en: In various places throughout the *Mahābhāṣya*,
there are statements of the form: "The teacher indicates [this] by his precedence."

In these [works], various statements are seen. Statements indicated by signs contained within the Sūtras are inserted therein. Those statements are of two kinds: those in the form of supplements (pariśiṣṭa) and those other than them. Among these:
The statements known as *paribhāṣās* were already recited in the form of rules even in grammatical treatises prior to Pāṇini’s grammar;
Pāṇini,
for his part, accepted them in his own *Aṣṭādhyāyī* by means of specific indicative marks (*liṅga*).
These have been clearly stated. As it is said in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*:

"In the ancient systems of grammar, these were merely matters of explicit statement (*vācanika*); here, in the system of Pāṇini, they are established by the logic of *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) and have been introduced through the *bhāṣya* and the *vārttika*."

"Those which are in the form of *paribhāṣās* shall now be explained. Thereupon, Sīradeva, having compiled those statements consisting of *paribhāṣās*, composed the work named *Paribhāṣāvṛtti*; [so too did] Nāgeśa.
He composed the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*. However,
as for those statements other than the *paribhāṣās* which are established by *jñāpaka*, and those [rules] mentioned in the *Mahābhāṣyopanyāsa*—
of these too...
Thinking that if some blind person were to be created by compiling [these works],
it might serve as a source of assistance for the learned, I have not made any effort here in this matter by any of the ancient scholars.
I remained reflecting on whether [this] was composed by him or not,

when by chance the venerable Pārthasārathi Miśra Bhaṭṭācārya— who is a lion among the illustrious grammarians, who has mastered the Vaikhānasa Āgamas, and who is honored by the Lord of Rāḍhā— himself...
Fifty years ago, this was printed in the Andhra script and subsequently submitted to the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies in Tirupati for publication in Devanāgarī.
Having seen the work titled *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* composed by Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa,
I experienced supreme joy; I have examined this book from its very beginning to its end.
This work, which does not deviate even by a hair’s breadth from the path shown by the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra, is highly authoritative;
yet, being extremely concise, it remains difficult to understand without a commentary. Therefore—
It was my thought that if this work were printed along with the *Lalitavivaraṇa*,
it would be of benefit to all; and likewise,
the venerable Bhaṭṭācāryas, with great devotion, undertook the composition of the commentary.
Being thus appointed, I have composed this commentary.
In this work, the *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, certain statements from the *Bhāṣya* have been omitted, and thus a certain deficiency exists. Therefore, those [statements]...
No words have been cited here from other sources; rather,
having compiled those [passages] that are most clearly established by authoritative tradition,
I have adopted only the concise style favored by Nāgeśa.
Having composed the root text titled *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, I also wrote its commentary titled *Vivaraṇa*. In that work,
the author has introduced various statements established by means of *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).
Some of those [statements] have been refuted by [the author] with the words, "This is not a proof," and so forth.
Therefore, having set aside such statements, we have compiled other statements that are accepted as authoritative.

Certain statements not included in the *Ḍhāḥsdvdr1;yānārūḍha* are observed to have been established in various places within the *Siddhāntakaumudī* by means of specific indicators (*jñāpaka*). Having considered the utility of these as well for supporting the correctness of certain words, this compilation has been made.
I composed the *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* in the second supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*).
Regarding the question of who the author of this *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* is—that is, who its composer is—it is Nāgeśa; however, there is no explicit evidence for this matter.

It is not found. Up to the present day, no scholars have indicated that any work bearing such a name was composed by Nāgeśa; nor is the name of Nāgeśa mentioned anywhere—in the beginning, middle, or end—within this work. Nor indeed is Nāgeśa [mentioned].

In his own work titled *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, which is cited in various other texts such as the *Śekhara*, he pointed to that work of his own. This being the case, the doubt arises: how is it determined that this [present] work was composed by Nāgeśa? [This is stated] in the Telugu script...
In the introduction to this *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*,

which is sealed by the venerable Pārthasārathimiśra himself, the teacher Pārthasārathi Miśra wrote as follows: "There is but one manuscript of this work belonging to my most excellent gurus in the southern region."

This work was composed by Setumāghavācārya, the son of the illustrious Maheśvara Bhaṭṭopādhyāya Sūri Ācārya, who was renowned as another Nāgeśa. Furthermore, it is stated by those very same [authorities] that "this book is proclaimed to have been composed by Nāgeśa. However, no original manuscript of this work is found in any library in the land of Bhārata.

It is possible to consider that the venerable Śrī Sucaritamiśra Ācāryas, having gone to the North and studied grammar, promoted its dissemination by teaching it in the South, and thus this *Mātṛkā* might have been composed by them at some point in the North.

In fact, upon a thorough examination of this work, I believe that no disagreement will arise regarding its authorship by Nāgeśa. In several places, a similarity between the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) found in the *Uddyota* and those in this work is observed. Therefore, it is possible to conclude that these two works—the present text and the *Uddyota*—have the same author.

I shall point out several passages for the purpose of illustration: (1) *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*, *Uddyota*: "Because it is an exception (*apavāda*), this is the statement of a partisan (*ekadeśyukti*); there is no fault because it is the statement of a partisan" (Sūtra 1.1.3, p. 13). (2) "The mention of multiple [bases] based on *altva* and so forth means the mention of multiple individuals based on that genus (*jāti*); such is the sense. This is the meaning thereof.

(17) (Sūtra 1.1.14) (3) Both of these [statements] are the assertions of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*). Following this, the statement in Bhāṣya 3.1.3 is also the assertion of a partial proponent. (4) How can there be purposefulness once it has been made known? Since there is no purposefulness even when it is made known, how can this statement in the Bhāṣya be the assertion of a partial proponent? This matter regarding its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) must be considered.

Therefore, in this context, the passage [Paṭha 110] which introduces an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) belongs to one who is a follower of the Ācārya (i.e., Patañjali). By that [evidence], even in the case of the root *bhāṣā*, [the form] *bibhitsati* is indeed established. Furthermore, by this, the form *cicchidīti*—which is a *yaṅ*-luṅanta (reduplication with elision of *yaṅ*) distinct from those two aforementioned usages—is also established; thus, it is incorrect in the *bhāṣā*. According to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that other *yaṅ*-luṅanta forms are simply ungrammatical (*asādhu*) in the *bhāṣā*.

(6) From this point forward, the mention of *maglopin* (a root that loses a portion of its penultimate syllable) is intended to indicate that the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* (behaving like the original element) does not apply hereafter; however, according to the Bhāṣya, this is merely the statement of a single partial view (*ekadeśyukti*). (Sūtra 7.4.2). This is the statement of a partial view.

Furthermore, Nāgeśa’s established position is that statements not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*, but imagined by someone according to their own whim as being established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), are not to be accepted. This was indicated by him at the beginning of the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, where he provided the qualification: "those introduced in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*."

Furthermore, as for the argument that rules such as "a rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory" and "the teaching regarding suffixes (*āgama-śāstra*) is not mandatory" lack authority because they are not observed in the *bhāṣya*, that is not correct; for they are indeed not observed in the *bhāṣya*.

Nāgeśa has clearly stated in this *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* that "there is no evidence for the restriction of grammatical correctness (*sādhutā*) based on a meaning that is not explicitly stated but merely indicated by a rule" (*Pariśiṣṭenduśekhara*, p. 232). Even in this collection of indicators (*jñāpaka*), all the statements have been cited exactly as they appear in the *Bhāṣya*.

No statement mentioned in the Siddhāntakaumudī and other such works has been included here that was not already stated by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. By this also, it is known that this work might have been composed by Nāgeśa. Apart from this, no further evidence is found for the authorship of this work by Nāgeśa. The appropriateness of the title of the work is itself an indicator.

It is not known whether this name was given by the author himself or by someone else; however, this work has been printed in the Āndhra script under this very title by the *Ḍḍhaṭṭācāryas*. The meaning of the title *Jñāpakasaṃgraha* is "a compilation of the *sūtras* that serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) of linguistic rules. Furthermore, the compilation herein follows the sequence of the eight chapters (*aṣṭādhyāyī*) exactly.

The name *Jñāpakasiddhavacanasaṃgraha* would indeed be appropriate; however, that name is too long. Furthermore, in the first edition, the name was given simply as *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*. Therefore, it is now being published under that very same title.

The style adopted in this work is such that, having cited a sūtra by way of a pratīka (initial word) from whose text a statement has been drawn, that statement is then presented along with its supporting evidence (*jñāpaka*). Certain errors present in the first edition have been removed in this edition; correct readings have been inserted within brackets marked with the symbol [ ].

I offer words of salutation to the venerable Pārthasārathimiśra Bhaṭṭācārya, who composed works such as the *Nyāyaratnamālā* and others, and who exerted great effort in bringing this text to light by making manifest his knowledge of the sacred scriptures.

Thus, having followed the request of Śrī Ḍḍhdhḍaddh;aṭṭācārya and having informed the Rāḥsdvdr1;ṣṭriya SaṃskḥTktgrRN;ata Saṃsthāna of the suitability for publishing this work, those who—being endowed with both ancient and modern learning, and being advanced in age, teaching, and administrative experience—secured the consent of the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies located in Tirupati and finalized the arrangements for its publication.
I offer my most profound salutations to the venerable Śrī V.E. Veṅkaṭarāghavācārya, the protector of the Prāṇas, expressing my own sense of blessedness in his presence.

Having examined this work and composed this preface in the form of a summary of its essence, these salutations are offered at the feet of the most venerable Śrī Anantaśayana Mayyaṅgār Maudayars, the presiding authorities of this seat of learning (vidyāpīṭha) and the heads of the Prajñācakrasaṃgha, who have graciously permitted [this undertaking].

Thus, I offer my heartfelt thanks to those who have assisted by consenting to the publication of this work, as well as to the authorities of the Bharatīvijaya Mudraṇālaya who have skillfully executed the printing. I am grateful to all these well-wishers.
December 15, 1972. N.S.
Rāmānuja Tātācārya.
Tirupati.

[This applies] according to its respective class (*yathājātīyaka*).
The form of another is understood as being of such a kind [in the case of] both [the preceding and following members];

133 a compound occurs with a preceding member of the same kind as the subsequent member; 152 when there is the exclusion of a particular attribute, there is the negation of that attribute; 187 as much as...

(76) There is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *yuc* and *re*. (70) A form (*rūpa*) functions as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*). (31) There is no prohibition regarding those substitutes (*ādeśa*) and so forth that differ in form. (113)

144. In some cases, the augment *suṭ* occurs even before a root beginning with a vowel following the prefix *sam*. 216. 175. There is elision of a final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) when *n* is elided (*nalope*). 203. The rule *sup supā* does not constitute a mandatory compound (*na nityasamāsaḥ*). 85. The rule of non-identity of form (vāsarūpa) does not apply here. The original element (*sthānin*) does not become the cause for the substitution. In a rule concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), the entire aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is the subject of the operation.

This prohibition does not apply to those [suffixes] for which the designation *pada* is established by virtue of beginning with *sva* (i.e., *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes). By this [rule], the third case ending is prescribed in place of the genitive in the context of *cheḥ*.
The Compendium of Indicators. First Chapter:
*aiuṇ*. 1.
Regarding the statement that the vowel *a* is both unmanifest (*vivṛta*) and taught [as such] during the stage of grammatical derivation, [the rule cited is] "a a" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.4.68).
Thus, the counter-argument serves as an indicator:
Śrīnivāsa, whose abode is on the peak of Vaikuṇṭha,
excels even the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) in bestowing the fruits of desire upon those who take refuge in him.

May some indescribable mass of compassion, who is served by hosts of supplicants arriving with various forms of entreaty, bestow welfare upon us. [He who] constantly [draws forth] the essences from many tantras...
I bow my head in reverence to the gurus, who are the foremost leaders of the world, intent upon the upliftment of the disciples.
2. Nāgeśa, whose intellect was sharpened by the study of the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā*, composed this *Jñāpakasaṃgraha*. It was previously published by Pārthasārathi in the Āndhra script. 3.
Commanded by that wise one, he undertook its exposition— a work measured in words rather than [mere] meanings, which delights the hearts of the learned. By this pretext,
whatever purification of the intellect arises from the thorough investigation of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts— [that is what is intended].

This is the supreme fruit of this [work]. Therein, the venerable Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology, has composed [this] commentary on the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*,
excluding the [original] verses.

Desiring to compose a work titled *Jñāpaka-saṃgraha*, which compiles the statements established as *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found scattered here and there, he first cites the following statement from the rule *aiuṇ*: "The vowel *a* is [already] taught."
When the author of the Vārttika stated that "the letter *a* should be regarded as an instruction (*upadeśa*) because it is eternal (*vivartatayā*),
for the purpose of including the letter *ā*," was this merely a restatement by the Vārttikakāra of what had already been established by the Sūtrakāra?
The purpose is stated:

when the objection is raised that the instruction on the *vivaraṇa* (exegesis) was already mentioned by the author of the *Vārttika* as something to be performed, the author of the *Bhāṣya* [responds].

[Objection:]— The purpose of that which is being taught as a distinct (vivṛta) sound is stated [in the rule]. How is it known that this [rule] teaches the restoration of the contracted (saṃvṛta) state for the vowel *a* when it is pronounced distinctly (*vivṛta*) as "a a"?
This is the intended meaning:

by means of the rule *a a*, the restoration to the original state (*saṃvṛtatva*) at the time of actual usage is established for that vowel *a* which was originally open (*vivṛta*) by its own nature during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), but had attained openness at that time. And this is the rule.

It exists at the end of the treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, it is understood that the letter *a*, which is taught in the sūtras preceding that [final] sūtra—such as those beginning the section on vowels (*svara*) and so forth—is indeed taught as a vowel (*vivaḥTktgrRN;ta*). And thus, just like the letter *a* being taught as a vowel, [the same applies].

In the *Vārttika*, it is stated that the purpose [of a rule] is being explained; however, in this context, the sūtra "a a" is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned purpose, because that sūtra possesses other purposes. Likewise, as stated [in the *Kāśikā*]: "In cases such as *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *atimālaḥ*..."

By the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the short vowel prescribed for the replacement of the long vowel *ā* would have to be the long vowel *ā* itself, because it is the closest (*sannikṛṣṭa*) to the original *ā* due to its internal similarity (*tadāntaryāt*); therefore, that [short vowel] is indeed included [as a possibility].
If it is asked: "How can the rule *a a* (Pāṇini 6.1.109) serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this purpose, namely that [the substitution] should occur?"—[the answer is:
No.
For if the vowel *a* were found anywhere in common usage (*loka*) or in the Veda (*veda*), then [the rule would apply] in place of the vowel *ā*.
Because of the proximity (*āntarya*) of the short *a* sound standing in its place, [the vowel] *vi* is understood as being elided.
There is no *a* sound elided anywhere that is not preceded by *saṃ*;
rather, it exists only when preceded by *saṃ*. And thus, the *a* sound exists only when preceded by *saṃ*.

The rule "a a" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), which states that [the final *a*] becomes [the initial *a*], does not have the result of establishing the status of being a *saṃvṛta* vowel for the short *a* in examples such as "atikhaṭva. Consequently, the rule [6.1.127] which prescribes the status of being *saṃvṛta* for the vowel *a* at the end of the treatise,
following the completion of the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), [is intended to apply to the final *a*].

This indicates that in the preceding sūtra, it is to be understood that only the vowel *a* (akāra) as it was taught [in the alphabet] is intended. Consequently, it is established that the Vārttikakāra explains the purpose only for that very *a* which was taught [in the alphabet] and subsequently modified.
Pratyāpatti (restoration) is the re-attainment of its own original state by that which has reached a modified state (*vikṛtatva*), namely, the attainment of its own original state once again.
For example, in the rule "In the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the letter *a* is taught as being modified," [the restoration is expressed] as *a a*.
The connection is that the statement of the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The rule is: *ṛ-la-varṇayor dīrghatvam* || 2 ||]
An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) follows the original form (*prakṛti*). This is because, in rules such as *kṣiyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.59), there is the mention of *iyaṅ*.
Furthermore, on the occasion of explaining the purpose of teaching the letter *l* in the rule *ṛlak* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), it was stated that one type of imitation arises from incapacity (*aśaktija*).
The purpose has been stated in the Bhāṣya. Likewise, it is said:
when a certain Brāhmaṇī woman, being unable to utter the word *ṛtaka*, uses the form *laḥtaka*, there follows an imitation of that usage, such as *brāhmaṇīlaḥtaka*.
This is called an imitation arising from inability. In that context,
when *brāhmaṇī-alaṅkāraḥ* is established, because the letter *l* is a vowel (*ac*),
the *ī* is replaced by a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) before it according to the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77).

The word *brāhmaṇyaḥ* becomes *brāhmaṇrlaḥ*. However, if the letter *l* were not taught in the *ṛla-sūtra*, and only *ṛk* were mentioned, then because the letter *l* would lack the status of being a vowel (*ac*), the rule *iko yaṇaci* would not apply.

Therefore, having stated that "the instruction of the letter *la* must be formulated," its refutation was provided. Likewise, there is the paribhāṣā: "An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like the original (*prakṛti*). And of that [paribhāṣā]—

An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like the original (*prakṛtivat*); that is to say, it becomes equal to the object being imitated (*anukārya*). The meaning is that whatever grammatical operation applies to the object being imitated also applies to the imitation. In this case, the word *ṛtakaśabdaḥ* is the object being imitated, and *latakaśabdaḥ* is the imitation.

Since the vowel *ṛ* in the word *ṛtaśaḥ* (in the form *anukārya*) is a vowel (*ac*), the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) applies just as it does in the case of the original form (*anukārya*). Likewise, because that same rule applies to the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) in the word *laḥTktgrRN;takaśaḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is established.
The intention is that the instruction [of the phoneme] *laḥ* need not be given.

As for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "an imitation follows the original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*), it is the mention of *iyaṅ* in rules such as "after *kṣi*, when followed by a long vowel" (*kṣiyodīrghāt*, Pāṇini 7.2.46). Likewise...
The word *kṣi* occurring in the Sūtra is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *kṣi* found in the Dhātupāṭha;
because an imitative word lacks the quality of expressing an action (*kriyāvācitva*), it lacks the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*).

By the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the substitution *iyaṅ* is obtained. However, Pāṇini has specifically mentioned *iyaṅ*; from this it is known that an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) functions like its original form (*prakṛtivat*). And so:

The suffix *iyaN* is prescribed after the verbal root *kṣi* (from the root *kṣi-dhātu*) by the rule *kṣiyaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.59]; however, since this rule can also apply to the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that form—the word *kṣiśas*—its purpose is fulfilled within its own domain. When someone says "pacantu pacantu" twice, the imitation of that is "dviḥ pacantu."
Since this compound (*pacantu śaśvad*) does not denote a verbal action, a means of action, or the like, it lacks the status of being a *tiṅ*-ending form;
consequently, the *nighāta* accent— which is prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), meaning that a *tiṅ*-ending word following another non-*tiṅ* word becomes unaccented— would not apply.
If it is accepted that imitation (*anukaraṇa*) occurs according to the actual pronunciation (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam bhavati*),

then just as the *nighāta* accent occurs in the original form (*anukārya*) *pacantu* which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix, that same accent will be established even in the imitation, namely the word *pacantu*. [Pāṇini 1.1.69]

On account of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *gonaugraḥ*—namely, that a grammatical operation prescribed for a whole does not apply to a part of it that is not itself a word—the parts such as *ā* and so forth, which resemble the sounds *ākāra* etc., and the sounds *ṛ* and *lṛ*... [in the rule *ṭheāāṅ*]... are [not treated as such].

The constituent parts [of diphthongs] resemble the letter *r* and the letter *l*; in the case of the diphthongs *e*, *o*, *ai*, and *au*, their constituent parts resemble the letters *a*, *i*, and *u*. In that regard, one must consider whether the grammatical operation prescribed for the individual phonemes beginning with *a* applies [to these diphthongs] or not.

In the case of *vicāra* (investigation), if one were to grasp the constituent parts of a phoneme (*varṇāvayava*) by means of perceiving the phoneme itself and then perform the grammatical operation (*varṇakārya*) upon them, then in examples such as *agne*, *indram*, *vāyo*, and *udakam*, [the rule would apply] to the *ik* portion following the letter *e*.
Because [the vowel *u*] is included by the mention of the letter *i*, and because the *u* residing in the syllable *o* is followed by a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) *i* in the word *indram*,
as well as because it is followed by a homogeneous *u*, the rule "a long vowel replaces two homogeneous vowels" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.101) would apply, resulting in a long vowel.
Anticipating this objection and in order to refute it, this statement was uttered:

"The rule does not apply to a member of that which is not separated by an intervening element. Here, the genitive case is used in a non-appositional sense (*vyadhikaraṇa*), meaning "of that which is a member of [something] not separated by an intervening element."
Of the part belonging to that collection which is not separated—

that is, of the part belonging to the collection [of the whole] which is grasped by a cognition having the form "one," and which has as its basis a cognition having the form "one" regarding the unity of the substratum.
The rule for that is as follows:

the meaning of the stated statement is that the rule regarding individual phonemes (*varṇa*) does not apply separately. And thus, in the case of the recitation of the *Buddhiguhya* [text], "the syllable 'e' is one," the part [i.e., the letter *e*] exists within the whole (*samudāya*) "e."

The meaning is that a rule concerning the *ik* vowel—which is not a constituent of the composite [word]—such as the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) and so forth, does not apply; thus, there is no possibility of the occurrence of a homogeneous long vowel in examples such as *agne indram*. The following provides the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this stated principle.
Regarding the phrase "gonaugrahaṇāt": this is the intended meaning— the inclusion of the term *go* (cow) in the rule *gedhdyaco'saṅkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat* (Pāṇini 5.1.39),
and [the inclusion of] *nau* (boat) in the rule *naudhdyacaḥ ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7).

The mention of *naugra-* in the rule (*sūtra*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the statement already mentioned. Therein, from the word *go-* in the first *sūtra*, and from a word joined with two vowels (*ac*), the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of "its cause" (*tannimitta*) or "its portent" (*utpāta*). Thus, [the form] *gavyam*.
"Dhanya" is the illustrative example. In that regard, regarding the word *go*, the vowel *o*—
which consists of the aggregate of the vowels *a* and *u*— is [understood] by the separate mention of its two constituent parts, *a* and *u*.
And since the word *go* would already be included by the term *dhātu* itself—

given that it contains the vowel *u* (as part of the suffix *-u*)— the explicit mention of the word *go* would otherwise be redundant; therefore, [its inclusion] serves to indicate that [the rule applies to] both the whole and its parts.

By the mention of *varṇa* [in the rule], it indicates that there is no inclusion [of other suffixes]. Thus, from the word *nau* (boat) and the word *dhvaja* (flag), in the sense of "one who crosses" (*tarati*), the suffix *ṭhan* is applied, resulting in the meaning "one who descends" (*avatarati*). The examples are *nāvikaḥ* (boatman) and *ghaṭikaḥ* (watchman).

In that regard, since the *au* in *naus* consists of a collection of two phonemes (*varṇa*), it possesses the status of being a "syllable" (*dhvactva*); thus, its inclusion would already be established by the term "syllable" (*dhvac*) alone. Therefore, the explicit mention of *naus* being redundant serves to indicate the aforementioned rule. And once that rule has been indicated:

In that [context], because the two phonemes *o* and *au* are not perceived as consisting of two distinct letters (*varṇa*), they do not possess the status of being "single-syllabic" (*ekāc*); therefore, their separate mention [in the rule] serves its purpose within its own scope. However, the result of this [separate mention] is to provide an indication (*jñāpana*).

In cases such as *agne indram*, the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) is exactly as previously stated. According to the view that "parts of letters are not included under the designation 'letter' (*varṇa*)," there would be no occurrence of *kṣumnādi* words, because they are not recited in the list of exceptions (*ta-paribhāṣā*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for the nasal following an *ṛ*-vowel is thus made known. [In the rule *ṛt-ṛ-laḥ*], the fact that vowels such as *ā* and other diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*)— which consist of parts of [the vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, etc.]— are not included by the mention of individual phonemes is established by the non-inclusion [of those parts].

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *mātṝṇām* is not established. This is because, when the form *mātṝnām* remains, there is no rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* following the vowel *ṛ*.
However, in the view that accepts the inclusion of *ṛ*, the status of being "following" is obtained by virtue of the *repha* (the letter *r*) situated between the *ṛ* and the *n*.

To the objection that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would be established by the rule "In the presence of *ra*, *ṣ*, *d*, *v*, or *r̥*, *n* becomes *ṇ*" (Pāṇini 8.4.1), [the reply is: even in the view that does not include the mention of *ṛ*, the *ṇ*-substitution for *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel is established on the basis of an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). Likewise...
The group beginning with *kṣu-bhuj* (the *kṣubhv-ādi* class) is recited as *naṭ* [ending in *ṭ*].

Its purpose, however, is the prohibition of the change of *n* to *ṇ* following an *ṛ*-vowel by means of the rule *kṣubhv-ādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.39). If, however, [the rule applied] to an *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel...
If [the substitution] were not to occur due to the absence of a rule (*sūtra*) that prescribes *ṇatva*,

then, because of the absence of the attainment of *ṇatva*, the reading of [the word] *kṣumnā* in the *gaṇa* beginning with *kṣumnādi*— which has the purpose of excluding that [substitution]— would be useless. Nor [is it the case that the rule applies] to the *n* following the *r* in the word *nārṇamani*.

It cannot be argued that its inclusion in that group [the *raṣābhyām* group] is for the purpose of ensuring the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; even so, this does not hold, because the inclusion of the word *tarpotiśaḥ* in that group serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned rule.
This is because, in the absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following an *ṛ*-vowel in the word *tarpotiśaḥ*, [the form would otherwise be incorrect].

Since there is no possibility of its occurrence, the absence of the rule *niḥṣṭhāvadhaḥ* indicates that the substitution of *ṇ* for the vowel *ṛ* in the word *ṛvarṇānna* indeed takes place. [Jñāpakasūtra:
Even so, there is no inclusion of those [words] whose *ṛ* is not elided (*apratyāhāra*).

This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in rules such as *uṇādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.1). [Vaiṭ] When the suffixes beginning with *ac* are excluded, and when the suffixes beginning with *at*, *ik*,
and so forth are excluded, the *itsaṃjñaka* (elements marked with *it*) situated between them [are also excluded].
There is no inclusion of the phonemes *ṇ*, *k*, and so forth, among the letters [of the pratyāhāra].

This is because of the specific mention [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] "uṇādayaḥ. If, by means of the mention of the initial vowel (*a*) and subsequent vowels, there were an inclusion of those situated in the middle as well, then since the phoneme *ṇ* would also be included, [the rule would apply].

In the rule *uṇ-śaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.136), when an *ac* vowel follows, one should have read the indication as *uṇādayaḥ* [with the long *ū*] in place of *ikaḥ* [the short *u*], because the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs when an *ac* vowel follows. Since the *uṇādi* suffixes are indicated [with a short *u*] without the *yaṇ* substitution taking effect upon an *ac* vowel, they are not included in the *pratyāhāra* *u*.
The meaning is that the *yaṇ* [substitution] is enjoined. Therefore, in examples such as *śrīkānta*, there is no *yaṇ* for the vowel *ī*.
Here, this applies even to those *it*s (vowels) situated between the initial consonants of the *hal*-pratyāhāra and the final consonants of the same.
The inclusion [of the vowels] is not accepted.

This being the case, we do not understand from where it was stated that there is no mention of both *act* and *atadvāpya* (the vowels other than *a*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Kaumudī*: "There is no mention of... [and so forth].

It has been stated thus: "the inclusion [of *it*]". In reality, however, the statement that the inclusion of *it*s occurs within the *ac*-pratyāhāra is established by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) as being simply "not [the case]";
there is no entry of the term *tadvyāpya* (that which is pervaded by it) therein. Nor...
It should not be said that there is a lack of inclusion (*agrahaṇa*) in the pratyāhāra [of vowels] beginning with *a* and so forth,

because it is possible to state that in the case of the *hal* [consonant] pratyāhāras, those consonants containing *hal* are devoid of their phonemes used for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha-varṇa*), due to the pronunciation of the vowel *a* used for the purpose of pronunciation.

For this very reason, in the *Ślokavārttika* on the rule *pratyayasthāt...* (P. 7.3.44), it is stated as "in the case of the mention of 'ac'" (*ajgrahaṇeṣu*), rather than "in the case of the mention of 'aj' and 'ac'" (*ajajgrahaṇeṣu*). This should be carefully considered by the wise. And this is clearly evident in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. [Jñā.ṭ] *hṛyavaraṭ* || 5 ||

The prohibition of doubling by the rule *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rules *halo yamāṃ yami* (8.4.64) and *jharo jhari* (8.4.65) are not operative here. Alternatively, [the fact that the rule is stated] is itself the refuge for the explanation.

In the *Vṛtti* on the sūtra *antaḥsthānāṃ yaralavānām aṇ-sūpadeśaḥ kimarthaḥ*, having observed the question "For what purpose is there the teaching of *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v* as *aṇ*s?", it is explained that when *sam yantāḥ* becomes *sam yantāḥ* and the *m* is replaced by an *anusvāra* according to *mo 'nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.23), and its *parasavarṇa* is applied, resulting in *saṃy yantāḥ*, the preceding *y* is included by the term *yargrahaṇa*; thus, by the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47)...

Thus, by doubling [the *y*], the form with three *y*s is established. Since the semivowels (*antaḥsthā*) are taught as *aṇ* in the *aṇ-sūtra*, and because the *y* lacks the status of being an *aṇ*, it cannot include its homogeneous nasalized *y* according to the rule *aṇudit*. Consequently, since the preceding nasalized *y* would not be included by the term *y* [in the doubling rule], there would be no doubling.

Therefore, the instruction of the letters beginning with *ya* is for the purpose of establishing their doubling (*dvitva*). Now, one might object: "Let there be doubling here; however, it need not be necessary because there would be a difference in form—namely, a form with three *y*s when doubling occurs, and a form with two *y*s when doubling does not occur. This objection cannot be maintained.

If it is argued that even though there are three *yakāra*s, because the middle *yakāra* is elided by the rule "ḍhalo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.64), the form with only two *yakāra*s is established—this would be so only if the elision in "ḍhalo yamāṃ yami" were obligatory (*nitya*). However, that elision is optional (*vaikalpika*).

And thus, since there is doubling [of the semivowels], the form consists of two *y* sounds in the case where the *y* is elided, and three *y* sounds in the case where it is not elided; therefore, doubling is necessary to establish this distinction in form. And that doubling is possible only if the semivowels (*antasthā*) are taught as vowels (*aṇ*), as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya according to the reasoning previously mentioned.

Regarding the doubt as to how it is known that the elision [of the *y*] in the rule *yamāṃ yami* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) is optional, the author of the Vārttika states: "The option (*vibhāṣā*) from [the preceding rule] *aci* continues [into this rule], or rather, this [present rule] prevents reduplication."

The meaning of this is as follows: In the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), it must necessarily be stated that the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over from the preceding rule *jhayo haḥ ghiṇi anyatarasyām* (8.4.62). Otherwise, the prohibition of doubling (*dvitva*) by the rule *śaro'ci* (8.4.49) would be rendered purposeless. By the rule *śaro'ci*, doubling is prohibited after a *śara* [consonant] before a vowel (*aci*).

The doubling (*dvitva*) prescribed by the rule *aco ra ṛtāṃ dvirvacanam abhyāsalo paśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105)—though here referred to as *aco raḥ... dvitvaṃ*—is prohibited. Here, the following objection might arise: "Let there be doubling in this case. Once doubling has occurred and the form *catūrṣu* is established, the desired form is indeed accomplished even by the elision of the first *ṣ* according to the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65). Therefore, the rule *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) is redundant."

In this regard, the following resolution must be stated: this sūtra indicates the optional application (*vikalpānuvṛtti*) of the rule "jharo jhari" (Pāṇini 8.4.65). Thus, when doubling has occurred, because the elision (*lopa*) is optional, there would result two forms: one with a single *ṣakāra* in the case of elision, and one with two *ṣakāras* in the case of the absence of elision.

In our view, however, forms such as *catuḥścatuḥ* are perceived as having only a single *ṣk* sound. Therefore, the rule *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) serves as a prohibition against doubling, thereby ensuring the meaningfulness of that sūtra. Furthermore, by this reasoning, it is established that the word *anyatarasyām* is also understood to carry over into the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), which is governed by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64).

Furthermore, in the case of *saṃyantā*, when the *y* is doubled, there arises a distinction between a form with two *y*s (in the view that the *yam* rule applies) and a form with three *y*s (in the view that the *yam* rule does not apply); the purpose of the section beginning with "the teaching of semivowels (*antaḥsthā*) as *aṇ*" is to ensure the establishment of this distinction.

Having taken all this into consideration, he cited the two sūtras "halo yamām yami" and "jharo jhari," and then stated that [the elision] occurs when there is the subsequent occurrence of a *jihvāmūlīya* or *upadhmānīya*. However, in that very same context, in the *Upasaṃhārabhāṣya*, it was stated: "This remains extremely doubtful for the teachers as to whether the subsequent occurrence of a *jihvāmūlīya* or *upadhmānīya* actually takes place or not."

Thus, having raised the doubt as to how this can be so, [the author] says: "The commentary (vyākhyāna) is the refuge. And in every case where there is a point of doubt, this principle is established: "The specific meaning is understood from the commentary; it is not a characteristic of the text that is subject to doubt. Accordingly, we shall explain that the word *viśeṣa* (specific/exception) from the two previously mentioned sūtras is carried over here.

Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever; this is the underlying intention (*bhāva*). [Regarding *jñā* and *laṇ*: In the rule *ḍhralopa* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), the mention of *aṇ* is by the preceding rule (*aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*) and not by the subsequent one (*tasya lopaḥ*). This is because the result is already established through the application of *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28); the specific mention of *aṇ* [in the former rule] is for that very purpose. Regarding the sūtra *laṇ*, such an investigation is undertaken: the letter *ṇ* is mentioned twice—once in *aiuṇ* and once in *laṇ*.

In that regard, when there is a doubt concerning the inclusion of *aṇ* and *iṇ*, the question arises: does this include [the vowel] by means of the preceding *ṇ* or by means of the subsequent one? In this doubt—

The author of the Vārttika stated that wherever the mention of *aṇ* and *iṇ* occurs, a determination can be made in every such case by means of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). He sets forth those instances in their entirety, beginning with the rule "ḍhralope... and so forth.

Regarding the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), there arises a doubt: is the term *aṇ* here denoted by the *ṇ* occurring earlier [in the *aṇ* pratyāhāra], or by the *ṇ* occurring later [in the *laṇ* sūtra]? The determination is that it is the *aṇ* mentioned by the former [the *aṇ* pratyāhāra] and not by the latter. What is the authority for this? To this, he says: *acaśca*. This is the underlying intention: The *aṇ* in the present rule is understood through the *aṇ* pratyāhāra, which begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *ṇ*. If it were understood through the *aṇ* pratyāhāra ending with the subsequent *ṇ* (as in *laṇ*), then in a word like *mālā*—derived from *mālāḥ* where the visarga is elided by the rule *ro’supi* (8.2.69)—the substitution of a long vowel would apply to the preceding *ā*, because the *ṇ* in *laṇ* follows the *ā*. However, since the *ṇ* in the *aṇ* pratyāhāra precedes the *ā*, the condition for the application of the rule (*pūrvasya*) is not met, and thus the fault does not arise. Therefore, the *aṇ* is determined to be the one defined by the *aṇ* pratyāhāra. Furthermore, the mention of *acaḥ* (in the rule *acaśca*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *aṇ* is indeed the one from the *aṇ* pratyāhāra; for if the *aṇ* were the one from the *laṇ* pratyāhāra, the mention of *acaḥ* would be redundant, as the *ṇatva* operation already applies to vowels by the general rule *alo’ntyasya* (1.1.52). Thus, the conclusion is that the *aṇ* is the one from the *aṇ* pratyāhāra.

If, in the rule regarding the elision of *ḍh* and *l* (*ḍhralopa-sūtra*), the term *aṇ* were to include the subsequent vowels [by the principle of *pratyāhāra*], then by that term *aṇ*, the letters *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o, ai, au, h, y, v, r, l* would be intended. And among those, the capacity for lengthening applies only to the vowels up to *au*. Consequently, when it is stated "the long vowel of *aṇ*," the result would simply be "the long vowel of a vowel" (*aco dīrgha*). This being the case, the mention of *aṇ* in the rule for the elision of *ḍh* and *l* would be redundant.

By the rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28), which means that wherever the terms "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), or "protracted" (*pluta*) are prescribed, the word *acaḥ* ending in the genitive case is supplied; thus, through the very presence of the word *acaḥ*, the lengthening of a vowel (*ac*) is obtained.

Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* (the term "aṇ" in the rule) being otherwise purposeless indicates that in this sūtra, the substitution is governed by the preceding rule alone. Consequently, in this sūtra, only the three vowels *a*, *i*, and *u* are intended to have their long forms substituted. Furthermore, since the word *ac* is brought into the scope of the rule, that [long vowel] would not be applicable [to other consonants]. Thus, the mention of *aṇ* serves its own specific purpose within its own domain.

Therefore, in rules such as *ātaḥ kṛ-kam-i-kṛṅ-tām* (Pāṇini 6.4.69), the purpose is the prevention of lengthening (*dīrgha-bhāva*). Now, even so, regarding the rule *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13), there arises a doubt as to whether the term *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [rule]. To this, it is said: "In the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, the *aṇ* is indeed the preceding one. As for the phrase "for this very reason": the meaning is that it is established precisely because the word *acaḥ* (from the previous rule) is present [as an adhikāra].

The meaning is as follows: by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ," a short vowel is prescribed for the *aṇ* group when the suffix *ka* follows. Examples include *jñakaḥ* and *kumārikā*. In that context, if *aṇ* were excluded by the subsequent [rule], then since only vowels (*ac*) among the letters up to *laṇ* possess the capacity to undergo shortening, the shortening would have been intended to apply only to vowels.

If that were the case, since the vowel (*ac*) would already be understood through the presence of the word ending in the genitive suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (i.e., *acaḥ*), the mention of *aṇ* in the rule for the substitution of *l* would be redundant. Therefore, this indicates that in this sūtra, *aṇ* applies only by the preceding rule. The purpose [of this indication], however, is to prevent the shortening [of the final vowel] in forms such as *gokā* and *naukā*. Everything else remains as before.

But even so, in the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), there remains the doubt whether the term *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [vowel]. Regarding this, [the author] says: "In the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*, although one could have simply said *acaḥ* (‘of a vowel’), the use of the term *aṇ* indicates that it refers only to the preceding [vowel]. [Commentary on *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*: Regarding the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*: although one could have stated *acaḥ* (‘of a vowel’) instead, because of the mention of *aṇ*, it must be understood as referring only to the preceding [vowel]. [Commentary on *vi.*: Regarding *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*: [The point is that the specific mention of *aṇ* restricts the reference to the preceding vowel.]

By the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, an anusvāra (nasalized vowel) is prescribed for an *aṇ* at the end of a word (*avasāne*), provided it is not a *pragṛhya*. In that context, if *aṇ* were intended as a reference to the subsequent [technical] term *aṇ*, one would simply have said *acaḥ*. Nor should it be argued that the term *aṇ* was used in order to also prescribe the nasalization of *ha, ya, va, ra,* and *la*.

By the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*," the term *apragṛhya-padena* includes both that which is similar to a *pragṛhya* and that which is a *pragṛhya*. Since the designation *pragṛhya* applies only to vowels (*ac*), and since a vowel is similar to another vowel by virtue of being a vowel, it would be possible for the word *apragṛhya* to include only a vowel (*aj*)—just as it includes a *pragṛhya*—by the same logic. Therefore, although one might have simply said *ac*, [the author] says *aṇ*.

Because [the rule] would otherwise be redundant. Thus, in this context, the mention of *aṇ* by the previous [rule] indicates that only *a*, *i*, and *u* are intended to be included here. That [intention] would not be established if only *ac* were stated; therefore, *aṇ* was mentioned so that its own portion [of the meaning] may find its application. However, its purpose elsewhere is that, in forms such as *kataḥ* and *TktgrRN;Ç*, the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the vowel *ṛ* does not occur.

But even so, regarding the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51), there arises the doubt as to whether the term *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [vowel]. To this, the answer is: *urajraparaḥ*. Since there is no possibility of *hya, va, ra, la* occupying the place of *ṛ*, and since only vowels can occupy the place of *ṛ*, it would have been sufficient to say *uraj*; therefore, the statement *uraṇ* is redundant.

It should not be argued that there is no consideration of parsimony (*lāghava*) versus prolixity (*gaurava*) between the two [rules] *ac* and *aṇ* because they possess an equal number of syllables; for when the term *aṇ* is employed, there arises the presence (*upasthiti*) of even more syllables than those presented by the term *ac*. Thus, the use of the expression *uraṇ* instead of *uraj* indicates that the term *aṇ* is to be understood as including the preceding *ṇ*-letter.

And likewise, if [the term] *aṇ* were not stated, there would be the inclusion of *ṛ*-sounds and so forth as well. Therefore, it is stated that *aṇ* is mentioned for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), which serves its purpose within its own scope (*svāṃśe*). However, its purpose elsewhere is seen in cases such as *mātṛṇām*, where the long vowel (*dīrgha*) that occurs in place of *ṛ* does not become followed by *ra* (*rapara*).

[Objection: But even so, in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), there is doubt as to whether *aṇ* refers to the preceding or the following [ṇ]; therefore, [the author] says: [Aṇudiditi: In the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (1.1.69), which specifies homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the term *aṇ* is taken with the following *ṇ*, not the preceding one. This is because the mention of *tapara* (specifying the duration of the vowel) in the subsequent rule *urṛt* (6.4.17) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Commentary: Regarding *aṇudid*: in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (1.1.69), which functions as a specifier of homogeneous sounds, *aṇ* is associated with the following *ṇ* alone, and not with the preceding one.

In this context, the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) in the rule *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, in forms such as *acīkṛtat* from the root *kṛ* belonging to the *curādi* class, after the formation of the *luṅ* aorist with *ciṇ*, doubling, and so forth—resulting in the sequence *acīkṛ-a-at*—the rule *urṛt* (7.4.7), which means that when a *ṇi*-affix follows, an *ṛ* may optionally replace the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) which is an *ṛ*-vowel, effects the substitution of *ṛ* for the letter *a*. Consequently, the form *acīkṛtat* is established.

In this context, the addition of the *t* (as in *ṛt*) is performed so that there may be only the vowel *ṛ* in place of *añ*, and not *añ*. For if, in the rule *aṇudit sūtra*, the term *aṇ* were understood by means of the preceding *ṇ*, then because *ṛ* is not an *aṇ*, it would not be a substitute for *añ* which has the same duration as *ṛ*; consequently, only *ṛ* would become the substitute and not *añ*. What [is the purpose of the *t*]?

Because of the presence of the *t* (the *tapara* marker), that [specification] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the subsequent mention of *aṇ*. Consequently, since the *ṛ*-vowel is also included within *aṇ*, it would also include its homogeneous counterparts, such as the letter *Añ*; thus, at times even the letter *Añ* might occur. To ensure that this does not happen and that only the *ṛ*-vowel occurs, the *tapara* marker is employed; thus, it fulfills its purpose within its own scope.

However, there is a specific purpose [for the *tapara* marker]: namely, that the *ṛ*-vowel is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for eighteen sounds. If it is argued that in the rule *ur ṛt*, even in the absence of the *tapara* marker, the *ṛ*-vowel being prescribed would not include its homogeneous counterparts because it is stated to be "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), and thus the *tapara* marker is redundant—here the author of the *Uddyota* says: "In the absence of the *tapara* marker, [the marker] serves the purpose of excluding other substitutes."

"Because they consist of their own forms, and because they are not intended to be enjoined as something previously unknown (*apūrva*), they lack the status of being things to be prescribed. Now, even if this is so, a doubt arises regarding rules such as *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.39), where it is uncertain whether the term *iṇ* refers to the *ṇ* that precedes or the one that follows. To this, he says: "The *iṇ* [is understood] only with the following [ṇ]."

In the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), although the term *iṇaḥ* alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of *yvōḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [Viṭṭhala’s Commentary: *Iṇ* is indeed [to be understood] with the subsequent *ṇ*. In the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*, by the expression *yvōḥ*, there is the inclusion of the *ivarṇa* and *uvarṇa*. And if *iṇ* were to be included with the preceding *ṇ*, then even by the word *iṇ*, there would be the inclusion of only the *i* and *u* vowels.

Furthermore, in the word *yvoḥ*, there is one *mātrā* for the *yakāra* and *vakāra*, two *mātrās* for the *okāra*, and half a *mātrā* for the *visarga*; thus, having extracted [these], they become three and a half *mātrās*. However, in the case of *iṇaḥ*, there is one *mātrā* for the *ikāra*, half for the *ṇkāra*, one for the *akāra*, and half for the *visarga*, making three *mātrās*; thus, there exists a lightness of half a *mātrā*.

Therefore, although one could have simply said "of *iṇ*" (*iṇaḥ*) for the sake of brevity, the statement "of *y* and *v*" (*yvoḥ*) indicates that [the rule applies] to an *ṇ* followed by an *iṇ*. Thus, if only "of *iṇ*" were stated, there would be the undesirable consequence of including *ṛ*-vowels and so forth as well; to prevent this, "of *y* and *v*" was stated, thereby fulfilling its purpose within its own scope.

However, there is another purpose: in rules such as *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam* (Pāṇini 8.3.78), the mention of the vowel *o* also includes the diphthong *au*; thus, in forms such as *goḥ* and *gauḥ*, the status of being a *śit* (having a *ś* as an indicatory letter) is established. Furthermore, the mention of the udātta accent in the rule *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaRudāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that qualities (*guṇas*) do not differentiate [the entity they qualify] (*abhedakā guṇāḥ*). *Vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1). The mention of the udātta accent in *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaRudāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that qualities (*guṇas*) do not differentiate [the entity they qualify] (*abhedakā guṇāḥ*).

In the sūtra *vṛddhir ādaic*, the Vārttikakāra stated that the addition of the *tapara* marker (the short *a*) after the vowel *ā* must be made for the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Since phonetic qualities (*guṇa*) serve as differentiators, when a vowel is pronounced with a certain quality, there arises the contingency of that name applying only to that specific quality. Therefore, the purpose of the *tapara* marker is to ensure that the name applies even to those vowels possessing other qualities.

Regarding that, two positions are presented concerning qualities (*guṇas*) such as nasality (*ānunāsikya*), accent (*udātta*), and so forth: whether they are differentiators (*bhedaka*) or non-differentiators (*abhedaka*). Having raised the doubt—"Both of these views have been stated regarding quality; which one here is logical? Is it that qualities are differentiators?"—it is concluded that it is indeed logical that qualities are differentiators. Why is this so? Because [the author] makes the mention of the term "acute" (*udātta*) in the rule: "In *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, [the final vowel becomes] *an* and is acute" (*asthidadhisaktthyakṣṇāmanaṅ-udāttaḥ*).

If the accents (*guṇa*) were non-distinguishing (*abhedaka*), then it would have been stated [by Pāṇini] simply as "pronounce the *udātta*"; this is the implication. Because the quality of being *udātta* is distinguished from the *anudātta* and others precisely by the pronunciation of the *udātta*, the exclusion of the *anudātta* and so forth is established even without explicitly stating them. Furthermore, since he has employed the word *yataḥ* as a separate term instead of pronouncing it [as part of a compound], it is understood that the accents are indeed distinguishing.

Furthermore, even when an acute accent (*udātta*) is pronounced, because that acute quality lacks the capacity to distinguish [the vowel] from others, there would be the inclusion of the grave (*anudātta*) *anaṅ* as well; therefore, the term "acute" (*udātam*) serves its purpose within its own scope by excluding that [grave accent].

Furthermore, since the vowel *ā* possesses some quality (*guṇa*) as an inseparable property when it is uttered, even if that quality were non-differentiating, the apprehension of the vowel *ā*—even when joined with another quality—would be established. Consequently, the purpose of the long *ā* (tapara) in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* would not be justified. This is the meaning of the section. [Pāṇini 1.1.2: *iko guṇavṛddhī*]

Therefore, the inclusion of the vowel *ā* in the rule *ato ḍhalādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) and the prohibition regarding *ṇi*, *śvi*, and *pratiṣedha* serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) that an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation does not take effect before *sic*. Since this is already established by the fact that the former is an exception (*apavāda*), this statement represents the view of a partial exponent (*ekadeśin*). Furthermore, the mention of *vṛddhi* in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* is for the purpose of being carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule *viṅti ca*.

Otherwise, that sūtra would establish merely the quality [of vṛddhi]; consequently, in forms such as *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*, vṛddhi would apply by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *sic* in the *parasmaipada*" (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

Having stated that there is no fault because the prohibition of *vṛddhi* also applies by the rule "when *vṛddhi* is prescribed and when *viṅt* [is applied]," he further says: "This is not necessary; for since the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs here due to its being *antaraṅga*, the vowel *u* will no longer exist at the end of the word, and thus *vṛddhi* will not take place."

Therefore, regarding the mention of *vṛddhi* in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this mention of *vṛddhi* serves as the basis for its existence there, and then stated: "The augment *sici* does not become *antaraṅga*; for if it were so, the author would not have made the mention of the vowel *a* in the rule *ato lāntasya*."

This is the meaning: by the rule "ato halāder laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.7), the optional *vṛddhi* of the short vowel *a* following a consonant (halādi) is prescribed before the suffix *sic* when followed by a *parasmaipada* ending beginning with *iṭ*. The examples are *akhādīt* and *akhadīt*.

It must be stated here that the phrase "of the letter *a*" (*akārasya*) was included so that, in the absence of such a specification, in rules such as *akoḥ sdvdr1;īt* and *amoḥsdvdr1;īt*, where the formulation would be *a-kuḥsdvdr1;-īt*, the *vṛddhi* substitution might otherwise apply even to the long *ū* in *mūla-* due to the presence of a *hal* (consonant) following a light vowel (*laghu*). To prevent this, it is said: "of the letter *a*."

If, however, an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) were to occur when *sic* follows, then—because it would be more internal than the *vṛddhi* which depends on both *sic* and the Parasmaipada suffix—the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would apply first. Consequently, since the vowel *o* would no longer be "light," the *vṛddhi* would not take place anyway; thus, the mention of the vowel *a* [in the rule] would be redundant.

And that [mention of *ak*] is purposeless, as it indicates the rule: "An internal element (*antaraṅga*) does not become superseded. Consequently, since the internal *guṇa* would not apply, the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u* would occur by virtue of its being subsequent (in the order of rules); therefore, the mention of *ak* is for the sake of preventing that, and thus it fulfills its own specific function.

Thus, the mention of the roots *ṇi*, *śvi*, and *ghrā* in the rule *ṇeraniṭi kṣaṇisyanijāguḥśvyeditām* (Pāṇini 7.2.5) also serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this statement. Accordingly, the meaning of that rule is: "There shall be no *vṛddhi* substitution for a root ending in *ṇi*, for one ending in *kṣaṇ* etc., for *śvi* with its *ṇic* suffix, or for a root having *e* or *it* as its *it*-marker, before the *sic* affix when it begins with *iṭ*."

*āṭnayīt* and *aśvayīt* are the illustrative examples. If *sici* were antaranga, then because of its antaranga status, the guṇa substitution would occur first; since the desired form would then be established, the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* would be unnecessary.

And that [rule] indicates that the *sici* augment does not become *antaraṅga*; consequently, since the internal *guṇa* substitution would not apply, and there would be the attainment of *vṛddhi*, the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* is for the purpose of prohibiting that [vṛddhi].

And thus, in cases such as *nyanuvīt*, when the internal *uvaṅ* substitution has not yet taken effect and the *vṛddhi* is about to occur, the rule *viṅti ca* establishes the prohibition of *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel. To ensure this prohibition is established, it must be accepted that *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel applies in the context of *sic*. For this purpose, it is settled that the mention of *vṛddhi* in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* is necessary.

In reality, however, since the rule for *vṛddhi* is established as an exception (*apavāda*) to the internal *guṇa*, once *vṛddhi* is obtained, the mention of the roots *ṇi*, *śvi*, and *gra* is for the purpose of excluding that *vṛddhi*. Thus, its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned statement is not tenable; therefore, [the desired form] is established by way of being an exception.

Because of the indicatory *k* in the suffixes *knus* and *san*—as seen in the rules *jñā-ṭ-kṅ-ti-cī* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), and *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9)—it is understood that this [rule] prohibits *guṇa* substitution even when it is conditioned by a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Therefore, the mention of "caused by that" (*tannimitta*) need not be made.

Regarding the rule *kṅti ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the author of the Vārttika stated: "In the rule *kṅti ci*, the mention of *kṅti* when there is a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is for the purpose of making the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) subject to that prohibition. In the rule *kṅti ci*, the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) is understood to follow. In that context, if *kṅti* were a qualifier of *ik*, then the meaning of the rule would be: "When a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix follows, there is no *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* for that *ik* which [stands before it]."

If that were the case, then in examples such as *ciṃtita* and *stuta*, since the letter *i* (ika) would indeed be followed by a *k*-marked suffix (*kit*), the exclusion of *guṇa* would apply. However, in cases such as *bhinnna* and *bhinnnavān*, in the form *bhin-ta*, the vowel *i* (ikāra) of the penultimate syllable (*upadhā*) would not be followed by a *k*-marked suffix because it is separated from it by the letter *d*; consequently, the exclusion of *guṇa* would not apply there.

Therefore, having supplied the word *tannimitta* (conditioned by that), the meaning of the sūtra should be described as follows: when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply conditioned by *kṅit*, they do not occur—this is the meaning of the sūtra. Consequently, since the *upadhā-guṇa* is also conditioned by *kṅit*, its prohibition is established, and thus the desired form is achieved.

Therefore, even for a penultimate (upadhā) vowel, the mention of "that which causes [the operation]" (tannimitta) is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Thus, in the case of the root *rudh* with the *yaṅ-luk* suffix, in the first person singular of the present tense (*laṭ*), at the stage where "roru īti" has been reached, the *guṇa* of the vowel *u*—caused by the affix *ti*, according to the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ"—is replaced by *o*, resulting in the form "roravīti."

In the absence of the apprehension of that cause, since the quality [of *guṇa*] was previously stated to be caused by that [cause], it lacks the status of being caused by that; thus, there is no prohibition of it, and the desired form is established.

Therefore, according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, the term "tannimitta" (having that as its cause) must be included in the rule *kiṅti ca* for two purposes: to prevent the substitution of *guṇa* in cases such as *ḍu dhāñ* ("to place"), and to ensure the absence of *guṇa* in cases such as *roravīti*.

However, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, wishing to establish the prohibition of *guṇa* by means of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the *ika* vowel in the *upadhā* position, rejected the mention of the condition "caused by that" (*tannimitta*). This is seen in the rule beginning with *trasigṛdhṛ...*—namely, the sūtra *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), by which the suffix *knu* is prescribed after the roots *tras* and others.

In this context, [the suffix] is designated by the letter *ka* with an *it*-marker (*itsaṃjñaka*). Its purpose is the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution in cases such as *gaḥTktgrRN;dhnuḥ* (from the root *gāh*), according to the rule *kṅti ca*. For if *guṇa* were prohibited for a suffix marked by *k* and *ṅ* only when it is followed by *i*, then because of the intervention of the letter *dha*, the *ṛ* would not be followed by a suffix beginning with *kn*; consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* would not apply.

However, the addition of the letter *k* in the suffix *kṛt* (*kakārānubandha*), when applied for that purpose, being otherwise redundant, indicates that there is a prohibition by the rule *kṅiti* even of that *guṇa* which is characterized by the presence of a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) and is separated [from the root] by an intervening element. Likewise, by the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), it is stated that a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a *hal* consonant that is in close proximity to an *ik* vowel shall be treated as *kit*.

In forms such as *jughoṣati*, the purpose [of the rule] is the absence of *guṇa* for the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *u*. Since the penultimate vowel is not followed by a *kit* suffix, the prohibition of *guṇa* would not otherwise apply; therefore, because there would be no purpose [for the rule], the mention of *kit* would be redundant. Consequently, the meaning is that this [mention of *kit*] indicates that there is a prohibition of *guṇa* characterized by the penultimate vowel.

And likewise, in cases such as *dhinno* and so forth, since the prohibition of *guṇa* is established by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the mention of "that which is caused by it" (*tannimittagrahaṇa*) is not necessary; such is the sense. [Jñā.ṭ] By the indicator consisting of the *ṅit* doubling of *yāsuṭ*, that operation which applies to substitutes ending in *ṅ* does not take place.

Regarding the statement "therefore, there is no prohibition of guna in *acinavam* and so forth," this is the opinion of the Vārttikakāra (on Pāṇini 1.1.5). [Objection: Now, one might raise the following doubt: when the suffix *liṅ* is applied to the root *ci*, and after the substitution of *am* for *iṭ*, the form *a-ci-nu-am* is established, then because the substitute *am* (which is the replacement for the *liṅ* affix) would be treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would possess the property of having a *ṅ* (as it is marked with *ṅ*); consequently, by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), there should be a prohibition of *guṇa*. [Reply: Anticipating this, he says: "By the rule regarding *yāsuṭ*. According to the sūtra *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅcci* (Pāṇini 3.4.103), which prescribes that *yāsuṭ* is *udātta* and has the property of *ṅ* when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ* or *ñ*, the prescription of the *ṅ*-property for *yāsuṭ* would be redundant.

In the case of *bhūyāt*, because the *tip* suffix in the place of the *liṅ* affix possesses the property of being *ṅit* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle, and because the *yāsuṭ* augment also acquires the status of being *ṅit* according to the maxim of "that which is added as an augment" (*yadāgama-nyāya*), one might object that the prescription of *ṅit*-ness is redundant. However, the prescription of *ṅit*-ness serves to indicate the rule: "Substitutes for [affixes] beginning with *ṅ* do not possess the property of being *ṅit*. Consequently, even though *tip* is a substitute for *liṅ* which begins with *ṅ*, it does not possess the property of being *ṅit*. Thus, the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* would otherwise be difficult to establish; therefore, the prescription of its *ṅit*-ness is purposeful.

However, the purpose of making this known is that in forms such as *acinavam*, because the substitute (*ādeśa*) possesses the marker *ṅ*, there is no prohibition of *guṇa*. The author of the Bhāṣya, having split the word *apit* in the sūtra *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4) and having carried over the term *ṅit* from the previous rule, has described two alternative interpretations of the sentence-meaning: either "that which is marked with *ṅ* is not *pit*," or "that which is *pit* is not marked with *ṅ*."

In this view, the dual number of *yāsuṭ* with the marker *ṅ* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), but rather it serves to prescribe *ti* and *v* where they would otherwise not apply, as in forms such as *mārjyāt*. Bearing this in mind, the author states: "This is the opinion of the Vārttikakāra. [The *pluta* vowel is established in vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) by the indicators (*jñāpaka*) of the rules *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11) and *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.125)].

Alternatively, the status of being established (*siddhatva*) for the *pluta* vowel is due to its being dependent on the same basis (*āśrayasiddhatva*), just as in the case of the substitution of *u* for *ru*. Having raised the objection that—since the addition of the *tapara* marker (*t* in *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*) excludes vowels of a different duration, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply to those of a different duration—the [author] provides the solution: since the *pluta* is treated as non-established (*asiddha*) when the *pragṛhya* designation is to be applied, the two-moraic *ī*-sounds and others of that same duration do indeed exist, and thus the *pragṛhya* designation will be successfully achieved.

Later, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* stated by way of objection: "The *pluta* vowel is established among the rules for vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), because this [rule], 'the *pluta* is as in its original state' (*plutaḥ prakṛtyā*), teaches the restoration (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the *pluta*. How does it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? Because an existing subject of an operation must undergo that operation."

By the rule *plutapragṛhyāḥ*, the elision (*abhāva*) of a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prescribed. If the protracted vowel were non-existent (*asiddha*) during vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), then, because the protracted vowel itself would not exist, it would be illogical to prescribe its elision by taking that protracted vowel as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*). Therefore, the intention is that the protracted vowel does not become non-existent during vowel-sandhi.

Regarding this, [the author] says: "In the case of *pluta*. The intention is that, in the general section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), this established status (*siddhatva*) is not being taught; rather, it is only being applied (*prakriyate*) within the specific context of the present discussion. With this in mind, he says: "Or else (*yadvā*). The reading "only in the present context" (*prakṛta eva*) is correct. The syntactic connection is: "The established status [of the rule], due to its being the basis for the *pluta* [vowel], applies only in the present context."

[The *Jñāpakapradīpa* states: The very mention of the word "single" (*eka*) in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14) indicates that when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, it is the class (*jāti*) that is intended. Its meaning is that there is no mention of multiple instances based on properties such as *altva* (the status of being a vowel). [The *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra* states: Let the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* be omitted.

Nor should it be argued that in the absence of *tad* (the suffix *t*), because the term *ac* is a qualifier of *nipāta*, the rule-meaning—that a *nipāta* ending in *ac* receives the designation *pragṛhya*—would imply that in examples such as *predaṃ brahma*, at the stage *pra-edaṃ*, the *nipāta* *pra* ending in *ac* would be *pragṛhya*, and thus no sandhi operation would occur. *Note: The original text contains several orthographic anomalies (e.g., ḍddhdhḍaddh;āve, viśeḥsdvdr1;aṇatvāt, pragaḥTktgrRN;hyasaṃjñā). These have been interpreted as *abhāve*, *viśeṣaṇatvāt*, and *pragṛhyasaṃjñā* respectively.*

Having raised the objection that if one accepts the meaning of the sūtra as being that "the designation *pragṛhya* applies to that vowel (*ac*) which is a particle (*nipāta*)—by relying on the fact that the particle is not specified as having the form of a vowel (*ajviśeṣaṇatva*)"—then since the particle *pra* lacks the nature of a vowel, it would not be subject to the *pragṛhya* designation, and consequently, the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) in the rule would be redundant; the author of the Bhāṣya replies: "In that case, then..."

Since this is established, when the mention of a single phoneme (*varṇa*) is being made, the fact that he mentions a single phoneme indicates that the Teacher intends: "In the mention of one phoneme elsewhere, there is the inclusion of the entire class (*jāti*). Thus, when there is a mention of a phoneme, there is the mention of multiple phonemes which are the substrata of that class. Consequently, by the term *ac*, there would be the mention of a collection of multiple phonemes based on their status as *ac*.

Furthermore, in examples such as *au akarot*, where the single phoneme *au*—which is a portion (*ekadeśa*) of the diphthong *au* and is designated as a particle (*nipāta*) when it functions as a case-ending—is subject to the technical designation of "heavy syllable" (*pragṛhya*), the substitution of *yaṇ* (the semivowel *y*) would not occur because the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is absent. Therefore, the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding such cases.

And when that [term *nipāta*] is restricted by its own capacity, only that single vowel which constitutes the form of the *nipāta* is understood as being the subject of the rule; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, the purpose elsewhere has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "That which was said—that the mention of *idam* and *el* is established because they denote a genus (*jāti*)—is thereby rendered appropriate."

The meaning of this is as follows: from the root *dam*, with the suffix *san*, the vowel *a* of the root is changed to *i* by the rule "damḍḍhḍaddh;a icca" (Pāṇini 7.4.56), resulting in the form *dimḍḍhḍaddh;a sa*. Then, because the suffix *san* is *kit* by the rule "ḥḍhḍhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;lantācca" (Pāṇini 1.2.10), the nasal *n* of the verbal stem's penultimate letter (*upadhā*) is elided by the rule "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Due to the absence of the augment *ṇiṭ*, the form *dhīpsati* is produced.

In this regard, the meaning of the sūtra *ḍhalantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10) is that a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant should be treated as *kit* when it follows a *hal* consonant that is in proximity to an *ic* vowel. In the state [of the derivation] *din + sa*, the suffix *san* does not follow a *hal* consonant (*na*) that is in proximity to an *ic* vowel; for the *san* follows the letter *bh*, and that *bh* is not in proximity to an *ic* vowel because it is separated by the letter *na*. Consequently, in the absence of *kit*-treatment, the elision of the *na* would be difficult to achieve.

If one accepts that the mention of "color" (*varṇa*) implies the mention of "genus" (*jāti*), then the purpose [of this rule] is established as follows: since there is proximity (*ekasamīpatva*) of multiple instances based on the genus *hal* (consonant), and because of its subsequent position, the suffix *san* becomes *kit*; when that [suffix] follows, there is the elision of the nasal *n* of the verbal root, resulting in the form *dhīpsati*. [The rule for the *gaṇa* of roots beginning with *jñā* is: *jñā-ādīnāṃ gaṇaḥ* (Sūtra 1.1.23).

In the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrā* (Pāṇini 5.4.110), there is no mention of the term *nadī*, because of the force of the mention of *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*. [Vaiśeṣika-ṭīkā: In the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), the mention of the word *saṅkhyā* (numeral) must be made.

The words *eka*, *dvika*, *trika*, *catuṣka*, *pañcaka*, *ṣaṭka*, *saptaka*, *aṣṭaka*, *navaka*, and *daśaka* are technical terms for numbers (*saṅkhyā-saṃjñā*); it should be stated that the word *saṅkhyā* (number) itself is also a technical term for a number.

Otherwise, as stated by the author of the Vārttika, because of the maxim that "between a conventional (*kṛtrima*) and a non-conventional (*akṛtrima*) term, the conventional meaning is understood," in the case of rules (*vidhisūtra*) containing the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*), the term "number" would refer only to conventional numbers such as *bhū* (one thousand million) and *gaṇa* (a multitude), and not to numbers like one (*eka*) and so forth.

Regarding that, an objection is raised in the Bhāṣya: "If, then, there is a cognition of the artificial in both the artificial and the non-artificial, then [the rule] ‘nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇīṣu’ would also apply here [to cases like *nadyāḥ kule*]."

The meaning is that if one accepts the logic of the *kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*, then in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī* (Pāṇini 2.4.22), the term *nadī* would refer only to those words ending in the vowels *ī* and *ū* that have been designated as *nadī* by the rule *yū stryākhyau nadī* (Pāṇini 1.4.3), and not to the word *nadī* itself.

The response to this objection is stated in the sūtra: "Because of the force of the sequence beginning with the Full Moon sacrifice and the sequence beginning with the New Moon sacrifice, it does not become a *bhāvyakarma* (a rite for the sake of a result)."

If the term *nadī* were to include the word *śarad*, which is designated as a *nadī* by the technical rule [Pāṇini 1.4.7], then since *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* also possess the designation *nadī*—being feminine nouns ending in long *ī*—their inclusion would already be established by that very rule [1.4.3]. Consequently, their separate mention in the sūtra would be purposeless.

Furthermore, that mention in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī* indicates that the word *nadī* does not denote a river that possesses the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "river" (i.e., a feminine noun ending in long ī or ū), but rather refers to something other than such a river. Thus, there is no fault [in the argument]; this is the intended meaning. This very point is stated [by the author] with the words beginning "nadī... and so forth.
