Immediately following that, in the sūtra *nadīpaurṇamāsī*, there arises the following concern: if the word *nadī* refers to what is commonly known in the world as a river, then words such as *gaṅgā*, *yamunā*, and so forth—which denote specific rivers—would also be included under the term *nadī* in that sūtra. Anticipating this objection, [the author states]: "The teacher’s usage indicates that [the designation *nadī*] does not apply to those specific [names]."

As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "When one recites this [text] during the autumn season, such as the month of Śrāvaṇa," the suffix *ṭac* prescribed by the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī* does not apply to words like *gaṅgā*, which denote specific rivers.

If that were the case, then the reading of *śarad-prabhṛtibhyaḥ* in [Pāṇini 5.4.107] would become redundant in examples such as *prativipāśam*. In such instances, the suffix *ṭac* is established by the rule *avyayībhāve śarad-prabhṛtibhyaḥ* (sūtra 5.4.107); therefore, that [reading of *śarad-prabhṛtibhyaḥ*] serves as its purpose.

In this regard, the point is as follows: since the word *vipāṭ*—which denotes a specific river—is included under the term *nadī* (river) in the rule *nadīpaurṇamāsī*, the suffix *ṭac* is established by that very rule; therefore, the inclusion of the word *vipāṭ* in the list of *śarad*-prabhṛti (autumn-beginning) words would be redundant. This redundancy serves to indicate that, in that particular rule (*nadīpaurṇamāsī*), the word *nadī* does not refer to a specific river. This is the underlying intention.

Regarding this, it has been said: "In the case of the rule for the suffix *śarat* and so forth, there is no mention of specific numbers because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the recitation of the word *viṃśati*. Likewise, in the rules for the substitutes of numbers, there is no mention of specific numbers such as 'one' (*eka*) and so forth, due to the prohibition in the rule for the suffix *kan*, namely 'atiśadantāyāḥ' (Pāṇini 5.1.22), which serves as an indicative."

In the sūtra *ekādiṅguṇavatuḍati* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), it was argued that the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) should be explicitly mentioned in the rule so that numbers beginning with one would also be established as having the technical designation of "number. To refute this requirement for a formal vārttika, it is demonstrated through a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) that the inclusion of numbers beginning with one is already secured by their mention in the specific rules (*pradeśas*) where the term "number" is employed.

Regarding the phrase "in the rules for the substitutes of numerals": in the prescriptive sūtras (*vidhisūtra*) that contain the term "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*), there is also the inclusion of numbers such as one (*ekādi*). The authority for this is the statement: "in the rule for the suffix *kan*."

The meaning is this: the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22), which prescribes the suffix *kan* after a numeral in the sense of "purchased with that," does not apply to numerals ending in *ati* or *śat*. For example, from *saptati*, one forms *sāptatikaḥ*; and from a numeral ending in *śat*, such as *catvāriṃśat*, one forms *cātvāriṃśatkaḥ*. In both cases, the suffix is *ṭhañ* according to the rule *tena krītam* (Pāṇini 5.1.37).

If, in the rule *vidhisūtra*, by the term *saṃkhyā* ("number"), there were no inclusion of artificial numbers such as *ekādi* ("one, etc."), then because numbers such as *viṃśati* ("twenty") and *catvāriṃśat* ("forty") would not be included under the category of "number," the suffix *kan* would not apply to them. Consequently, the restrictive rule *atiśadantāyāḥ* ("of that which ends in *ati* or *śat*") would find no scope for application.

Therefore, that prohibition [of *niṣṭhā*] indicates that even those beginning with "one" (*eka*) are included in the rules concerning numbers (*saṃkhyāpradeśa*). [Pāṇini 1.1.24: "Words ending in *aṣṭan* are called *aṣṭan*. The mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in *aṣṭan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its status as *aṣṭan*. The mention of the long vowel in forms ending in *ā* is for the sake of [the suffix] *maṭ* (i.e., *nuṭ*).
In the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the mention of *upadeśa* must be made. It should be stated that a number ending in *a* or *n* in its original form (*upadeśa*) receives the designation *aṣṭan*.

Otherwise, in cases such as *śatāni śāstrāṇi*, since it ends in *n* after the addition of the augment *num*, it would receive the designation *aṣṭan*; consequently, by the rule *aṣṭabhyaḥ luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), there would be the undesirable result of the elision (*luk*) of the case endings *jas* and *śas*.

Regarding the form *aṣṭānām*—when *aṣṭan* + *ām* is established, since the rule "ātvam aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84), which prescribes the substitution of *ā* for the final *n*, is both subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nitya*), the *n* is replaced by *ā*. Consequently, because the word no longer ends in *n*, the designation *ṣaṭ* (ṣaṭ-saṃjñā) does not apply. Since *ṣaṭ* is absent, the augment *nuṭ* prescribed by "ṣaṭ-catur-bhyo hal-ādau" (Pāṇini 7.1.55) would be impossible. Having raised this objection, [the author] considers cases such as *śatāni sahasrāṇi*.

By the rule *sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhir animittaṃ tadvighātasya* (an operation conditioned by a specific combination of elements does not cause the destruction of that very combination), the designation *ṣaṭ* is blocked; thus, even though the substitution of *āt* is applied in the case of *aṣṭānām*, the designation *ṣaṭ* is established by the authority of the evidence (*jñāpaka*) found in the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. That [evidence] is: "the mention of the long vowel in the rule for *aṣṭan*."

By the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.182), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is prescribed for the case endings beginning with *śas* that follow the word *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel. In that rule, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is made for the purpose of excluding the acute accent of the *sup* suffix in the form *aṣṭasu*.

Furthermore, if the designation *ṣaṣṭha* were not applied to *khaṭvā-tva*, then in the word *aṣṭasu*, by virtue of its being subsequent to the rule "aṣṭana" (Pāṇini 6.1.182), the rule "jhalyupottamam" (Pāṇini 6.1.180)—which means that in a word ending in a case-suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, the penultimate vowel becomes acute—would apply. Consequently, the vowel following the *ṭ* would become acute due to this "penultimate accent" (*upottamasvara*), thereby establishing the desired accentuation.

What is the use of such prolixity? One might argue that because [the rule] *aṣṭanaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*), it would set aside the accent prescribed by *jhaly upottamam* and, by virtue of the rule *aṣṭanaḥ*, the accent of the nominal suffix (*vibhakti*) alone would apply. To this it must be said: [this is not so].

In the view that admits the substitution of *ā*, since the substitute *āt* (which results from the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*) lacks the designation *aṣṭan* according to the principle established in the *Bhāṣya*, the penultimate vowel (*upottama-svara*) would not apply there; consequently, the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* would have its own scope of application, and thus it could not function as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [penultimate accentuation].

Furthermore, because of its status as a subsequent rule (*paratva*), in the case of *aḥsdvdr1;ṭasu*, only the penultimate accent (*upottamasvara*) would apply; thus, since the accent of the suffix (*viḥḍddhdhḍaddh;aktisvara*) does not even arise, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) made for the purpose of excluding it would be entirely redundant. And that very mention serves to indicate that the designation *aḥsdvdr1;ṭ* applies even to the word *aḥsdvdr1;ṭan* when it possesses the quality of being long (*kṛtātva*).

Furthermore, even in a case such as *khaṭvāḥ*, when the rule "jhalyupottamam" (Pāṇini 6.1.180) would otherwise apply for the accentuation of the penultimate syllable, the rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.172) is introduced. By the principle of "that which does not apply [otherwise] is superseded" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the rule "aṣṭanaḥ" itself operates as an exception (*apavāda*). Similarly, in the case of *aṣṭasu*, even under the alternative where the vowel is not long, the accent would apply due to the operation of that exception; therefore, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is made in order to prevent that.

The phrase "it must be done" (*kartavyam*) indicates that its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope. However, regarding its utility elsewhere, the intended meaning is that since the designation *haṭ* applies to *kṛt* as well—as established in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84)—the augment *nuṭ* is successfully established by the rule *aṣṭacatvāriṃśadadhryaśca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55). [Commentary on *sarvādīni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27): Regarding the designation *sarvanāman*, for this very reason, due to its being a *nipāta*, there is no substitution of *ṇa* [for the initial *na*].

The words *purāṇa* and *purātana*, being included in the *paṭ-samāsānta* group beginning with *paṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.32), are established as such. Regarding the rule *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27), one might raise the objection that since these are classified as *sarvanāman*, the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) would require the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*. Anticipating this, the solution is provided that the substitution of *ṇa* is avoided due to their being *nipātana*s (irregularly formed words). To this, it is further replied: let there be the absence of *ṇa* by virtue of the *nipātana*, but let the *ṇa* that is otherwise required by the rule remain; for the purpose of a *nipātana* is...

Having raised the objection that the intention [of the rule] is to establish the correctness of that specific form (*tadrūpa-sādhutva*) and not to exclude other forms, the *Bhāṣya* provides the following resolution: "Since the substitution of *ṇa* would otherwise apply, this *nipātana* (irregular derivation) is prescribed; it will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to that. This refers to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "In the case of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of 'pronoun' (*sarvanāman*)."

When *tanu-sam-tata* is established, the form *satataśaḥ* is considered correct due to the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *m*, by virtue of the rule *aparasparāḥ kriyāsātatye* (Pāṇini 6.1.144), which is a technical substitution (*nipātana*). Since this elision-substitution is introduced before the elision [of *m*] has already taken effect, it would supersede that elision. Consequently, the form *saṃtatam* would not be established.

Likewise, in the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu...* (Pāṇini 4.3.104), the word *purāṇa* is prescribed as a nipātita (irregularly formed) term; consequently, this would result in the sublation (*bādha*) of the word *purātana*. Fearing that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word *purātana* would thus not be established, [the author] states: "The pair *purāṇa-purātana*."

Thus, the correctness of *saṃtata*, *satata*, *purāṇa*, and *purātana* is established solely by their inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, and not by means of a specific grammatical *nipātana* (irregular formation). Therefore, there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault; this is the intended meaning. In the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, the maxim is cited: "Nipātanās are indeed exceptions. [Jñā.ṭ] *Pūrvaparā* (Sūtra 1.1.34).

First comes the list of word-groups (*gaṇapāṭha*), and afterwards the list of rules (*sūtrapāṭha*). This is known from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *pūrvādibhyo vā* (Pāṇini 5.3.38), where only nine words beginning with *pūrva* are mentioned. In the list of rules, there are exactly nine items beginning with *pūrva*.

Regarding the rule *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.34), for what purpose are *pūrva* and the others listed individually in the *jas* case-ending? For while they are indeed distinguished by their specific meanings in the list (*gaṇa*), they are always read there specifically for the sake of the designation "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). In that regard, the rule should have been stated simply as *pūrvādīni nava*.

Anticipating the objection that this [work] might have been acquired through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the author] states: "This would indeed be so if the *gaṇapāṭha* were prior and the *pāṇinisūtrapāṭha* were subsequent."

Having resolved that this is not the case because there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*), the *Bhāṣya* establishes, by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), that the *gaṇapāṭha* predates Pāṇini’s *sūtras*: "In that case, the Teacher’s [Pāṇini’s] own statement indicates that 'that is the earlier recension' and 'this is the later recension,' namely, when he makes the mention of 'nine' in the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*" (Pāṇini 5.4.70).

"Only nine, beginning with *pūrva*," it is said. Regarding that—the mention of "nine" in the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*—is made for the purpose of excluding [the inclusion of] more than nine, such as *tyad* and others, from the list of *pūrvādi*. Thus, the *gaṇapāṭha* (list of words) begins with *pūrva*.

If the list of gaṇas were previously arranged in a fixed order, then by the rule "pūrvādiḍḍhyaḥ," the words beginning with *tyad* would also be included; therefore, to exclude them, the mention of the word *nava* must be made.

However, when the *Pāṇini-sūtra* precedes the *Gaṇapāṭha*, then because the nine terms beginning with *pūrva*—namely *pūrvapara*, etc.—are specifically designated by the three sūtras [beginning with] *pūrvādīnāṃ navānām* (P. 1.1.34), there would be no possibility of including the nine pronouns beginning with *tyad* under the rule *pūrvādibhyaḥ* (P. 7.1.16). Consequently, the subsequent mention [of those pronouns] would be redundant; thus, [the existence of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is established].

The intention is that antiquity is inferred. "Sūtra-pāṭha" means the recitation of Pāṇini’s sūtras. [Jñānaprakāśa] states: based on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.1) and others, there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words such as *pūrva* by way of excluding *dvi* and so forth.

Regarding the doubt as to why the three sūtras beginning with *pūrva-parāvara-* are recited in detail instead of simply reading "the nine beginning with *pūrva*" for brevity in that very same sūtra, the resolution is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The purpose of this, however, is so that there may not be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the exclusion of 'two and so forth' (*dvyādi-paryudāsena*)."

Kaiyaṭa explains his intention as follows: After listing *tyad* and the others in the [gaṇa], some have also listed *pūrva* and the others. In that case, by the rule "after *kim*, pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and numerals (*saṅkhyā*), the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are applied" (Pāṇini 5.3.2), there would arise the undesirable consequence of excluding the suffixes *tasil* and so on from *pūrva* and the others. To remedy this, the technical designation *sarvanāman* is then applied to them once more, whereby the suffixes *tasil* and the rest are prescribed.

"Therefore, the exclusion of *dvitva* and so forth is accomplished by this [rule]. Immediately following that, the author of the Bhāṣya, wishing to refute this objection, states: "This purpose also does not exist. The authority of the Teacher makes it known that for these [elements], the exclusion is not effected by the exclusion of *dvitva* and so forth; for he provides the exceptional rule (*nipātana*) stating 'that which was previously established is not valid [for what follows]'."

Furthermore, if there were a prohibition of *tasil* and other suffixes following words such as *pūrva* by means of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth, then the mention of the word *pūrva* in the form ending with *tral*—as in the rule "pūrvatra"—would be invalid. The meaning is that, by the authority of this very mention, it is indicated that there is no exclusion of *pūrva* and the others through the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth.

Having kept all of this in mind, [the author] says: "By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the term *uttaratra* from the Vārttika—"If it is argued that there is no substitution of *jaś*, then because of the absence of *ḍha* in what follows, there would be the contingency of an exception (*apavāda*)"—is referred to.

Regarding the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), which states that what ends in a *kṛt* suffix and what ends in *m* or *e* is indeclinable (*avyaya*), the word *praśān* does not receive the designation of indeclinable by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations as if a suffix were present). This is because its inclusion among the *svarādi* group serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) for this point. In the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*, two interpretations of the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* have been presented: the first interpretation is that an indeclinable is that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix, or ends in *m* or *e*.

The second explanation is that whatever ends in *kṛt* (primary suffix) or *m* (the letter *m*) should be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Regarding this second explanation, one might raise the objection that when the root *tam* preceded by *pra-* takes the *kvip* suffix and that suffix is elided, even though the suffix has disappeared, the form *pratām* would still possess the status of ending in a *kṛt* suffix by virtue of the rule on the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and its status of ending in the letter *m* would remain evident; thus, it would incur the designation of an indeclinable. Anticipating this, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "The teacher’s intention indicates that... [and so forth].

The term *praśān* receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of its suffixal characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because this [author] recites it in the list of *svarādi* [indeclinables]. If the designation of an indeclinable were to apply by relying on the quality of ending in *kṛt* [suffixes] through the suffixal characteristic, then [the following would occur]:

Since the substitution of *n* for *t* (*natva*) is not established even when the suffix *śatṛ* is present, the word *praśān* does not end in *m*. Furthermore, by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, it does possess an ending in *kṛt* (the suffix *śatṛ*). Thus, since its status as an indeclinable would already be established by the rule "kṛnmejanta" (Pāṇini 1.1.39), the inclusion of *praśān* in the *svarādi* list would not be necessary for the purpose of assigning it the technical designation of "indeclinable. Therefore, the fact that it is nevertheless read there indicates that it does not receive the designation of "indeclinable" by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule. This is the meaning.

This very point has been stated [by Patañjali] with the words beginning "ending in *kṛt*," etc. [Jñānaprakāśa]: In the absence of three or four [suffixes], the prohibition of the long vowel for a *nām* ending in the rule "na tisṛcatasṛ" (Pāṇini 6.4.4) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In the commentary on the sūtra *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), the principle of *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* is cited, and its various applications are enumerated. Among these, "the application of the feminine suffixes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*" is also mentioned as one such purpose.

In the case of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, when followed by the nominative-accusative dual endings *jas* and *śas*, the forms *tisaḥ* and *catastraḥ* are substituted. Since these substitutes end in the vowel *ṛ*, the rule *ṛn-nebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5)—which prescribes the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* after stems ending in *ṛ*—would apply. However, that application is precluded by the principle of *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*.

Taking the coincidence of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as the cause (*nimitta*), the two rules [Pāṇini 4.1.63 and 4.1.75] prescribing the suffixes *tis* and *catas* do not apply when the cause for the suffix *ṅīp*—which would obstruct them—is present. The intention is that if *ṅīp* were applied, it would intervene between the stem and the case-ending, thereby destroying the coincidence of the case-ending that serves as the cause.

And the author of the Bhāṣya refuted this purpose—which was put forward as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the existence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—by first establishing its non-existence: "This purpose also does not exist. The authority of the Teacher (*ācārya-pravṛtti*) indicates that *ṅīp* does not occur when *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are present."

When this [sūtra] teaches the prohibition of the lengthening of the vowel in the *nām* (genitive/locative plural) ending by stating "not in *tisṛ* or *catasṛ*," it implies that the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after these two. For if *ṅīp* were applied to *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, there would be an intervention by that suffix, and since the condition of being followed by a *nām* ending would be absent, the lengthening prescribed by sūtra 6.4.3 (*nāmi*) would not even arise; thus, what purpose would the prohibition of lengthening serve? Since the prohibition of lengthening is indeed stated, it makes known that *ṅīp* does not occur after those two.

Consequently, since the absence of the *ṅīp* suffix in *tistraḥ* and *catastraḥ* is established by that very same indicator (*jñāpaka*) which [also] applies to the *jaś* and *śas* endings, the absence of *ṅīp* here does not serve as an illustration for the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*; this is the point. This is precisely what is stated in the passage beginning with "the absence of *ṅīp* in *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*," and so forth.

But surely, if the inclusion of the term *saṃnipātalakṣaṇa* is not accepted, then in forms such as *yā*, *sā*, and so on, the suffix *ṭāp* would not occur. This is because, when *sau* follows the words *yad* and *tad*, the *d* of *tyadādīnām aḥ* is changed to *a*, and after the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), since the stem ends in *a*, the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* would require *ṭāp* to be applied. Yet, that [suffix] does not occur.

Anticipating the objection that a short vowel (*atva*) caused by the conjunction of two vowels (*saṃnipāta*) cannot itself be the cause for the destruction of that very conjunction—such as the elision (*lopa*) of the *t* in *tāpam*—the author states: "The rule of *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* is non-eternal (*anityā*), as evidenced by indicatory marks (*jñāpaka*) such as the grammatical rule *na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45)."

According to the principle stated previously—that when a suffix is applied to a feminine noun, if the *ṭāp* were not present due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* [the rule that a grammatical operation caused by a specific configuration is not triggered when that configuration is destroyed]—then the mention of a form ending in *ṭāp* in the sūtra *yā sā* (Pāṇini 7.2.89) would be inconsistent. Therefore, the meaning is that the authority of this very mention establishes the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*. Consequently, in forms such as *rāmāya*, [the rule] *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102)...

Thus, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by Pāṇini 7.3.102. Otherwise, since the substitution of *y* (for *ya*) would have been caused by the combination with the final *a*, it could not serve as a cause for the lengthening that destroys that very combination; therefore, the lengthening would not occur—this is how it should be understood. In the rule *suḍanapuṃsakasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.43), by stating that this is an *asamartha-samāsa* (a compound whose members do not have a mutual relationship), it is indicated that the particle *a-* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "prohibition" and is not a living being (*aprāṇika*).

In the commentary on the sūtra *viḍvanoranapuṃsakasya*, it is stated: "This should be regarded as an *asamartha-samāsa* (a compound whose members lack semantic connection), namely *anapuṃsakasya*. There is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the negative particle *nañ* and the word *napuṃsaka*. With what, then? With the verb *bhavati*. [The meaning is: 'it does not occur in the case of the neuter.'"

By this, having accepted an *asamartha-samāsa* (an "impossible compound"), the Sūtra is explained as being intended for a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation). In that case, if the indeclinable *a* were to have some sense of negation, then by accepting *a napuṃsakasya* as two separate words, the *prasajya-pratiṣedha*—meaning "it does not apply to the neuter"—could be obtained even without resorting to an *asamartha-samāsa*.

The assumption that this is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound whose members do not have their own independent meanings) would be an unnecessary strain and should not be resorted to. Furthermore, the fact that such a [separate] indeclinable *a* with the meaning of negation does not exist is indicated by the very recourse to that [assumption]. Therefore, the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya* is as follows: he stated it in that way because he considered the word *anapuṃsakasya* to be a compound (*samasta-pada*), and that its status as a compound could not be maintained without it having the meaning of negation.

By this, those who interpret the Śruti passage, "If one knows Brahman as non-existent," by treating *asat* and *brahma* as separate words and explaining it as, "if one does not know that Brahman is existent," are to be refuted. [Jñānendrasarasvatī’s Commentary] The rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (by the rule *idudupadhasya*, Pāṇini 8.3.41) does not apply to a letter following a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of *ṛ* and *u*. Thus, in *bhrātuḥ-putra-grahaṇa*, the *ṣ* is not substituted.

[The Vita: But surely, by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, which prescribes that the substitute *aṇ* for the vowel *ṛ* is followed by a *ra*-sound, it is implied that even an *aṇ* occurring in place of both *ṛ* and another vowel is followed by a *ra*-sound; for that single substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not lose its status as having *ṛ* as its locus (*sthāna*).

Furthermore, in the case of *mātuḥ* from *mātaḥ* + *ṅsi*, when the vowels *ṛ* and *a* are replaced by *u* followed by *r* according to the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111), the form becomes *mātur s*. Then, by the rule *rāt sasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), the *s* is elided and the *r* is converted to a visarga (*visarjanīya*), resulting in *mātuḥ*. Subsequently, upon the conjunction with the word *karoti*, the visarga—which is not a suffix (*apratyaya*)—is subject to the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41), which prescribes the substitution of *ṣ*.

Nor can it be argued that the phrase *apratyayasya* means "of that which has a suffix as its constituent part," because since the vowel *a* is a constituent part of a suffix, its substitute—the visarga—must also be a constituent part of a suffix, and thus how could it attain the status of being *padānta*? For even if one somehow explains the substitution of *u* for *a* as having a suffix as its constituent part, it remains difficult to establish that the visarga—which occupies the place of the *r* that was itself a constituent of that *u*—is likewise a constituent part of a suffix.

Furthermore, suspecting that the occurrence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would be unavoidable, he says: "The mention of *bhrātṛṣputra*. According to the previously stated method, even in the word *bhrātṛṣputra*, since *ṣatva* is established by the rule "idudupadhasya" itself, the inclusion of that word in the *kaskādi* group—being otherwise redundant—indicates the following: there is no *ṣatva* for a letter following an *ekādeśa* (a single-substitute replacement).

The meaning is that the substitution of *ḥ* (visarga) for *r* does not occur after a *visarga* which has as its cause the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.87] regarding single-substitution (*ekādeśa*). Similarly, the substitution of *ḥ* does not occur after an *ukāra* (*u*) which has as its cause the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.111] *ṛta ut*; thus, in the case of *mātuḥ karoti*, there is no occurrence of *ḥ*. However, in the word *bhrātuḥputraḥ*, the establishment of *ḥ* is achieved because it is included in the *kaskādi* group. This is the intended sense.

In the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, however, it is stated that a [substitute] caused by a rule for a single substitute (*ekādeśa-śāstra*) does not possess the status of being a *repha*. In this context, it should be understood that when a *u* is produced by a rule for a single substitute, the visarga—which occupies the place of the *repha* that was a constituent part of that *u*—is considered to be caused by a rule for a single substitute.

In response to the doubt as to how this [rule] was read in the *Kaumudī* when it has not been included in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Manoramā* states: "In the original source (*ākara*), however, the prevalent reading is *ekādeśaśāstranimittāt*. There, the meaning is: 'from that *o*-sound for which the rule of single-substitution (*ekādeśa-śāstra*) is the cause. In the *Śabdaratna*, however, it is stated that the result is the prevention of the substitution of *ṛ* (ṛtva-nivṛtti) in examples such as *oḥ puyajñi* and *adhiḥ*.

And because that [form] is Vedic (*chāndasa*), it is stated that it is read only with the suffixes *ṣaṣṭhī* and *saptamī*. Furthermore, the reading with the fifth case-ending (*pañcamyanta*) for forms such as *bhaimiśra* and others has been fully justified; enough of this elaboration here. [Jñā.ṭ] Regarding *ṅcci* (Pāṇini 1.1.73): although the desired form would be established by the rule "for the *loṭ* [imperative], *er* is replaced by *u*, and for *tuhī*, *stāt* is substituted in the benedictive (*āśīḥ*)," the addition of the marker *ṅ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *tātaṅ* is a replacement for the entire stem (*sarvādeśa*).

[Objection: But surely, by the rule *ṅcci*, it is stated that a substitute (*ādeśa*) bearing the marker *ṅ* (itsaṃjñaka) takes the place of the final letter. And since the substitute *tātaṅ* also possesses the marker *ṅ*, one might suspect that by the rules *tu hyoḥ* and *ha eti*, *tātaṅ* would replace both the final *u* and the final *i*. To address this doubt, he says: "In the section concerning *eruḥ* for the *loṭ* [imperative]. Even without the presence of the marker *ṅ*, [the rule *eruḥ* applies]. (Sūtra 6.4.103).

Since the substitution of *tāt* is prescribed in the section on final substitutions (Pāṇini 3.4.86), its status as a final-substitution (*antyādeśa*) is established; thus, the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* in *tātaṅ* would otherwise be redundant. This redundancy serves to indicate that *tātaṅ* is not a final-substitution, thereby signaling that the marker *ṅ* has the function of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

Consequently, since the rule *añcu* (Pāṇini 1.2.12) has already fulfilled its purpose with respect to roots such as *śīṅ* that do not have any other meaning, it serves the purpose of preventing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions; thus, the substitute *tāt* does not apply to the *loṭ* imperative ending *hi*. And so, because *tāt* consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is understood to be a replacement for the entire original form (*sarvādeśa*). [Jñāpakasūtra] *anekāl* (Pāṇini 1.1.55).

In this context, the mention of *śit* in the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya* indicates that the status of having multiple phonemes (*anekāltva*) does not belong to *anuṣvadha*. [Objection: But surely, since rules such as *āṬś*, *iś*, and *śī* would already be established as replacing the whole by virtue of having multiple phonemes, the inclusion of the term *śit* in the sūtra *anekāl śit sarvasya* is redundant; to this, he replies: "In this context," etc.

Therefore, having joined the suffix *anuṭ* (which is an *anubandha*), the status of being "multi-alphabetic" (*anekāltva*) is not relied upon [for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole]. If it were *anekāl* after discarding the *anubandha*, only then would it be a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). However, in the case of forms such as *āṬś*, since they lack the status of being *anekāl* without the *anubandha*, they would not obtain the status of being a substitute for the whole; thus, the mention of *śit* is for the sake of ensuring that these are substitutes for the whole—this is the intended meaning.

Therefore, it should be understood that the result of this [rule] is to indicate that in cases such as *arvaṇas taḥ*, the substitution is not universal (*sarvādeśa*). In this treatise, certain paribhāṣās of this kind have also been included; we do not know their intended purpose. [Jñāpakas: The rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56) [is established]; for in the case of an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply, as is known from the fact that suffixes such as *śyan* are marked with the indicator *ś*.

Or rather, it is established by continuing the word *ṣaṣṭhī* from the previous rule, such that "the substitute is like the original with respect to what is indicated by the genitive case. If the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were merely a transformation of the operation (*bhāvanāvipariṇāma*)—meaning that when there is occasion for an operation on the substitute, the operation must be performed on the original—then [the following objection would apply].

Having raised the objection that even when the suffix *ka*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3)—is applied, the operation belonging to the suffix *aṇ* would still occur by virtue of the principle of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the author] replies: an operation prompted by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not take place when its exception (*apavāda*) is present. Thus, since the suffix *ka* is an exception, the operation prompted by the general suffix *aṇ* does not occur; therefore, there is no fault.

In this regard, the evidence (*jñāpaka*) is the addition of the marker *ś* in rules such as *śyan* and others, which are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *śap*. If, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the operation prescribed for the general rule (*utsarga*) were to apply to the exception, then even in the case of *yan*, the operation conditioned by the absence of the marker *ś* (i.e., the presence of *ś*) would occur through the status of being a substitute for *śap*; consequently, the addition of the marker *ś* in *śyan* and other such rules would be purposeless.

And this indicates that what is prescribed by an exception (*apavāda*) does not operate when there is a general rule (*utsarga*). Alternatively, in the sūtra "the substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānin*)," one carries forward the word *ṣaṣṭhī* from the sūtra "the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [is used] in connection with the original" (Pāṇini 1.1.49), transforms it into the instrumental case, and supplies the word *nirdiṣṭasya*; thus, [the meaning is]: "of that which is indicated by the genitive."

I would explain [the rule] as follows: "That which is prescribed in place [of something else] is like that original (sthānivat). Furthermore, the suffix *kap* is not prescribed in place of an *aṇ* that is specified by a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭa*). Therefore, it is not *sthānivat*, and thus there is no fault. This twofold resolution has been set forth in the foundational treatises (*ākaragrantha*). Regarding this, [it is said]: "It is not an exception (*apavāda*)," and so forth. As for the word "established" (*siddha*), the remainder of the sense is: "The maxim [is] 'an exception does not [invalidate] what is prescribed as a general rule (*utsarga*').'"

[Commentary on Jñā.ṭ: When a substitute (*ādeśa*) is to be applied, the rule *āḍhḍhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.35) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no substitution of *āḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;rīṭ*. [Commentary on Vi.ṭ: According to the *sthānivadbhāva* rule itself, if a substitute were to behave like its original (*sthānin*), then in the case of the present tense marker *laṭ*, in the second person singular, the substitute for the root *brūñ* would be *āḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;*.

Having stated this, [the author] notes that the augment *īṭ* would apply to the subsequent *thala* suffix by the rule *bruva īṭ* (Pāṇini 7.3.93), and that a prohibition of this must be stated, as declared in a Vārttika. Refuting that, Bhartṛhari stated: "A prohibition of *īṭ* need not be stated; for by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is established that *īṭ* does not occur after [the root] *brū*."

If it is asked what the evidence is [for this], the prescription of *thatva* (the substitution of *th*) in the rule "āḥsthah" is the evidence. Likewise, the rule "āḥsthah" prescribes the substitution of the phoneme *th* for *āḥ* when followed by a *jhal*-beginning suffix; "āttha" is the illustrative example.

If, by resorting to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) here, the *brū* root were [treated as such] and consequently the augment *īṭ* were applied to the suffix *thal*, then since *thal* would begin with the vowel *ī* and not with a consonant (*jhal*), how could the substitution of *th* for *t* occur when that suffix follows? Therefore, this indicates that the substitution of *th* prescribed when a *jhal* sound follows does not apply when *īṭ* is present.

If it is argued: "But surely, by the rule *āḍhḍhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;sthaḥ*, the substitution of *th* is prescribed when followed by a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound that has previously occurred (*bhūtapūrva*). Even though the suffix *thal* lacks the status of beginning with a *jhal* sound now due to the addition of the augment *īṭ*, since it previously possessed the status of beginning with a *jhal*, one might take that as the basis for the substitution of *th*. Thus, because there would be no point [in the rule], how can it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?"—if one were to rely on the principle of referring to what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*), then...

Since even for [the substitutes] *ṇal* and so forth, there exists the state of having been preceded by a *jhal*-beginning [affix] by taking their original form (*sthānyavasthā*), it would follow that the letter *ṭi* occurs after all five [of these substitutes].

If this were the case, [the author] would have prescribed the substitution *ātha* by the rule "The *ātha* substitute occurs for the five beginning with *bruva*, and also for *bruva*" (Pāṇini 3.4.84) without mentioning the term *liṭ*, and he would not have composed a separate rule stating "in *liṭ*. Since a separate rule has been composed, it is understood that the principle of referring to what occurred previously (*bhūtapūrvagati*) is not accepted here. Consequently, among the five [suffixes], only *thal* is one that begins with a *jhal* consonant.

If *tasya* were to possess the property of beginning with a *jhal* sound, then the substitution of *tha*, which is prescribed when a *jhal*-beginning suffix follows—as in *tasya bhagnam*—would be without scope (*anavakāśa*). Therefore, it indicates that there is no elision (*lopa*) of the genitive ending. Having taken all this into consideration, [the author] says: "The substitution of *āth* must be performed."

Regarding the rules *gotaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.90) and *otaḥ* (6.1.93), the inclusion of the *ta*-par marker (*taparakaraṇa*) serves as an indicator that, in cases such as *citraguḥ* and *catraguḥ*, the *ṇit*-quality and the substitution of *ā* do not apply. In the commentary on the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, there arises the concern that in the word *gośaḥ* (the genitive plural of *go*), both the *ṇit*-quality and the substitution of *ā* would apply. Anticipating this objection, the author of the *Akara* states that due to the force of the *ta*-par marker, the *ṇit*-quality and the substitution of *ā* do not occur. This is indicated by the citation: *gota iti*.

This is the intended meaning: if an ādeśa were to be treated like its original (sthānivat), then in the case of *citraguḥ*—where the analysis is *citragāvo yasya* (he whose cows are variegated)—the suffix *su* would follow the word *go*, because after the shortening of the vowel *o* to *u* by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), that *u* would, by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānin*), still possess the quality of being *o*; thus, since the condition for applying the rule *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90) would be met, [the suffix *ṇit* would have to be applied].

Since that [suffix] is *ṇit* by the rule *sū. 7-1-90*, when it follows, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (*sū. 7-1-15*) would result in the *vṛddhi* substitution of the vowel *u*. Consequently, in the case of *trigum*, because the *u* would—by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*—be an *o*-vowel, the rule *āṬto'mśasoḥ* (*sū. 6-1-93*) would then result in the replacement of both the preceding and following vowels with *ā* when *am* follows an *ac*. This is the objection.

The resolution, however, is as follows: since the term *otaḥ* is used with a long *ṭ* (tapara) in both rules, it is a rule concerning an *al* (a phoneme); and because of the principle that "what is not a rule concerning an *al* does not apply by way of substitution" (*analvidhau*), there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). The purpose of the long *ṭ* is the exclusion of the vowel *u* in the rule *guṇaḥ*. If the rule were to apply there as well by way of substitution, then the use of the long *ṭ* would be meaningless.

[Commentary on *Pāṇini 1.1.59*: *dvirvacane'ci*] The mention of the term *aj* [in the rule] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies even when the original form (*rūpa*) [is not directly present]. The example *jeghrīyate* is provided as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to that. [Commentary on *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*] Now, an objection: the meaning of the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) is that when a vowel (*ac*) which is the cause of reduplication (*dvitvanimitta*) follows, a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānivat*).

Furthermore, in the view that this is an *atideśa* (extension) of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), forms such as *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ* would not correctly establish the long vowel *ā*. In the case of *cakr-atuḥ*, when the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution to become *r*, resulting in the intermediate stage *kr-atuḥ*, the doubling (*dvitva*) prescribed for a monosyllable (*ekāc*) cannot apply because the stem is now vowelless. Even if it were to apply by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), due to the nature of an *atideśa* of the operation, it would result in the doubling of the very form already specified after the *yaṇ*-substitution.

Furthermore, when *cakr-atuḥ* is established, if [the rule] were applied to the beginning of a root starting with a consonant (halādi), the form would result only in *cakratuḥ*. Fearing that the form *cakratur*, characterized by a reduplication (*abhyāsa*) containing the vowel *a*, would not be established, [the author] states: "But [there is] the mention of *ajgrahaṇaṃ*."

The intended meaning is this: regarding the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, one should not consider it a "transfer of operation" (*kāryātideśa*), in the sense that whatever grammatical operation applies to the original element (*sthānin*) also applies to its substitute (*ādeśa*). Rather, it is a "transfer of form" (*rūpātideśa*), in the sense that whatever form the original element possesses, that same form is attributed to its substitute.

And likewise, in the case of *cakratuḥ* from *kṛ*, when the *yaṇ* substitution is applied, by the extension of the form of the original element (*sthānyātideśa*), the form *kṛ*—characterized by the vowel *ṛ*—is doubled, and thus the form *cakratuḥ* is established without any fault. As for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the extension of form, it is the mention of the term *ac* (vowel) in the rule *aci* [Pāṇini 1.1.56]. The purpose of that [mention] is to prevent the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) in cases such as *jeghrīyate*.

From the root *ghrā*, by applying the rule *ī ghrā-dhmroḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.31), the vowel *ā* of the root is replaced by *ī*, resulting in *ghrī*. This form is then doubled, yielding *ghrīghrī*. Following the rules for the elision of the initial *ṛ*-class vowels (*ṛṭ-ṛṣ-ṛbhyo hali*), the substitution of *c* for *j* (*cutva*), and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*), and finally applying the rule *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82) which effects *guṇa* substitution in the reduplicated syllable, the form *jeghrīyate* is obtained.

In that context, because *yaṅ* is the cause of reduplication (*dvitvanimitta*), when it follows, there would be a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*) for the substitute *ī* (from *ā*) by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*; consequently, upon the reduplication of *ghrā*, the form would result in *jaghrāyata*. To prevent this, the mention of *aj* (a vowel) [in Pāṇini 1.1.59] was made. Once that is established, the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* applies to a substitute of a vowel (*ajādeśa*) only when a vowel (*ac*) that is the cause of reduplication follows.

However, since even that which is the cause of doubling (*dvitvanimitta*) lacks the status of being a vowel (*actva*), there is no substitution of the form *ā* for the *ī* by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva* when that [cause] follows. Thus, when *ghrī* undergoes doubling, the form *jeghrīyate* is established. In that case, if one adopts the view of the transfer of the operation (*kāryātideśapakṣa*), then only the operation of doubling itself is transferred to *ghrī*; consequently, because there is no transfer of the form *ā*, there is no fault even if *sthānivadbhāva* applies—so what is the use of mentioning the term *ac*?

The mention of *kṛt* and *aglopi* in the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* indicates that the extension (*atideśa*) of *sthānivadbhāva* prescribed by that sūtra is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*). [Jñāpakasamuccaya: The mention of *ṭhoḥ pū* and *aṇji* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the existence of *sthānivadbhāva* after a causative suffix (*ṇi*). [Vivaraṇa: But surely, in forms such as *avacāvayiṣyati* and *avacukṣāvayiṣyati*, the augment *suṭ* would apply to the roots *av* and *kṣu* when they are followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)?

In that context, when the suffix *ṇic* follows—as in the case of the root *nau* where the vowel *u* undergoes *vṛddhi* by the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115), followed by the substitution of *āv*—the form *nāv-i-sa* results. At this stage, if one were to apply the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) to the substitution of *āv*, thereby extending the form of the long vowel *au* to the substitute, then upon doubling the word *nau* in the sequence *nau nau isa*, the form would become *nunāvayiṣati* after the elision of the augment *abhyāsa* and the subsequent substitution of *āv*. However, in that case, the application of *sthānivadbhāva* is difficult to justify.

By the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for an *aj*-substitute is stated only when an *ac* vowel follows that which causes reduplication. Here, however, since the *ṇic* suffix is not the cause of reduplication, one might ask how the *aj*-substitute applied after it could possess the status of a substitute. To this, [the author] says: *oḥ puyaṇji*.

And likewise, there is indeed the status of *sthānivadbhāva* for a substitute (*ajādeśa*) that occurs before the causative suffix *ṇic*; in this regard, the rule "oḥ puyaṇjyapare" (Pāṇini 7.4.80) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). The meaning of that rule is: when *san* follows, if there is a base (*aṅga*), then the vowel *u* belonging to its reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) shall undergo *itva* (change to *i*), provided that *p*, *y*, *ṇ*, *j*, or *k* follow, with an *a*-vowel preceding them. The example given is *yiyaviṣati*.

In this context, if the term *puyaṇji* were not stated, then even in forms such as *avanunāvayiṣati*, the substitution of *i* for the *u* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would occur. To prevent that, the term *puyaṇji* is stated.

Furthermore, if there is no *kathānivat-bhāva* (the status of being like the original) for what is performed in the causative (*ṇau*), then a reduplicated syllable containing the vowel *u* would be difficult to find here; thus, since the substitution of *i* would not apply simply because the *u* is absent from the reduplication, what would be the purpose of including the mention of *puyaṇji*?

And this [rule] indicates that when a *ṇi* suffix is present, there is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*); such is the understanding. Regarding the rule *pratyayasya luk* (Pāṇini 1.1.61): by virtue of the expression *pratyayasya* and because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *lugvā duherdyanoddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), it follows that *luk* and the other elisions (*lopa*) are replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).

In the rule *pratyayasya luk-ślulupaḥ*, the Vārttikakāra stated that the mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is for the purpose of establishing that *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Refuting this, the Bhāṣyakāra says: "This purpose is also unnecessary. The tradition of the Teacher makes it known that *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are replacements for the whole."

When this [elision] is about to take place by the rule "luk vā duhr-dhṛṣ-tṝ-stṝ-sru-śn-ūṅām ātmanepade dantye" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.102), which prescribes *luk*, [the author] teaches *luk* by the rule "lug vā duhr" (*Pāṇini* 7.3.73). By the rule "lug vā duhr," the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ksa* after roots such as *duh* is optionally prescribed when a dental [suffix] beginning with *taṅ* follows.

Examples such as *adugdhā* and *adhukṣata* are cited here. In that regard, although the elision [of the *saP* suffix] is already established in the rule "ghorlopo leṭi vā" (Pāṇini 7.3.70) by simply carrying over the term "elision" (*lopa*) from that sūtra, the explicit mention of "elision" (*luk*) serves to indicate that the disappearance (*adarśana*) prescribed by the mention of "elision" (*luk*) is a total substitution (*sarvādeśa*). However, in the case of "elision" (*lopa*), the disappearance applies only to the final phoneme.

Even when *luk* (elision) would be a substitute for the final [element], the desired result is established simply by the recurrence of the word *lopa* (elision); therefore, what is the purpose of mentioning *luk*? However, the mention of *luk* is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that it is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). This is the underlying intention. This very point is stated [in the commentary] with the words "by the force of the rule *pratyayasya*" and so forth. This is according to the view of the Vārttika.

According to the opinion of the venerable Bhartṛhari, however, [the elision of suffixes occurs] because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule "there is optionally elision (*lug vā*) after [a suffix ending in] *duḥ*. [Pāṇini 1.1.62: "When a suffix is elided (*pratyaya-lope*). Because of the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 1.1.63: "When a suffix is marked by *lu*, [an operation affecting] the stem (*aṅga*) does not take place," it is understood that elision (*lopa*) applies to *luk* and the other types of suffix-elision as well.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, it is stated by the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* that even when there is the elision (*lopa*) of an affix, an operation conditioned by that affix still takes place. In that case, when there is a *luk*-elision of an affix, an operation conditioned by that affix does not occur, because *luk* is not considered a form of *lopa*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *pañca* and *sapta*, when the case endings *jaś* and *śas* are elided by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), the forms *pañcan* and *saptan* would not possess the status of a *pada*. Due to the absence of *pada*-status, the elision of the final *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur. Therefore, one must assert that *pada*-status is established by relying on the fact that they end in *su* through the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle.

One might suspect that the rule regarding the treatment of a stem (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies only when there is an elision of a suffix (*pratyayalopa*) and not when there is a disappearance by *luk* (*pratyayaluk*); however, this is not to be feared, because of the prohibition: "When [a suffix] is marked with *lu*, there is no [application of] the stem-operation" (*na lumatāṅgasya*). This prohibition—that when a suffix is elided by terms such as *luk*, the treatment of a stem (*aṅgakārya*) based on the suffix does not apply—is only appropriate when there was an actual application of the suffix-treatment to begin with. A prohibition is illogical if the treatment had not already been applicable.

When an element is elided by *luk*, the designation of "elision" (*lopa-saṃjñā*) applies to that *luk* only through the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), because that rule speaks of the "elision of an affix" (*pratyaya-lope*). Therefore, the underlying intention is that the fact that *niḥ* cannot otherwise be accounted for serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *luk* and other such markers are also considered forms of "elision" (*lopatva*). Regarding the sūtra *tasminniti* (Pāṇini 1.1.66): in these two sūtras, under the view that they designate case endings, the seventh and fifth cases do not simultaneously designate [the respective loci].

This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84). [Viṭṭhala’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If it is accepted that the maxim *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66) prescribes the status of being 'prior' (*pūrva*) for what precedes, and the maxim *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) prescribes the status of being 'subsequent' (*para*) for what follows, then in a rule of prescription where both the locative (*saptamī*) and the ablative (*pañcamī*) case-endings occur—"

In that case, there would be the assumption of an ablative case for both the preceding and the following [words]. Consequently, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) would apply to both of them. For example, in the rule *tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātuke'nudātam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the word *tāsyādiḥ* would be assumed to be in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), thereby displacing the locative case (*saptamī*) of the word *lasārvadhātuke*.

Likewise, regarding the locative case [saptamī] "in *lasarvadhātuka*" and the ablative case [pañcamī] "after *tās* etc.," one should understand the former as being in the sense of the latter. Similarly, regarding the locative case "in *lasarvadhātuka*" and the ablative case "after *tās* etc.," one should understand the former as being in the sense of the latter. Anticipating the objection that the property of being unaccented (*anudātatva*) would thus apply to both, he says: "In these two rules..."

If, by means of the mutual assumption resulting from the mention of two [conditions], the meaning of the sentence were such that the *anudātta* accent of the *tāsī* and other affixes occurs when they are *lasārvadhātuka* and there is a *lasārvadhātuka* [affix] present, then even in rules such as "āda-guṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87), since the word "aci" is understood by anuvṛtti, one would have to rely on the mutual assumption of both [conditions]. Consequently, by explaining it as "there is guṇa substitution for an *avarṇa* before an *ac*, and for an *ac* following an *avarṇa*," the guṇa of the preceding and following sounds would be established.

The rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84) would otherwise be rendered purposeless. Since that sūtra has been composed, one does not resort to the assumption of both the ablative (*pañcamī*) and the locative (*saptamī*). If both were resorted to, because the ablative designation is stronger, the ablative alone would cause the assumption of the subsequent [element], and thus the *guṇa* substitution would apply only to the latter. Therefore, the sūtra *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* exists for the sake of establishing the *guṇa* substitution for both the preceding and the following elements.

Furthermore, in rules such as *tāsyanudāttet* (P. 6.1.186), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is interpreted as having the force of the locative (*saptamī*), meaning "after that which begins with *tāsī*. Consequently, the anudātta accent applies only to the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following *tāsī* and the like, and not to both the preceding and following elements. This is the intended meaning, and thus there is no fault. [Jñāpakasūtra: *yena vidhiḥ* (P. 1.1.72)]

By the statement *akor* in the rule *nedamadasorakoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.11), it is indicated that when a portion of a word is mentioned, the whole word to which that portion belongs is understood by that mention. [Objection: Even if one follows the interpretation of the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* ("that by which a grammatical operation is prescribed applies to that [word] and to what ends with it"), the substitution of *śī* for the nominative plural suffix *jas* would not apply after *sarvakaḥ*, because *akac* has been added to it. Likewise, [the same would apply to other cases].

When *sarva* is followed by the suffix *jas*, and *akac* is added, resulting in *sarvaka-jas*, the form *sarvaka* lacks the status of being called *sarvaśas* (the word *sarva* with the suffix *śas*), and consequently lacks the status of ending in *sarvaśas*. Therefore, whether one applies the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ prātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.10) or the rule *sarvanāmāntāt prātipadikāt* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.4.10), in either case the inclusion [of *sarvaka*] does not occur, and thus the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17) does not apply.

In this way, regarding the form *hinati* in the phrase *evaṃ hinati*, since only the root *hi* is a verbal root (*dhātu*), the form *hinat*—which possesses the suffix *śnam*—is not a verbal root because it follows immediately after the affix. Consequently, one might raise the objection that the final acute accent (*antodātta-svara*) prescribed by the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162) would not apply. Anticipating this, [the author] states: "Not so, except for *idam* and *adas* when followed by *akaḥ*," and so forth.

The sūtra *nedamadasorakoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.11) teaches that the substitution of *e* for the following genitive case ending (*ṅasi*) does not occur after the pronouns *idam* and *adas* when they are followed by the suffixes *ak* or *akac*. In this context, the phrase "when followed by *ak* or *akac*" excludes those instances of *idam* and *adas* characterized by the addition of *akac*, such as *imaka* and *amuka*.

In that context, since the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is stated for the forms *idam* and *adas* when they end in *-viḥ*, how could it apply to those two when they are specifically characterized by the suffix *-akac*? Therefore, even though the word "of *aka*" (*akor*) is not explicitly mentioned, because the exclusion is established through the very distinction of the forms, the fact that the term "of *aka*" (*akor*) would otherwise be redundant indicates that it includes as a part of itself the forms ending in *-viḥ*. And thus, [the rule] applies to *idam* and *adas* which fall within the scope of this distinction.

Since it is a part of that [word], it would be included by the inclusion of *idam* and *adas*; therefore, for the purpose of excluding it, the term *akaḥ* is meaningful. Likewise, because the word *sarvakaśas* is also included by the word *sarvaśas*, [the restriction is necessary].
Since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) exists [in *sarvaka*], when the suffix *jas* following it is replaced by *śī*, the form *sarvake* is established. Similarly,
in the case of *hinad* (from *hinasti*), the augment *śnam* which has arrived as a constituent part of *hinad* is included by the mention of *hinad*.

The intention is that since *han* is also a verbal root (*dhātu*), the rule "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) applies, and thus it is established as having an udātta accent on the final syllable. This very point is also stated in the maxim: "That which falls in the middle of [a word] is included by the mention of that [word]."
"Of those whose measure is delimited" means "of those whose measure is circumscribed.

"The state of being such" means "the state of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) and so forth. [Note: *Jñānendraguru* explains that the rule "pūrvādiniḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.86) and "sapūrvācca" (5.2.87) constitute a division of the grammatical rules.]

The rule *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* ("the treatment as if possessing a designation applies except in the case of a nominal stem") is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this. [Objection: Now, if it were stated in the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72) merely that "the designation should apply to that which ends with the qualifying element," then in the rule *roṇī* (4.2.78),...
Considering that the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the sūtra [Pāṇini 4.3.79] would apply only after the word *roṇī* ending in *ajakaroṇī* and not from the word *roṇī* alone,

and that consequently the form *rauma* would not be established, [the author] has formulated this rule for the sake of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of both the base ending in *vaśiṣṭha* and of that [suffix itself].

This has been explained in the *Ākara*. In that context, the portion "and of that" (*tasya ca*) is not to be accepted. One might raise the objection that even in the absence of that [portion], the suffix *aṇ* would be established by taking the word *roṇīśa* as ending in the word *roṇī* through the principle of "designation as if it were so" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). [The author] addresses this doubt...

Regarding the mental application (*manasikāra*)—by means of [the rule] beginning with *pūrvādiniḥ* and so forth—it is thus: since the designation-like status (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is prohibited within the domain of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the word *roṇī* lacks the status of ending in the word *roṇī*; and of that...

The intention is that one must necessarily state "there would be a designation" (*saṃjñā syāt*). As for the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for the paribhāṣā "the status of being like that which has a designation [does not apply] when followed by a non-prātipadika," it is the rule *pūrvādiniḥ*.
The section on *yogavibhāga*: By formulating the single sūtra "pūrvāt sapūrvād iniḥ," [the author] intends that in forms such as *kṛtapūrva*,
because the word *kṛta* and so forth precede it,

and because the word *pūrva* alone— by virtue of the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it designates)— is also considered to have something preceding it (*sapūrvaka*).
Since the suffix *ini* can be established in both cases for the words *pūrvin* and *kṛtapūrvin*, the division of the rule into two parts— namely,
*pūrvādiniḥ* and *sapūrvācca*—
is made by the authority of the grammatical tradition (*ācārya*) when the context concerns nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
The term *bhāva* (the state) signifies that it is made known that the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not exist.
Thus ends the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter. [Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the sūtra "tasyāditaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.32):

The statement regarding the *anudātta* nature of *deva* and *brahman* in the rule *svaritasya...* and so forth is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this section [of the Veda] follows the rule *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66), as in the examples *idaṃ kāṇḍam*, *idaṃ kāṇḍam*. [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra, p. 159: *tasyādita udātamardhahrasvam* (Pāṇini 1.2.32).

In the *Śikṣā-sūtra*, having established the meaning of the rule that the first half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) of a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel is designated as acute (*udātta*), [the author] introduces the rule "its beginning is acute" (*tasyādita udātam*,
Pāṇini 1.2.32) and then the rule "that which follows an acute or circumflex is more depressed" (*udātasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ*, Pāṇini 1.2.40).

The nine sūtras ending with the Sūtra-paryanta—beginning from the sūtra *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66)—are to be recited after that point. Having stated this, the purpose is declared: "So that the correct formation [of the circumflex accent] may occur from a circumflex vowel (*svarita*)."
"From a *svarita* [vowel], the following *anudātta* vowels [become *pracaya*] when there is a *saṃhitā* [of more than one syllable]" (Pāṇini 1.2.39).
This is its meaning: in the passage "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri," after the word *me*, which is *svarita*, the following...
Because *gaṅge* is addressed, it is unaccented (*anudātta*);

consequently, according to the rule "after a *svarita*, in the case of a following *saṃhitā* of unaccented [syllables], there is monotony (*ekaśruti*)," it possesses *ekaśruti*. However, the word *me* has a *svarita* accent.
According to the rule *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.39), when the single accent (*ekaśruti*) is to be applied,
the circumflex (*svarita*) produced by the rule *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

If the position after a *svarita* did not exist for words such as *gaṅge*, *praḍddhdhḍaddh;aḥTktgrRN;tīnām*, then the *ekaśruti* (monotone) would not be established according to the reading of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* as it stands. However, if the aforementioned nine *sūtras* were placed immediately after "udāttādanudātasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.66), [the result would be different].

Since the single rule prescribing the [svarita] accent— "svaritātsaṃhitāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.39)— is also situated within the nine rules [of the first two pādas], it is immediate [to the preceding]; therefore,
the rule "udāttādanudātasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.66) which precedes it is not considered *asiddha*.
Since the *meṣa* (the sheep) [in the example] is established as having a circumflex (*svarita*) accent,

there is no objection to the single tone (*ekaśruti*) for the subsequent unaccented (*anudātta*) words beginning with *gaṅge*, *pra*, and *tīrthāni*. Nor is it the case that the rule for the single tone of unaccented syllables is prescribed by relying on the word "from a circumflex" (*svaritāt*).

It should not be argued that this effort is futile because, since a *svarita* vowel would be non-existent (*asiddha*), it would be impossible to rely on the rule "from a *svarita*" (*svaritāt*), and thus the existence of the *svarita* as established (*siddha*) is understood; for where there is no possibility of a *svarita* being non-existent, one may indeed rely on the rule "from a *svarita*" and proceed from there.
Because the sūtra serves its purpose by prescribing a single accent (*ekaśruti*) for the following unaccented vowels;

just as in the example "kāryaṃ devadattayajñadattau," where the word *kāryam* ends in a suffix (*ṇyat*), and by the rule "titsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185), it has a circumflex (*svarita*) at its end. From that...
In the case of two following unaccented [vocatives], such as *devadatta* and *yajñadatta*, there is *ekaśruti*.

Here, because the rule "the *ti* [of a suffix] is circumflex" (*titsvaritam*) belongs to the third section (*tripādī*), there is no possibility of its being considered non-existent (*asiddha*); thus, in this instance—

The purpose of the sūtra is thus established by its prescribing a single uniform tone (*ekaśruti*) for the following *anudātta* syllables based upon the *svarita*. Consequently, in the case of "imaṃ me gaṅge," the aforementioned nine-fold [classification] of the previously mentioned inconsistency is resolved.

The *Bhāṣya* states that the reading [of the sūtra] should be placed immediately after *udāttādanudātasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66). Having thus explained the placement of these nine sūtras in the eighth chapter,
the *Bhāṣya* also provides the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) for this very point right there.

In the *Mahābhāṣya*, it is stated in the passage: "The rule 'anudāttau suppitau' (Pāṇini 3.1.4) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this entire section of sūtras [from 1.1.62 onwards] follows after [the rules concerning] 'deva' and 'brahman'.
By the sūtra "anudāttau suppitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4), [it is established that] the words *deva* and *brahman*, etc., [are followed by suffixes that are *anudātta*].

An *anudātta* is prescribed for the *svarita* occurring within the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*. For example, in the citation "devā brahmāṇa āgacchata," regarding the two words "devāḥ" and "brahmāṇaḥ," [the *anudātta* is applied] by the rule "āmantritasya ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.198).
The first syllable becomes udātta. Then, since the remainder is unaccented (an-udātta), the anudātta is prescribed for that [syllable] by the rule "udātādanudātasya svaritaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.38).
In that context, when the anudātta is to be applied according to the rule "devabrahmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.38),...

Since the circumflex (svarita) accent is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *udāttādanudātasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.66), only the grave (*anudātta*) remains; thus, the prescription of the grave for that [circumflex] again would be purposeless. This purposelessness indicates that the section consisting of nine sūtras following the rule *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* is to be understood as a separate unit.
And according to that principle, by means of the subsequent rule "devabrahmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.38), which belongs to a different section consisting of nine sūtras,
the preceding rule "udāttādanudātasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.66)—
which prescribes the svarita accent— is not rendered non-existent; thus, the mention of the anudātta [in the subsequent rule] is purposeful.
The sūtra *jñāpakaparaḥ* [is] a statement intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Having taken all of this into consideration, he says: "of the *svarita*, etc.
While the term *svaritasya* is being carried over [from a previous rule], this [sūtra] prescribes the *anudātta* for *deva* and *brahman*.
The meaning is that the rule *devabrahmaṇoranudāttaḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned point.

[Jñā.ṭ] The rule *apṛkta ekāl* (Pāṇini 1.2.41)—this mention of the term *eka-* (single) also indicates that when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, it includes the entire class (*jāti*) of that phoneme. [Vi.ṭ]

"‘This also’ (*idamapi*): by the word ‘also’ (*api*), the mention of the term *ekāc* found in the sūtra *nipāta ekāc* (Pāṇini 1.1.14) is included. This has already been explained previously, so it will not be explained here again. [Jñānendrasarasvatī’s commentary: *arthavad adhātuḥ*..."

(Sūtra 1.2.45) || Regarding the term *apratyaya* ("not a suffix"), since it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation), the fact that the accentuation rule *noṅdhātvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.175) prohibits the accent on the suffix *viṅ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that bases ending in *ṅī* and *ṅīp*, etc., possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [Vṛtti: *arthavād dhātur apratyayaḥ...*]

In the rule *prātipadikaṃ*, according to the view that the term *apratyayaḥ* expresses a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—meaning "that which is not a suffix"—the meaning of the sūtra would be: "A word ending in a suffix and a suffix itself do not receive the designation *prātipadika*. Consequently, [the following would apply:]

When *brahmabandhu* + *striyām* [is formed], by the rule *ṛn-nebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *brahmabandhū*. Then, by the rule *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the long vowel of the homogeneous class (*savarṇadīrgha*) is substituted, resulting in *brahmabandhū*. Regarding this single substitute (*ekādeśa*):

Anticipating the objection that, because the suffix *ṅīp* (ṅīṣ) would be treated as if it were subsequent (*paravadbhāva*) due to its being a suffix, the form *brahmabandhū* would end in a suffix and thus lose its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), thereby preventing the derivation of case endings such as *su* (*svādi*), [the author] establishes that a word ending in *ṅīp* possesses the designation of a nominal stem.
He establishes this by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words "of the word *apratyaya*," etc.

The underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: even though a word ending in a *ṅit* suffix is followed by another suffix, it still retains the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In this regard, the indicator is the rule "noṅdātvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.175).

This is a counter-exception (*pratiṣedha*) to the accentuation of the suffix *śas* and others. By that aforementioned rule (*sūtra*), it is established that when *aṇ* is substituted for the root vowel, the suffixes beginning with *śas* following that *aṇ* shall not be acute. The example provided is *brahmabandhvāḥ*.

The prohibition of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) for *śas* and other case-endings following a stem ending in *ṅ*— on the grounds that such a stem would lack the status of a nominal base (*prātipadika*) and thus suffixes like *śas* would be difficult to obtain— serves to indicate, by way of making known the status of the *ṅ*-ending stem as a *prātipadika*, that case-suffixes (*vibhakti*) arise after it. This is the meaning.

In the *Haimaśabdānuśāsana*, however, the formulation of the rule is seen as "svādaya utpadyante ṅyantāt" (*svādi* suffixes arise after a verbal root ending in *ṅ*). The purport of that rule is also precisely the same meaning as stated above,
due to the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the prohibition "na ṅsidbuddhyoḥ" (Sūtra 8.2.8).

The negation "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) by means of the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*) is not an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). In that very same sūtra, in the case of the *prasajyapratiṣedha* view, when *rājan* + *s* is established, after the lengthening of the vowel and the elision of *su* by the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ*, in the form *rājān*, there is the elision of *n*.

By the rule *prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7), the form *rājā* is observed [to be derived] through the elision of the *n*. That would not be possible; for even though the case-ending (*su*) is elided, because it is "ending in a suffix" by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that a grammatical operation applies as if a suffix were present), the technical designation *prātipadika* is excluded by the principle that "that which ends in a suffix is not a *prātipadika*."

Anticipating the objection that there might be a loss of the *nalopa* (elision of the final *n*) due to the absence of the designation "suffix" (*pratyayasaṃjñā*), he resolves the difficulty by stating:

"Not [in the case] of *ṅsi* and *ṅmu*" (*na ṅsiṅmuḍbhyām*). This is because it is established as a principle that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the operation conditioned by a suffix) does not apply when the specific prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) is in force. Thus, there is no fault.

"Because of the restrictive indicator (*jñāpaka*). By the rule *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ*, it is stated that the elision of the *n* should not occur in the dative singular (*ṅi*) or in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). [This is illustrated] in the phrase *parame vyoman*.

In the *Chandas* [Vedic literature], there is the extraction [of forms] such as *udāḥ*. Here, after the elision of *ReĀ*, one might assume the status of being "ending in a suffix" (*pratyayāntatva*) by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule;

however, because of the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) does not apply. Consequently, since the elision of *n* caused by the nominal stem status would not occur, the rule prohibiting the elision of *n*—namely, "na"—[is required].

The rule *ṅsiṃḥcdvddhddhed;uddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138) would otherwise be rendered meaningless. However, it has been established that this rule indicates—by relying on the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix)—that the prohibition *apratyaya* (not being a suffix) does not apply here. Therefore, there is no fault; such is the conclusion. [Jñā.ṭ]
In the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.63),
because of the mention of the term *dvandva*, it is indicated that every *dvandva* compound is optionally singular (*ekavacana*). And thus:

"Tiṣya-punarvasū"—this is what is to be excluded [from the rule]. Alternatively, there is the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) according to the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* ("the genus of non-living things [is singular]"). Here, "possessing breaths" (*prāṇavantaḥ*) does not refer to living beings; rather, it is the vital breaths themselves that are "possessing breaths. [Vi: But surely, in the case of the dual compound of lunar mansions, "tiṣya-punarvasvoḥ"...]
In the sūtra *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.34),
what is the purpose of the phrase *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*? Is it not the case that in its absence,
even the singular (*ekavacana*) would undergo dualization (*dvivacana*), and consequently...
It should not be argued that the form *tiṣyapunarvasu* ending in the singular would not be established;

for when *tiṣya* and *punarvasū* form a *dvandva* compound, a singular ending is difficult to obtain, as there is no possibility of a singular ending taking the place of the dual. Nor [is it the case that] *tiṣyaśca punarvasū*...
It should not be argued that because of the rule for singularization in a *dvandva* compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the singular number is required here since it is a *samāhāra* [of parts];
for the formation of a *dvandva* is prescribed only for parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth. Nor is it the case that...

By the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, it should be stated here that the dvandva compound [of the nakṣatras] undergoes the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*). This is because of the prohibition regarding non-living beings (*aprāṇinām*).
Consequently, since the word *tiṣyapunarvasu* does not exist in its singular form, [the rule does not apply].

Raising the objection that the phrase “of the singular” in the sūtra *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* is redundant because the possibility of a dual number does not arise [in the case of these two stars], [the author] replies: for this very reason, that [phrase] indicates the rule that every dvandva compound is optionally singular. And thus:

In the case of the *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* compound "tiṣyapunarvasū," when the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) applies, the expression "tiṣyapunarvasu" would otherwise take the singular number. To prevent this and ensure the dual number is maintained, the phrase "of the dual number" (*dvivacanasya*) has been stated.
As for the fruit of making this known,
