it is stated in the Bhāṣya that in the case of a *dvandva* compound of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) such as "the Bhābhravas and the Śālaṅkāyanas," the grammatical correctness of the singular ending— as in "Bhābhrava-Śālaṅkāyana"— is established.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting of the mention of the word *bhū* here.
"That which is to be excluded" refers to [the application of] the word *bhū-vacana*.

The meaning is that it is the object to be excluded. In reality, however, since the two stars Tiṣya and Punarvasu are not designated as living beings in common worldly usage, the genus (jāti) based on Tiṣya and Punarvasu is distinct for each Manvantara due to the difference in the constellations.
And because it is stated that [the word] *saṃhitā* denotes a collection (*samūha*), and since it is a class-name for non-living beings,
the rule *jātiraprāṇinām* applies to bring about a singular form; the purpose of this is so that the singular number of *sā* does not become a dual.

It is appropriate to say that "the speech of the *ṛk* and *yajus* is the breath," as stated [by the author] with the words "or rather" (*yathā vā*). The meaning is that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) themselves exist here [in the stars]; because the existence of living beings is dependent upon the *Tiṣya* (Puṣya) and *Punarvasu* constellations, it can somehow be said that *Tiṣya* and *Punarvasu* are the "breaths" (*prāṇa*), but not that they possess "breathing life" (*prāṇitva*).

Consequently, the intention is that the exclusion "not for a person" (*apraṇinām*) does not apply. Regarding the rule *bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.68): since this would already be established by the rule *pumān striyā* (1.2.67), this present sūtra serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the following meaning: "In cases where, beyond the general rule, there is a specific qualification characterized by that [general rule], the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) applies according to the rules beginning with 'the elder over the younger' (*yatrordhvaṃ prakṛtestallakṣaṇo viśeṣastatra vṛddho yūnā*)."

[Objection]: Now, in the section concerning the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among many), since the brother is mentioned with the sister and the son with the daughter, the rule "bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.68)—which has the meaning that "brother and son" are used [as a single term] when [spoken of] with "sister and daughter"—would be redundant.

Anticipating the objection that the purpose [of the present rule] is already served by the sūtra *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), he states its meaningfulness as being intended for a specific technical indication (*jñāpana*): "Only when it is 'the male with the female'. This means that the sūtra *pumān striyā* applies only in those cases where a specific distinction characterized as male or female exists only after the genus (*prakṛti*), and not within the genus itself.

Just as in the case of "ḍhac12;ṃḥdyaṇoddhd;saśca ḍhac12;ṃḥdyaṇoddhd;sī ca," the term "ḍhac12;ṃḥdyaṇoddhd;sa" is common to both instances. Since the distinction occurs only after that [common element], when the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule "pumān striyā" (a male term remains with a female term) applies, the form becomes "ḍhac12;ṃḥdyaṇoddhd;sau."

Therefore, in the case of *haṃsaśca varaṭā ca*, there is no application of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule, because even though they belong to the same genus (*prakṛti*), there is a difference [in gender]. In the case of *bhrātā ca svasā ca* as well, since there is no difference in the genus itself, the rule *pumān striyā* (a male term remains when a female term follows) does not apply; thus, the rule *bhrātṛputrau* is meaningful as it prescribes *ekaśeṣa* in that specific instance. This is the intended meaning.

Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter. [Jñānaṭīkā: *bhūvādayaḥ* (Sūtra 1.3.1). The inclusion of the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) indicates that there is indeed a recension [of roots] external to the Sūtra. [Vivaraṇaṭīkā: Now, one might object: in the Sūtra "roots begin with *bhū*," the inclusion of the word "beginning with" is redundant. Likewise...

If the author of the Sūtras, having recited the roots beginning with *bhū*, were to refer to them by the term "the *bhū*-class" (*bhvādi*), then the Sūtra should have been recited simply as "those [roots] are to be conjugated" (*te dātavyāḥ*).

And even if the author of the Sūtras had not recited "bhūvādayaḥ" (the roots beginning with bhū), one might still object that it would be impossible to refer to them by the expression "bhūvādayaḥ" and so forth; anticipating this doubt, he says: "The mention of 'ādi' (etcetera)."

The intention is that the author of the Sūtras employed the word "ādi" (beginning) in order to indicate that the *dhātupāṭha* exists as an expansion of the Sūtras, so that it may be easily understood that the reference to the roots situated therein is made by means of the term "ādi."

Furthermore, having completed those roots such as *maṅ* and *mad* which are recited in the Sūtras, the author of the Sūtras states, "those are roots" (*te dhātavaḥ*). Consequently, even for forms such as *āṇavayati* that are not recited there, the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) would still apply. Therefore, it should be understood that the expression "bhūvādayaḥ" (beginning with *bhū*) is stated in order to establish the designation "root" only for those [forms] actually seen in the Sūtras, Vārttikas, Bhāṣyas, and the lists of root-groups (*gaṇapāṭha*).

[In the *Jñāpaka-ṭīkā* on *Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.3.4]: "It should be stated that [the rule] does not apply to a *taddhita* suffix. This was rejected because it was understood that even when *tham* is excluded by the letter *u*—which serves to protect the *it*-designation of the *m*—there is an implied prohibition against its application to *taddhita* suffixes. However, now [the suffix] ending in *yā* (*dānīm*) is formed with the letter *y*, which has been elided in the formal statement (*nirdeśa*).

[Objection: But surely, by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*, the designation *it* is prohibited for the dental stops (*tavarga*), *s*, and *m* when they occur in the position of case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Then, from the word *kim*, by the rule *kimo’t* (Pāṇini 5.3.12), the suffix *at* is added. The letter *t* of this suffix receives the designation *it* by the rule *ādirantyena sahetā* (Pāṇini 1.1.71) and is subsequently elided by the rule *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Furthermore, by the rule *kvāti* (Pāṇini 7.2.105), *kim* undergoes the substitution *kvā*. Thus, the form *kva* is established. In that context, because the suffix *at* is a *taddhita* suffix, it is designated as a *vibhakti* (case-ending) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1).

Regarding the sūtra *Pāṇini 1.3.5* (*na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*), one might raise the objection that since the suffix *vi* is designated as a *vibhakti*, the *t* occurring therein would be barred from receiving the *it*-designation by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*. Anticipating this, the author of the Vārttika stated: "It should be specified that [the prohibition applies] when it is not a *taddhita*."

The intention [of the Vārttikakāra] is that since the designation *it* is prescribed for the *tavarga* (the dental stops) and so forth only when they stand in the place of the suffixes of *taddhita*, the *it*-designation indeed applies to the letter *t* situated within a *taddhita* suffix. This Vārttika, however, has been refuted by the Bhāṣyakāra, who established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no exclusion of the *it*-designation for the *tavarga* and so forth when they occur within a *taddhita*.

Regarding the statement, "it should be stated that [the suffix] is not a *taddhita*," this connects with the phrase "and this has been rejected. By the rule "idamasthamuḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.94), the suffix *thamu* is prescribed after the word "idam" in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*). Furthermore, the letter *u* in this suffix is designated as an *it*.

In response to the objection that the inclusion of the vowel *u* here is unnecessary and that the suffix could simply be *tham*, [the author replies: if that were the case, the letter *m* would acquire the technical designation *it* by the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) combined with *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). To prevent this, the vowel *u* has been joined [to the suffix]. Consequently, the resolution must be stated that because *m* is not the final element in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), it does not receive the designation *it*.

However, even though the suffix *tham* is taught with a final *m*, since it receives the designation of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.27), the letter *m* would not be subject to the *it*-designation by the very rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4). Therefore, the pronunciation of the vowel *u* [in *thamu*]—which is performed for the purpose of protecting that *m* from the *it*-designation—is redundant.

Furthermore, that [rule] indicates that the designation *it* (the marker *it*) is not applied to the suffixes *tha*, *thu*, *sa*, and *m*. Consequently, since the letter *m* of the suffix *tham* would otherwise be subject to the *it*-designation, the pronunciation of the vowel *u* is purposeful for the sake of excluding it.

By that very fact, the exclusion of the *it*-designation will not apply even to the suffix *at* when it occurs within a *taddhita* formation; thus, the Vārttika stating "it must be said: 'not when it is a *taddhita*' (*ataddhite*)" is unnecessary—this is the underlying intention.

Now, one might object: since the rule *tu-smābhyām nād* (Pāṇini 1.1.35) does not apply when a taddhita suffix beginning with *vi* or *ḍ* follows, this would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, in the word *idānīm*, the letter *m* at the end of the suffix *dānīm*—which is prescribed by the rule *dānīm ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.18)—would incur the designation *it*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But *dānīm* is made to end in *y*. That is to say, the suffix is indeed *dānīmya*, ending in *y*.

Furthermore, that *ca* [in the sūtra] is not heard because it has been elided by the rule "lopo vyorvali" (Pāṇini 6.1.66), since it takes the form of a *ca* when followed by a *val*. Consequently, since the *m* is not final in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), it does not receive the designation *it*. Nor should it be argued that if the suffix were to end in *y*, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the *y* in forms such as *idānīm*; for the intention is that the *y* is elided by the rule "saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.23), as indicated by the mention of the [suffix] with the *y* already elided.

The elision of *śi* is understood to occur by the rule *lopo vyor vali*. [Jñāpakas: By the rule *tasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.9), and by the indicatory evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *dadātidadhātyorvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.139), there is no non-distinction (*ananubandhakātamasārūpyam*) based on the presence of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). By the indicatory evidence in the rule *śitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55), there is no non-distinction (*ananubandhakātamasārūpyam*) based on having multiple indicatory letters (*anekāltvam*).

Because of the mention of *māṅ* as having undergone the substitution of *ā* in the rule *udīcāṃ māṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.19), the state of being non-anubandha is not intended [for that substitute]. It is more logical that the anubandhas are exclusively single, because they serve as markers (*saṃjñā-kārakatvāt*).

Regarding *anudāttaṅtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12): the optional rule stated in *anupasargādvā* (Pāṇini 1.3.43) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the restriction regarding the affixes (*vikaraṇas*) is stronger [than the general rule]. This is because the application of the restriction occurs even when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa*. This was made clear in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *śadeḥ śitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.60). Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter.

Regarding the rule *vipratiṣedhe* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), the mention of *ūṭh* in the rule *vāha ūṭh* (6.4.132)—namely, that "an external element is as if unestablished"—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). In the word *indra*, there are two vowels. Of these, one is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), and the other is replaced by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). Consequently, *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*).

In this regard, since there is no possibility of the application of *vṛddhi*, the prohibition (*na* in *na samāse*) is redundant; being so, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the operation applies to both the preceding and following words, and that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not *antaraṅga*. This is because the mention of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49)—which follows the rule *pratyayavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.4.13)—is an indicator for the rule *gatikārakapūrvasyāpi* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.2.49).

*Su-pitiṅ-antam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14): This inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in") in this rule is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the principle that "when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*), that which ends with it is not included. [Note: All these rules, being of the nature of paribhāṣās, have been explained in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*; therefore, they are not explained here.]
We do not know how it came about that certain such [corruptions] have also been included in this collection of indicators (*jñāpaka*).

The statement "the word *dhava* denotes a class" (*jātiśabda*)—as indicated by the sūtra 1.4.21—is an indicator that the term *jātiśabda* refers to a word denoting a genus (*nānādravyavācin*), and not to a word denoting magnitude (*vaipulyavācin*).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, by the rule *dvitve'rthe dvivacanam*, the dual suffix is prescribed when the meaning is duality. In that context, duality is of two kinds: extension (*vaipulya*) and a specific number (*saṃkhyāviśeṣa*).

In that case, because there is no specific indicator (*viśeṣa-darśana*), the dual number would apply to both meanings. Consequently, one might object that in the expression *bahu-rodana* ("much weeping"), since "abundance" (*vaipulya*) is intended by the context (*prakaraṇa*), the dual number would follow;
anticipating this objection, he says: "the designation of the dual number."

Since the genus *bhūtatva* (the state of being an element) is one, and since it ought to be indicated by the singular form "element" (*bhūta*), the use of the plural expression "elements" (*bhūtāni*) indicates that which denotes multiple substances.

The term *bhūmikrama* mentioned here is the same as that introduced in the phrase "the sequence of the stages" (*bhūmikrama*); it does not refer to the term *bhūmikrama* used in the sense of "vastness."

This is the intended meaning: although the number "two" is one, because the substratum of the number "two" is itself dual, the duality residing in that substratum is superimposed upon the number "two," and thus it is said to be "two."

The dual number is prescribed [for the word *śrotra*]. Consequently, the meaning of the sūtra results as follows: the dual number applies to that quality of hearing (*śrotṛtva*) which has as its substratum that which possesses hearing.

Since the basis for the vastness (*vaipulya*) that consists of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is one, there is no mention of "vastness" with respect to that vastness which is of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and rests upon that single basis.

Since the substratum of the number-form "duality" (*dvitva*) is manifold, the term "duality" applies specifically to that which possesses the form of duality. In this regard, regarding these suffixal rules (*pratyayaniyama*), since indeclinables (*avyaya*) do not attain the status of being words (*pada*), a restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*) must be stated. Alternatively, the restriction of the suffix may depend upon the intended meaning (*prakṛtārtha*).

In rules such as *dvivacanaikavacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.22), *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21), and so forth, the status of being restrictive (*niyamārthatva*) is accepted. And restriction (*niyama*) is of two kinds: restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*) and restriction regarding the meaning (*arthaniyama*).

The restriction regarding the suffixes is as follows: the singular suffix occurs only when there is one [object], the dual suffix only when there are two, and the plural suffix only when there are many. Furthermore, the restriction regarding the meaning is as follows: the singular suffix occurs only for one, the dual suffix only for two, and the plural suffix only for many.

In that case, if the suffix were applied immediately after the base, indeclinables such as *uccais* and *nīcais* would not obtain the designation of "word" (*pada*), because they would not end in a consonant (*hal*). Furthermore, [the suffix] is a suffix (*pratyaya*).

If [the suffixes] were restricted to a specific number, then because these indeclinables (*avyaya*) are devoid of number, the designation *pada*—which is conditioned by being a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*)—would not apply. And in the absence of *padatva*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r* for *s*) and so forth. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that precisely because of this impossibility, one must abandon the restriction on the suffixes and instead adopt a restriction based on meaning (*arthaniyama*). Regarding those [indeclinables]: In those cases...

Thus [it is said]. In these cases, such as the singular number and so forth, there is no fault even under the view that the rule concerns the suffix (*pratyayaniyamapakṣa*). The restriction is made without regard for the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); and singularity and the rest are indeed the meanings of the base.

Consequently, by the restrictive rule that the singular number applies only to a single entity (*ekasminnevaikavacanam*), the application of the singular number is excluded from duality and plurality—which, as numbers, belong to the same genus as unity—only to that extent. However, the singular number is not thereby excluded from the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) when it is devoid of number (*niḥsaṃkhya*), such as in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Therefore, with the intention that even for indeclinables (*avyaya*) their status as words (*padatva*) is not contradicted because they are established as being capable of having case-endings (*svādya*), he says: "or depending on the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtārthāpekṣo vā*). He recites the *Vārttika* which establishes the two previously mentioned rules: "The meanings of the case-endings (*sup*) are the object (*karman*) and so forth, as well as number (*saṃkhyā*); likewise for the verbal endings (*tiṅ*). Therein, the restriction is well-known; or rather, the restriction applies to the bases (*prakṛti*). [Viṭṭhala: Regarding the phrase "therein, the restriction": *Note: The original text contains various non-standard characters (ḍddhdhḍaddh, ḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd, TktgrRN, tsdvdr1) which appear to be transcription artifacts or specific encoding markers. They have been omitted from the translation.*

The meaning is that there is a restriction regarding the object (*arthaniyama*). Alternatively, the restriction concerns the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*). Regarding the former, because of the *jñāpaka* rule "avyayādāpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82), the case-endings (*sup*) are elided after indeclinables (*avyaya*). According to another view stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "taddhitaśca" (Pāṇini 1.1.31), the singular number is the general rule (*autsargika*) for indeclinables.

[Objection: Let it be that the lack of restriction regarding case endings depends upon the general sense—that the singular number applies only to oneness (*ekatva*) and not to any other meaning whatsoever. Even so, the production of case endings (*svādi*) after indeclinables (*avyaya*) is established by means of an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark); thus he says: "In that context, the meaning" (*tatrārthe*). This means that even under the view that the singular number and so forth apply only to meanings such as oneness (*ekatva*), etc.

If, by the rule of conditionality (*pratyayaniyama*), the case endings (*sup*) were excluded from indeclinables (*avyaya*) because they are numberless (*niḥsaṃkhya*), then, since no case endings would arise after indeclinables, the prescription of their elision (*luk*) in the rule *avyādāpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82) would be purposeless. Yet that [prescription] was indeed made; it therefore indicates that case endings do arise after indeclinables.

Therefore, the objection that the status of being a *pada* (word) is untenable is refuted; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the rule "from indeclinables (*avyaya*), [the case endings] *sup* [are produced]," the term "*sup*" refers to the nominative plural. The phrase "they are produced" (*utpadyante*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. In reality, however, not all case endings are produced from indeclinables, but rather only the singular; thus it says, "from indeclinables."

In the commentary on the sūtra *taddhitaś-cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, after stating the arrangement of the sūtras as *dv-ekayor dvivacanaikavacane* and *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, [it says]: "The singular number (*ekavacanam*) [is used] for one, the dual number (*dvivacanam*) for two, and the plural number (*bahuvacanam*) for many."

Having adopted the arrangement of the sūtra as "ekavacanam," it is stated that the singular number is the general rule (*utsarga*), while the dual and plural numbers apply when there are two or many objects, respectively, acting as exceptions (*bādhaka*).

Consequently, by the general rule "the singular number," the singular is prescribed in the absence of duality and plurality. Therefore, since indeclinables (*avyaya*) lack number and thus lack both duality and plurality, only the singular number as stated in the general sūtra will apply to them; this is the established conclusion.

Is it by the general rule that the singular number of the first case (*prathamā*) alone occurs, or is it rather that the singular number of every case occurs? This is another point. The rule *adhi-parī anarthakau* (Pāṇini 1.4.93) indicates that even particles (*nipāta*) which are devoid of meaning are treated as having meaning. This is intended to establish the designation *karmapravacanīya* for those [particles] by setting aside the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*.

Alternatively, since they do not possess a distinct meaning, the verbal root expresses the action (*kriyā*) denoted by itself. The rule stating that "those whose meaning has already been expressed may also be used" serves as an indicator of this fact. [Vi.Ṭ: Now, one might object: "By the sūtra *adhiparī anarthakau*, the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the particles *adhi* and *pari* when they are meaningless. It cannot be argued that this prescription is intended to prevent the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*, because [the definition of those terms] requires connection with an action (*kriyā-yoga*)."

The designations *gati* and *upasarga* are prescribed [by Pāṇini]. One might raise the objection that these two designations would not apply to particles (*anarthaka*) because they lack connection with an action, since their meaning consists merely in being connected with a verbal root. Anticipating this, the author maintains the utility of the rule by stating that it serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory proof): "This indicates" means that it is indicated that even for meaningless particles such as *āṅ*, *pari*, and so on, whatever grammatical operation applies to a meaningful word also applies to them.

The designations *gati* and *upasarga* apply to meaningful items when they are joined with a verbal action. Since these two designations would otherwise also apply to the meaningless *adhi* and *pari*, the rule for the designation *karmapravacanīya* is established to prevent that. The result of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is that the statement made in the *arthavat-sūtra*—"the designation *prātipadika* must be stated even for a meaningless particle"—is not necessary. In reality, however, even *adhi* and *pari* are not meaningless.

The view is that "all prefixes (upasargas) are illuminators of the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). In this regard, other prefixes illuminate the qualifiers residing within the action denoted by the verbal root. However, *adhi* and *pari* illuminate the action expressed by the verbal root itself, but not the qualifiers residing therein. This was stated in the rule *anarthakāḥ* precisely because of this [distinction]. Thus, the "connection with action" (*kriyāyoga*) consists solely in being an illuminator of the action.

Since the terms *adhi* and *pari* also possess the sense of "existence" (*sadbhāva*), they would have attained the designation of *gati* and the designation of *upasarga*; therefore, by means of this [rule], the designation of *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed to set aside those [other designations]. Thus, the sūtra is not purposeless. For this very reason, it is also not the case that it serves as a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) for the aforementioned statement. With this intention, he says: "Or rather, because there is no other meaning."

The meaning is that there is no expressed meaning (dyotya-artha) consisting of a specific quality belonging to that [action] which is distinct from the action denoted by the verbal root (dhātu). Regarding the word "indicator" (dyotaka): the meaning is "that which indicates. Now, if *adhi* and *pari* are indicators of the very same meaning already expressed by the verbal root, then their employment would be redundant, according to the maxim that "those whose meaning has already been stated are not employed. To this, he says: "even though their meaning has been stated."

The intention is that this very point makes it known that there is usage even of words whose meaning has already been expressed. Just as in the case of "Bring the two Brāhmaṇas," where duality is already understood by the dual ending itself, the repetition is used for the sake of even clearer comprehension, so too such repetition is not contradictory; this is what the rule "adhi-parī anarthakau" (Pāṇini 1.4.93) indicates. [Jñā.ṭ] "laḥ parasmaipadam" (Sūtra 1.4.99).

The mention of *parasmaipada* in the rule for the *sic* suffix when there is strengthening (*vṛddhi*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation *puruṣa* does not supersede the designation *parasmaipada*. [Objection: But surely, in the rule "laḥ parasmaipadam" (*Pāṇini* 1.4.99), the mention of *parasmaipada* need not be made; rather, the mention of *parasmaipada* should be made right there in the section on "laḥ" (*Pāṇini* 3.4.77).

In the first chapter, within the section prescribing the technical name *parasmaipada*, because there is a governing rule for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the suffixes *ti, tas, jhi*, etc., are assigned both the designation of *puruṣa* (person) and the designation of *parasmaipada*. One might suspect that the latter, being posterior, would sublate the designation of *parasmaipada*; however, fearing that the prescription of the *parasmaipada* designation would then find no scope of application (*sāvakāśa*) in the case of the *śatṛ* and *kvasu* suffixes, [the author] says: "In the case of *sic*, there is vṛddhi."

If, by the designation *puruṣa*, the designation *parasmaipada* were to apply to *tiṅ* and so forth, then the mention of *tiṅ* and so forth by the term *parasmaipada* in the rule "There is vṛddhi for *sic* before *parasmaipada*s" (Pāṇini 7.2.1) would be inconsistent.

Therefore, the intention is that the designation *parasmaipada* is not superseded by the designation *puruṣa*; this is what is being made known (*jñāpyate*). [Jñā.ṭ] And regarding the rule *vi-bhak-tiś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104): when the phrase "three each" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) is supplied as an ellipsis, the designation applies by virtue of the statement beginning with "*aṣṭana ā*" (Pāṇini 7.2.84).

In the case of its replacement by *naḥ*, because the rule "tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi" (Pāṇini 7.1.28) prescribes the substitution of *na* for *śas*, and because it says "of the first two [cases]" (*prathamayoḥ*) when it could have simply said "of *au* and *jas*" (*auṭ-jasoḥ*), it is made known that the mention of the "triple" (*trikagrahaṇa*) applies to the prescription of the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, in the rule *vi-bhak-tiś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104), does the phrase *trīṇi trīṇi* ("three by three") carry over from the rule *tiṅ-strīṇi-trīṇi* (Pāṇini 1.4.100), or not? If it does carry over, then the designation *vibhakti* would apply only to a group of three, not to a single one; and that being the case, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the word *arvan* would not occur when followed by each individual case-ending beginning with *jas*.

By the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for *aṣṭan* when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). However, there is no difficulty [in this rule] because there is no triad [of case-endings] following the word *aṣṭan* simultaneously. If the phrase "three by three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) were not carried over [from the previous rule], then each of the case-endings beginning with *sva* would individually receive the designation "case-ending," and consequently, the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* would be established even when followed by each individual ending.

Nevertheless, regarding the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), since the term "first two" (*prathamayoḥ*) refers to the case-endings (*vibhaktyoḥ*), it denotes the collective pair of case-suffixes named "first. Consequently, there are two possible positions: either the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one) would occur only when followed by *su* and *au*—by virtue of the continued application of the condition *aci* (before a vowel)—and not when followed by *jas* and so on; or [it would occur] only when *au* and *jas* follow. Thus, both these positions remain possible.

Anticipating this objection, he provides the following solution: "In the case of *anuvaḥ* [in the rule] *trīṇi trīṇi*... Even though, according to the view that it is a collective (*samudāya*), the designation *vibhakti* (case-ending) belongs only to the aggregate consisting of three, because the three cannot be used simultaneously, the force of the explicit statement of the *ātva* (substitution of *ā*) implies that the term *vibhakti* applies to each individual part of the aggregate. Thus, since the rule for *ātva* is prescribed when a constituent part of the aggregate follows, it applies to each single one.

There is no fault [in our position], because the substitution of *ā* is established even from the subsequent rule (*parataḥ*). [The word] "becomes" (*bhavati*) is understood; the sense is that the substitution of *ā* occurs for the base ending in *aṣṭan*. Regarding the phrase "three each" (*trīṇi trīṇi*), in the view where it is not understood as a recurring term (*anuvartate*), although the designation of "case-number" (*vibhakti-saṃjñā*) applies to each individual [word], he demonstrates in the commentary on that [sūtra]—namely, "In the mention of those two"—that in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, only the first two triads [of case-endings] are intended, and not the two suffixes (*pratyaya*).

The phrase "three, three" means that there are no subsequent vowels [to follow]. According to the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi*, the word *śas* refers back to the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the lengthening of the preceding vowel to match its class), and it prescribes the substitution of *na* for the letter *s* which is a constituent part of the suffix *śas* following that [long vowel].

In this context, if the word *tasmāt* were not included [in the rule], then in the derivation of *etān gāḥ paśya*, where *go + aśas* is established, the rule *āṬtaḥ amśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.93) would cause the single substitution of *ā* for both the *o* and the *a*. At the stage *gās*, the letter *s* would also undergo the change to *ṇ*. To prevent this, the word *tasmāt* is stated. Since the *ā* in *gās* is not a long vowel resulting from the substitution of a homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the letter *s* does not follow a homogeneous long vowel, and therefore the change to *ṇ* does not occur.

Furthermore, if [the rule] *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* were intended to mean that the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitution occurs only after the two first case-endings, namely *āṬ* and *jas*, then what would be the purpose of the rule *tasmād*? By its being formulated, it indicates that by the rule *prathamayoḥ*, only the two sets of three case-endings (*tri-ka*) are understood. Therefore, since the *pūrvasavarṇa* long vowel is established for *am* and *śas* as well, there is no defect whatsoever.

Alternatively, if the substitution of the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* for *au* and *as* were already observed [elsewhere], one would have formulated the rule simply as "āṬjasoḥ pūrvasavarṇa. Thus, the intention is that this [rule] indicates that the mention of *au* and *as* applies only to the first two triplets (the nominative and accusative). By the word "ca" in the expression "ityuktyā ca," the prescription of *natva* is conjoined. Thus ends the first chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.
The rule *pāre-madhye ’ḍ-dvitīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.18), with the inclusion of the word *vā*,
indicates that the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of compounds and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) is optional (*vikalpa*). This means that their formation may or may not take place.

Regarding the statement "the exception is permanent": when this [rule] is applied, by one application there is the exclusion of the first vowel (*vṛtti*), and by the other application there is the exclusion of the second vowel; thus, the exception is considered non-permanent. [Vi.Ṭ: But surely, in the case of "pāre-madhya-"]...

In the rule *ṣaṣṭhī vā*, the mention of the word *vā* (“or”) is purposeless. Nor should it be argued that its purpose is to prescribe the compound optionally, so that in the alternative where the compound does not occur, the sentence *pāraṃ gaṅgāyāḥ* would also be considered grammatically correct.

Since the option is established by the very fact that the *mahābhāṣya* is authoritative, even though the sentence would be grammatically correct (*sādhu*) under the alternative view that this compound does not exist according to the *mahābhāṣya*,
[the rule] "ṣaṣṭhī" [is stated].
Since the correctness of a genitive tatpuruṣa compound is not desired [in this context],
the compound *gaṅgāpāram* would otherwise lack grammatical validity; therefore,
this is for the purpose of demonstrating the correctness of the genitive compound.
It should not be said that [the compound] is *vāgraḥ*. For in the rule for the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound,
specifically in the sūtra "pāre-madhye," the elision (*lopa*) of the case-ending is applied by way of the subsequent mention (*anuvṛtti*) of both [terms].

Even for the compound *pāremadhya*— which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*— there is an option (*vikalpena*) because the section governing the formation of *avyayībhāva* compounds applies here as well.
The term *bādhakatva* (sublating force) [is used] because, in the absence of this [sublation], there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*);
since that too is optional, in its absence the sentence remains grammatically correct (*sādhutva*), and thus the desired result is established. Therefore, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed.

Anticipating the objection that [the word] is redundant, he establishes its purposefulness by way of indicating a specific qualification of the statement— namely, "or this. According to the manner previously stated, being redundant, the mention of "or" (*vā*) indicates as follows:

The compound is optional. In that regard, if there is any exception (*apavāda*), it is always an exception to the general compound (*utsarga-samāsa*). Therefore, in the rule concerning the exception...

Even in the view that accepts the validity of the sentence [as a whole] through the *anuvṛtti* of the word *mahat*, it is only the correctness of the sentence that is admitted, and not that of the *utsarga-samāsa*. And thus,
even when the mention of the word *vāk* is absent in the present context...

Even when the suffix *ṅasi* (genitive singular) is present, this [suffix] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). In the alternative where this [suffix] is not applied, only the syntactic well-formedness (*vākya-sādhutva*) would be obtained, and not the genitive compound. For that purpose...
The mention of "option" (*vāgrahaṇa*): when that [option] exists, the ungrammaticality of the sentence arises through the force of the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*);
furthermore, by the mention of "option," the general rule (*utsarga*) is also permitted in certain cases.

Thus, the correctness of all three— the compound with the word *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive), the compound with the word *saptamī* (locative), and the *avyayībhāva* compound— is established. And so, in this manner,
within the section governing the *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there occurs an apavāda-sūtra (an exception rule).

It should be noted that if there were no sublation (*bādha*) by a specific rule (*apavāda*), then because the general rule (*utsarga*) would be eternally uncontradicted, the conclusion would follow that the scriptural injunction of the general rule (*utsarga-śāstra*) is not intended to apply; this is how it must be understood here.

It should be understood that the purpose of this [rule] is to indicate that even though the *bhūta* suffix is optional, it nevertheless permits the grammatical correctness of the sentence in its alternative form, and thus does not permit the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound). This is because, when this [suffix] is employed, [the compound is formed].
The meaning is that [the compound] is prohibited when *vā* is uttered.

And thus, because there exist two words expressing an alternative (*vikalpa*)—namely *vā* and *iti*—in that case, the compound is prescribed by one of them, namely *vā*. Consequently, it is understood that even a sentence is correct in one alternative (*pakṣe*).

Furthermore, an exception (*apavāda*) is stated by means of an alternative (*vikalpa*); by that, even the general rule (*utsarga*) becomes as if suspended—this is the meaning. [Jñānaśrīmitra’s Ṭīkā on Pāṇini 2.1.36: "The fourth case ending is used in the sense of 'for that purpose' (*tadartha*)," according to Pāṇini 6.2.43.
The *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of the first member [of a compound] is indeed a *prakṛtivikṛtibhāva* (an original state that has undergone modification),

as indicated by the inclusion of the term "in the sense of" (*arthe*) in sūtra 6.2.44 and "and after a word ending in *kta*" (*kte ca*) in sūtra 6.2.45. Likewise, this is known from the mention of "one whose happiness has departed" (*hṛtasukha*).

The compound *tadartha* is formed precisely by means of the dative case used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). [Vijayīndra: Now, according to the rule *caturthī tadartha* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), a word ending in the dative case expressing a modification (*vikṛti*) is compounded with a word expressing the material cause (*prakṛti*).

It must be stated that a compound is prescribed [only] with that which ends in *su*-affixes; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of forming a *tādarthya* (purpose) compound even in cases such as *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking"). And in this way, compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder") are not established, because [the word] *aśva* and *ghāsa* [would not form a compound].

The modification [of the word *aśva*] is due to the presence of the state of being a modification of the original form. Furthermore, the compound *aśvaghāsaḥ* (horse fodder) does not take the form of a compound ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which expresses a relationship consisting of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*).
It should not be argued that there is no fault even in the absence of a *caturthī* compound in cases such as *aśvaghāsādi*,
because [in the case of a *caturthī* compound] it would be formed by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36).

In the case of the *pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara* (the accent of the original form of the first member), there is a difference in accentuation between the two options: the *caturthīsamāsa* (dative compound) follows the rule of the *prakṛtisvara*, whereas under the option of the *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound), the rule "samāsasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.223) applies, resulting in an *antodātta* (acute on the final syllable) accent for the compound.
Thus, due to this difference in accent, the grammatical effect of the *caturthīsamāsa* is accomplished by means of the *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*.

Anticipating the objection that this is impossible to state, [the author] replies: even the accentuation of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies only in cases where there is an actual modification of the original form (*prakṛtivikṛtibhāva*). Thus, even in the case of the compound *aśvayaghasaḥ*, the final syllable of the compound remains accented high (*samāsāntodātta*) according to the rules of accent.

Considering the resolution that, due to the absence of a distinction [between types of compounds], words such as *aśvaghāsa* are correct only as *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compounds, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first member, which is prescribed by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36),
is also [to be understood in this way].

The proof that this occurs only in cases where there is an increase or decrease in the original substance is indicated by the rule "caturthī tadarthe" (Pāṇini 2.1.36). The underlying intention is as follows:
if [the compound] were not governed by the rule "caturthī tadarthe," which prescribes...

If the *prakṛtisvara* (original accentuation) of the first member were to occur even in cases where there is no *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of modification), then the two rules— "in the sense of [a word]" (*arthe*, Pāṇini 6.2.44) and "and when a *kta*-suffix follows" (*kte ca*, Pāṇini 6.2.45)— would be rendered useless.

In examples such as *devatārtham*, when a word ending in the dative case— such as *devakata*— is followed by the word *artha*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the preceding member is prescribed by the rule *arthe*.
Similarly, in examples such as *goḥḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;tam*, when a word ending in the dative case follows a word ending in the suffix *-kta*, [the same accentuation applies].
The *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) is prescribed by the rule "kte ca.
In that regard, since the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) would be established in both cases by the very rule "caturthī tadarthe," a further prescription should not have been made.

Furthermore, the accentuation prescribed by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.3.13) indicates that the relationship of *prakṛti-vikṛti* (material cause and product) exists only in cases such as the offering of a cow for the sake of a deity (*devatārtha*). Therefore, in instances such as *gohitaṃ* ("beneficial to the cow"), [the rule does not apply].
Since the accentuation would not otherwise be obtained due to the absence of the conditions for *prakṛtisvara* and *vikārasvara*,

two rules— "in the sense of [a purpose]" (*arthe*) and "after [a word ending in] *kta*" (*akte ca*)— are provided to ensure its attainment. Thus, the meaning of this section is that by means of these rules, the accentuation and other properties of compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* are established even though they are *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*s (genitive compounds).

In order to reject the *vārttika* which states, "it should be stated that [the word] *artha* always forms a compound," the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) was made in the *Mahābhāṣya*. There are two rules: one is "caturthī" (Pāṇini 2.1.36), and the other is "tadarthārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.37). Regarding these:

The meaning of the sūtra *caturthī* is that a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthyanta*) is compounded with a word ending in *su* (the nominative singular suffix). And the meaning of *tadarthārtha* is that the word *artha* is substituted for the final member (*uttarapada*) which has that [fourth-case word] as its purpose. Consequently, [the compound] *brāhmaṇāya payaḥ* [is formed].

When the compound is formed as *paya-*, the subsequent use of the word *payaḥ* again is for the purpose of indicating that the word *payaḥ* is the substitute [for the final element of the compound]; this is the resulting meaning. If, however, the rule (*yoga*) is divided in this way, then [the result is] *chātrāya*.
Regarding the doubt that even here in the word *rucitam*, there might be a substitution of the word *artha* for the word *rucita*, the commentators have stated:
"The teacher [Pāṇini] indicates [this rule]: 'A dative case ending used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that) is compounded, but not [when it denotes the recipient of a gift]."

Since the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣv anudātto ṅc ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.103) is established by the alternative formulation (*nyāsa*) *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣv ṛdittvapi ca liṅ*, it indicates that augments (*āgama*) are *anudātta*. It has been stated that this very point also serves as an indicator for the meaning that augments are to be treated as if they were non-existent (*avidyamānavat*).

This pair [of arguments] is also the statement of a partisan (ekadeśin). [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāradīpikā: Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "udātta" (high-pitched) in the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅcci*? For by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*), the suffix already possesses an acute accent.
Since the acute accent (*udātta*) of *yāsuṭ* would also be established [by that rule], and since the substitutes for *liṅ*, namely *tip*, *sip*, and *mip*,
are unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule "suppitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4), it follows that *yāsuṭ*, being a part of them, would also be unaccented.

It must be stated that the word *udātta* is mentioned for the purpose of establishing that [the augment] is high-pitched (*udātta*) when it occurs. If that were the case, the sūtra would have been formulated simply as "yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu picca liṅ";
for in that formulation, by the rule "apicca liṅ," the property of being *pit* would be extended (*atideśa*) to all substitutes of *liṅ*.

Anticipating the objection that since *pit* (the *p*-marker) does not apply, the *anudātta* (unaccented) status is not established and the accentuation as *udātta* (acute) by the rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*) would alone prevail—
rendering the mention of *udātta* redundant— the author states "yāsuṭ" to show its purposefulness as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the rule "augments are unaccented" (*āgamā anudātāḥ*). Likewise...

The intention is that because the *āgama*s (augmental suffixes) are unaccented (*anudātta*), it was stated that the *yāsuṭ* [augment] must also be accented (*udātta*) so that it does not incur the same status of being unaccented. Regarding the phrase "this very [rule]," etc., it means that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) has been stated; the words "in the rule 'the first syllable is accented' (Pāṇini 3.2.3)" are to be supplied.

Since *yāsuṭ* is itself a suffix (*pratyaya*), its acute accent (*udātta*) would already be established by the rule that a suffix is acutely accented on its first syllable; therefore, the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is acutely accented serves as an indicator of the meaning: "augmentations (*āgama*s) are as if non-existent. And when they are non-existent—
It has been established therein that when the suffix itself is acute by virtue of being the first member of a compound,
the unaccented nature of the augments is secured through the non-acute (anudātta) status of the *śi* ending.
And so it is said:

The intention [of the author] is that the mention of "udātta" (acute accent) serves its purpose for the sake of excluding the *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent that would otherwise result from the application of the rule *śeṣanighāta*. [Objection: But surely, since the *yāsuṭ* augment is conditioned by the *parasmaipada* (active voice), it should apply after the substitution of the *l*-suffixes have taken place.

Since the accent of the affix would have been acute either by its being *antaraṅga* (more internal) or by its being *para* (subsequent), the *yāsuṭ* would consequently be either unaccented or, due to the non-acute nature of the *śi*, anudātta (grave). How, then, is it that the explicit mention of "acute" (*udātta*), which is made for the purpose of establishing an acute accent, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?
Anticipating this very objection, he states that this is the assertion of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*), saying: "Both of these... [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.8:

*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*]. This is because the rule [Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.37: *aśvāghasyāt*] prescribes the vowel *ā* for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ī* in the *kyac* suffix; this serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark).

Regarding the rule *aghaśaṃsadviddhaddhed;dāc chandasi parecchāyāṃ kyac*: [Objection] But surely, in the sūtra *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the word *ātmanaḥ* is connected with *supaḥ*; and consequently, from that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) and expresses the desire for oneself— [The following text follows: ...from that [suffixal element], [the affix *kyac* is applied]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a grammatical commentary on Pāṇinian rules concerning the application of the affix *kyac* in Vedic literature.)

The meaning of the sūtra is understood as follows: the suffix *kyac* occurs when there is a desire for an object. This being the case, in the Vedic passage "mā tvā vṛkā agāyavaḥ," the suffix *kyac* would not apply to the word *agha* in the sense of "desiring harm" (*aghamicchanti*), because the suffix *vaḥ* (the desiderative marker) has already occurred.

One desires the destruction of one’s own sin, but not the sin of another. Thus, raising the objection as to how the *kyac* suffix can be applied here—since the word *agha* (sin) does not possess the capacity to cause the blindness of others—the author replies: "In the Veda (*chandasi*), [the suffix] occurs even when the desire for the blindness of another is intended. The authority for this is the rule: "After *aśva* and *agha*, [the suffix *kyac* is applied] in the sense of *āt* (desire)."

And regarding that sūtra, the meaning is that when the affix *kyac* follows the words *aśva* and *agha*, the substitution of the vowel *ā* occurs [for the final letter]. In this context, the affix *kyac* is applied to the word *agha* only when there is a desire for another (*parēcchā*). For in the world, no one would desire evil (*agha*) for themselves; rather, one desires evil for another. Thus, by prescribing the substitution of *ā* for the word *agha* when *kyac* follows, Pāṇini implies his approval of the application of *kyac* after the word *agha*.

Therefore, from this *jñāpaka*—namely, the rule *aghaśaṃsaduhāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.148)—it is established that the suffix *kyac* occurs even in the sense of "one who desires the removal of sin" (*agham icchati*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*); such is the intention. Regarding the rule *namovarivaścitraṅaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.19): those words ending in *kyac* and other such suffixes denote an action (*kriyā*). This is because of the *jñāpaka* provided by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), which prescribes the technical designation of "root" (*dhātu*) for those ending in *san* and others. The purpose of this is that the suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and so forth, apply to them. Furthermore, these suffixes like *tavyat* apply to the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment). And the *sādhana* belongs to the action alone.

Even the *bhāva* (the abstract action) is indeed a *kriyā* (action). However, in the case of an external instrument (*parasādhana*), there is no arising of *naiḥśreyasa* (ultimate liberation), because an instrument is necessarily accompanied by an agent. This is because a suffix arises only for that specific verbal root (*dhātu*) which possesses that particular instrument. Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* stated in the rule *vi-ṣṭhā-śabdā-karma-piba-māna-vad-vas-tṛp-añc-ut-ruha-jīry-ati-śada-sado-ḍhā-ka-raṇa-mi-man-i-ṇi-śran-tha-granth-ā-cari-x-mā-bhū-sthā-āv-asa-ha-krama-ga-ma-jan-dhā-ṛd-ji-riṣaḥ kyac*: "In the case of suffixes such as *kyac*, there is a specification of the meaning of the suffix."

And this is its meaning: from the root *namas* (to bow), the suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of worship (*pūjā*); from the root *varivas*, it is applied in the sense of service (*saparyā*); and from the root *citraṅ*, it is applied in the sense of wonder (*āścarya*). Thus, even in the sense of the *kyac* suffix, [the verbal activity] should be understood as "it exists" (*bhavati*). Otherwise, that which ends in *kyac* would not be expressive of an action (*kriyāvācakatva*).

Having refuted this *Vārttika*, the venerable Bhartṛhari has established that forms ending in *kyac* and other affixes denote action by means of an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*). He states: "those ending in *kyac* and others. By the word "others" (*ādi*), the affix *ṇiṅ* is included. By the rule "Those ending in *san* and others are verbal roots" (*Pāṇini* 3.1.32), the technical designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is prescribed for forms ending in *kyac* and others.

And the purpose of that [rule] "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is to establish the formation of *tavyat* and other suffixes, which are prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.96] as being added after a root. Furthermore, *tavyat* and the others are prescribed when there is a means (*sādhana*) consisting of an object (*karman*) or other factors. And a means belongs to an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, if that which ends in *kyac* and so forth were not expressive of an action, then—due to the absence of an action expressed by it—the suffixes *tavyat* and the rest, which are prescribed for the means of an action, would not apply to words ending in *kyac* and so forth.

Consequently, the prescription of the technical term *dhātu* (verbal root) for [words ending in] suffixes such as *tavyat* would be purposeless. Since the designation *dhātu* has been stated, it follows that words ending in *kyac* and other such suffixes are understood to denote action (*kriyā*); this is the underlying intention (*bhāva*). Now, one might object: "How can it be said that *tavyat* and the others [denote] the means (*sādhana*)? For by the rule "The suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* occur only after those two [roots and nouns]" (Pāṇini 3.4.70), *tavyat* and the others are prescribed even in the sense of *bhāva*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Let it be so."

Nevertheless, since suffixes such as *tavya* and others occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*)—that is, after that which signifies existence—and because a word ending in *kyac* and so forth has as its primary referent the action (*kriyā*) expressed by it, the absence of such suffixes as *tavya* even when there is existence after a word ending in *kyac* etc. makes it difficult [to derive them]. Thus, the prescription of *tavya* and other suffixes after a root, as well as the prescription of the technical designation "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) for that which results in those fruits, necessarily implies that a word ending in *kyac* and so forth is expressive of an action.

The resolution [of this objection] is as follows: even *bhāva* (the state of being) is indeed an action (*kriyā*). Now, one might object: although forms ending in *kyac* and other affixes lack the denotation of an action, they denote a substance (*dravya*) by virtue of being *svārthika* (retaining their original meaning). Furthermore, the result of the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is the derivation of suffixes such as *tavyat*, which denote the action and its factors (*kāraka*) expressed by another word—as in "look at the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśya*), where the word "tree," though denoting a substance, is intended as the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing.

Anticipating the second objection, he says: "But in the case of *parasādhane*. Since the word *sādhana* (means/agent) is relative, when there arises an expectancy as to "in whose accomplishment [is the suffix used]," it is understood that the suffix is applied to that verbal root whose meaning has that particular agent as its means of accomplishment.

Just as when it is said, "one should behave toward one's mother," and upon the doubt arising as to whose mother, it is understood to be "one's own mother," so too, because the second case endings and others are prescribed after a nominal stem (*pratipadika*), and because the nominal stem denotes a substance (*dravya*), their production occurs for the sake of another [the action] by virtue of the authority of the grammatical rule.

The suffixes beginning with *tavyat*, however, which denote action, find their scope within other verbal roots (*dhātu*) for the sake of their own derivation; they do not arise after those ending in *kyac* and the like, which have another as their means of derivation. Thus, the very prescription of the technical term "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) for these words ending in *kyac* and so forth—which results in the application of suffixes such as *tavyat* when expressing their own derivation—is the proof that they denote action; this is the intended meaning. [Pāṇini 3.2.21: *muṇḍamiśra*...]

Because of the rule prescribing the substitution of *ḍha* for *la* and *atva* (the substitution of *a* for *ṛ*) as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is elision (*lopa*) when the suffix *kṛt* is applied to the form *vṛddha*. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "The suffix *ṇic* is prescribed after *muṇḍa*, *miśra*, *ślakṣṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *vrata*, *vastra*, *dhānya*, *kāla*, *kalā*, *lābha*, *tūsta*, and so forth, in the sense of 'one who causes to become' (*karoti*)," the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed after words such as *muṇḍa* in the sense of performing that action.

In that [sūtra], two words, *ḍhauk* and *kal*, are recited. From this it is understood that for these two words ending in *i*—namely *ḍhauki* and *kali*—the substitution of *a* is prescribed when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Nor is it explained in that manner for the sake of establishing the existence of *sanvadbhāva*; rather, as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "In the Kali age, when the *ṇic* suffix follows [the roots] *ci*, *kliś*, and *bhyas*, the forms *acīklṛpat* and *ajījabhat* are desired. These two forms are possible only when the *ṇic* suffix is present, because they are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātita*).

In the case of *ajaḍhdyahulat*—derived from *aja-aṭ-dhyaṇ-ul-t* where the *a* is elided by the rule "ṇer niṣṭhāyām aviṣaye" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), resulting in *aja-aṭ-dhya-ul-t*, followed by reduplication according to "caṅ" (6.1.11) and the elision of the *ṇi* suffix—the form stands as *ajaḍhdyahulat*. Since the base (*aṅga*) has lost its vowel (*aglopi*), the rule "anaglope" (8.4.93) prohibits the application of the *sanvadbhāva* treatment. Consequently, the substitution of *i* for the short *a* prescribed by "sanyataḥ" (7.4.89) does not occur.

Furthermore, if the suffix *ṇic* were applied after the word ending in the vowel *i*, namely *ḍhali*, then—due to the extension of the status of being treated as *iṣṭhan* by the rule "as if followed by *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavat*)—the elision of the final *ikāra* would apply by the rule "of *ṭi*" (*ṭeḥ*), and the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply by the rule "after a vowel, before *ñ* or *ṇit*" (*aco ñṇiti*). Since the latter (*vṛddhi*) takes precedence, the *aikāra* would result from *vṛddhi*. Once that *aikāra* is elided by the rule "of *ṭi*," because the *aikāra* is not a short vowel (*ak*), its elision does not occur; thus, there is no elision of the *ag* [portion].

Since the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *anaglope* has been stated, and since the substitution of *i* for *a* by the rule *sanyataḥ* would apply when there is the *sanvadbhāva* prescribed by *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), the form would become *ajīgarat*; thus, *acīkalat* would not result. Therefore, it must be explained that the causative (*ṇic*) is formed from the roots *kṛt*, *khṛt*, *gṛh*, and *lih*.

According to the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* (Pāṇini 7.4.2), the fact that the word *aglopi* is mentioned in the wording of the sūtra indicates that elision (*lopa*) is stronger than vṛddhi. Consequently, even in the case of *ahali i at*, elision takes precedence over vṛddhi; thus, when the final *i* of *ahali* is elided, the base (*aṅga*) remains "one whose [final] vowel has been elided" (*aglopin*). Therefore, due to the prohibition contained in the phrase "provided there is no elision" (*anaglope*), [the rule does not apply].

Because the state of being like *san* (*sanvat*) would otherwise apply [by rule 7.4.79], one might suspect that the specific prescription of the short *a*-ending (*adantatva-nipātana*) is redundant. Anticipating this objection, the author states: "of *hrī* and *kali*. Since the prescription of the short *a*-ending would be redundant according to the reasoning previously stated, it serves to indicate that when the suffix *kvip* is added to the roots *hrī* and *kali*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the augment *vṛddhi*.

And likewise, in the case of a root ending in *i* followed by *ṇic*, if *vṛddhi* were applied first and then [the *i*] elided, the root would become *aglopi* (having its penultimate vowel elided); consequently, due to the absence of the *san-vat* rule, the substitution of *i* for *a* by the rule "sanyataḥ" would not occur. Therefore, the *ṇic* suffix is stated here with the intention that the *vṛddhi* should take place after the elision.

And thus, in the case of *ḍhulla*, *kala*, and others ending in /a/, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] occurs, resulting in the form *ā*. Even though that /ā/ is subsequently elided, because of the prohibition "when there is no elision of an *a*-vowel" (*anaglope*), the rule for *sanvadbhāva* does not apply; consequently, the substitution of /i/ for the *abhyāsa* (reduplication) vowel does not take place—this is the established position.

In the *Dhātupradīpa*, however, it is observed: "The substitution of *at* for *ṛ* and *lṛ* is for the purpose of preventing the application of the rules regarding *san*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāva*). One must understand that even this statement has its purport (*tātparya*) in some way directed toward the meaning already stated. Regarding the rule *cleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44): because the *kit* designation is applied to *sic*, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no elision of the *n* in a stem ending in *sic*. Consequently, the fact that *sic* is marked with the *it* designation (*idittva*) may be dispensed with (*pratyākhyeya*), since the status of being *it* is established through the principle of "that which occupies the place of another" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: in the place of *cli*, there is a substitute beginning with *sij*; in that substitute, both the letter *c* and the letter *i* are seen to be marked with the technical designation *it*. Among these, the addition of the letter *i*—which is called an *it*—is redundant. Nor can it be argued that its addition is for the sake of an operation triggered by the *iditva* (the status of having an *it*) of the element ending in *sij*. For likewise...

Regarding the form *amaṃsta*, one might argue that because the suffix *sic* has an indicatory *i* (*it*), the rule for its elision does not apply; thus, since the stem ending in *sic* would not have an indicatory *i*, the *n* of its penultimate syllable would be dropped by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). However, this objection is invalid. Because the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14) prescribes that *sic* following the root *han* is marked with an indicatory *k* (*kit*), this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of *n* does not occur after a stem ending in *sic*. Consequently, the absence of *n*-elision in *amaṃsta* is established.

Likewise, according to the rule—"from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *ā*, in the *luṅ* [tense], *cli* [is substituted], and for *cli*, *sic* [is substituted]"—when the form *ā han s ta* is established, the *s* of *sic* becomes *kit* by the rule "*hanaḥ sic*" (Pāṇini 1.2.14).

In that case, following the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), the nasal *ṇ* is elided; then, by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.27), the *s* is elided, resulting in the form *āḍhḍhacyaṇoddhṛta*. In this context, the prescription of *kit*-status for the suffix *sic* would be redundant if it were *anidit* (lacking an *it*-augment). If that were so, [the form would be] *āḍhḍhacyaṇoddhṛt*.

Since the form *aiṣīt* is established even without the prescription of *kitva* for the suffix *sic*—because the final *s* of the stem ending in *s* is elided by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), which prescribes the elision of the penultimate *n* when a suffix beginning with a consonant and marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows—the prescription of *kitva* for *sic* serves no purpose. However, its inclusion is intended to indicate that the elision of the penultimate *n* of a stem ending in *sic* does not occur [even when a suffix beginning with a consonant follows], as per the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ*.

And thus, the prescription of *kit*-ness for the suffix *sic* is purposeful for the sake of establishing the elision of the nasal *n* in the example *ahyan*. Furthermore, by the statement that in *amaṃsta*, the elision of *n* does not occur because it belongs to a stem ending in *sic*, the absence of *nalopa* is established; therefore, the *iditva* (the assignment of the *it* designation) of *sic* is not necessary. Consequently, let there be no *iditva* for *sic*; let it simply be *sac*. This is the conclusion. This very point is stated [by the author] with the words "because of the making of *sic* a *kit*" and so forth.

Because *cli* has the marker *it*, the *sic* that arises in its place is understood to have the marker *it* by virtue of the rule of "substitution as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, it is argued that the marker *it* for *sic* is entirely useless—this is what is meant by the phrase "by virtue of substitution as the original. However, in reality, since it has been demonstrated that all observed results are established even without the marker *it*, the attempt to establish the presence of the marker *it* through "substitution as the original" is superfluous.

Therefore, it should be noted that the author himself stated in the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota* that the Vārttika "because of the status of being non-penultimate (*ididvāsthānivat*)" is the statement of a partisan (*ekadeśyukti*). [Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the rule *vāsarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94): due to the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *dadātidadātyorviḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.139), there is no requirement for non-homogeneity (*asārūpya*) with respect to the suffixes belonging to the same section (*anudhikāra*).

"By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;śaśvatorlaṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.116), it is understood that the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply to those substitutes for *luṅ*. [Vi.ṭ: These two statements are of the nature of prohibitions (*pariṣedha*), and thus they are not explained here. Thus ends the first quarter (*pāda*) of the third chapter. [Jñā.ṭ: Regarding the rule *ṭhcareḥsdvdr1;ṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16):"]

In the rule *adhyakṣāse-nādāyeḥ ṣṭran* (Pāṇini 3.2.17), because of the mention of *adhyakṣa* as an example, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix occurs only in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and not in the sense of the object (*karman*). [Viṭ: Now, one might ask: why does the suffix *ṭa*, which is prescribed by the rule *careḥ ṣṭran* (Pāṇini 3.2.16) when the word *su* is an upapada, not occur in the case of *kurūṃś carati*?

Nor should it be argued that in the rule *careḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.140), because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *adhikaraṇe* from the preceding rule *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* (3.2.15), the suffix does not occur when a direct object (*karman*) is the governing word (*upapada*). This is because the term *karmaṇi* is also continued [from the previous rule].

Otherwise, there would be no possibility of obtaining the suffixes prescribed by the subsequent sūtras when a word in the accusative case (*karman*) is the *upapada*. Anticipating this objection, he establishes [the point] by means of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the sūtra "careṣṭaḥ," which applies only when the *upapada* is in the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*), and not in the accusative: "and in the case of *akṣa*, *sena*, and *ādi*. For if the sūtra "careṣṭaḥ" were to apply even when the *upapada* is in the accusative, then...

Since the form *ḍhikṣācara* is established by this very suffix *ṭa* in the rule "he moves through the dice" (*ḍhikṣāṃ carati*), the mention of *ḍhikṣā* in the sūtra "after *ḍhikṣā*, *senā*, and *ādi*, [the suffix] *ṭa* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.2.16) is redundant. And that [redundant mention] indicates that the rule "after the root *car*" (Pāṇini 3.2.17) applies only when there is an *upapada* denoting a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

And likewise, since the mention of *ḍhakṣāgra* is for the sake of the suffix *ṭa* when a word in the objective case (*karman*) is an upapada, its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope. However, its practical utility is as follows: in examples such as *kurūṃś carati*, the suffix *ṭa* does not occur after the root *car* when an object is an upapada; this is the established rule (*bhāṣya*). [Jñā.ṭ] *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61).

By stating "even here, despite the presence of a prefix," he indicates that in other rules where "prefix" (*upasarga*) is mentioned, the mention of "prefix" does not apply. Consequently, the instruction regarding the mention of "prefix" in the rule *vadaḥ supy anupasarge* (Pāṇini 1.3.75) need not be stated.

In the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidachidajinīrājām upasarge 'pi kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.61), the author of the Vārttikas stated: "The inclusion of *su* among *sad* and the others. The meaning of this is that the suffix *kvip* occurs after the roots beginning with *sad* when *su* stands as an upapada.

Regarding the example "sīdati vedau" (he sits on the altar), when the root *sad* takes the suffix *kvip* with the word "vedi" as a following member (*upapada*), the form "vedisat" is derived. Now, if it is said that *kvip* occurs when a word ending in *su* is the *upapada*, then [the following applies]: [The rule: *bhāṣyakāra* states: "If it is said that *kvip* occurs when a word ending in *su* is the *upapada*, then..."

Since the prefix *su-* also ends in a *su*-affix, it is included by the rule *supi* itself; therefore, one might object that it is unnecessary to state "also when there is a prefix" (*upasarge 'pi*) in the sūtra. Anticipating this doubt, he stated that such a statement must be made for the sake of providing a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*). His intention is as follows: although the inclusion of prefixes is already established by the mention of *supi*, the explicit mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) serves as an indicator that where a suffix is prescribed with a *sup*-ending word as an upapada, it does not apply when a prefix is the upapada.

And likewise, the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*) in the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.61) is purposeful for the sake of the *kvip* suffix even when a prefix is present as an *upapada*. Its specific utility, however, is that the *kyap* suffix prescribed by the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.106) does not occur when a prefix is present as an *upapada*.

And thus, it is established that in that very sūtra, the vārttika stating "the mention of the root *grah* without a prefix (*anupasarga*) must be made" need not be formulated. For this very reason, in forms such as *pravādyam*, the suffix *kyap* does not occur after the root *vad* when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an upapada. All of this is intended by the statement: "even when there is a prefix here. [Jñāpakasūtra] *ātman-māne* (Pāṇini 3.2.83).

The prescription that the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following the root *tās* (of the periphrastic future) is unaccented (*anudātta*) indicates that even when the accent of the *vikaraṇa* is present, it does not supersede the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*. [Regarding this, under the rule *thātamamāne khaś ca*, it is stated by the *vārttika* "and in the case of the object acting as the agent" (*karmakartari ca*) that the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *man* when it denotes self-reflection (*ātmakarmakamanana*), provided a word ending in a nominal suffix (*sup*) is the governing term (*upapada*), and the sense is that of the object acting as the agent (*karmakartṛ*).]

The intention of the speaker here is this: when the suffix *khaś* follows, by the rule "that which has an action similar to that of the object [takes the designation of the object]" (Pāṇini 3.1.87), the status of being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) applies, and consequently, the suffix *yak* occurs by the rule "the suffix *yak* before a sārvadhātuka [affix]" (Pāṇini 3.1.67). Thus, in the form *darśanīyamānī*, the audible presence of the letter *y* is the result.

Regarding this, the following objection arises: "Let there be no mention of the object (*karman*) here. Let this suffix *khaś* be prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) alone. Since the root *man* belongs to the *divādi* class, when the suffix *khaś*—which denotes the agent—is applied, followed by the *śyan* augment, the form *darśanīyamanyam* (containing the letter *y*) is indeed established."

And although *rūpa* is not established [in this way], even so, there would be a difference in accent (*svara*): when *yaka* is present, the accent is acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*); whereas when *śyan* is present, the accent is acute on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*) according to the rule "the initial syllable of a root ending in *ñ* or *ṇ* is always acute" (*ñnityādir nityam*, Pāṇini 6.1.197). This must be stated [as a counter-argument]. However, because the accent of *śyan* is superseded by the accent of *khaś*, the state of being acute on the final syllable (*antodātatva*) is established.

Even so, first there is *khaś* and its accent, and immediately after that, *śyan* and the accent prescribed by it; since the accent of *śyan* would be superseded by the accent of *khaś* due to the rule of "the later [rule] prevails over the earlier" (*paratva*), the initial syllable would necessarily become udātta. To resolve this doubt, he states the solution based on a statement established by a *jñāpaka*: "of what follows *tās*" (*tāseḥ parasya*).

The intention here is as follows: by the rule *tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the lack of acute accent (*anudātatva*) is prescribed for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following that which ends in *tās*. For example, in forms such as *kartā*, the *ā* of *tās*—which is a substitute for *luṭ*—becomes unaccented. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accentuation of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).

If the *śit* accent were stronger than the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), then, when the suffix-accent is present, the *tās*-accent would override the suffix-accent; thus, since the unaccented nature of the suffix would already be established by that very rule, the prescription of the unaccented status for the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās* would not be necessary.

Since the fact that [the affix] *tās* is unaccented (*anudātta*) has been stated, this very point is made known: even when present, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* does not supersede the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*. Thus, in forms such as *kartā*, the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) would otherwise apply; therefore, the prescription of the unaccented status for what follows *tās* is intended to prevent that.

And thus, in cases such as *darśanīyammanya*, if the suffix *śyan* were used, then since that [suffix] does not cause the addition of the *khakha* accent, there would be only the final acute (*antodātta*) accent; and even with *yak*, there is only the final acute accent. Thus, because there is no difference in accent, the desired form is established by *śyan* alone. Therefore, it is proper that this *khaś* occurs only in the active voice (*kartari*), and the mention of the "agent who is also the object" (*karmakartṛ*) need not be made. This is the conclusion. [Pāṇini 3.2.118: *laṭ sme*]

This makes it known that what was characterized by a particular mark in the past no longer possesses that mark in the present. [Regarding the rule *laṭ sme*: the meaning of this sūtra is that when *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *laṭ* occurs for the past non-recent (anadyatana) and non-evident (*parokṣa*) tenses. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *liṭ*. Examples include such expressions as *nalena sma purādhīyata* ("Nala was studying in the past").]

And in that same *Sūtra*, there are two *Vārttikas*: "In the case of *sma* and *purā*, [the suffix] is used for the immediate past (*bhūtamātra*), not for the recent past (*adyatana*). The meaning of this is as follows: in the first *Vārttika*, the group of five rules beginning with "after *sma* and *purā*, the *laṭ* [suffix is used]" (*sū.* 3.2.118), ending with "and after *purā*, the *luṅ* [is used], provided *sma* does not follow" (*sū.* 3.2.122)—namely, "after *sma*, the *laṭ*," "also when it is not proximate," "after *na* and *nu*, in response to what has been seen," "after *na* and *nu*, optionally," and "after *purā*, the *luṅ* [is used], provided *sma* does not follow"—is intended.

It is observed that in that context, the suffix occurs only for the past (*bhūta*). However, a suffix characterized by "smara" (the particle *sma*) does not occur for the present day (*adyatana*). Consequently, by the three rules—"*laṭ sme*" (Pāṇini 3.2.117), "*aparokṣe ca*" (3.2.119), and "*puri luṅ cāsme*" (3.2.122)—a suffix is prescribed for a non-present-day (*anadyatana*) specific past.
