Regarding the rules "nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane" (Pāṇini 3.2.120) and "nanvorvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 3.2.121), one must adopt the established distinction that these suffixes are prescribed only when there is a mere statement of what has occurred (*bhūtamātre*). However, the intention of the Vārttikakāra is that this distinction is not obtained from the sūtras themselves. In reality, however, this distinction is indeed obtained from the sūtras alone; thus he says: "This makes it known."

From the commencement of the subsequent sūtra, "aparokṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.119), it is understood that the mention of *parokṣa* (non-evident) from the preceding sūtra, "laṭ sme" (Pāṇini 3.2.118), is carried over [into this rule]. Consequently, since the mention of *anadyatana* (not of today) is also connected with the mention of *parokṣa* there, it is established that the sūtra "laṭ sme" has as its scope both the non-evident (*parokṣa*) and the not-of-today (*anadyatana*).

The rule *aparokṣe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.119) specifies the non-remote (non-immediate) past tense (*anadyatana*). However, in the rule *puri luṅ cāsme* (Pāṇini 3.2.122), the explicit mention of the *luṅ* suffix indicates that the non-remote past tense (*anadyatana*) is understood [to apply] by implication.

For if this were a rule for the mere past tense (*bhūtamātra*), then, by the continued application of the mention of the term *bhāṣā* from the sūtra "nanvor vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 3.2.121), the present tense (*laṭ*) would be prescribed optionally; consequently, in the alternative where [the present tense] does not occur, the aorist (*luṅ*)—which is prescribed for the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*)—would come into effect.

The mention of *luṅ* is purposeless [in this context], because it has already been established that *luṅ* is not prescribed for the non-current day (*anadyatana*) by the rule *puri*. However, according to the view that *luṅ* is indeed prescribed there, the mention of *luṅ* is for the sake of including *luṅ*. Thus, it is established that this set of three rules (*trisūtrī*) refers to the past not belonging to the current day (*anadyatanabhūta*).

Regarding the two middle rules—"nanau paḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.120) and "nanvorvibhāṣā" (3.2.121)—since the mention of the "remote" (*parokṣa*) tense in these rules serves as a negation of both the "remote" and the "non-remote," it also negates the mention of the "imperfect" (*anadyatana*) tense that occurs in conjunction with them.

The intention is that since the suffix *nivaḥ* has already been established by the rule itself as referring exclusively to the sense of "habitual action" (*bhūta-mātra-viṣayatva*), the mention of the *vārttika* regarding the portion concerning the sense of the object (*viṣaya-vibhāga*) is redundant. Regarding the rule *nindā-huṅ-śuṅ-bhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.146): because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the prescription of the suffix *vuñ* after roots meaning "blame" (*nindā*) and so forth, in the case of suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), all suffixes beginning with *taḥ* (the *tṛc* suffix) do not occur by way of the optionality of non-identity of form (*vā-sarūpa*).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: Is not the prescription of the suffix *vuñ* by the rule "nindādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.146) and others redundant? For the desired form is already established by the suffix *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule "ṇvultṛcau" (Pāṇini 3.2.133), since there is no difference between the two in terms of form or accent.

In the case of the word *nindaka*, when the suffix *ṇvul* is applied, the vowel preceding the suffix becomes acute according to the rule *liti* (Pāṇini 6.2.193); thus, the *i*-kāra of the root is acute. Even in the case of the suffix *vuñ*, the initial of the entire formation is acute by the rule *ñnityādirnityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197). Therefore, since there is no difference in accentuation, there is likewise no difference in the phonetic form.

Although there is no difference in accent for a monosyllabic root, there is indeed a difference in accent for a polysyllabic root. In this sūtra, the root *asūya* is indicated; consequently, in the word *asūyaka*, formed with the suffix *vuñ*, the first syllable of the entire compound is udātta.

However, since there is a difference in accentuation—namely, that in the case of the *ṇvul* suffix, the letter preceding the suffix is followed by a *sakāra*, which becomes *eyaN*, and thus the vowel is acute—it must be said that the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.36] exists for that purpose. One might object: "In that case, let the rule simply be 'asūyo vuñ'; the mention of 'blame' (*nindā*) and so forth is redundant. Anticipating this doubt, he establishes its utility as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for a specific statement: "for blame and so forth" (*nindādibhyaḥ*).

The meaning is this: in the absence of the suffixes *niṅ* and others, forms such as *nindaka* would not be established. Nor should it be argued that by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the suffix *ṇvul* is established optionally as an alternative to *taḥ* (the *tṛc* suffix), since *ṇvul* is a superseding factor (*bādhaka*). Why? Because... [text fragment]

Since the desired form is established from that very [suffix], the mention of "nindā" and so forth in the *vuñ* rule would otherwise be redundant; this redundancy indicates that the *vāsarūpa* principle does not apply to suffixes having the same meaning as those beginning with "tacchīla. Consequently, the *ṇvul* suffix would invariably supersede *vuñ*. Thus, the mention of "nindā" and so forth in the *vuñ* rule serves its purpose within its own scope (*svāṃśe*) for the sake of establishing forms such as *nindaka*.

In other cases, when there is a specific purpose—namely, in the presence of suffixes prescribed in the *tācchīlika* section—the general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*) does not apply. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the suffixes such as *taḥ* and *tṛc*, which would otherwise be obtained by the principle of *vāsarūpa*, do not occur in the case of *tācchīlika* formations. [Pāṇini 3.2.150: *jucaṅkramya...*]

In this context, because of the specific mention of *pada* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*) do not coexist with other suffixes expressing habitual action in the form of a *vāsarūpa* option. However, because of the specific mention of *dīpa* in the rule "sūdadīpe," there is a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *yuc* with the suffix *ra*.

[Objection]: But surely, by the rule *ju-caṅkramya-dandramya-saṃsargi-bhrāj-ujjvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ yaḥ*, the suffix *yuc* is prescribed after the roots *ju*, *caṅkram*, *dandram*, *saṃsarg*, *bhrāj*, *ujjval*, *śuc*, *laṣ*, *pat*, and *pad* to form words denoting those who habitually perform the action and so forth. In that case, the mention of the root *pad* in this rule is redundant.
Since that [root] is marked with the anudātta accent and begins with a consonant (hal), the suffix *yuc* is established by the general rule itself, namely, "anudātetśca halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.149).

Nor is it the case that, by the specific rule *laḥ karmariṇa ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), which prescribes the suffix *ghañ*, and by the specific rule *laḥ parasmaipadāni* (Pāṇini 1.4.99) followed by *śīlito’bhyastaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.178) and *laṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣahanakamagamaśruva ukañ* (Pāṇini 3.2.154), the suffix *ukañ* supersedes the suffix *yuc* prescribed by the general rule [of *śīlita*], such that [the form] would be [derived with] *ukañ*.

Regarding the purpose of including the word *pada* here in the rule for *yuc*: one might object that the mention of *gra* [in Pāṇini 3.3.63] is unnecessary, because by the principle of *vāsarūpa*, the suffix *ukañ*—which is not identical in form (*asarūpa*)—optionally supersedes *yuc*, and thus *yuc* would be established even without it in certain instances. Anticipating this objection, he states that the mention of *pada* is for the sake of providing an explanatory indication (*jñāpana*), saying: "Because of the mention of *pada* here... [and so forth].

The inclusion of the word *pada* in the aforementioned manner, though seemingly redundant, indicates that in the case of specific rules (*apavāda*) governing *tācchīlika* suffixes, the general rules (*utsarga*) governing *tācchīlika* suffixes—which would otherwise apply by the principle of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*)—are barred. Thus, the purpose of including *pada* is to ensure that even the suffix *yuca* is established in place of *ukañ*, thereby making its mention meaningful. This is the underlying intention.

But if it is indicated in this way, then the mention of *dīpi* in the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.153) would be redundant. For by that rule, the suffix *ṇyuc* is prescribed for *dīp*, which is already obtained by the rule *anudātetashca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149).
For that [word], the suffix *ra*, prescribed by the rule *namikampismyajaskamahiṃsadīpo raḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.167), serves as an exception (*apavāda*).

Since both [the suffixes *u* and *aka*] are *tācchīlika* (denoting habitual action), one might object that when the exception (*apavāda*) suffix *ṇvi* is present, the general rule (*utsarga*) suffix *yuc*—which is *tācchīlika*—would not apply because it is not obtained by the authority of the aforementioned *jñāpaka*. Consequently, one might suspect that the inclusion of the root *tīp* in the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca* would be purposeless for the sake of establishing its exclusion. Anticipating this, [the author] states that precisely for this reason, through the indication of the statement "there is co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *yuc* with *reṇ*" (*yuco reṇa samāveśaḥ*), that [purpose is achieved].

The meaning of "meaningful" (sārthakam) is as follows: regarding the rule *sūdadīpa-* etc., because of the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *yuc* with the suffix *rap*, the suffix *yuc* might occasionally also apply to the root *dīp*. Therefore, the mention of *dīpi* [in the rule] is for the purpose of excluding that possibility—this is the sense. Furthermore, the purpose of this indication is that in cases such as *kamrā kanyā* ("the desiring girl"), the suffix *yuc* may optionally occur; by means of this, forms such as *kamanā kanyā* are established.

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter. [Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the rule *tumun-ṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10): the re-enactment of the prescription for *ṇvul* indicates that when a verb expressing an action is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*) denoting an action performed for the sake of another action, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not apply by the principle of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*). Consequently, the mention of *laṭ* in the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3) is intended to provide an occasion for the application of *ṇvul*. [Vi.ṭ] Now, an objection: the prescription of *ṇvul* in the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām* is redundant.

Since the suffix *ṇvul* is established by the general rule "*ṇvultṛcau*" itself when a verb denoting an action is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*) and the time [of the main action] is future, the forms such as "the eater goes" (*bhoktā vrajati*)—meaning "he goes in order to eat"—are already established.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *ṇvul* in the rule "laḥ T-kṛt śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.23)—which prescribes the *l*-suffixes, including *ṇvul*, when a verb is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*) denoting an action for the sake of another action—is intended to prevent the supersession (*bādha*) of *ṇvul* by those specific suffixes mentioned in the subsequent rules.

One might raise the objection that, by the rule of *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), the suffix *ṇvul* is optionally available alongside *laṭ* because it does not sublate it, and thus *ṇvul* would be established even in the alternative case. Anticipating this, [the author] states: "The re-enunciation of *ṇvul*. Thus, this serves to indicate that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply when a verb (*kriyā*) is the subordinate element (*upapada*) denoting an action performed for the sake of another action. Consequently, the re-enunciation of *ṇvul* is for the purpose of ensuring that *ṇvul* does not sublate *laṭ*.

Consequently, the suffix *ṇvul* is established even in the sense of "one who obstructs" (*bādhaka*). And by that [suffix], the affixes beginning with *ta*, which have *ṇvul* as their source, are invariably replaced by *laṭ*. Therefore, the intention is that expressions such as "the agent (*kartā*) goes" are not used—just as one does not say "the doer (*kāraka*) goes"—in the sense of "he goes while performing an action. [Commentary on Pāṇini 3.3.58]: *gṛdhivañcyoḥ pralambhane* (The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* take the Ātmanepada when meaning "deceiving").

Because the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for "theft" (*steya*) by the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.75], whereas it is not prescribed for "non-theft," and because it is not prescribed for non-theft, the specific mention of the root *ci* (to gather) in the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.58] indicates that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule "thāthaghañktā... " (Pāṇini 6.2.144) does not apply to the verb *cinoti* preceded by the prefix *niḥ*.

[Objection]: Now, in the rule prescribing the suffix *ghañ*, namely *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), the mention of the root *ci* preceded by *niḥ* is redundant. This is because the form is already established by the suffix *ac* itself, according to the rule *erac* (3.3.56), which provides the meaning "certainty" (*niścaya*).

In the view that [the suffix] is *ap*, there is an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātatā*) by virtue of being *cit*. Even in the view that it is *ap*, there is an acute accent on the final syllable by the rule "thā-tha-dhañ-ktā-jña-ca-prabhṛti-kāṇām" (Pāṇini 6.2.144), because there is no distinction regarding the accent. Nor should it be argued that the prescription of *aci* in the rule "cheṣṭādāne cerasteye" (Pāṇini 3.3.40) is for the purpose of precluding *ghañ* when the act is not theft; for by the prohibition "asteye," *ghañ* does not apply in the case of theft anyway.

In the case of *asteya* (non-stealing) and *adattādānaviramaṇa* (abstinence from taking what is not given), the suffix *ghañ* alone is prescribed, and not *ap*. Thus, having raised the objection that the rule for adding *ap* after the prefix *ni-* to the root *ci* would be redundant, [the author] indicates—precisely because of this—that the final acute accent (*antodātta*) prescribed by the rule "thā-tha" etc. does not apply to *ni-caya*.

And likewise, in the case where it is treated as a suffix (*apratyaya*), because the accentuation rules beginning with *thāthādi* do not apply, the vowel following the letter *ca*—namely the vowel *ā* in *cayaśas*—is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). That same [word] remains acutely accented on the middle syllable even in the case of *niścayaśas*, according to the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), which prescribes that a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix following a prefix, an agentive factor (*kāraka*), or a secondary word (*upapada*) is acutely accented on the middle syllable. Thus, *niścayaśas* is acutely accented on the middle.

In the alternative view (*apakṣe*), because of the difference in accent—specifically the rule that [a word ending in] *ac* has the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*)—the formation of the word *caura* from the root *cur* with the suffix *ap* would not be established when the sense is "taking by force" (*hastādāna*) rather than "stealing" (*steya*), as the required accent would be at the end of the *ac*. Therefore, the resolution is stated [in the commentary] beginning with "of stealing" (*steyasya*) etc., namely that the suffix *ap* is prescribed after *cur* preceded by *nis* in this specific context. Regarding the phrase "in the rule for *ghañ*" (*ghañvidhau*), it means "in the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.40]: 'After *cur*, [the suffix *ghañ* is used] in the sense of taking by force, provided it is not stealing.'"

"Because it has not been seen [to apply] otherwise" (*aniḥśeṣadarśitatvāt*). The word "of the suffix *ap*" (*appratyayasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. [Regarding the rule *praiṣātisarga* (Pāṇini 3.3.163): This statement concerning the *kṛtya* suffixes, being intended to exclude the *loṭ* [suffix], indicates that after the section on the feminine (*strī*), the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpavidhiḥ*) does not apply.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: "In the rule *praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca*, let the mention of *kṛtya* suffixes not be made. Since *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed generally for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), they will apply elsewhere as well, just like the *praiṣa* (commands) and so forth."

Nor should it be argued that the mention of "kriyā" (action) here is for the purpose of preventing the *loṭ* [imperative] mood from subverting the *kṛtya* suffixes in cases such as *praśastadr̥ś* and others—lest there be no scope for the *kṛtyas*. For, by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the *loṭ* may optionally subvert them, and thus the *kṛtyas* would still be established in the alternative case. Anticipating this objection, [the author says]: "In that case, then... (*evaṃ tarhi*)... [and so on].

That [mention of *kṛtya*] is for the purpose of making known that the rule of optional forms (*vā-asarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply after the section governing feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*). And thus, since this sūtra, "The [suffixes] *pra*, *iṣ*, *ṇa*, *dv*, *ra*, *ati*, and *sarga*" (Pāṇini 3.3.56), exists after the governing heading "In the feminine, *ktin*" (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the maxim of optional forms (*vā-asarūpa-nyāya*) does not apply here. Consequently, since the suffix *loṭ* would invariably supersede the *kṛtya* suffixes, the mention of *kṛtya* is for the sake of establishing their coexistence (*samāveśa*)—this is the view.

Regarding the statement "it is a non-authoritative word": one should not argue that the rule *vāsarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94) is redundant as a means of providing this information, because its purpose is already established by the very phrase *astriyām* therein. For by that [phrase], it is understood that the option regarding different forms (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply within the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of "in the feminine" (*striyām*). This is because the intention is that the prohibition (*na*) does not apply beyond the governing scope of "in the feminine."

It should be understood that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the word *striyām* ("in the feminine") is severed precisely at the sūtra *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.114). Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter. Regarding the sūtra *udīcāṃ māṅo vyatihāre* (Pāṇini 3.4.19): here, the mention of *māṅ*, which has undergone the substitution of *ā* (i.e., *māṅ*), indicates that the status of being non-*anejanta* (not ending in a vowel other than *a*) does not apply when a suffix is added after an *anubandha* (indicatory letter).

[Commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*: This has been explained elsewhere; therefore, it is not commented upon here. [Commentary on the *Jñāpakasamuccaya*: By the rule *lasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77), because the marker *ṇ* is attached to *ṇal*, the letter *l* in the various *lakāras* does not receive the designation *it*. [Commentary on the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra*: But surely, in forms such as *pacati*, the suffix *ti* replaces *laṭ*; and according to the rule *laśakkataddhite* (Pāṇini 1.3.8), the letter *l* is designated as *it*.]

Furthermore, since *laṭ* is marked with the indicator *l*, its substitute *ti* (and by extension *t* etc. would also possess the *lit* quality by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule; consequently, one might object that the *lit-svara* (the acute accent on the *liṭ*-substitute) would apply in forms such as *pacati*. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "Because of the marking of *ṇal* as *lit*. Since the *lit* quality of *ṇal* is already established through the *sthānivadbhāva* of *ti*—which itself is the substitute for *liṭ*—the explicit marking of *ṇal* as *lit* serves to indicate that the technical designation *it* does not apply to the *lakāra*s such as *laṭ*.

And thus, since the *lit*-status belongs only to the substituend (*sthānin*) and not to the substitute (*ādeśa*), it is difficult to establish that status for the substitute; therefore, the inclusion of the *liṭ* suffix in the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.193] is meaningful. Consequently, in forms such as *pacati*, the *tiṅ* suffixes and others do not possess the *lit*-status, and thus there is no possibility of the accentuation prescribed for *lit* suffixes. However, in the actual text of the Bhāṣya, the formulation of the statement is seen as: "The *lit*-status is not assigned to substitutes of *la*."

It should be noted that in both cases, the result is exactly the same. Regarding the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79): it must be stated that there is a prohibition of *āna* in the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānām*; or, it has already been stated; or, the statement of the substitution for *sānu-bandhaka* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the operations involving *it* apply to the stage of the substitute (*ādeśa*).

[Commentary on vi.ṭ: Now, one might raise the objection: "By the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*, which prescribes the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* of those *ātmanepada* suffixes that follow a *ṭit* *lakāra*, would this not also apply to the *ṭi* of the suffix *āna-* in forms such as *pacamāna-*? For *āna-* is also an *ātmanepada* suffix that occurs in place of a *ṭit* [suffix]. Anticipating this doubt, he states "by the rule beginning with *sūtra*... and so forth, based on the Vārttika: "*In the case of the substitution of *e* for a *ṭit*, there is no prohibition of *āna-*, provided it is an *ātmanepada*. Thus, there is no substitution of *e* for *āna-*.

In reality, the rule *gāṅ liṭi* (Pāṇini 2.4.49) prescribes the substitute *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ*. Since the root *iṅ* possesses the marker *ṅ*, the substitute *gā* would also acquire the status of having the marker *ṅ* by virtue of the principle of "the substitute being like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, the inclusion of the letter *ṅ* in the substitute is redundant; this redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that wherever a substitute is taught with an attached marker, the operations triggered by the designation of that marker (*itsaṃjñā*) do not apply to the substitute itself. This is what has been stated.

And thus, because the suffix *śānac* is prescribed in place of the *anu-bandha*-less *śatṛ* by the rule "laṭaḥ śataṅ-śānacau," the substitution of *etva* (the replacement of *a* with *e*) caused by the *ṭit* designation does not apply to *śānac*. In cases such as *pacate*, however, since [the suffixes] beginning with *ta* are prescribed in place of the *anu-bandha*-less *laṭ* by the rule "lasya," *etva* will indeed apply to them; therefore, there is no fault. With this intention, he says: "Or it has been stated."

In the *vārttika* on the sūtra "gāṅ liṭi," the word "iti" is understood [as a marker]. And here—the commentary (*pradīpa*) on the sūtra "gāṅ liṭi" should be consulted, which states: "In a case where a suffix (*pratyaya*) such as *sānu* or *bandha* is mentioned, the substitution (*ādeśa*) takes place even while the *it*-designation (*itsaṃjñā*) has not yet been assigned; or, once the *it*-designation has been assigned, the operations dependent upon it do not take place. Thus ends the third chapter.
[Fragmentary Text] ...of the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka] ... Chapter Four.

[Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the rule *ajādya* (Pāṇini 4.1.4): the Vārttika "and *śūdrā*, when preceded by *amaṇḍa*," indicates that there is an application of the rule to that which ends in [the specified stem]. [Vi.ṭ] In the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*, [it says] "śūdrā..."
The *Vārttika* states: "Or, [the suffix] is applied before the word *jāti*. This means that if the *śūdra* caste is to be denoted, the word *śūdra*—preceded by *amaḥ*—takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
Thus, the word *śūdra*, which is listed in the *ajādi* group, takes *ṭāp*.

It is obtained in a general sense. In that context, if the word *śūdra* possesses the two qualifications of denoting a genus (*jāti*) and the absence of being preceded by a *māṅgalya* [auspicious] prefix, then the suffix *ṭāp* applies.
Alternatively, the distinction (*vyavasthā*) is established by the *vārttika*. In that case,
the qualification "preceded by *ama-ṛṣi*" would be redundant,
because the word *māhiṣya-śūdra* is not included in the list of words beginning with *aja*.

For the suffix *ṭāp* is not applicable [in this case]. Nor should it be argued that the word *śūdraśabda* is recited among the *ajādi* (the group beginning with *ajā*) words, and therefore, by the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*), the word *maṇḍūkaśūdraśabda* would also be included;
for the rule of extension to what ends in [a specific element] applies only when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself possesses that [element].
It should not be argued that even a *śūdra* who possesses [the word] *mahat* would be included [in the scope of the rule];

for there is a prohibition against the application of the "rule of the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) when the base (*prātipadika*) itself already possesses [that element]. Anticipating this objection, [the author] intends to indicate that the "rule of the final element" does indeed apply in the case of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*).
Regarding the phrase "and a Śūdra woman":

thus, by the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to that which ends with [the specified term]), the word "Śūdra" would include the compound "Amaśūdra" as well; therefore, the mention of "Ama-" at the beginning is for the purpose of excluding that.
The purpose of this indication, however, is that just as in the case of *bhavatī*— where the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6) because it ends in an *ugit* vowel—
the suffix *ṅīp* would also apply by the principle of extension (*tadantavidhi*) to words ending in *ati-bhavat* because they end in an *ugit* vowel.
The derivation of the form is "it descends" (*avatīti*), "she descends" (*avati*);
this is the intended meaning. "In this [section]" means in the section on feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*).
[This refers to] *Pāṇini Sūtra* 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*) and 4.1.104 (*vāmadevāḍḍyaḍḍyaṅ*).
(Śūtra 4.2.9) Thus, regarding the doubling [of the consonant], it is stated: "In the mention of *an-anuc-chva-dha-ndha-kra-gra-ha*, there is no mention of *sa-anuc-chva-dha-ndha-kra-gra*;
in the mention of that..."

The statement "the addition of *na* is not for the purpose of excluding *andhaka* and others" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the two rules. [Jñā.Ṭ] The very mention of the modification (*vikāra*) in the rule *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83) indicates that "that which has undergone a partial modification is not different from the original."

The mention of the word *vā* in the rule *pīlāyā vā* (Pāṇini 4.1.118) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "the suffix *aṇ* does not occur when there is the scope for an exception (*apavāda*). [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra] Regarding the rule *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83), what are the operations (*prakriyās*) that occur prior to *prāgdīvyataḥ*?

If it is intended that *aṇ* applies to those [suffixes] beginning with *āṬ*, then in the rule "from here up to *prāgdīvyataḥ*, the suffixes that occur have the meaning of those [words]," it is intended that *aṇ* applies to those very meanings. In the first case,
there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of *aṇ* even when *iñ* and other suffixes are prescribed as exceptions (*apavāda*).

Since the two [options] would have the same object of reference (*ekaviṣayatvena*), there could only be an alternative (*vikalpa*), and not the relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). Regarding the second position,
that "the rule for *iṭ* applies when the meaning is present," this is stated in another grammatical treatise (*prakriyāntara*).

The suffix *aṇ* has scope [to apply] because it would otherwise be superseded by *iñ* and other suffixes arising due to the specific restriction of a single meaning; thus, there is no fault. In that regard, even in the first position (*pakṣa*), there is no fault.
To establish this, [the author] says: "Or by *pīlā*"; that is, the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule.

If the suffix *aṇ* were to apply even in the scope of an exception (*apavāda*), then the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra "pīlayā vā" would be purposeless. This is because [the suffix *aṇ* would already apply] from the word *pīlā*.

Regarding the sense of offspring (*apatya*), when the suffix *ḍhak* would otherwise apply by the rule "after a word of two syllables" (*dvyacaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.1.121)— which is an exception to *aṇ*— the suffix *aṇ* is again prescribed optionally as an exception to that *ḍhak* by the rule "optionally after *pīlā*" (*pīlāyā vā*).
If *aṇ* were not applied even in the presence of an exception (*apavāda*) to it...

Alternatively, even without this sūtra, since the application of *aṇ* could be established optionally through the attainment of *samāveśa*, the sūtra would be rendered useless; therefore, it is made known that *aṇ* does not apply in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) such as *iñ* is intended. Consequently, in cases where *iñ* and others are intended, *aṇ* does not occur.

The sense is that there would be an over-extension (*prasakti*). [Jñānaṭīkā] Since one could have simply said "before *ṭhak*" (*prāk ṭhakaḥ*), the statement "before *dīvyat*" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*, Pāṇini 4.1.83) indicates that the meaning is not restricted. [Vivaraṇaṭīkā] But surely, why is "before *dīvyat*" used instead of "before *ṭhak*," since the latter would be more concise?

It has not been stated. Anticipating the objection that by the word *ṭhak* [in the rule], the sūtra "From *prāgvahat*, *ṭhak*" (Pāṇini 4.4.1) is being referred to, [the author] says: the phrase "prior to *dīvya*" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*) was stated for the purpose of making known that the suffix *aṇ* occurs only for those meanings which occur prior to *dīvya*.
Therefore, it is understood that the suffix *aṇ* occurs even in the sense of *cha* (as taught by Pāṇini 4.2.80), because it precedes the rule "prāgdīvyataḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.83).
In that context, if it were stated simply "before *ṭhak*," then *aṇ* would not apply in the absence of *ṭhak*; hence [the rule specifies] "before *dīvyat*."

Thus, the statement is purposeful. The purpose of making this known is that when two suffixes, *aṇ* and *iñ*, would both apply to the same base (*prakṛti*) for the same meaning, the suffix *iñ*— which has its own scope elsewhere— supersedes the suffix *aṇ*.

Intending to state that the existence of the *bādhya-bādhaka* (the sublated and the sublater) relationship has been determined, he says: "The suffix *ṭhak* should be stated as [occurring] before. The word "this" (*ayam*) means the suffix *aṇ*. [Pāṇini 4.1.90: *yūni luk* || "In the case of *gotra*, *ukṣan*, *ṛṣi*, etc. ...]

In the rule prescribing the suffix *vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.39), the mention of the terms *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and others is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in common usage, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers specifically to the remote ancestor. Furthermore, in common parlance, a descendant is metaphorically designated as the "lineage. For example: "What is your lineage, young man? "I am a Gārgyāyaṇa. [Vi.]

The meaning of the rule *ṭhyūni luk* is as follows: when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that falls under the category *prāgdīvyatīya* is intended to be applied, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan*-suffix; once that [elision] has been effected, whatever [suffix] would otherwise apply from a particular base applies from that same base. Of that...

At the time of enumerating the purposes [of the treatise], the Vārttika rule "iñ and ṇya are used everywhere" was cited. The extraction of *iñ* is illustrated by the example *Āupagavīyaḥ*. From the base *Upagu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the sense "the offspring of Upagu," resulting in *Āupagavaḥ*. Then, from that base, the suffix *iñ* is applied in the sense of a grandson (*yuvāpatya*), resulting in *Āupagaviḥ*. From that...

When the suffix *ccha* is intended to be applied, there is first the elision (*luk*) of the *iñ* suffix *yu* (the patronymic suffix). Once that has been elided, the suffix *ccha* is applied, resulting in the form *aupagavīyāḥ*. What is the purpose of this elision (*luk*) here?
Even if the *iñ* were not elided, when the suffix *ccha* is applied by virtue of the rule for *vṛddha* [nouns], the form would still be *aupagavīyāḥ*.

In response to the doubt regarding the establishment of the form [of the word], the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "When there is an extension (*atideśa*) as if it were an established rule (*vṛddha*), the suffix *iñ* would result, and by the rule 'after a *gotra* [name],' the suffix *aṇ* would apply."

The meaning of this is as follows: by the Vārttika, "Under the governing rule *prāgdīvyataḥ*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the treatment of *yuvan* as being like *vṛddha*," the suffix belonging to *yuvan* is extended the same operations as those of *gotra*. Consequently, in the absence of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule *iño gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.112).
The suffix *cha* is prescribed after this [word *yuvan*]. Therefore, it must be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ*.
Regarding that, the Bhāṣya states: "There is no fault; this extension (*atideśa*) is rejected.
And thus, because there is no extension of the status of being a *gotra* to *yuvan*, [the rule does not apply].

Even if there were no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "iño gotre" would not apply; rather, only the suffix *cha*, characterized by the term *vṛddha*, would apply. Thus, since the desired form is established, the elision of *iñ* by the rule "yūni luk" is unnecessary for the example "aupagavīyāḥ. Therefore, this [elision] is not an illustration [of the necessity of the rule].
The intention of the Bhāṣya is that [the rule] cannot be established.

Therefore, if the extension (*atideśa*) of the term "old" (*vṛddha*) to the "young" (*yuvan*)— that is, the extension of the *gotra* designation— is rejected, then how can the purposes (*prayojana*) stated for the extension of the *gotra* designation be accomplished?
To this doubt, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Those [forms] are established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
The intention here is as follows: the collection of the descendants of Garga is *gārgyāyaṇakam*.
Regarding the *Gārgyāyaṇakas*: "something belonging to the Gārgyāyaṇas" (*gārgyāyaṇakam*);

[the derivation is as follows: "this has its origin in Gārgyāyaṇa" (*gārgyāyaṇa-ṛḍddhdhḍaddh;aktirasya*) = *gārgyāyaṇakaḥ*. The purpose of the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffix *vuñ*—which applies when based on a *gotra* name—to the term "yuvan" (youth), as if it were "vṛddha" (elder), has been stated. Among those [purposes], in the first case:

In the example *udāharaṇe*, [the derivation is as follows]: the descendant in the lineage (*gotra*) of Garga is *Gārgya*, formed by the suffix *yañ* according to the rule "gargādibhyo yañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.105).

The young descendant (*yuvan*) of Gārgya is *Gārgyāyaṇa*, formed by the suffix *phak* according to the rule "yañiñośca" (Pāṇini 4.1.101). From that, in the sense of a collection (*samūha*), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

By the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhra-* (Pāṇini 4.1.39), the suffix *vuñ* is applied, resulting in the form *gārgyāṇakam*. In this case, since the *phak* suffix, which is a *yuvan*-suffix, is treated as if it were a *gotra*-suffix, the suffix *vuñ* is subsequently added by the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhra-*.

"Let there be a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of an aggregate (*samūha*). Having established that this is the purpose of the extended application (*atideśa*) by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the extended application was subsequently rejected.
Likewise...

Regarding the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.39), the words *rājanya* and *manuṣya* in that sūtra denote those who possess Vedic lineages (*śāstrīyagotra*). Furthermore, the word *manuṣya* is established by the addition of the suffix *yat* according to the rule *rājaśvaśurādyat* (Pāṇini 4.1.161).

In that regard, since the suffix *vuñ* is already established for [the descendants of] the *rājanya* and *manuṣya* classes by the very mention of *gotra* in the rule "gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājāhuñ" (Pāṇini 4.2.39), what is the purpose of mentioning *rājanya* and *manuṣya* separately? [The answer is: these two [mentions] indicate that the term *gotra* occurring after the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on "offspring" (*apatya*) refers to the worldly (*laukika*) *gotra*.

In common usage, *gotra* refers merely to offspring. This is because the word *gotra* is employed in the world even for the offspring of a younger generation, as seen in such instances as, "O young brahmin, what is your *gotra*? to which the reply is, "I am a Gārgyāyaṇa. Furthermore, in worldly usage, words such as *rājanya* (kshatriya) and *manuṣya* (human) denote specific castes (*jāti*) and do not signify a *laukika-gotra*; therefore, since they could not be included by the mention of *gotra*, they are mentioned separately.

And thus, according to Gārgyāyaṇa, since even a word ending in the *pha* suffix (denoting the son of a youth) has the meaning of a worldly lineage (*laukika-gotra*), it is included by the mention of "lineage" (*gotra*) even without the extension of the designation "as if it were a lineage" (*gotravat-pravṛtti-atideśa*). Consequently, because the suffix *vuñ* is established for the sense of a collection by the rule "gotrokṣo... [Pāṇini 4.3.160], the extension of the designation is rejected.

Having reflected upon all this—namely, by means of the rule beginning with "iti vuñvidhau" [Pāṇini 4.3.126]—the word "param" means "subsequent to the section on *apatya* (descendants). [Jñāpakasūtra: "The suffix *anaṅ* occurs when there is immediate succession" (Pāṇini 4.1.104). This means that the suffix *ṛk* does not occur when there is immediate succession.

Since the term *gotra* is established by virtue of its governing context (*adhikāra*), the fact that this prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is taught indicates that those [terms] such as *bhida* which are mentioned (*kathyante*) or recited (*paṭhyante*) in the list beginning with *anaḥ* apply even to what immediately precedes them.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: from the sūtra as it is heard—"After *bhidā* and the rest, when there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the suffix *añ* is applied"—it is understood that the suffix *añ* occurs after *bhidā* and the rest in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) only when there is immediate succession, that is, without any interval. If that were the case, then in the sense of "the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) of Kuśika," the form *Kauśika*—derived from the word *Kuśika* with the suffix *añ*—would not be established.

Anticipating the objection that—since Kuśika was a seer (*ṛṣi*), his son Gādhi was also a seer, and his son Viśvāmitra was also a seer, there is no interruption in the lineage of seers, and thus by the rule of exclusion [of non-sequential cases], this [case] constitutes immediate sequence (*ānantarya*)—the author says: "In the case of seers, there is no [immediate sequence]. Immediate sequence means *only* when there is no interval. The locative case in "in the case of seers" (*ṛṣau*) is used to express the locus as a limit (*avadhi*).

And thus, the meaning of the rule *anaḥ TktgrRN;ḥsdvdr1;yānantarye* is that the suffix *añ* does not apply to denote a descendant immediately following [the original progenitor] according to the *Ṛkṣadvṛddhi* [tradition]. The intention is that there is no obstruction whatsoever to the application of *añ* to denote a lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) from the word *kuśika*.

One might object: since the term *gotre* is supplied by anuvṛtti from the rule *gotre kuñjādibhyo ḍhak chaphañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.98), this present rule applies only to the offspring of a *gotra*. Consequently, because there is no possibility of it applying to the immediate offspring (*anantarāpatya*), the statement "the suffix *naḍ* [is used] when there is no immediate succession" is redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the governing influence (*adhikāra*) of the word *gotra*."

In the *ḥcdvddhddhed;idādigaṇa*, both the *anaḥTktgrRN;* suffixes and the *anaḥTktgrRN;* suffixes are recited. Among these, the statement "in the case of immediate succession (*anaḥTktgrRN;*ānantarya)" is intended to indicate that the suffix *añ* occurs even for the immediate offspring (*anantarāpatya*). By this, the form *nānāndra*—meaning the immediate offspring of a *nanāndṛ* (husband's sister)—is successfully derived by means of *añ*. Similarly, *pautra* and *dauḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;tra* are also thus established.

The point is that since the word *bhṛgu* is recited in the *ṛṣy-aṇ* group (*ṛṣyādigaṇa*), the rule "the suffix *añ* occurs after words denoting a seer when forming a descendant of a *gotra*" is restricted to that specific scope. [Jñāpaka Sūtra: *ārag udīcām* (Pāṇini 4.1.230). Since the suffix *āra* is already established by the previous rule, the explicit mention of *āra* indicates that this suffix applies even from other [bases] besides those ending in *rak*.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, from the word *godhā*, by applying the suffix *ḍhrak* in the sense of offspring according to the rule "godhāyā ḍhrak" (Pāṇini 4.1.129), and then applying the augment *āraṅ* according to the rule "āraṅ udīcām" (Pāṇini 4.1.130) in the opinion of the Northern grammarians, the form *gaudhāraḥ* is derived.

Here, one might object that since the word *godhāśva* ends in the vowel *ā*, the form *gaudhāra* could be established even by the suffix *rak*; therefore, the prescription of the suffix *ārak* would be purposeless. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "It is established by *rak*. This means that the suffix *āra* is also prescribed after words that do not end in *ā*, such as *mauṇḍāraḥ* and *jāṇḍāraḥ*.

The intention is that those [forms] are not established by virtue of having the suffix *rak* as their final element; thus there is the statement [of the rule]. [Commentary on Jñāpaka: And therefore, from the sūtra *ataśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.177). In this sūtra, the word *ataḥ* is a reference to that which ends in *at*, because of the specific mention of elision (*luk*) for [the suffixes] *avanti* and others.

[Commentary on Vṛtti: Now, since the word *iti* in the sūtra *ataśca* functions as a qualifier of the *tadrāja* [suffix], when the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the meaning understood is that there is elision of the *tadrāja*-designated suffix ending in *a* when it occurs in the feminine.

And thus, in the sense of "the offspring of Āmvaṣṭha" or "the offspring of Sauvīra," from the word *āmvaṣṭha* and the word *sauvīra*—both of which denote a country (*janapada*) and a Kṣatriya—the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhet-keśalājād-añ-ñyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.169). Because of the presence of the vowel *i*, both forms become *āmvaṣṭhyāḥ* and *sauvīryāḥ*; and [by the rule] *ataś-ca*... [the elision of the feminine suffix follows].

Fearing that the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] would apply by the rule *sū. 4.1.177*, [the author] states: "By the word 'from this' (*ataḥ*), there is a reference to that which ends in it. Thus, in the rule *ataśca* [4.1.175], the extension of the rule to what ends in that (*tadantavidhiḥ*) does not occur. The meaning of the rule is simply that there is elision of the *tadrāja* suffix in the feminine when it consists of the form *akāra*. Examples include *śūrasenī* and so forth. From the word *śūrasena*, the suffix *añ* is applied, and its elision occurs.

However, although *ñyaṅ* ends in the vowel *a*, there is no elision (*luk*) because it lacks the actual form of the vowel *a*; this is the established position. The fact that the inclusion of the word "ending in" (*tadanta*) is not required here is indicated by the statement: "because of the explicit mention of elision (*lugvacana*) for *avantī* and others."

By the rule *striyām avanti-kunti-kurubhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.174), the elision (*luk*) of the *ñyaṅ* suffix following the *tadrāja* [secondary] suffixes *Avanti* and others is prescribed. If, under the rule *ataś ca*, the elision were also prescribed for a *tadrāja* suffix ending in *a* by means of the principle of extension (*tadantavidhi*), then since the elision of even the *ñyaṅ* following *Avanti* and others would be established by *ataś ca* alone, what would be the purpose of the rule *striyām avanti*?

The intention is that the *Khaṭvāṅga* commentary on that sūtra, by stating "and therefore," indicates that there is no rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to forms ending in those stems) in this sūtra. [Jñā. The prohibition "not from *prācya* [clans] such as *Bharga* and *Yaudheya*" (*sū.* 4.1.178) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the elision (*luk*) [of the secondary suffix] after [clans] beginning with *Parśu*. [Vi. Regarding the sūtra "and therefore" (*ataśca*, 4.1.177), it is stated: "The elision (*luk*) must be prescribed for [clans] beginning with *Parśu*."

The word *parśūḥ* is a derivative form (*ḍddhdhḍaddh;āḥsdvdr1;yam*). Its meaning is as follows: in the sense of "the female descendant of Parśu," the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *parśu* by the rule *dhyañ-magadha* (Pāṇini 4.1.170). That [suffix] is elided by the rule *ataśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.177). Then, by the rule *parśvādi-yaudheyādibhyo 'ṇ-añ-au* (Pāṇini 5.3.117), the suffix *aṇ* is added again in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

Since that [suffix] occurs in the section on *bha* (the *ḍhann-prakaraṇa*), its elision (*luk*) is not otherwise applicable; therefore, its elision is prescribed by this rule. Consequently, the form *parśūḥ* is established through the application of the suffix *ūṅ* by the rule "ūṅ utaḥ. With the intention that this statement is unnecessary because the elision is already established by a *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), he says: "Not [in the case of] the Easterners," and so forth.

The elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix following an *i* that is read in the *yaudheya*-class of gaṇas is prescribed by the rule: "Not [the elision] of those from the East, nor of those beginning with *bharga* or *yaudheya*" (Pāṇini 4.1.178). The example is *yaudheyī*. In the sense of "the female descendant of Yudhā," the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule "after a word of two syllables" (sūtra 4.1.121).

Then, by the rule *svārthe’ñ* (Pāṇini 5.3.117), when the suffix *añ* is elided (*luk*), the suffix *ṅīp*—which would otherwise be introduced by the rule *añantalakṣaṇa*—is replaced by *ṅīn* according to the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.73), resulting in the form *yaudheyī*.

If the elision (*luk*) by the rule *ataśca* did not apply even to the *tadrāja* suffixes derived from the fifth class (Pāṇini 4.1.173), then, because there would be no possibility [of such an elision], the prescription of the elision of the suffix *añ* for *yaudheya* and others—which is taught as an exception (*pratiṣedha*)—would be purposeless. Therefore, the meaning is that this exception (*pratiṣedha*) indicates that the elision of the vowel *a* occurs for those [suffixes] following the group beginning with *parśu*.

One might object: since the form *yaudheyī* is established by the suffix *ṅīp* according to Pāṇini 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*) even without the suffix *añ*—derived from the word *yaudheya*, which ends in *ḍhak*—what is the necessity for *añ* here? If this is raised, the answer is no. For when *ṅīp* is applied, the word becomes *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable) due to the *nivṛtti-svara* (the accentuation that follows the disappearance of the original accent); however, when *ṅīn* is applied, it becomes *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Thus, the intention is that there is a difference in accent (*svara*). Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter.

[The *Jñāpaka-ṭīkā* states: Regarding the rule *tadasminn astīti deśe* (Pāṇini 4.2.67), because the word *tat* is mentioned twice in the rule *tad asyāsty asmin* (Pāṇini 5.2.94), it is indicated that in some cases even a single *yoga* (sūtra) may be understood as following [from a previous context], as if it were repeated. However, the rule *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59) was stated by the Teacher through oversight; it could have been formulated differently.

[Commentary on vi: Now, at the beginning of the section on the *cāturarthika* suffixes, four sūtras are recited which set forth four distinct meanings: "When it exists in that place, [the suffix is applied] to denote the name of that place" (Pāṇini 4.2.67), "That by which one has been led away" (4.2.68), "The dwelling place of that" (4.2.69), and "Not far from that" (4.2.70).]

In this regard, the author of the *Bhāṣya* initiated a certain inquiry as to whether these four [rules] combined constitute a single sūtra, or whether these four are separate sūtras. He states that the rule "in a place, it has that name" (*deśe tannāmni*) forms a compound with all four: "that exists in it" (*tadasminnasti*), "it is prepared by that" (*tena nirvṛttam*), "it is its dwelling" (*tasya nivāsaḥ*), and "it is not far from it" (*adūrabhavaśca*).

The suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur in the sense of "it exists in this" when a country is to be understood as having the name of the base [to which the suffix is added]; the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur after a word in the instrumental case in the sense of "settled by him" when a country is to be understood as having that name; the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur after a word ending in the sixth case in the sense of "his dwelling" when a country is to be understood as having that name; and [they occur] in the sense of "not far from it."

The meaning of the four [sūtras] in sequence is as follows: "When a country is to be understood, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur after words ending in *ṛ*, *śatṛ*, *la*, and *anta*, provided they denote that [country]. Examples: *Audumbara*: because there are *udumbara* trees in this country. *Kauśāmbī*: the city so named because it was founded by Kuśāmba. *Śaiśira*: the region inhabited by the Śiśiras. *Vaidiśa*: the city not far from Vidiśā.

These are the illustrative citations. In that regard, according to the view that these four [sūtras] constitute a single sūtra by being combined, the rule *deśe tannāmni* would not apply to the four parts of a compound. For there can be no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of one member belonging to a single yoga within another member that constitutes that same yoga.

If that were the case, then in the sūtra *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59), the second occurrence of the word *tat* would be redundant; for the first *tat* could simply be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the phrase *veda* as well. Anticipating this objection, he says: *tad asyāsty asminn iti*. This is the intended meaning: [The sūtra *tad asyāsty asminn iti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94) provides the basis for the suffix *matup*, which is required here to form the word *mīmāṃsaka* from *mīmāṃsā*. Without this rule, one might incorrectly apply the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *tad adhīte tad veda*, resulting in the undesirable form *mīmāṃsika*. The point is as follows: [The suffix *matup* is introduced after a nominal stem ending in *a* or *ā* when the sense is "he has that" (*tad asyāsti*) or "that is in him" (*tad asminn asti*). Thus, the intention is this: [By applying the rule *tad asyāsty asminn iti matup*, the correct form *mīmāṃsaka* is established.]

In the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94), by accepting that the word *tat* from the preceding part is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) even into the portion *asmin*, the commentary explains it as *matup* in the sense of *tadasmin*. Here, within a single rule, the carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *tat* is observed in the subsequent portion *asmin*. For there would be no carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) across different parts of a single rule.

Regarding the rule *tadasyāsti tadasminnasti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94), one should have made a double mention of the word *tat*. Since he does not do so, it indicates that there is an *anuvṛtti* (carrying over) even within a single sūtra. If this were the case, one might object that the second occurrence of the word *tat* in the sūtra *tadadhīte tadveda* (4.2.59) would be redundant. Anticipating this, he says: *tadadhīte* [is] "composed through negligence."

Kaiyaṭa states that the meaning is: "It was composed through negligence (*pramāda*), characterized by a lack of attention toward brevity, for the sake of easily understanding the auspicious words. Regarding the rule *kartṛ-ādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.95): here, the proposal to extend the application of the word "from a village" (*grāmāt*) from the previous rule by stating "it should be stated as 'and from a village'" has been rejected. In the rule *kartṛ-ādibhyo ḍhakañ*, it is said: "'And from a village' should be stated."

The *vārttika* states: "The term *grāmeyaka* [should be taught]. This is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*: "In that case, it must be stated. It need not be stated. In the rule 'from *katrya*-type words, the suffix *ḍhakañ*', the word 'from a village (*grāmāt*)' is understood to carry over. To this, [the opponent] replies: "In this case, it is said that 'from a village' is carried over"—the remainder of the sense being that it is carried over from the rule "from a village, the suffixes *ya* and *khañ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.94).

Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter. [Jñāna-ṭīkā: *Pūrvāhṇe* (Sūtra 4.3.24)]. The statement of non-elision (*aluk*) in the rule "*ghakālataneṣu*" (Pāṇini 6.3.17) indicates that the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs after a word ending in the locative case (*su-banta*). Although the semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) resides in the locative-ending word itself, nevertheless, because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), one might expect the suffix to be added to that [stem] alone; therefore, this matter must be established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

By the rule *vi-bhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām*, the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭyuL* are prescribed after the words *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*, and the augment *tuṭ* is also applied to them. Examples include *pūrvāhṇetanaṃ* and *aparāhṇetanaṃ*.

Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika stated that since the seventh case endings (*saptamī*) are heard in the words *pūrvāhṇe* and *aparāhṇe*, their status as having a case-ending (*subanta*) must be asserted. His intention was that, because of the governing rule "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a nominal stem" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.1), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) should be added directly to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, the author of the Bhāṣya established the derivation of the secondary suffix from a word with a case-ending (*subanta*) by means of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), and thereby rejected the Vārttika.

Regarding this, [the author] says: *ghakālataneṣu*. By the rule *ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.17), which prescribes the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case (*saptamī*) following a word denoting time when followed by suffixes containing the letter *gh*, *kālā*, or *tana*, it is indicated that the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from the nominal stem itself. Otherwise, since the locative case would not even exist, how could there be any possibility—whether of elision (*luk*) or non-elision (*aluk*)? This is the sense.

[Objection: Is it not the case that this is not something to be established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? For, since the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of [words] that are *samartha*," and because the *Samartha-sūtra* states—by the words of the Bhāṣya—"What, then, is *samartha*? It is a word (*pada*) whose sequence of phonemes has been fixed, which is capable of bringing about the meaning"—it follows that the secondary suffix arises from the very word ending in the suffix (*sūbantapada*). [Response: To this, he says: "Even though... (*yadyapi*), etc., and "Nevertheless... (*tathāpi*), etc.

In the section on secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the rule "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī* or *ā*" (*ṅy-āpprātipadikāt*) also continues to apply. Therefore, for consistency with that, the meaning of the term "samartha" (capable/competent) must be stated. And that [meaning] is: when a case-ending (*sup*) is present, that which is capable of conveying a meaning is "samartha. Thus, the sense is: a secondary suffix is added to a primary nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is first [in order] and is capable of conveying a meaning when a case-ending is present.

Furthermore, since the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* would apply to the nominal stems *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*, there would be no hearing of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). Therefore, by means of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), one must establish the derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) from a word ending in *su* (the nominative singular), and then justify the hearing of the locative case-ending through the non-elision (*aluk*) prescribed by the rule *ghakālataneṣu*. This is the intended meaning. [Jñā.ṭ] The explanation of that [is given under] Sūtra 4.3.66.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it is well known that the term *vyākhyāna* (explanation) applies only to a book (*grantha*). [Objection: But surely, according to the rule—"And [the suffix] after the name of that which is to be explained" (*tasya vyākhyāna iti ca vyākhyātavyanāmnaḥ*)—it is stated that a *taddhita* suffix occurs as prescribed after a word denoting that which is to be explained ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), when an explanation is to be expressed. Thus, just as in examples such as "a book explaining the *sup*s" (*supāṃ vyākhyānaḥ saupaḥ granthaḥ*), [one might expect a similar formation for] Pāṭaliputra’s...

One might object that even in cases such as *vyākhyānī sukosalā* ("the commentary on Sukosalā"), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix would apply; for since the arrangement of walls and so forth in Sukosalā is exactly like that in Pāṭaliputra, Pāṭaliputra is thus "explained" (*vyākhyāyate*) by means of Sukosalā, and thus the condition for the application of the rule exists. Anticipating this objection, [the author notes] that because of the inclusion of the word "name" (*nāman*) in the phrase *vyākhyātavyanāmnaḥ*, [the suffix applies only] to the name of a work consisting of words that is well-known as something to be explained. Therefore...

Intending to show that there is no fault as stated above, he says: "The explanation refers only to those works consisting of words. This means it refers only to those works whose nature is composed of words (*śabdātmaka*). By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), there is an exclusion of non-verbal things such as Pāṭaliputra and the like. [Jñā.ṭ] Vāsudevārjunau (Pāṇini 4.3.98).

This very explanation makes it known that the word mentioned first is the one that is cited. Furthermore, "Vāsudeva" is there the name of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). [Objection: But surely, according to the rule *vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun*, the citation should have been made as *arjunavāsudevayoḥ*.

Anticipating the objection that, because the word *arjuna* has fewer syllables than the word *vāsudeva*, it ought to be placed first according to the rule *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34), he says: "This very [word... and so forth.

This designation is made not only because that which has fewer syllables is used first, but rather to indicate that even when two words have an equal number of syllables, the one that is more significant (abhīkṣṇa) should be placed first. Between Arjuna and Vāsudeva, Vāsudeva is mentioned first because he is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Therefore, the intention is that the prior placement of the word *vāsudeva*—which denotes the most excellent form of the Blessed Lord—is appropriate; by this, forms such as *tāpasagirī* are established. [Jñānendukaumudī on Pāṇini 4.3.140] |||anudātādeśca|| (Sūtra 4.3.140) ||| The rule *anudātādeśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.140) [is applied].

The reading of *garbhiṇī-śabda-pāṭha* in the *Akṣādi* group indicates that as soon as the second vowel becomes manifest (*prāduṣbhāva*), the preceding *anudātta* accentuation (*pūrva-nighāta*) should take effect. For if it were otherwise, after the word *gabhasti*—which begins with an initial acute (*ādy-udātta*)—the suffix *ṅīp* would be applied, and from that form ending in *ṅīp*, only the suffix *aṇ* would be applicable, not the suffix *añ* characterized by the *anudātta*. Thus, the purpose [of the *pūrva-nighāta*] is clearly evident.

The mention of "pada" (word) is for the purpose of defining the scope of the sentence, so that it does not apply beyond it. Regarding the rule *anudātādeśca*: its meaning is that the suffix *añ* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) beginning with an *anudātta* vowel, in the senses of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). Examples include *dādhityam* and *kāpityam*.

And regarding that sūtra, there is the Vārttika: "In the rule prescribing *añ* after a word beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), an addition must be made for words ending in *ṅīṣ* that have an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudāta*). Its meaning is as follows: it must be stated that *añ* also occurs after a word ending in *ṅīṣ* whose initial syllable has an udātta accent, when the meanings are "modification" (*vikāra*) or "part" (*avayava*). The example is *kauvalam*, meaning "a modification of *kuvalī*" (the jujube fruit). The word *kuvala* has an acute accent on the first syllable according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* rule "and for *grāma* etc. (*grāmādīnāṃ ca*). From that [word *kuvalī*], by virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; then, *añ* is added in the sense of a modification.

If it is argued that since the suffix *ṅīṣ* added to the word *kuvala* after the initial syllable is acute (*udātta*)—and because the suffix *ṅīṣ* is acute by its own accentual rule (*pratyayasvara*), while the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule of "the rest being unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), the word *kuvalī* remains unaccented (*anudātta*)—then the suffix *añ* would be established here by the sūtra itself, so what is the necessity for the Vārttika? This is not so, because even though the *ṅīṣ* is acute, the rule of "the rest being unaccented" does not apply here.

Regarding the rule *anudātaṃ padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), which states that a word is unaccented except for one [vowel], here it must be stated that the suffix *śas* is unaccented. Furthermore, that rule concerns words (*pada*). The intention is that *kuvalīśas* is not a word because it lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*subanta*). Following that, there is the Vārttika: "Or rather, [it is unnecessary] because that which is capable [of forming a compound] begins with an unaccented vowel."

And this is its meaning: the term "anudātādeḥ" (beginning with an unaccented vowel) is not a qualifier of "ṅyāpprātipadikāt" (from a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix or a long vowel). If it were so, since the word *kuvalīśa*—ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*)—does not possess the quality of beginning with an unaccented vowel according to the previously stated rule, there would be no occasion for the doubt: "How could *añ* be applied after that? Rather, it is a qualifier of the "samartha" (semantically connected) element, and that which is semantically connected is precisely that which ends in a case-suffix (*sup*).

Consequently, the meaning of the rule *anudātādeḥ su-antād añ* is as follows: from the word *kuvalīśa*, after the suffix *su* has been produced, the suffix *añ* is applied because it ends in *su*. Since the form ending in *su* is a *pada*, by the operation of the rule *anudātaṃ padam ekavarjam*, the single vowel *ī* (of *kuvalī*) is acute (*udātta*) and all else is grave (*anudātta*). Thus, because the sequence *kuvalī ṅs* does not begin with a grave vowel, the suffix *añ* is applied, and the form *kauvala* is established according to the very method of the rule.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, holds that the phrase *anudātādeḥ* ("beginning with an unaccented vowel") is a qualifier only of *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix or a consonant"), and not of *su-bh-antāt* ("from a word ending in a case-suffix"). If it were otherwise, then in the case of *vāco vikāraḥ* ("a modification of speech"), since the case-ending (*sup*) would be udātta by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the nominal stem ending in the case-suffix would be considered *anudāttādi*; consequently, the suffix *añ* would apply [by Pāṇini 4.3.140]. Therefore, [the Bhāṣya] says: "tarhi... [and so on].

Regarding the doubt as to how the suffix *añ* can be established from the word *kuvalī*—which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅī*—since it lacks the status of a nominal stem (*padatva*) and thus the elision of the final syllable (*śeṣanighāta*) does not apply, and consequently it lacks the quality of being "beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātādi*), the following resolution is offered: it is accepted that in a certain word, at the very moment the second accent becomes manifest, an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) takes the place of the previously existing accent.

Regarding the word *kuvalaśā* (the feminine form of *kuvala*), the rule *grāmādīnāṃ ca* prescribes an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*). Consequently, by the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the vowel *ī* becomes acutely accented. When this second accent is manifested, it supersedes the preceding initial acute accent, and that [initial] becomes grave (*anudātta*). Thus, because the word *kuvalīśā* begins with a grave accent, the suffix *añ* is established by the very rule [under discussion].

If it is asked what the authority is for adopting [the reading] "as many as the second vowel" and so forth, the answer is that the *Gārhīṇī-śabdapāṭha* is the authority, as it is the collection (*gaṇa*) of the *gārhīṇīs*. The *gārhīṇīs* are a group (*samūha*).

In this sense, since the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule *anudātāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44), the word *garhāṇīśa* is recited in the *ḍhakṣādi* group (Pāṇini 4.2.38) for the purpose of establishing the suffix *aṇ* as an exception to that. If the word were subject to the *nighāta* accent, then its inclusion in that list would be redundant. Likewise...

The word *ārtiga* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *man*, according to the Uṇādi sūtra "artigaś ca man" (Uṇādi Sūtra 458). From that [base], the suffix *in* is applied. Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by virtue of the word ending in *n*.

Since the word *garhaṇī*—ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—lacks the status of being a *sū* (a nominal stem ending in a consonant), it lacks the status of being a *pada*; consequently, when the rule "anudātaṃ padam" applies, the initial udātta accent of the word *garhaṇī-bhartṛ* does not disappear. Thus, because the rule "anudātāder añ" does not apply, the word *garhaṇī* is included among the *kiṃkṣādi* group [of words that take the suffix *añ*].

By the recitation for the purpose of establishing the *añcu* augment, the reading indicates that as soon as the natural accent (*svarita*) of the second [syllable] becomes manifest, at that very moment the previously established accent of the preceding [syllable], namely the *nighāta*, occurs.

And likewise, since the initial acute accent (*ādyaudāta*) previously prescribed for the time of *insvara* becomes a circumflex (*svarita*), the rule for the suffix *añ* conditioned by having an initial anudātta would otherwise apply; therefore, the inclusion of the word *gargara* in the *hakṣādi* group is purposeful, as it serves to prevent that. The author [Patañjali] demonstrated that the purpose [of this inclusion] is the establishment of forms such as *kauvala*, where the suffix *añ* is successfully applied.

Having reflected upon all this—namely, that [the world] consists of the senses and so forth—the meaning is: "at whatever time" (*yāvaty eva*) means "at whichever time" (*yadā eva*). "At that very time" (*tāvaty eva*) means "at that very time" (*tadā eva*). "Otherwise" (*tathā hi*) means "in another way" (*anyathā*). "The suffix *añ* characterized by the anudātta accent" refers to the remainder of the rule: "The suffix *añ* after a word beginning with an anudātta vowel" (*anudātāder añ*, Pāṇini 4.2.44). Therefore...

In the sūtra *anudātaṃ padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), the mention of the word *pada* is redundant. This is because it has already been established that even prior to the application of *su*-suffixes, the unaccented (*śeṣa-nighāta*) state is attained at the time when the second accent would otherwise apply. To this, he replies: "The mention of *pada* is for the purpose of limitation. That is to say, it serves to restrict the scope.

The inclusion of the term *pada* (word) is for the purpose that, when the status of being a word (*padatva*) is about to be established, only that [syllable] which possesses it should have the anudātta accent, excluding the single [subsequent syllable], so that this does not apply to a collection of words (*padasamūha*). This is the underlying intention. Thus ends the fourth chapter. Now begins the fifth chapter.
[From the Jñānendukaumudī: The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in the locative case, provided it is not one of those beginning with *prākkrīta*. (Pāṇini 5.1.1)]

Regarding the rule *asamāse niḥṣṭhyūtodikhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.20): the mention of *niḥṣṭhyūta* and so forth in this non-compound (*asamāsa*) context is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition against *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to a form ending in the specified word) does not apply to the preceding rules. [Vivaraṇa: Now, regarding the phrase "in a non-compound"...]

In the rule *niḥṣyandādir dhyaḥ*, the exclusion of compounds (*asamāsa-grahaṇa*) is redundant. For if that were absent, the suffix *ṭhak* would apply by this very rule even from the compound *paramaniḥṣyanda-*, whereas it is intended that only *ṭhañ* should apply. And thus:
It should be stated that the mention of the compound [in the rule] is for the purpose of excluding the word *paramaniḥsveda*. This is because,

according to the principle that a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) which possesses a specific suffix excludes the application of that suffix to a word ending in it, the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed after words such as *niḥsveda* would not apply.

Having raised the objection that since the word *paramaniḥśreyasa* (supreme beatitude) is established even without the inclusion of the term *divyāvabhāsa* (divine manifestation)— because [the compound] does not end in *niḥśreyasa* and so forth— the [desired] result follows even without the mention of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), [the author] proceeds as follows:

The mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) in the preceding sūtras is for the purpose of indicating that by the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is also the inclusion of that which ends in it. And thus, by that same principle, it applies here in this sūtra as well.

Since the rule for *tadanta* (extension to forms ending in those stems) would apply, the suffix *ṭhak* could also occur even after words such as *paramaniḥsveda*; therefore, the mention of *asamāsa* (non-compound) is meaningful in order to prevent that. However, the purpose of this indication is [to justify] the rule: "After *khala*, *yava*, *māṣa*, *tila*, *vraśca*, *naḍa*, *khaṇḍa*, *cūrṇa*, *brahman*, and [the word *kuśala*], [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied]" (Pāṇini 5.1.7).
The suffix *yat* prescribed after words such as *khala* occurs even after those ending in *khala* and so forth. Thus, from *kṛṣṇatileṣu* (in black sesame), [the form] *kṛṣṇatilyaḥ* is derived;
likewise from *rājamāṣeṣu*.
Thus, the formation of *rājamāṣa* and so forth is established.
All of this is stated later—namely, "in the case of *niṣka* and so on.
[Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the sūtra 5.1.24 (*viṃśatitriṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvun*): the suffix *kha* is applied after *viṃśati*.

The mention of the suffix *kan* ending in [the word *viṃśaka*] in this rule (*sūtra* 5.1.32) indicates that the suffix *kan* is applied to the words included in this very rule [by the previous rule, 5.1.24]. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "The suffix *ḍvun* is applied after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat* when not used as a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*")...

The suffix *ḍvun* is prescribed after the words *viṃśati* and *triṃśat* when they denote a price (*nīyartha*). For example: *viṃśakaḥ*, *triṃśakaḥ*. In this context, since the condition "provided it is not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) is not explicitly stated, [the rule would otherwise apply] even to names.

Even in the case of a numerical value (*viṣayārthe*), the suffix *ḍvun* would occur; however, in that context, it is intended [only] for forms such as *viṃśatikaḥ* and *triṃśatkaḥ*. Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "when not used as a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*).
But in the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), we have *viṃśatikaḥ* and *triṃśatkaḥ*.
Thus, in both cases, the suffix *kan* is difficult to obtain. Having raised the objection that the suffix *kan* is prohibited by the rule "After a numeral ending in *ati* or *śat*,
[the suffix] *kan* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 5.1.22), [the author] states in the rule "From *viṃśatika*, [the suffix] *kha*" (Pāṇini 5.1.32).

There is no fault [in this], because it is taught that the suffix *ka* occurs after the words "twenty" (*viṃśati*) and "thirty" (*triṃśat*) when they are uttered with the suffix *kan*; thus, the utterance [of the word] ends in the suffix *kap*. Nor is there [any other objection].

The word *viṃśatika* alone was uttered by the author of the Sūtra. Therefore, it must be asked: even if the correctness (*sādhutva*) of the word *viṃśatika* is understood through that, how is the correctness of the word *triṃśatka* to be understood? [It is understood] by means of the word *viṃśatika*.

The intention is that by means of the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the sūtra containing the word "twenty" (*viṃśatiśaḥ*), it is indicated that the suffix *kan* applies even to the two [ordinal numbers] consisting of twenty and thirty which are included in those sūtras; this is because the status of being an indicative mark depends upon its connection with a grammatical rule (*yoga*). [Jñāna-ṭīkā]

In that case, by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.2.116), the seventh case (*saptamī*) occurs after a word ending in the seventh case, as indicated by this very indicator. [Commentary: Now, one might object: "By the rule *tatra tasyeva*, the suffix *vati* is prescribed in the sense of 'like' (*ivārtha*) after words ending in the seventh case and words ending in the sixth case. For example: *mathurāyām iva*..."

Examples such as "the wall in Strughna is like that in Mathurā" (*mathurāvat strughne prākāraḥ*) and "Yajñadatta’s cows are like Devadatta’s cows" (*devadatasyeva devadatavat yajñadatasya gāvaḥ*) illustrate this. In these cases, when the word *iva* is used in conjunction with the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*), the locative case is employed to express similarity (*sāmya*).

Raising the objection: "Even though [the word] *sādṛśye* (in the sense of similarity) exists, since the locative case is not prescribed by any rule in connection with the particle *iva*, how can the prescription of the suffix *vati* after a locative-ending word in the sense of *iva* be consistent?"— having raised this doubt,
[it is replied that] because of this very prescription of *vati* after a locative-ending word in the sense of *iva*, there is an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) regarding the use of *iva*.

He resolves that there is no fault whatsoever by pointing out the indication [of the rule] that "the seventh case-ending is optional"—"from this very [rule]"—by means of the word *iva*. The word "yoga" (connection) is to be supplied.
The result of this indication, however, is as in the case of "like gods" (*deveṣv-iva*) or "like Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇeṣv-iva*).
The application of the term *nāman* and so forth is thus established and becomes valid.

[Jñā.ṭ] What does this indicate regarding *kimidaṃbhyām* (Sūtra 5.2.40)? This very [rule] indicates that after *kim* and *idam*, the suffix *vatup* is applied. [Vi.ṭ] But surely, regarding "*kimidaṃbhyām*..."

Regarding the rule *ve ghaḥ*: does this prescribe the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of the suffix *vatup* following *kim* and *idam*? Examples include *kiyān* and *iyān*. In that regard, since *vatup* is difficult to obtain after *kim* and *idam*, [the rule would otherwise be redundant].

The formulation regarding the *dhātu* (the base) is inconsistent. One might raise the objection that, according to the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the suffix *vatup* is prescribed only after the words *yat*, *etat*, and *tad*; however, anticipating this, he says: "This very [point]... What is this? [It refers to] the two...

The intention is this: since the prescription of *ghatva* for the letter *va*, which is a constituent part of that [suffix], would be untenable in the absence of the suffix *vatup*, the suffix *vatup* is inferred to occur after the interrogative pronouns *kim* and *idam* on the grounds that the prescription of the substitute (*ādeśa*) would otherwise be inexplicable. (Jñā.ṭ [Jñāpakasamuccaya] 8th Āhnika)

[The rule] *aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.127) indicates that [the rule] *asaṃkhyādeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.58) implies [the principle]: "That which ends in [a specific element] applies to the whole compound" (*tadantavidhi*). By this, the form *ekaviṃśatitamaḥ* is established. [Vi.: But surely...]
By the rule "ṣaṣṭhāṣṭābhyāṃ ḍaṇ asaṃkhyādeḥ," since the suffix *ḍaṇ* is prescribed after words other than those denoting numerals,
the augment *tamap* is invariably applied to the *ḍaṇ* that follows a word expressing a number. [Thus,] *ṣaṣṭhitama*.

This is an illustration of such cases. In that context, if the phrase "from asaṃkhyā and so forth" were not stated, then even in the case of *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*, the augment *tamaṅ* would necessarily occur by virtue of the rule:
"The word *viṃśati* and those following it optionally take the augment *tamaṅ*" (Pāṇini 5.2.56).
If it is argued that "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is perceived through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then the purpose of the rule *asaṃkhyādeḥ* must be stated.
