That is not correct, because by the mention of the word *ṣaṣ*, there is a prohibition of the extension of a rule to what ends with that [word] (*tadantavidhi*) when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) already possesses the suffix *ḍa*.

Anticipating the objection that this sūtra would not apply because the inclusion of the word "eka" (one) in the rule for the suffix *ṣaṣṭha* (sixth) would preclude it from applying to the word *aṣṭan* (eight), [the author] says: "after *aṣṭan*, *ādi*, and so forth. And thus:
Being rendered useless by the aforementioned reasoning, the expression "of *asaṃkhyā* etc.

indicates that, within the section on the suffix *-tamaṭ*, there is the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) [to include compounds ending in these]. Consequently, even from words such as *ekaṣaṣṭi*, this sūtra applies the rule of extension to produce the form permanently.
Since the suffix *ḍat* would otherwise entail the addition of the augment *tam*, the phrase "not beginning with a numeral" (*asaṃkhyādeḥ*) is stated to prevent that.
This is because the word *ekaśas*—being composed of the initial constituent *eka*, which denotes a number—is not "not beginning with a numeral. Therefore, [the rule does not apply].
[This is] a difficult point. The result of this [rule] is to provide an indication (*jñāpaka*); by means of that, the twenty-first is established.

This is because, in the rule *viṃśatyādibhyas-tamaḍ-anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.56), the term ending in those [words] is also included through the application of the principle of inclusion of what ends in them (*tadantavidhi*).

By that [rule], even from the word *ṣaṣṭi*, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is replaced by *tamaṭ*, whereby *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ* is established. However, if there were no application of the rule regarding the inclusion of the final member (*tadantavidhi*) within the section concerning *tamaṭ* for the suffix *ḍaṭ*, then [the suffix would apply] only to that which ends with the word *ṣaṣṭi*.
The point is that because the word *eka* is not included in the rule *viṃśatyādirhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.56), the suffix *tamaṭ* would not apply to the suffix *ḍaṭ*;
consequently, the form would have been simply *ekaḥṣaṣṭhaḥ*. [Jñānendrasarasvatī]
And [the suffix yañ] is applied after the group beginning with *sidhma* (Pāṇini 4.2.97).

Since the desired form would have been established simply by reading *adanta-picchādi-tunda-ādi* as a single compound, the fact that they are read separately indicates that the option (*anyatarasyām*) in the rule *laṅ-anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.103) implies a conjunction (*samuccaya*). This is because the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the rule *keśād vo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.109) is repeated here [to indicate such a conjunction].

For the purpose of inclusion: some maintain that this [suffix] is prescribed after *dyu* and *ruha* for the sake of obligatoriness (*nitya*), while others desire it as an optional (*anyatarasyām*) rule. This is because those rules which fall between two alternative rules (*vibhāṣā*) are considered obligatory (*nitya*).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, in the rule "sidhmādiḍhya," the word "anyatarasyām" is understood from the preceding rule "prāṇisthād āto laj anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.2.96). Thus, it follows that after the class of words beginning with *sidhma*, the suffix *lac* optionally occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).

The meaning of the sūtra is explained as follows: this being the case, since there are words ending in *a* in the *sidhya*-class (*sidhyādi-gaṇa*), the suffix *lac* is optionally applied to them. In the alternative where *lac* does not occur, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* would also apply by virtue of the rule "ata iniṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.2.115).
The suffix *matup* is seen [in the word *anubala*].
Anticipating the objection, "How is this established?", [the author] says, "ending in a vowel" (*adanta*), etc.
The intention is as follows: since particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, the term *anu* is understood in this sūtra.
The particle *anyatarasyām* here has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not the sense of option (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, by the mention of *anyatarasyām*, the suffix *matup* under discussion is conjoined [with the suffix *lac*].
Thus, the meaning of the rule is: "From the class beginning with *sidhma*, both *lac* and *matup* occur. Consequently...

There is no possibility of the application of the suffixes *ini* and *thañ*. If it is asked what the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is for the fact that the particle *anyatarasyām* here has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), the answer is: the separate mention of the *piccha*-group and the *tunda*-group in the rules [Pāṇini 5.2.100 and 5.2.117] is the indicator. Likewise...
Regarding the rule *tuṇḍādibhya ilac ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.117), there is a single sūtra.
In that context, four suffixes (*pratyaya*) are observed: *ilac*, *ini*, *ṭhan*, and *matup*.
If, by virtue of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), all four suffixes [are applied],...
Even the *sidhma* group (*sidhmādi*) would be a part of this very same class [of words],
by virtue of its being included in the *anuvṛtti* of the rule "from *loman*, *pāman*, and *piccha*, the suffixes *śa*, *na*, *ila*, and *ka*" (Pāṇini 5.2.100).

The four suffixes beginning with *piccha* would also apply [to words] beginning with *tuṇḍa*. This being the case, by the very recitation of *tuṇḍa* and others in the *picchādi* group, the four suffixes—beginning with *loman* and *pāman*—are established for the *tuṇḍādi* group. Thus, regarding the *tuṇḍādi* group...

The separate rule *ilac ca* is redundant. Alternatively, since the suffixes for words such as *piccha* are already established by the inclusion of *piccha* and others in the *tunda*-group, the four suffixes are obtained by the rule *tundādibhya ilac ca*; therefore, in the rule *lomādipāmādi*, [the mention of *picchādi*] is unnecessary.

The inclusion of *picchā* and so forth [in the *sidhmādi* group] is redundant. Consequently, the separate recitation of these two groups—*picchādi* and *tundādi*—as well as the formulation of separate rules for them, is improper;
thus, the option (*anyatarasyām*) in the rule "sidhmādi-bhyaś ca" (Pāṇini 5.2.97) is stated.

This indicates that the meaning is one of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not one of option (*vikalpa*). And thus, although two suffixes would be established through the conjunction of the *matup* suffix already under discussion, the fourfold group of suffixes beginning with *tunda* would not be established for words such as *piccha*, and so forth. Therefore, [the suffixes] beginning with *piccha*...
The rule *tuṇḍādibhya ilac ca* was formulated after *paṅktiviṃśati...* [Pāṇini 5.1.59].
Since that rule is introduced immediately after the rules for the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan*, the particle *ca* (and) conjoins *matup* with *ini* and *ṭhan*, thereby establishing four suffixes.
However, because the suffixes *ini* and *thañ* are taught prior to the rules for *sidhma-ādi* and *piccha-ādi*,
the suffix *matup* mentioned previously is the one conjoined by the term *anyatarasyām* (meaning "optionally"),
which serves as a conjunction; thus, according to them, there are only two suffixes.

The systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is established. However, in the view that [the suffix] has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*), the intention is that in the case of its absence, all suffixes—whether introduced by the preceding rule or the subsequent one—would apply according to their respective scopes. [This is indicated by the rule] *sidhmādibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.97).

He presents another indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the mention of the word *anyatarasyām* in the Sūtra is intended to signify a conjunction (*samuccaya*), by means of the rule "keśād vaḥ" and so forth.
This refers to the rule: "After *keśa*, [the suffix] *va* is optionally [used]" (Pāṇini 5.1.109).

Since the result is established by merely repeating the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) in the subsequent rule, that [mention] would otherwise be redundant; therefore, it indicates that the mention of "optionally" in the preceding rule is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). And thus, from that [word], as in the case of *keśāt*...

In this context, if the suffix *la* were understood in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), the suffix *ti* would be stated in the sense of option (*vikalpa*). Consequently, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* would also be obtained. It is for this very reason that the four forms—*keśavaḥ*, *keśī*, *keśikaḥ*, and *keśavān*—are established.
This is the intention [of the author].

Others, however, maintain that the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* in the rule *keśād vo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.109) is for the purpose of indicating the obligatory (*nitya*) application of the preceding rule *dyudrubhyāṃ maḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.107); otherwise, *anyatarasyām* would have been included there as well.

Because, if this [rule] were to apply, that [preceding rule] would also result in being non-obligatory (*anitya*); thus, in that very sūtra, he indicates the non-application (*nivṛtti*) of the term *anyatarasyām*. This is precisely why it is said that those rules which occur between two optional (*vibhāṣā*) rules become obligatory (*nitya*).

This has been stated elsewhere. Furthermore, since there is no other purpose for the inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* in the rule *keśād vaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.55), how can it serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the sense of conjunction?
They say that [the suffix] *ḍa* should be prescribed. He restates that: "In the sense of 'always' (*nitya*), one [suffix is used] after *dyauḥ* and *drūḥ*.

However, in reality—since it is possible to establish its obligatory nature by adding the word "obligatory" (*nityam*) to the rule "In the sense of 'always,' *m* [is substituted] for the final vowel of *dyauḥ* and *drūḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.1.84)—for that purpose, [the author resorts to the following sūtra].
The inclusion of the word "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is not appropriate;

therefore, the mention of "anyatarasyām" is merely an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark). It should be noted that this very lack of propriety is what is indicated by the phrase "eke" (some). [Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.117: *ekagopūrvāt*]

The inclusion of the word *nityam* (always) in the rule "ekagopūrvāṭṭhañ nityam" indicates that the suffix *ṭhañ* continues to apply even prior to this specific yoga. [Objection: But surely, in the rule "ekagopūrvāṭṭhañ nityam," the word *nityam*...

It is not useless. Nor can it be argued that, in the absence of *nitya*, the term *anyatarasyām* would carry over from the rule *keśād vo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.109), and consequently, the suffix *matup* might optionally apply in certain cases; therefore, the mention of *nitya* is for the purpose of excluding that [optionality]. This is what must be said.
Since the term *anyatarasyām* from the preceding sūtra has been withdrawn (*nivṛtti*) and therefore cannot be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here,
the inclusion of the word *nitya* is for the purpose of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this reason, [the rule applies] here...

The inclusion of the term *nityam* ("always") in the sūtra indicates that the option (*anyatarasyām*) mentioned in the preceding sūtra is understood to carry over here. Thus, since that option would also apply here, the matup suffix might optionally occur; therefore, [the term *nityam*] is used for the purpose of excluding that.
The intention is that the suffix *ghañ* is compulsory. However, the result of this notification is that the rule *vrīhyādibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.116) is optional.
[Jñāpakasiddhi] *praśasyasya śraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.60): This prescription of the substitute *śra-* applies specifically to the words beginning with *aja* and *ada*.
This indicates that even for those [words] which are not *guṇavacana* (denotative of qualities), the suffix applies provided they begin with a vowel (*ajādī*).

[Objection: But surely, in the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ*, one should carry over the word *ajādī* from the rule *ajādī guṇavacanādeva* (Pāṇini 5.3.58), and having transformed it into the locative case, [apply it here].

The meaning of the sūtra is explained as follows: when the suffixes beginning with *aj* follow, the substitute *śra-* occurs for the word *praśasya*. The suffixes beginning with *aj* are *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. In that context, [the substitution applies] to the word *praśasya*.

Anticipating the objection that the prescription of the substitute *śra-* for *praśasya* is not applicable because [the word] does not denote a quality (*guṇa*), [the author] indicates that for this very reason, the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* occur even after words that do not denote a quality. Consequently, [the rule applies] even from that which is not a word denoting a quality.

Intending to show that the prescription of the substitution of *śr* is appropriate because the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow words beginning with *praśasya*, he says: "of the two beginning with *aj*" (*ajādyoḥ*).
This means when *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow. The phrase "this prescription of the substitution" refers to this very rule.
The meaning is "the prescription of substitutes such as *śra*"; this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), including also the prescription of substitutes such as *jya* and so on.

"Of these, *praśasya*, *vṛddha*, etc. means "of *praśasya*, *vṛddha*, and so forth. [Pāṇini 5.4.14] "After a word ending in *ṇac*, in the feminine"—here, the mention of the word "feminine" (*strī*) indicates that [suffixes] are also used in their own sense (*svārthika*).

"Gender and number transcend their natural limits. [Objection: But surely, in the rule *ṇacaḥ striyāmañ*, the suffix *añ* is prescribed after a word ending in *ṇac* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), provided it is feminine (*striyām*).
This term *striyām* is construed with the suffix *añ*. In that context, regarding the phrase *striyām*:

It is redundant. Since the suffix *ṇac* is prescribed for the feminine by the rule "In the case of the exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*), [the suffix] *ṇac* [is used] in the feminine" (Pāṇini 3.3.43), the suffix *añ*, which is prescribed in its own sense (*svārtha*) after a stem ending in *ṇac*, follows the gender and number of the base according to the maxim: "Suffixes added in their own sense (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the original form (*prakṛti*)."
Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] applies only to the feminine—as in the case of *dhavitrī*—it is stated:

"In that case, since the meaning is already established, the fact that he employs the term 'feminine' (*strī*) indicates that suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) deviate from the gender and number of the base. Therefore...

With the intention that the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) was stated for the purpose of establishing the feminine gender of the suffix *aṅ* by excluding other genders when they might otherwise apply, [the author] says: "In this context, there is the mention of 'feminine'. However, the result of this indication is [seen in forms such as] *guḍakalpā drākṣā*.
"Clarified butter is like oil, and rice-gruel is like milk"—this is established as proven in the *Bhāṣya*. Thus ends the fifth chapter.
[Fragmentary text] ...of the Tattvārtha [Sūtra], Chapter Six. Now begins the seventh chapter.
In the rule *dāśvān sāhvān* (Pāṇini 6.1.12),

the mention of the term "non-homogeneous vowel" (*asavarṇa*) in the rule *aco ñṇiti* (6.4.78) indicates that a rule pertaining to phonemes (*vārṇa*) is weaker than a rule pertaining to grammatical operations (*āṅga*).

For without the increase of the *guṇa* vowels, a doubling of a consonant followed by a non-homogeneous vowel does not occur. [This is to be understood as a refutation (*parihārya*) and is therefore not explained further. [Jñāpakasūtra: "Not when there is *samprasāraṇa*" (Pāṇini 6.1.37). This very prohibition indicates that [the rule applies] to the preceding [vowel].

[Regarding the word *parasya*: it means "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*). [Commentary: Now, by the rule "na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam," it is stated that when a *samprasāraṇa* vowel follows, the *yaṇ* of the preceding vowel does not undergo *samprasāraṇa*. [As in the case of] *yūnaḥ*.

This is an illustration, beginning with the word *yuvan*. When the suffix *śas* follows the word *yuvan*, the form *yuvan-as* remains. Then, by the rule "śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.133), there is a vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the letter *va* into *u*. Thus, when the form *yu-u-an* is established— [the subsequent rules apply].
When the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied by the rule *samprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), resulting in the sequence *yu-un*,

the form *yūnaḥ* is established through the application of the long vowel for homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*). In that context, although the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) would also apply to the letter *y*,
it is prevented by the rule *na samprasāraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.37) regarding the substitution of the letter *v* by the letter *u*.

It is established that when a *samprasāraṇa* follows, the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *y* does not occur. This is consistent only if the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* occurs first in the word *yuvan*;
however, [in your view] it occurs first for the letter *y*.

If the *samprasāraṇa* were performed [simultaneously], then because the condition of being preceded by a *samprasāraṇa* would be absent, the elision (*niḥsṛṣṭa*) would not take effect. Consequently, the *samprasāraṇa* of both [consonants] would occur such that the *yakāra* undergoes *samprasāraṇa* first, and subsequently the *vakāra*.
Anticipating the objection that this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasajyate*), he states: "This very prohibition (*niṣedha*) makes it known.
For if *samprasāraṇa* were to occur for both [vowels], the purpose of the prohibition would be rendered useless.

And by the prohibition [of *samprasāraṇa*] for the preceding [vowel], it is made known that the *samprasāraṇa* applies to the following *yaṇ*, not to the preceding one. Consequently, when the *samprasāraṇa* of the following [vowel] has been performed,
since the [application of *samprasāraṇa*] to the preceding [vowel] would also have occurred, the prohibition is established.

The intention is that there is the fulfillment of the purpose for that which has no further application (*niḥśeṣa*). Regarding the rule *pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), the mention of the two case endings (*vibhaktyoḥ*) here serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the word *tasmāt* in the subsequent rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ* (6.1.103) refers back to the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the preceding sound).
In the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, the term *prathama* indicates that which has become the first among those arranged in sequence within a certain arrangement;
this is known from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *dīrghājjasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105).

The meaning results in [the reference to] the two initial *bhūtas* (elements) among those that constitute the arrangement of the *sac-dvddhddhed;* (the *sacchabda*). In that regard, which are the two initial *bhūtas*?
Is it the two *vibhaktyoḥ* (case-endings), or rather the two *pratyayayoḥ* (suffixes)? Such is the doubt. Now, [one might object]: "In the rule *iko yaṇaci*..."

From this [sūtra 6.1.77], the word *aci* is understood to carry over. And that is a qualification of the phrase *prathamayoḥ*. Consequently, the meaning established is "of the two nominative cases beginning with a vowel. In that context, although the nominative singular suffix *su* does not begin with a vowel, [the rule still applies].
By taking the "ajādi" (beginning with a vowel) status from another constituent element, it is possible to state that the first two [elements] possess the "ajādi" status; however,
this is not the case for the two suffixes (*pratyaya*) when they are included in the *grahaṇa*.

Because *su* and *śas* do not belong to the class beginning with *aja*, and because *au* and *jas* are not among the first [cases], the interpretation that "the two suffixes beginning with *aja* are the first" is untenable. Consequently, the mention of "the first two" must refer exclusively to the first two case-endings (*vibhakti*). Where [is this stated]?

If it is argued that there is no possibility for doubt [regarding which two are meant], we say no; for the phrase "beginning with *aj*" (*ajādī*) itself is the qualifier of "the two nominative endings" (*prathamau*). Thus, since they are established as being "beginning with *aj*," the meaning is:
"after those two nominative endings which [are so designated] in relation to other suffixes beginning with *aj*. After those two, [the rule applies].

Since it is also possible to explain that the rule *pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ* applies specifically to the two suffixes *au* and *jas*, one might ask: does the term "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*) refer to the first two case-endings, or [to the first two vowels]?
Because there is doubt regarding the two suffixes [of the first case], the state [of the rule] remains as it was; therefore, he says:

"here. In the sūtra *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103), when the two suffixes beginning with vowels (*aja-dyauḥ*) are mentioned as the first two, it refers specifically to the suffixes *āṬ* and *jas*.

By that rule [Pāṇini 6.1.102], the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ) would be substituted. However, in the case of the suffix *śas*, since the substitution of the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding does not apply, how could the letter *s*—which is a constituent part of *śas*—be subsequent to that which has undergone the substitution of the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding? How could it possibly exist?

Therefore, by using the word *tasmāt* (from that), the author of the Sūtras implies his acceptance of the long vowel resulting from the same preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) even for the neuter; the sense is that in the rule *prathamayoḥ*, there is no inclusion of the dual number alone. [Jñā.ṭ]

And because of *samprasāraṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.108). The rule for the substitution of *āṅ* with *pir* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) is stronger. For example, in *adya + ūḍha* > *adhyūḍha*, the *guṇa* substitution—which is an internal operation—is applied first to the root and the prefix (*dhātu-upasarga-yoga*). Thus, the prefix undergoes the change first.

The connection is with the *dātu* (the giver), not with the word *adyaśas* (fame); for the word *adyaśas* is connected with the entire compound. Regarding the rule *samprasāraṇācca*, there is the Vārttika: "In place of the *guṇa* resulting from *āt*, there is the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrghatva*) before *āṅ* and *abhyāsa*. *Āiṅ*.

And in the case of *āṅ*, when both *ādguṇa* and *savarṇadīrgha* are applicable, only *savarṇadīrgha* occurs and not *ādguṇa*; this is the purpose [of the rule]. The citation "āṅ idyoḍhā" is an example. When "adya ā" becomes "adyoḍhā," in the state where "adya" and "ā" [are present], [the rule applies].

When *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence) applies, as in *adyā uḍhā*, the form *adyoḍhā* is established by *ādguṇa*. However, if first *eC aC > ai au* (*aiṅ aic*) were applied, resulting in *ady-au-ḍhā*, and then *guṇa* were applied to these two, the form would become *adyauḍhā* due to *vṛddhi*; such is the intention of the Vārttika. But is this Vārttika not improper? At the outset...

If a long vowel were produced by the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), then the prescription of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule *omāṅośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.95) would become redundant. Likewise, in the case of *śiva ā īśvaraḥ*,
where *ā* and *īśvaraḥ* undergo the *ādguṇa* substitution, [the result would be] *śiva*.

When *eḥ* is thus established, and the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88) would otherwise apply to produce a vṛddhi, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is prescribed as an exception to that. Furthermore, if the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) were to occur first instead of the guṇa substitution in *ādguṇaḥ*, then [the form would be] *śiva ā anayoḥ*.

One might object: "Once the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* has occurred, and subsequently the *guṇa* [by P. 6.1.87], the form is already established as *śiveḥ*. What, then, is the purpose of prescribing the single-substitute (*pirarūpa*) rule? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The single-substitute [is prescribed] by *āṅ*. And thus, [the rule is necessary for cases where there is] an *antaraṅga* [operation].

The formulation of the augment *āṅ* is for the purpose of making known the rule that "that which is more internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger. Since the operation of the *guṇa* substitution [of *ā* + *i* = *ai*] is internal because it is an operation dependent upon both the root and the prefix, [the form] becomes *āi*.

Thus, since the *guṇa* substitution would subsequently apply to these two [vowels], the undesired form *śivaidhi* would result; therefore, the rule prescribing *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent vowel) for *aiṅ* is meaningful as a means of preventing that *guṇa*. This is the intended sense. [In this context,] the prefix (*upasarga*) is first combined with the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.

The reason why *yoga* is not [formed] with the word *adyaśas* is provided by the rule *tu*, which states that there is no connection (*saṃbandha*) between the prefix *āṅ*— which has the sense of a locus (*adhāra*) in the case of the word *adya*—
and the word *adya*. This is because a locus requires a verb, and the prefix *āṅ* does not denote an action.

Action (*kriyā*) is expressed by the combination of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and a prefix (*upasarga*). Therefore, the connection with the suffix *śas* occurs only through the combination of the root and the prefix, and not by the prefix *āṅ* alone, which does not denote action; such is the sense. [Jñā.ṭ] Regarding the unaccented (*anudātta*)...

And regarding *yatra* (Pāṇini 6.1.161): because the augment *ayac* is marked with the *cit* indicator, it is indicated here that the rule "the end" (*anta*) does not apply. Thus, by implication, the beginning is acute (*udātta*). [This refers to] the rule *anudātasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ*, which means: when an acute vowel is elided after an anudātta vowel.

The meaning is that an acute (*udātta*) [vowel] takes the place of that grave (*anudātta*) [vowel]. In this context, either it refers to the acute [vowel] of that cause (*nimitta*) depending upon which the elision of the acute occurs where no acute exists; or, disregarding its status as a cause, it refers to the acute [vowel] that follows a phoneme (*varṇa*) in which no acute exists.

Alternatively, the explanation of that accent may be that it is called *udātta* because of the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *u*. This is what is intended [by the author]. In that regard, according to the first position, one should carry forward the word *anta* from the sūtra: "The final syllable of a *ghañ*-formed stem ending in a *kṛt* suffix with a penultimate *ṛ* is *udātta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.159).

The meaning of the sūtra is established as "the end of that which lacks an udātta [accent] is udātta. However, in the second alternative, since an udātta is prescribed for the vowel itself that is anudātta, the term "end" (anta) does not apply because there is no further result [to be achieved]. And thus, in the second alternative, it means "the beginning of the anudātta [syllable] is udātta."

The result [of the analysis] is as follows: in the first alternative, it results that the end of the *anudātta* (unaccented) syllable is *udātta* (accented). When the doubt arises as to which of these two alternatives is better, [the author] states that the second alternative alone is superior—namely, "because of the *cit* designation applied to *ayac*. This is because this [suffix] has two constituent parts (*avayava*).

In the sense of "that which has three parts," the suffix *tayap* is applied according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* (Pāṇini 5.2.42) after the words *dvi* and *tri*. Furthermore, for this *tayap*, the substitute *ayaj* is applied by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyaj vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.43). Thus, [the form] *traya* is derived from *tayap*.

The suffix *pit* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Consequently, the *ayac* that replaces it is also unaccented by virtue of the rule *sthānivadbhāva*. When this [suffix] follows, the *ikāra* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Thus, in the forms *dvayam* and *trayam*, [the following applies]: *anudātasya ca*...

By the previously stated rule, "yatrodātalopaḥ," since the initial *a* of *aya* would have been acute (*udātta*), the suffix *ayac* is marked with the *cit* accent so that it may instead be acute at the end (*antodātta*). Furthermore, if the word *anta* were to carry over (*anuvarteta*) from the rule "anudātasya ca," then [the rule would apply] to that which is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Since the word *aya* is already acute (*udātta*) by its very nature as a *dhātu*, and since the desired result is thus established, what is the purpose of making the affix *ayac* marked with the *cit* accent? Therefore, the application of the *cit* accent indicates that the word *anta* does not carry over (*anuvartate*) into this rule. If it does not carry over, then for this *aya* which is [otherwise] unaccented (*anudātta*), [the rule applies].

When "udātta" (acute) is mentioned, since there is no reason to bypass the first [element], it follows by implication that it refers to the initial [syllable] alone. Therefore, the purpose of applying the *cit* marker to the suffix *ayac* is meaningful, as it serves to indicate that the final syllable is acute.
The result of this rule-statement (*jñāpana*) is the establishment of the acute accent for the vowel *ā* in the form *vindāte*.

Otherwise, the internal vowel *e* would be udātta. According to the rule "tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātam" (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the suffix *āte* following the root *vid* in the sense of "discernment" (*vicāraṇe*) would be anudātta.

By this rule (*sūtra*), [the *śna*] is unaccented (*anudātta*). Because *śnam* is an affix (*pratyaya*), it is accented (*udātta*). Then, when the *ś* and *n* are elided by the rule "of *śna* and *as*" (*śnasor allopaḥ*), the accentuation of the vowel *ā* is observed according to the aforementioned rule.
However, if the mention of the final letter (*antagrahaṇa*) were not repeated, only the vowel *e* would be accented.
It should be understood thus: [Pāṇini 6.1.182] "After a long vowel belonging to a word ending in *aṣṭan*."

The mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "eight" (*aṣṭan*), and it serves as an indicator for the optional substitution of *ā* (*ātvavikalpa*) for the sake of the suffix *nuṭ* when the word ends in *ākāra*. [Objection: But surely, regarding the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt*...

The meaning is that a *vikti* (case-ending) beginning with *śas* and following after a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is acute (*udātta*). The citation "aṣṭāsu" is an example. Here, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) need not be included. Nor, in its absence, would there be any issue regarding the form "aṣṭasu."

Since the word *su* following the term ending in *ras* [from *aśiṣṭasu*] would otherwise be acute-accented by the rule *su-ut-tama-jas-ām udāttaḥ*, it must be stated that the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is for the purpose of preventing that. This applies in the case of the form *aśiṣṭasu*.
By the rule *jhalyupottamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.180),

which means that in a word ending in a case-suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, the penultimate (*upottama*) syllable shall be acute (*udātta*) when followed by a suffix marked with the markers *ṣ*, *ṇ*, *ṭ*, *t*, *c*, or *u*,
[the penultimate syllable] becomes acute.

Since the vowel *ā* following the letter *ṭ* is itself udātta, the word *su-* does not acquire udātta status by the preceding rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 6.1.172). Nor can it be argued that even in the case of *aṣṭāsu*, the penultimate accent (*upottama-svara*) would prevail due to its posteriority; for this objection is refuted by the principle of *yena nāprāpte*.

It must be resolved that in the case of *aṣṭānām*, the penultimate accent (*upottama-svara*) possesses the status of an exception (*bādhakatva*). And likewise, by the same logic, in the case of *aṣṭasu* as well, the penultimate accent is set aside [by the final acute] because it is an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, [the form] becomes *aṣṭābhyaḥ*.
It should not be argued that the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is purposeful because it serves as a means to prevent [the application of] the *viḍ-bhakti* accent;
for in the case of the word *aṣṭāsu*,
when the *ṇatva* (nasalization) of the *n* occurs, there is an absence of the status of ending in *n* (*nakārāntatva*) due to the prescribed change of *n* to *a*.
Since the accent prescribed by the rule *jhaly upottamam*— which is formulated in dependence upon the designation *aṣṭan*— would not otherwise apply,
and since that [accent] would necessarily result [in that case], the sūtra *aṣṭanaḥ* is composed.

Because it is impossible to state [otherwise], there is an absence of an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, in the case of *aṣṭasu*, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), only the penultimate accent (*upottamasvara*) will occur.
Even if the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) were not admitted, because that elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), [the word] remains one ending in *n*.
Because it is designated as having the *ṣaṣṭha* (sixth) name, the low-pitched (*upottama*) accent is applied.
Consequently, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) would be redundant; therefore, he says:
"The mention of 'long' is for the sake of the sixth [vowel]. Thus, the mention of "long" serves to establish the substitution of *āt*.
This is for the purpose of making known that the designation *ṣaṭ* applies even when [the word] is declined [in other cases]. And thus,
in the case of *aṣṭāsu* as well, since the designation *ṣaṭ* applies, the rule *aṣṭanaḥ* is commenced precisely because the *upottama*-accent would otherwise have been required.

By the principle of non-attainment (*aprāptinyāya*), the rule *aṣṭana* does not function as an exception (*apavāda*) [to the preceding rule]; thus, in the form *aṣṭāsu*, the *upottama*-accent does not apply. By the same logic, since the rule *aṣṭasu* would also be an exception [to the general rule], the accent of the nominal suffix (*vibhaktisvara*) would have applied [instead].
The mention of *tīrtha-grahaṇa* (the inclusion of the word *tīrtha*) is for the sake of including that [suffix] by way of being its door; thus, it achieves its purpose within its own scope.
As for the result of making this known elsewhere, it is stated: "for the sake of the *nuṭ* augment in the case of a stem ending in long *ā*" (*ākārāntasya nuḍarthaḥ*).
This refers to the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.84) in the context of *aṣṭana ām*.

The point is that when the substitution of *ā* for the letter *n* is applied, even a word ending in *ā* is designated as *aṣṭan* by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*); consequently, by the rule "aṣṭacatuḥ-bhryaśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.55), the augment *nuṭ* is added to *ām*, and thus the form *aṣṭānām* is established. Alternatively:

Because the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* prescribed by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* is compulsory (*nitya*), in the locative plural form, only the form containing the long vowel, *aṣṭāsu*, occurs, and not the form containing the short vowel, *aṣṭasu*.
And likewise, having raised the objection that the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would be redundant as it excludes those [cases],

[the author] states that the mention of the long vowel is for the purpose of making known that the *ātva* (substitution of *ā*) being prescribed after *aṣṭan-* is optional. And thus, in the alternative case where *ātva* is absent, [it applies] to the forms of *aṣṭan-*.

Thus, since *rūpa* also exists as a real entity (*sadbhāva*), the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in that rule is meaningful for the purpose of ensuring the non-application of the accent prescribed by the rule "aḥsdvdr1;ṣṭanaḥ"; this is stated because there is also an option regarding the substitution of *ā*.
Thus, the single long vowel *ai* (in *aikṣi*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for two rules;
the intention is that because it would otherwise be impossible [to account for], it can indicate even multiple meanings.
It is stated "and so forth" (*ceti*) to suggest this very point. However, in reality, regarding the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, [the following applies].
Because the designation *ṣaṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) relative to the substitution of *āt*, when the designation *ṣaṭ* is to be applied,
that *āt* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being external (*bahiraṅga*).
Consequently, since the designation *ṣaṭ* is established by virtue of the word ending in *n* [before the substitution], the *nuṭ* augment caused by that designation applies by the rule "nopadhāyāḥ."

Since the form *iṣṭa* is established by the rule *dīrgho na-lope ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), there is no need for a further explanatory purpose (*jñāpana-phala*). Therefore, it should not be taught that "the designation *śat* applies when the substitution of *ā* has been made," because the substitution of *ā* occurs by virtue of the [preceding] rule. Thus, the substitution of *ā* is [already] established.

The mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal suffix (*vacana-jñāpakatayā*). And the purpose is the establishment of two forms, such as *aśiṣṭaḥ* and *aśiṣṭābhiḥ*. Consequently, it appears that in the rule *ātva-vikalpasya ca*, the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of *vā* (or).

[Pāṇini 6.1.185] states: *titsvaritam*. This indicates—by means of the *tapara* marker (*u*) in [Pāṇini 6.1.131], *diva aut*—that when a vowel is being designated by the letter *u*, it includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). And thus, in the case of *au*, this serves to exclude the long vowel.

Regarding the rule *tapara*: the necessity of including the letter *t* in the mention of suffixes (*pratyaya*) has been refuted by relying on the letter *d* found in the substitutes (*ādeśa*). In the *tapara* sūtra, the letter *d* is also included as a variant form (*cartva*) of the letter *t*. [Vi.]

In the rule *ṭhitisvaritam*, there is the *vārttika*: "The mention of *ti* refers specifically to an affix (*pratyaya*). Its meaning is as follows: it must be stated that only an affix ending in *ti* becomes *svarita*. Otherwise, in the case of *kirati*, [the rule] *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) would apply.

Since the *ikāra* being prescribed by the sūtra would also possess the quality of *tit*, it would consequently incur the status of *svarita*. Desiring to refute this vārttika, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "In the rule *Añtaḥ id*, the substitute *ikāra* is *dit*; and since it is not *tit*, the *svarita* accent does not apply."

Thus he spoke. Regarding this, if a division (*cheda*) were made as *antaḥ it*, then the substitute for the original long vowel would be the closest corresponding (*antaratama*) long vowel, namely the letter *i*. Anticipating the objection that if the *tapara* marker (*aḥ*) is employed, then only a short vowel of that same duration (*tatkāla*) would be understood, [the author] says:
Having resolved that, by the restrictive rule (*paribhāṣā*) "there is no inclusion of homogeneous vowels when [a vowel] is being substituted," the short *ik* vowel alone remains;
therefore, the substitute is indeed *id*, which includes the letter *d* as an inherent part of the suffix, provided that...
If it is stated that there is no inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*) when [the vowel] is being substituted,
then in the case of *amūbhyām*, at the stage *adā bhyām*, the long *ā* following the *d* would [be subject to substitution] by the rule *adaso 'ser dādudo maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80).

The letter *u* mentioned in the sūtra would not be a substitute for its homogeneous counterpart, the long *ū*, because it is being prescribed [as a short vowel]. Consequently, in the form *amūbhyām*, there would be only the short *u*;
thus, [the author] raises this objection once again.

It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In that case, the Teacher’s traditional teaching (*ācāryapravṛtti*) indicates that when the vowel *u* is being pronounced, it includes the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*).
This is because he [uses] the vowel *u* in the rule 'diva ut' (Pāṇini 6.1.131)."
"He makes [the vowel] followed by *t* long (*taparaṃ karoti*). Having reflected upon this, he states:

"By saying 'it indicates the state of being followed by *t* (*taparatvam jñāpayati*),' and so forth. Regarding its own scope (*svāṃśe*), he says: "And thus, in the case of *dyauḥ* and *dyubhyām*," where, after the form *div* has become *dyu*, it stands as *dyu-bhyām*.

Because the letter *va* is followed by a *jhal* consonant, the rule *ca-cha-voḥ śū-ḍ-anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) applies, resulting in *ū*. When *dyū* is established by this, the letter *ū* undergoes the substitution of *u* according to *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), and with the subsequent application of *yaṇ*, the form *dyauḥ* is established as *dyubhiḥ*. In this case:

The point is this: since the vowel *u* being substituted [for *as*] would, by virtue of the rule for including homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), include its long counterpart, it would result in the substitution of *ū*; therefore, the use of *ut* with a long *ṛ* (taparakaraṇa) is meaningful as a means to exclude that possibility. However, its purpose elsewhere is seen in forms such as *amūbhyām*.

Now, one might object: since the vowel *u* prescribed by the rule *diva ut* is a *ti*-element, the term *pratyaya* (suffix) must necessarily be included in the word *ti* in the rule *titsvaritam* in order to prevent that *u* from being circumflex (*svarita*). Therefore—
Regarding the mention of the *tit* designation:
likewise, in the rule *diva ut*, the substitute is simply *ut*. Consequently, by the very absence of the *tit* designation, the *svarita* accent would not otherwise apply.
The sense is that the substitution of *e* and *ai* for *pra* and *ati* respectively is not mandatory.
Now, if *ud* were the substitute, then by the application of the rule "taparas tatkālasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.70),
the substitute would also have to be the long vowel *au*.
Anticipating the objection that [the rule] might not apply, he says: "In the *tapara* sūtra.

Thus, in the rule *taparaḥ*, the letter *da* becomes *ta* by the rule of *cartva* (the substitution of *ta* for *da*), resulting in the sūtra *taparaḥ*. The meaning of the sūtra is: "A sound followed by *t* or *p* is the name for its own duration. Consequently, [the vowel] *ud* is indeed of its own duration.

The form *pravaḥ* [is derived] from *pra-vah*, as in the example *pravaḥtetaḥ na dīrghasyāpatiḥ*; this is the established view (*bhāvaḥ*). The mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) in this context (Pāṇini 6.1.192) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), a composite unit (*saṅghāta*) is the subject of the operation. The mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a grammatical commentary (*bhāṣya* or *vṛtti*) on Pāṇinian sūtras, specifically discussing the technical term *pūrva* and its role in accentuation rules.]

There is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rules governing accents (*svaravidhi*) that the locatives [in such rules] are locatives of the final member (*tadantasaptamī*). [Objection: But surely, by the rule "In the case of *dhī*, *hrī*, *bhī*, *kṣu*, *mad*, *jana*, *dhana*, *daridra*, and *jāgara*, [the acute accent falls] on the syllable preceding the suffix when it is marked with *P*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.192),...

It is prescribed that for roots ending in a long vowel (*ḍīpratyayānta*) followed by a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix, the syllable preceding the affix shall be acute (*udātta*). The example given is *juhoti*;
here, the vowel *o* preceding the affix [is acute].

The state of being acute (*udātatva*). In the absence of this sūtra, the acute accent would apply by the rule *anudāte ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.190). In that case, what is the purpose of mentioning the term *pratyaya* [in the sūtra]? It is not [for the sake of the word] *hibhyāni*, where, in the absence of that [mention of *pratyaya*], the suffix *ni* would be followed by *pit*.

The acute accent (*udāttatva*) would apply to the *āṭ* that precedes [the suffix]; however, it is observed that the accent applies only to the *ciṇ* that precedes the *āṭ*. For that purpose, the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is made. And when that is present, by the rule regarding augments (*yadāgamanyāya*), the *āṭ* which has been added becomes part of the suffix; therefore, the accent applies to what precedes the suffix.

When it is stated that [the vowel] is acute (udātta), one must state that the mention of the suffix (pratyaya) is for the purpose of ensuring that the acute accent applies specifically to the vowel *ā* that precedes the *ṇi*, as in the case of "āni."

Even in the absence of the mention of a *pratyaya* (suffix), since it is stated that "that which precedes a *pit* [suffix] is acute," and because *pit* has not been mentioned here, the *āṭ* augment is also understood by the mention of *pit*; thus, when *āni* follows,
from that...

Anticipating the objection that since the first [vowel] itself would be acute, the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) would be redundant because the augment *āṭ* does not acquire an acute accent, he states its purpose as being indicative (*jñāpaka*):
"The mention of the suffix here... and so forth. Likewise...
Furthermore, being redundant according to the aforementioned method, the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) indicates that in rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*),

a combination (*saṃghāta*) is intended. Consequently, let there not be the acute accent (*udātatva*) for the preceding combination starting from *āni* and *itaḥ*, but rather let there be the acute accent for the vowel preceding the suffix, as is desired.
The intention is that the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is for the sake of [the rule] *syāt*.
However, the result of this indication is stated in the Bhāṣya as follows:
"The low-pitched (*anudātta*) nature of [suffixes] beginning with *cit*, *svara*, and *tāsi* is due to conflict (*vipratishedha*)."

"What was stated is logical: 'it becomes *ḍhatva*. This is its intended meaning: in the case of *āsīnaḥ* and *śayānaḥ*, because the suffix *śānac* is marked with *cit*, the final vowel of the root would have been udātta by rule.
However, according to Pāṇini 6.1.186, "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following a verbal root taught with an *anudātta* marker, or one ending in *ṅ* or *t*, is *anudātta*."

Thus, although the *anudātta* accent would also apply to the *śānac* suffix, since both [the *anudātta* and the *udātta*] would be applicable, the Vārttikakāra stated in the rule *tāsyanudātet* that, according to the principle "in case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam*, Pāṇini 1.4.2), the *anudātta* alone takes effect due to its posteriority.
And that [rule] is only applicable if the entire complex (*saṃghāta*) were the subject of the operation in the rule concerning accents (*svaravidhi*);

otherwise, by the principle "of the first of the following" (*ādeḥ parasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.54), there would be the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) for the initial *ā* of the suffix *śānac*, and the high-pitched accent at the end (*antodāttatva*) for the final syllable by the rule "of a *cit*-marked element" (*citaḥ*).

Due to the absence of contradiction, the application of the rule for conflicting sūtras would not be possible. However, if the entire cluster were intended to have its own accent, then the fact that the cluster *āna* is unaccented (anudātta) would contradict the fact that its final element is accented (udātta);
thus, there is a conflict in this way.
According to the *Vārttika*, the statement that [the suffix] is unaccented due to its subsequent position is correctly established;
for in the very rule *ḍhīhrī* (Pāṇini 6.1.192), the locative case ending in *piti* is heard, and thus,
by the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), [the operation applies to what precedes it].

Anticipating the objection—"Since [the rule] *parihṛddhḍaddh;āḥsdvdr1;ayā pūrvasya* will apply [by the general principle], what is the purpose of the mention of *pūrva* in the sūtra *pratyayātpūrvaṃ piti* (Pāṇini 6.1.192)?"—he states: "The mention of *pūrva*... [is for the sake of... .

And likewise, in the rule concerning vowel accents (*svaravidhi*), the mention of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of indicating that locative cases (*saptamī*) there are locatives of the final member (*tadanta-saptamī*). Furthermore, in the view that [the term refers to] the final member,
the *bhī-prabhṛti* group is cited as an example where the son (*pit*) follows.

The meaning of the sūtra would then be that "it (the vowel) becomes udātta up to that [final] point. In this case, all vowels of the suffixes would become udātta by turns. Since it is desired that only the single vowel preceding the suffix be udātta, the word "pūrva" (preceding) is included for that purpose.

Its purpose regarding its own scope is fulfilled. However, its purpose as a *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) is seen in rules such as "upotamaṃ riti" (Pāṇini 6.1.216). In that context, when the suffix *rit* follows, the acute accent (*udātta*) is not prescribed for the penultimate syllable (*upotama*), but rather for the word ending in the suffix *rit*.
"That which is immediately preceding it is observed to have the udātta accent" [referring to *jñā.ṭ*:

*saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204)]. The statement that the first member of a comparison is udātta is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is a prohibition of the application of affixal accent (*pratyayalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) in the case of the accent characterized by *anuḥcdvddhddhed;* (i.e., the *kṛt-svara*). [referring to *vi.ṭ*: "But surely..."]

The rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam*— which prescribes that the first syllable of a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is acute-accented when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*)— is redundant. For even in the absence of that rule, in cases such as *cañceva cañcā*,
the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.97) would still apply.

It should not be asked how the initial acute accent (*ādyaudāta*) is established in the word *cañcā*— which is derived with the elision (*lup*) of the suffix prescribed by Pāṇini 5.3.98 (*lum manuṣye*)— since the initial acute accent is established by the very rule "the first syllable of that which ends in *ñ* or *n* is always acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.198), by resorting to the principle of "treating as if present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) the suffix *kan* even though it has been elided.

Raising the objection that, because the initial acute accent (*ādyaudāttatva*) does not fall under the jurisdiction of the *aṅga* (the stem), the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63)—which prohibits the application of suffix-based operations—would not apply here, the author replies: "of the upamāna" (*upamānasya*). Thus, since the accent in cases such as *cañca-* would already be established by the general rule of suffix-based operations (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the rule "saṃjñāyām upamānam" (Pāṇini 6.2.80) would otherwise be redundant. Being thus purposeful, it indicates that suffix-based operations do not apply to an accent caused by a subsequent element (*anubandha*).

And thus, because the designation *it* for the vowel [of the suffix] in the rule "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [acute]" (*ñnityādirnityam*) is caused by that very designation, when that [designation] is to be applied, the status of the suffix as a *pratyaya* (by virtue of Pāṇini 1.1.62) does not apply to the element *cañcā*. Consequently, since the initial acute accent (*ādyaudāta*) would not otherwise apply, the rule "in a name, the upamāna [is acute]" (*saṃjñāyāmupamānam*) is meaningful as the means to achieve that accent; such is the intention.

The purpose of this indication [of the accent] is as follows: in examples such as *gargāḥ*, where the meaning is "the descendants in the lineage of Garga," the suffix *yañ* prescribed by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105) undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañoś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64). If one were to rely on the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) for that elided suffix, the initial acute accent (*udātta*) would have been required by the rule *ñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197). [This indication prevents that result.]

And that [prohibition] does not apply here because of the indication that the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not operate when a vowel characterized as *anudātta* follows. [Jñā.ṭ] In rules such as *notarapade'nudātādāvapaḥpṛthivī* (Pāṇini 6.2.142), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *apaḥ*, *pṛthivī*, and so forth, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle: "In the formulation of accentual rules (*svaravidhi*), a consonant is treated as non-existent."

In the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), the exclusion of *anāvaḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the principle that "in the attainment of the accent of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*), a consonant is as if non-existent. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *anantaraḥ* ("immediately preceding") in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) indicates that when a specific condition is stated, it applies even to a compound preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*.

[Viṭ] The derivations (*pariṣkāra*) of these three [terms] are not explained here, as they have already been recited in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*. [Jñā] By the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu* (Pāṇini 5.4.140), the mention of the word *mūrdhasu* indicates that *viṣva* is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*).

By the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197), when the words *pād*, *dan*, or *mūrdhan* follow *dvi* or *tri* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable is prescribed.

In that regard, examples of the word *mūrdhan* [ending in] *śas* are *dvimūrdhaḥ*, *trimūrdhaḥ*. According to the rule *dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.115), the suffix *ṣa* is applied here as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Since that compound-final suffix is obligatory, it is more appropriate to cite it precisely as it is taught [in the rule], namely with the compound-final suffix applied, as in *pāddanmūrdhasu* (Pāṇini 6.2.197).

Having raised the objection that—since the rule begins with *pād* ending in the suffix *kṛt* (the *ac* suffix), it would be more appropriate to mention the word *mūrdhan* in the same way—one notes that because the word *mūrdha* is mentioned in the sūtra as *pāddanmūrghasu*, it is indicated by this very fact that the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsāntapratyaya*) is optional.

And likewise, the rule in the Sūtra "mūrdhasu" is formulated by relying on the alternative view that the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not apply. Therefore, even when the suffix is not applied—as in *dvimūrdhā* and *trimūrdhā*—the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is established by the elision of the suffix according to the rule *bahu-vrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*. With this intention, he states: "The mention is 'mūrdhasu'."

The purpose of this indication, however, is seen in examples such as *supathī nagarī*, where the suffix *kap*—prescribed by the rule *inaḥ striyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.152)—does not necessarily apply because it is optional. Furthermore, this statement is already covered by the maxim: "The rules governing compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) are not universal."

In the *Pariśiṣṭenduśekhara*, it is stated that the inclusion of the word *rājan* among the *aśvādi* group in the rule *prateraṃśvādayastatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.2.193)—which prescribes an udātta accent on the final syllable—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [rule]. [Jñāpakasamuccaya: *hr̥dayasya hr̥llekha-yadaṇ-lāseṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.50)].

In the context of the subsequent rule (*uttarapadādhikāra*), the mention of *lekhagrahaṇa* (the mention of *lekha*) indicates that the mention of *rupagrahaṇa* (the mention of *rūpa*) is understood. This is because, in the rule "khityanavyayasya," the inclusion of the term "anavyayasya" (of that which is not an indeclinable) implies the mention of that which ends in *khid*.

[VI.Ṭ] But surely, in the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*, by the mention of the suffixes *yat* and *aṇ*, and by the paribhāṣā "when a suffix is mentioned, there is the mention of that which ends with it and begins with the element from which it is prescribed," there follows the mention of forms ending in *yat* and *aṇ*.

One might raise the objection that since the substitution of *hrasva* (short vowel) for *hrasva* occurs only when followed by a *yat* or a *ṇat*, it would not apply to the words *hrasvam* and *hrasvārtham* when they stand alone. Anticipating this, [the author] states: "because of the mention of *hrasva-lekha-grahaṇāt*."

If there were a mention of "aṇanta" (ending in an *aṇ* suffix) here [in the rule], then since the word *lekha* itself ends in an *aṇ* suffix, the substitution of *śa* for *hrasva* (the short vowel) before it would already be established; consequently, the explicit mention of *lekhagrahaṇa* would be redundant.

The Teacher indicates by the mention of *lekhagrahaṇa* that by the term *aṇ*, only the form itself (*svarūpa*) is understood, and not that which ends in *aṇ*. Thus, since there is no possibility of grasping the word *lekha*—which ends in *aṇ*—by means of the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *lekha* is made.

Alternatively, because an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon its context, it is indicated that under the governing heading of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), there is no inclusion of a word ending in [a specific element] when only the suffix itself is mentioned. Consequently, in the case of *kumārī gauritarā*, the rule "gharūpakalpapū—" (Pāṇini 6.3.43)—which prescribes the shortening of the feminine suffix *ṅī* when a suffix designated as *gha* follows—does not apply to a word ending in *gha*. This is the intended meaning.

If it were understood in this way, then the shortening prescribed by the rule *khityanavyayasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.66) would apply only when *khit* follows immediately, and not when a word ending in *khit* follows. Consequently, one might raise the objection that in forms such as *śunindhayaḥ*, where the word *dhayaḥ* ending in *khit* follows, the shortening would not occur. Anticipating this, he says: "In the rule *khityanavyayasya*... [and so forth].

If there were no mention of that *tadanta* (ending in that) here as well, then, because an indeclinable followed by *khi* would be difficult to find, the short vowel (*hrasva*) would not apply to an indeclinable at all; consequently, the prohibition "not [an indeclinable]" (*anavyayasya*) would be rendered meaningless. Since that prohibition is indeed stated, it indicates that the mention of *tadanta* exists in this rule.

And likewise, in rules such as *doḥsdvdr1;āmanyamaḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;ḥ*, the restriction *anavyayasya* (of that which is not an indeclinable) is meaningful for the purpose of excluding short vowels. The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is that its utility lies in the establishment of the short vowel in forms such as *śuniṃdhaya*, where a suffix ending in *khid* follows.

[Commentary: By the rule *samaḥ sami* (Pāṇini 6.3.93), and because the rule *naḍḍhivaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.116) prescribes the substitution of *sam* for *sama* when followed by a word ending in the suffix *kvip*—which belongs to the class beginning with *añcu*—the principle that "when a root is mentioned, it includes that which begins with it" applies here as well. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *samaḥ sami*, the substitution of *sam* for *sama* is prescribed when *añcu* ending in *kvip* (i.e., not ending in a *pratyaya*) follows.

"Samyak" is an illustrative example. Likewise, by the rule *nañ-hu-vid-dhṛti-ruci-sthiti-niśrita-ku-ṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.75), a long vowel for the preceding member is prescribed when followed by words ending in the suffix *kvip*, such as *naddha* and others. "Upānat" and so forth are illustrative examples.

In that case, let the mention of *kvip* not be necessary. Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that [mention], the two rules would also apply in cases such as *samañcanam* and *upanahanam*; for since those two rules fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), those two rules operate only when a subsequent member in the form of *añcu*, *nahyādi*, or similar suffixes follows.

In the word *samañcanam*, although *añcana* is the final member (*uttarapada*), there is no fault because *añc* is not the final member. The status of being a final member belongs to the root *añc* alone only when the suffix *kvip* is present; otherwise, it would be difficult for that verbal root to even possess the status of a word (*pada*).

And thus, having raised the objection that the mention of *kvip* is redundant because the suffix *kvip* is already included by the very heading (*adhikāra*) "after the final member of a compound" (*uttarapade*), he says: "because of [the rule] *añcateḥ paścamasya*. Accordingly, the mention of *kvip* is made for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*).

Where a word ending in the locative case is employed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for a verbal root (*dhātu*), it is indicated that the rule of "extension to what begins with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies even in the absence of an explicit mention of the suffix *al*.

And thus, since *añceḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.98] and *naḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;vaḥTktgrRN;tī* [Pāṇini 6.3.75] would be taken as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the term *uttarapade*, and by the rule of "specification of the beginning" (*tadādividhi*), the meaning of the sūtra would be: "When a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) begins with a verbal root such as *añc*, then the substitution of *sam* for *saṃ* and the lengthening of the vowel of the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) occur. This would be the resulting interpretation of the sūtra.

If that were the case, then in examples such as *samañcanam* (the act of bending together) and *upanahanam* (the act of binding), the rule would also apply because the subsequent member *añcana* contains the constituent element *añc*. Therefore, the mention of the suffix *kvip* is made [in the sūtra]. By this, the two aforementioned rules operate only when preceded by a word ending in *kvip*, such as *añc* and others; thus, there is no fault—this is the intended meaning.

The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is as follows: in the rule *ataḥ kṛ-kami-* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the term *kṛ* in that specific qualification refers to a subsequent member that has *kṛ* as its initial constituent. Consequently, the substitution of *s* for *t* is established even in the case of *ayaskāra*. Otherwise, the substitution of *s* would only occur when *kṛ* is a verbal root ending in *kvip*, as in *ayaskṛt* and similar forms.

[From the rule *janasanakhanām* (Pāṇini 6.4.42) and *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64): Then, by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ lopo bhavati iṭi ca ajādau kṅiti*, there is elision [of the long *ā*] after roots ending in *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *jahāti*, and *sā*, when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*, or when the augment *iṭ* follows. This is for the purpose of establishing the substitution of *ī* which will be discussed later. From that [rule], *īt*: the suffixes beginning with *dhv* are understood to follow, and *ī* is substituted for those beginning with *dhv*.

By the rules *erliṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.67), *vānyasya* (6.4.68), *nalyapi* (6.4.69), and *mayateridanyatarasyām* (6.4.80), the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final vowel] before the suffix *yat*. Since this is already established, the fact that Pāṇini composes a heavy (prolix) rule indicates that even when a matter is established by brevity (*laghu*), there is still a conflict (*vipratipatti*) [that must be resolved].

And [the mention of] *goda* and so forth [in the rule *godāyo 'nupasarge*] is for the sake of preventing the substitution of long *ī* (*ītva*) in such cases. How, then, is this [mention] rendered purposeful once [the prohibition of *ītva*] has been established? Therefore, this statement is merely the opinion of a partial exponent (*ekadeśin*). Regarding the *Vārttika* on the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.42), which states: "The substitution of *āt* [for the final vowel of *san*] occurs by way of priority over the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*)," its meaning is as follows: [The elision of the nasal in *san* is taught by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (6.4.24). The substitution of *āt* is taught by the present rule. Since both would apply to forms like *saṃjighāṃsati*, there is a conflict (*vipratipatti*). According to the principle that when two rules apply simultaneously, the one taught later takes precedence, the elision of the nasal would prevail. The *Vārttika* asserts that the substitution of *āt* prevails instead.]

When the suffix *kta* is added to the root *sad*, resulting in the form *sant*, the substitution of *ā* for the vowel occurs by this [present rule], and following the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*), the rule "anudātopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37) would apply to delete the final consonant. However, because of the principle "in case of conflict, that which follows prevails" (Pāṇini 1.4.2), the substitution of *ā* alone takes effect due to its subsequent position in the rules. Thus, the form becomes *sāta*.

One might object: "In this case, a conflict (vipratipatti) is not applicable, because according to the maxim 'when a preceding rule is not established, there is no conflict due to the absence of a subsequent one,' even though the status of being unestablished (asiddhatva) applies here, a conflict does not arise. Anticipating this objection, he will state that there is no fault, because it is taught that a conflict does indeed occur [in such cases].

And in that regard, the inclusion of the term *hrasva* in the sūtra *ghumāsthāgāpājaḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;atisāṃ ḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;li* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since it is possible to explain its status as an indicator only if it would otherwise be redundant, he demonstrates that redundancy with the words beginning "the elision of *ā* occurs before *iṭ* and [before an affix marked with] *ṅ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*).

The intended meaning here is as follows: In the rule *ghumāsthā* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), if the mention of *hal* were absent, then even in the case of *godah* (*go-dā-ka*) and *kambaladah* (*kambala-dā-ka*), the substitution of *ī* would occur at the stage *godā-a*.

However, since the mention of *hal* is present, the suffix begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) and does not begin with a consonant (*hal-ādi*); therefore, no fault arises. And if [the *hal* were] absent...

In the case of mutual conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), by the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), because two operations are mutually non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to one another, even when the substitution of *ī* is applied, that [substitution] would be non-existent; consequently, by the elision of the *ā* according to *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), the form *goda* would be established, and thus the mention of the suffix *aṇ* would be purposeless.

And the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes indicates that the rule concerning conflict (*vipratishedha-sūtra*) applies even when the [suffix] has not yet been established. Thus, since *ītvam* (the substitution of *ī*) would occur by virtue of its higher status, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* is for the purpose of preventing that; this is one way in which it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The second alternative, however, is that after prescribing *ī*-change (*ītva*) without qualification, one can then enjoin the elision of the long *ā* (*āllopa*) before vowels beginning with *a* as an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, after the rule "there is elision of *ā* before *iṭ* and [before a suffix beginning with a vowel]" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*), the rule "of *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *aja*, and *hā*" (*ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām*) follows; the meaning is that there is elision before a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kṅiti pare*). This elision is prescribed before a suffix beginning with a vowel that has *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter for the purpose of establishing the *ī*-change.

Therefore, [the rule] "īt ghumāsthādīnām īt ca" [means that] *ī* is substituted for the roots *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, and so on. And thus, when the sūtra is formulated in this manner, since the distinction is established—namely, that *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, and so on take *ī* before affixes beginning with *ch* (i.e., those marked with *ṅ* and *k*), while there is elision (*lopa*) before affixes beginning with vowels and marked with *ṅ* and *k*—the mention of "before *ch*" becomes redundant. Being thus redundant, it serves to indicate the existence of a conflict (*vipratishedha*).

Therefore, in the case of *godah* (from *go-dā*), because [the substitution of] *ī* would apply by superseding the elision of *ā* due to its subsequent status, the mention of *hal* is meaningful for the purpose of preventing that. The purpose, however, is that in forms such as *sātaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* is established because it is subsequent to the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). This is the meaning of the section.

However, even if *hal-agrahaṇa* (the mention of *hal*) is not accepted, since the desired result is established by the elision (*lopa*) itself—having set aside the *yoga* for the sake of preventing the substitution of *ī* in cases such as *godaḥ* according to the principle of the previously mentioned sūtra—the mention of *hal* would lack its own scope of application (*cāritārthya*). Therefore, this statement is the assertion of a partisan (*ekadeśin*), and not [the final view].

The statement of the Siddhāntin begins with "How [is it] made known? This is also clearly seen in the Uddyota. [Regarding the rule] *huśnuvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.87): the mention of *hu* and *śnu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) occurs even in the case of the present participle suffix (*śānac*).

If it is argued that by the statement in the Bhāṣya, "tena bhāṣāyām api checa chida iti etat siddham bhavati," the very ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) of other forms ending in *yaṅ* and *luṅ* is intended in the Bhāṣya.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might raise the objection: since the word *cchandasī* ("in Vedic") is understood to carry over from the rule *chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73) into the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (2.4.74), the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) would apply only to the Veda. Consequently, the use of forms ending in the elided *yaṅ* (*yaṅluganta*) in the common language (*bhāṣā*) would not be grammatically correct. Anticipating this doubt, he establishes that the elision of *yaṅ* is valid even in the common language by means of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). Here:

Regarding the statement *juhuḥ* and *śraṇvan*: by the rule *juhuḥ-śnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*, it is established that for the root *hu*, for a stem ending in the suffix *śnu*, and for a multi-syllabic stem (*anekāc-aṅga*) where the vowel is not preceded by a consonant cluster (*asaṃyoga-pūrva*), a *yaṇ*-substitution occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) within the domain of a *sārvadhātuka*. Examples include *juhvati* and *śraṇvanti*.

In that context, it is understood that [the rule] *huśnuvoḥ* applies even without [the explicit mention of] *hu* and *śnu*. For, when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, there exists no other base (*aṅga*) besides one ending in *u* that has more than one vowel (*anekāc*), apart from *hu* and *śnu*. Thus, the mention of *huśnuvoḥ* would be redundant.

Furthermore, in Vedic usage—as in the example *yuvaṃ yoyuvatīnāṃ vaḥ*—there exists no form such as *yoyu*, which ends in the vowel *u* and is preceded by a non-conjunct consonant (*anekāj*) that begins with a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*). Therefore, it must be stated that the mention of *śnu* [in Pāṇini 6.4.77] is for the purpose of including forms like *yāvayati*.

By the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), because the suffix *śatṛ* is treated as *ārdhadhātuka*, it lacks the status of being *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, that rule [of Pāṇini] does not apply there.

Thus, since the mention of *śnu* and *nu* would otherwise be purposeless, this very mention—being otherwise redundant—indicates (*jñāpayati*) that even in the *bhāṣā* (common speech), forms ending in *yaṅ-luk* are grammatically correct.

Furthermore, in the *bhāṣā* (vernacular), regarding forms such as *yoyuvatī* ending in the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), the rule *chandasyubhayathā* does not apply. Therefore, in order to prevent the substitution of *yaṇ* when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix *śatṛ* follows, the inclusion of *śnu* and *hrasva* in [Pāṇini 6.4.87] serves its purpose within its own domain (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*).
The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is that forms such as *bebhidī* and *cecchidī*, which end in the elision of *yaṅ* in the *bhāṣā*, are grammatically correct.

If it is argued that because only *cchidīti* and *cecchidīti*—the two forms with the *yaṅ*-lopa suffix—are cited as examples, other roots with the *yaṅ*-lopa suffix would not be valid in the *bhāṣā*, [we reply: by that very fact, [it is established] that they are valid even in the *bhāṣā*. [This is based on the rule *ata eka...* (Pāṇini 6.4.120).]

The rule *phaliḥ* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *ay* [for *e*] is established as non-existent (*asiddha*). The prohibition regarding *śas* and *idam* is the indicator that the substitution of *etva* [for *ai*] applies even when there is a difference in form. Because the inclusion of the letter *t* in the rule for the substitution of *at* for *śna* and *as* indicates that the principle "that which is *asiddha* here" (*asiddhavad atra*, Pāṇini 6.4.22) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the form *dehibhūtuḥ* is established.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, in the case of *jahatur*—where *jahaṇ-jahaṇ* becomes *jahatur*—once the substitution of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) has occurred, the rule *abhyāse car ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54) applies the *jaś*-substitution (changing the *ṇ* to *j*). However, when the subsequent operations of *etva* (the change of *ha* to *e*) and the elision of the *abhyāsa* are to be performed, that *jaś*-substitution is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

Since the *aṅga* [stem] possesses the property of not having an *ādeśa* as its initial element, the rule *ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120) applies. Thus, when the roots *phal* and *bhaj* undergo reduplication in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], resulting in the forms *phal-phal-a-tuḥ* and *bhaj-bhaj-a-tuḥ*, and after the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* and *jaśtva*, the forms *pa-phal-a-tuḥ* and *ba-bhaj-a-tuḥ* are established.

Since the *aṅga* [stem] begins with a substitute (*ādeśa*), the rule *ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120) does not apply; therefore, it must be stated that the mention of *phal* and *bhaj* is for the purpose of establishing the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*).

If the *jaś*-substitution resulting from the *abhyāsa* (reduplication) were *asiddha*, then, because of that *asiddha* status, the rule "ata ekahalmadhye" would already establish both the *etva* (change to *e*) and the elision of the *abhyāsa* simply by virtue of there being no initial substitute (*anādeśāditvāt*). Why, then, is the mention of those two specifically made in the rule "taśphala"?

And this [mention of *phal*] indicates that when the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*) are to be performed, the substitution of *et* for *ai* is already established. Consequently, since the substitution of *jaś* is established and the [substitution of *et*] does not apply because it begins with a substitute letter (*ādeśādi*), the mention of *phal* serves to establish both the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication; thus, its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope.

The purpose [of this rule] is that in forms such as *cakhāda* and *jaghāna*, because the substitution of the *jaś*-class sounds (*jaśtva*) for the doubled consonants is established as already accomplished, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) would not occur, since these [consonants] would be considered the beginning of a substitute (*ādeśādi*).

[Objection: If this were so, then in forms such as *pecatuḥ* and *dedhatuḥ*, because the original unaspirated (*pragṛhya-carāṃ*) would become original unaspirated and the original voiced unaspirated (*prakṛti-jaśāṃ*) would become original voiced unaspirated, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication would not occur due to being the beginning of a substitute. [Response: To this, [the author] says: "In the case of *śit* and *siddha*... (referring to the rule *śitsiddhayoḥ*).

By the rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* (Pāṇini 6.4.126), the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*) for the roots *śas* and *dad* are prohibited. However, in this case as well, because the substitute *cira* for *car* begins with a consonant (*ādeśādi*), it lacks the status of beginning with a vowel (*anādeśāditva*). Consequently, since the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication would already not apply by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* (Pāṇini 6.4.120), what is the purpose of this prohibition?

Furthermore, by the prohibition [of the rule *kḥTktgrRN;ataḥ*], it is indicated that the prohibition does not apply to a case where the substitute (*ādeśa*) is different from the original form (*sthānī*) and constitutes the initial part of the stem (*aṅga*), such as in the case of the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*). Thus, for a stem whose initial part is a substitute different from its original form, the prohibition [of the rule *kḥTktgrRN;ataḥ*] does not take effect.
