If, by the rule *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the final letter), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the final *t* were intended to be optional, then the sūtra would have been formulated simply as *vāṃreḍitasya*. This is because, since the substitution of the subsequent form for the final letter is already established as obligatory by the preceding sūtra (Pāṇini 6.1.98), only the optionality itself would need to be prescribed.

Likewise, by stating the rule "nāmr̥ḍitasyāntyasya tu vā" (Pāṇini 6.1.99), [the author] indicates that the single-substitute *pararūpa* does not apply to the final [phoneme]. Consequently, when the *pararūpa* of the final phoneme of the reduplicated form *at* would otherwise have been obtained, that is prohibited; thus, the prescription of the option for the final [phoneme] finds its purpose in its own domain.

And thus, in the case of *paṭat* as well, since the substitution of the single form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*) for the final letter is already established, the intention is that this is not the purpose of the paribhāṣā: "When a rule is meaningless, it does not apply to the final letter. [Jñānapaṭala] "The word itself is the meaning of the word" (Pāṇini 1.1.68). The mention of the term *rūpa* (form) indicates that there exists for a word something other than its mere form.

Because the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84) indicates that the numeral ending in the letter *a* is designated as *aṣṭan*, it follows that when the technical designation *śabda* applies, there is no application of the rule regarding its own form (*svarūpavidhi*).

[Objection]: Now, in the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*, since the word *sva* denotes "one's own," it is understood first by the sense of hearing independently of any connection with other words; thus, by the word *sva*, only its own form (*rūpa*) is grasped. Therefore, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the word *rūpa*?

[Objection: "The mention of its form. And thus, from the mention of its form, it is understood that the word possesses its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is distinct from its form and characterized by its meaning. Likewise, from the mention of its form, it is understood that the word possesses its own essential nature which is distinct from its form and characterized by its meaning.

And thus, the mention of the word "form" (*rūpa*) is for the purpose of communicating that the nature of the word is qualified by its meaning. By this, it is understood that in this treatise, only the form of the word as qualified by its meaning is accepted, and not that which is devoid of meaning.

And thus, since the meaningfulness [of the item] is understood from the sūtra itself through the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*), it is established that the restriction regarding the mention of "meaningful" need not be applied. Furthermore, it should be understood that the argument concerning "being first presented" (*prathamopasthitatva*) and so forth is set aside by the mention of "form" (*rūpa*). Now, one might object: let there be no such thing as the technical name "word" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*).

Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of such [technical] names, the mention of their own forms (*svarūpa*) would also occur in the *Śikṣā-śāstra* regarding designations such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so forth; for in the rule *ṛṇāntā ṣaṭ*, by the term *ṣaṭ*, [the number six is intended].

Thus, since the technical name *śatṛ* is established for that which has the form of *śatṛ* by virtue of its own nature (*svarūpa*), and since the technical name *śas* is established for that which ends in *n* by the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana-prāmāṇya*), the mention of the letter *ṣ* [in Pāṇini’s rule] would otherwise be redundant. This redundancy serves to indicate that the rule regarding one's own form (*svarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply in the case of technical names (*saṃjñā*). This is the case in rules such as *ṭi-ghu-ādi*.

The meaning is that since the establishment of the original form (*svarūpa*) occurs through the absence of elision (*lopa*), the rule "the term *saṃjñā* applies up to the suffix *kṛt*" would be unnecessary; such is the intention. [Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.18: "A *ktvā* suffix followed by an augment *iṭ* does not cause elision."

The mention of *jhal* in the rule *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9) indicates that the prohibition of *kit*-status applies only to that which is original (*aupadeśika*), and not to that which is transferred by extension (*atideśika*). [Objection: But then, one might argue that there is no need to mention *ktvā* in the rule *na ktā seṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.18). Nor can it be said that in the absence of that mention, the prohibition of *kit*-status would apply even to the *niṣṭhā* suffixes in forms such as *gudhitah* and *gudhitavān*, whereby the *upadhā-guṇa* (penultimate vowel strengthening) would consequently occur.

Regarding the sūtra *niṣṭhā śīṅsvidimidikṣvididhṛṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19), although the prohibition [of *iṭ*] is already established by the rule *na seṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.18), this [present] sūtra serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The restriction is that the *niṣṭhā* suffixes following only the roots beginning with *śīṅ* are *kit*, and not others. Consequently, in forms such as *gudhitaḥ*, there is no fault, because the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not prohibited from being *kit*.

Nor should it be argued that even in such cases as *papiva* and *papima*, the elision of the *ā* of *papā*—occurring in the stages *papā iva* and *papā imaḥ*—would not take place because the suffixes *iva* and *imaḥ* are marked with *k* and *ṅ* (indicating they are *kit* and *ṅit*), which would prohibit elision due to the presence of the augment *iṭ*. This is because the elision is established by taking *iṭ* itself as the cause. Furthermore, one should not argue that even so, in forms like *jagmiva* and *jaghiva*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) by the rule "there is elision of the penultimate vowel of the roots *gam*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas* when followed by a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* except for *anaṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.98) would not occur. [This objection is invalid, as the elision is indeed established.]

The fact that the *liṭ* suffixes are not treated as *kit* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the existence of the augment *iṭ*. The very indicator is the mention of the term *jhal* [in the rule *jhalo jhali*]. By the rule *iko jhal*, the *kit* status is prescribed for a *san* beginning with a *jhal* sound that follows a stem ending in an *ik* vowel; examples include *bibhitsati* and others. In that context, by the mention of *jhal*, it must be stated that the *kit* status of a *san* beginning with a vowel—such as in *śiśayiṣate*, which possesses the augment *iṭ*—is thereby excluded.

However, since the term *ktvā* is not mentioned in the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, there would be no prohibition of *kitva* for any *seṭ* suffix whatsoever; consequently, because there would be no prohibition of *kitva* even for a *seṭ* *san* suffix—as in the case of *śiśayiṣate*—the mention of *jhal* in the rule *iko jhal* would be rendered purposeless, as its result [the prevention of *guṇa*] would already be achieved.

The formulation of that [rule] indicates that, in the sūtra *na seṭ*, the prohibition applies to the original (*aupadeśika*) *kit* status and not to the transferred (*ātideśika*) one. Since the *san* suffix with a *seṭ* augment lacks original *kit* status, but rather possesses it through transfer by the rule *iko jhal*, the mention of *jhal* was made so that the prohibition in *na seṭ* would not apply to it; thus, the rule serves its purpose within its own scope.

The point is this: in examples such as *jagmivān*, the prohibition by the rule *na seṭ* does not apply to the *kit* status—which is extended [to the suffix] by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5). Consequently, the elision of the *iṭ* augment (by the rule *kṅiti ca*) is established. [Now, the rule for the designation of *kāla*: *parokṣakālo 'c* (Pāṇini 1.2.27).

The rule *pluta-pratiṣedhaḥ praśnānantarayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.93), which prescribes a *pluta* vowel for a single-mora (*mātrika*) vowel, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a single-mora vowel does not occur at the end [of a word]. Furthermore, the prescription of a long vowel (*dīrgha*) by the rules *ato dīrgho yañi* and *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.101–102) is an indicator that a single-mora vowel does not occur in the middle [of a word].

The prescription of the *pluta* vowel as having two morae (*dvimātra*) in the rule *omaḥ ḍvyādāne* (Pāṇini 8.2.87) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a two-mora vowel does not occur at the end of a word. [Commentary: Now, one might object: in the rule *eṅ pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), the term *eṅ* is a collective mention (*praśleṣanirdeśa*) of vowels consisting of one, two, and three morae. In that context, through a correspondence based on the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*), the designation *hrasva* (short) is assigned to the one-mora vowel, the designation *dīrgha* (long) to the two-mora vowel, and the designation *pluta* to the three-mora vowel.

In this regard, how is it understood that this is a notation of *praśleṣa* (conjunction) consisting precisely of those [vowels] arranged in sequence—one *mātrā*, two *mātrās*, and three *mātrās*? Whether there be a one-*mātrā* [vowel] in the middle or at the end, whether there be a two-*mātrā* [vowel] at the beginning or at the end, or whether there be a three-*mātrā* [vowel] at the beginning or in the middle.

Furthermore, fearing that the established rule—that only a single-mora [vowel] is short (*hrasva*), and so forth—would not hold, he says: "The mention of *pluta* for the one-mora [vowel]. If there were an indication at the end of the one-mora [vowel], then, according to the principle that "whatever is at the end has the designation *pluta*," it would have to be stated that the one-mora [vowel] has the designation *pluta*.

Furthermore, in the case of *ḥḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;* (he), since the single-mora *i*-sound (*ikāra*) is already a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, the prescription of its protraction by the rule "*viḥḍddhdhḍaddh;āḥsdvdr1;ā paḥTktgrRN;ḥsdvdr1;ṭaprativacane ḥḍhddhac12;eḥdyaṇoddhd;ḥ*" would be redundant. Therefore, that prescription indicates that a single-mora vowel does not become protracted at the end [of a sentence].

Thus, if a *mātrika* (one-mora) sound were to occur in the middle, that which is in the middle would be designated as "long" (*dīrgha*), because a single *mātrā* constitutes length according to the rule "atodīrgho yañi. Consequently, the prescription of a three-mora (*pluta*) sound—which consists of two *mātrās* [in addition to the preceding long vowel]—would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, this indicates that a two-mora sound does not occur at the end.

And thus, since it is established that a one-mora (*ekamātra*) vowel is placed at the beginning because it cannot be placed at the end or in the middle of the *mātrika* [section], and a two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel is placed in the middle because it cannot be placed at the end, it follows by implication that the three-mora (*trimātra*) vowel is placed at the end. Consequently, the designations "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), and "protracted" (*pluta*) for the one-mora, two-mora, and three-mora vowels are established respectively; this is the underlying principle. [Pāṇini 1.3.1: *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*]

In the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the mention of *śnu* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not occur for a suffix. Furthermore, the prescription of the substitution of *au* for *div* in the nominative singular (*divaḥ sau autvam*) indicates that the case-endings beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are produced from the verbal root *div*. [Viṭ: Now, an objection: by the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*, the designation *dhātu* is prescribed for those items such as *bhū* and others that are recited in the Dhātupāṭha.

Likewise, regarding the form *trasnū*, there arises the possibility of the substitution of *uvaṅ*. Since *nu* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha, in the case of *trasnu + āṬ*, *nu* would be considered a verbal root (*dhātu*), and consequently, the rule "aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.77) would apply, resulting in the substitution of *uvaṅ*. It should not be argued that this doubt is misplaced on the grounds that while *ṇu* is read in the Dhātupāṭha, *nu* is not, nor does *nu* share the same phonetic form (*sārūpya*) as *ṇu*. For even if *nu* were not explicitly listed, the doubt remains valid.

In the application [of the rule], since the suffix *nu* is indeed a verbal root (*dhātu*), its similarity (*sārūpya*) exists even in the word *trasnu*, where the suffix *nu* occurs; therefore, the mention of *śnu* [in the rule] is necessary. For if the substitution of *uvaṅ* were to apply to the suffix as well, then because the element *na-* would also be a verbal root when the suffix *śnu* is present, the substitution of *uvaṅ* would already be established, and the mention of *śnu* would be purposeless.

And this [rule] indicates that the substitution of *uvaṅ* does not occur for that which consists of a suffix and has the same form as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus, there is no fault. Now, even so, in the case of the word *div* which is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), since it has the same form as the *div* read in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), it would receive the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*); consequently, because of the prohibition "not a verbal root," its designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadikasaṃjñā*) would not be established.

Furthermore, one might suspect that the derivation of case endings such as *su* would not occur because [the word *div*] lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); anticipating this, [the author] states: "divaḥ saḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.84]. By the rule "diva aut" (Pāṇini 7.1.84), which prescribes the substitution of *au* for *div* when followed by the nominative singular ending *su*, it is shown that since the ending *su* would otherwise be impossible due to the absence of the nominal-stem designation for *div*, this rule—which would otherwise be inconsistent—indicates that case endings such as *su* arise even from the verbal root *div*.

Therefore, there is no fault; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). In reality, however, these two indicators (*jñāpaka*) have been presented without relying on the principle that only those words denoting action, such as *bhū* and others, receive the designation "root" (*dhātu*). It should be noted that in the case of *trasnu*, even though there is similarity in form to a root, the designation "root" does not apply—whether one considers the element *nuṅ* [of the suffix], or the word *div* [as a base], or the word *nu* itself as an underived (*avyutpanna*) term—precisely because they lack the quality of denoting action.

[Pāṇini 1.3.7] *jñapa-ṭ cuṭū*. The inclusion in the list of certain roots such as *undi* (meaning 'to moisten') and *skandi* (meaning 'to move' or 'to leap'), which are marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ* (*irit*) and are not followed by the augment *num*, indicates that the rule for changing *i* to *it* does not apply to this class of roots. [Vṛtti: Regarding the sūtra *cuṭū*, there is the Vārttika: "The addition of *ḍhṛ* must be included. In cases such as *rudhir*, it must be stated that the *ṛ* is designated as *it*.

By the rule *irito vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.57), the augment *aṅ* would not apply. Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the letter *r* has the designation *it* by the rule *ḍhralopaṃ dhuṭi* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) [or rather, here referring to the general principle of *it* markers], and the letter *i* has the designation *it* by the rule *upadeśe'janunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.2); for if that were the case, the rule conditioned by being *idit* would also apply, and consequently, in forms such as *bhetā* and *chetā*, the augment *num* would be required by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58).

Therefore, because the designation *it* cannot be applied to the individual components, the intention of the Vārttika is that the designation *it* must be stated for the entire aggregate "ir. However, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that since the designation *it* is already established for each component individually, it need not be stated for the aggregate. Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the application of *num* due to the *it*-designation.

Because certain roots marked with the indicatory letter *iṛ*—such as *undī* in the sense of "cleansing" (*niśāmane*) and *skandi* in the sense of "motion and leaping" (*gati-śoṣaṇayoḥ*)—are recited in the Dhatupatha with the augment *num*, it is indicated that the rule for roots marked with *iṛ* does not apply here. Therefore, he explained that there is no occurrence of *num* in forms such as *bheteta*, citing the rule *undir niśāmane* and others. [Jñāpakapradīpa, Sūtra 1.3.67: *ṇer aṇau*]

The prohibition regarding *anādhyāna* (non-contemplation) indicates that the *ātmanepada* occurs for verbs of this class. [Objection: But surely the meaning of the rule *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartānādhyāne* is: "The *ātmanepada* occurs after a causative (*ṇi*-stem) provided that the action which was in the non-causative (*aṇi*) state is expressed by the same [causative] form, and the factor that was the object (*karman*) in the non-causative becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative, except in the case of contemplation (*adhyāna*). In that case, the term "*anādhyāne*" (except in the case of contemplation) would be redundant.

Having raised the objection that since only those actions whose agents are themselves the objects (*karmavadbhāva*) are subject to the *karmavadbhāva* rule, and since actions such as *adhyāna* (thinking about) have agents who are not themselves the objects, they cannot be subject to *karmavadbhāva*, [the author] states "except when there is *adhyāna*" (*anādhyāne*) to show its purpose: namely, that it indicates the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for actions of this class, precisely because of that very reason. Thus, its meaningfulness is established.

In this context, the meaning is that when those which are objects (*karman*) of roots ending in *ṇic* become the agent (*kartṛ*) of those same roots when they are in the *ṇic*-form, then the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs even though the action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha-bhāvakriyatva*). Consequently, Kaiyaṭa maintains that the *ātmanepada* is established in such examples as *paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam* ("the servants see the king") and *darśayate bhṛtyān rājā* ("the king causes the servants to see himself").

Those who wish to know this truth through direct observation should consult the *Kaumudī*, which is a commentary on this Sūtra, as well as its sub-commentary, the *Bālamanoramā*. [Pāṇini 1.3.79: *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*]. Due to the indicatory evidence (*jñāpaka*) regarding the optionality (*vāvacana*) for roots beginning with *dyut* and others, the Ātmanepada does not occur when the Parasmaipada is otherwise required.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: even though the *parasmaipada* is prescribed by the rule "anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ," there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that only the *parasmaipada* must occur; therefore, in its alternative case, the *ātmanepada* might also occur. To this, he says: "Because there is an option (*vāvacana*) for the roots beginning with *dyut*."

If the ātmanepada were to occur even when there is a rule for the parasmaipada, then in the rule *dyudbhyo luṅ* (Pāṇini 1.3.91), the optional prescription of the parasmaipada by carrying over the word *vā* from the preceding rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90) would be purposeless; for both sets of verbal endings would be established even without the recurrence of the word *vā*.

Furthermore, the mention of the word "or" (*vā*) is an indicator (*liṅga*) for the non-application of the substitution of the *ātmanepada* in place of the *parasmaipada*. Therefore, there is no fault; this is the established conclusion (*bhāva*). [Jñānapaṭala, from *ā kaḍārādekā saṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.4.1)]

The mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*) in the rule *ḍhākror anyatarasyām* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when the designation of object (*karma-saṃjñā*) applies, the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) does not occur.

[Objection: But surely, by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), it is stated that in examples such as "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to go to the village," the agent (*kartṛ*) Devadatta in the non-causal (*aṇyantā*) state receives the designation of object (*karman*) in the causal (*ṇyantā*) state. Just as Devadatta possesses the status of an object because he is the locus of the result produced by the operation denoted by the causative suffix (*ṇij*), he likewise possesses the status of an agent because he is the locus of the operation expressed by the verbal root itself. Thus, Devadatta remains an agent even in the causal state.

Furthermore, one might object that because two designations (saṃjñā) would apply simultaneously to the deity, the two powers (bhakti) associated with those two designations would result in a confusion of functions. Anticipating this, [the author] says: *hṛkroḥ* ("of *hṛ* and *kru*"). If the agent who causes another to act (*prayojyakartṛ*) were to possess both designations, then even for *hṛ* and *kru*, there would be the inclusion of "motion" (*gati*) and so forth.

Having read the rule *pāṭham*, one should not have included the word *anyatarasyām*. By that [omission], it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that when the prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) receives the technical designation of "object" (*karma*), the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) does not apply to him. Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no fault. [Vārttika: *vipratiṣedhe param* (Pāṇini 1.4.2).

The inclusion of *gaura* and others in the list of words beginning with *śva* (in the *śvan-ādi* group) indicates that the accent of a *nighāta* (elided or unaccented word) does not descend upon a following word. Regarding the rule *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* ("when there is a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails"), there is the *vārttika*: *antaraṅgaṃ ca*. The meaning of this is that an *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned) operation is stronger [than a subsequent one].

And its purpose is demonstrated by the immediately following *vārttika*: "The substitutes *yaṇ*, *aikāra*, *aukāra*, *guṇa*, and *vṛddhi*, as well as reduplication, elision (*al-lop*), and accent, [take precedence] over [the application of rules]. In that context, regarding the point that the single-substitute rule (*ekādeśa*) prevails over elision (*al-lop*) due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*), the example given is *śunā*.

When *śvan* + *a* + *an* + *ā* is present, by the rule *śvayuvamaghonām* (Pāṇini 6.4.133), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), resulting in *śu* + *a* + *an* + *ā*. At this stage, both the elision of *an* (*allopo'naḥ*, 6.4.134) and the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) by *saṃprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108) apply. Among these, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the *pūrvarūpa* alone takes effect. Now, one might object: "In this case, whether there is the elision of *an* or the *pūrvarūpa*, there is no difference whatsoever in the resulting form."

If it is argued that describing the greater strength (*balīyastva*) of an internal element (*antaraṅga*) in this context is irrelevant, we say no. When the *ḍhilopa* occurs, because the vowel *a* is acute (*udātta*), when that [vowel] is elided, the acute quality is transferred to the following unaccented (*anudātta*) suffix by the rule "anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.161). Thus, *śunaḥśepa-* becomes oxytone (*antodātta*).

But when one perceives the *pūrvarūpa* [the single substitute], then by the rule "A single substitute for [an udātta and an anudātta] is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the single substitute *u* becomes udātta, while the remaining portion remains anudātta; thus the word *śunā* becomes *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable). Therefore, because there exists a difference in accent (*svara*), [the two forms are distinct].
Having thus accepted the distinction between accents (*svara-bheda*) and described its purpose, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have refuted that distinction of accents in order to reject it.

Likewise, in the case of *śunā* (in the form *tathā ḍhḍhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;-śunā*), even though the elision of the *al* suffix occurs, the accent of the original base (*udātanivṛttisvara*) applies to the word *śvan*. Since the word *śvan* ends in *n*, its form is established by the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*), so what is the purpose of including it in the *gaurādi* group? It is not the case that *ṅīp* is unnecessary, for since *ṅīp* is marked with *p* (indicating it is *pit*), it would be unaccented (*anudātta*); consequently, in the word *śunī*, the vowel *ī* would become unaccented.

However, because the suffix *ṅīṣ* is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *ī* in *śunī* is acute; thus, since there would be no difference in accent, the inclusion of [the word *śvan*] in the *gaurādi* list is for the sake of making it oxytone (*antodātta*). Therefore, one must state how that [inclusion] can serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Even when the suffix *ṅīp* is present, in the derivation of *śunī* from *śvan* + *ī*, after the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) has occurred and the form *śu-an-ī* is established, the vowel *a*—which is originally acute—is elided by the rule *allopo’naḥ*. Consequently, by the rule *anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ*, the following grave (*anudātta*) vowel *ī* becomes acute, thereby establishing that the word is oxytone (acute on the final syllable). Thus, the inclusion of the stem *śvan* in the *gaurādi* list is redundant; its very redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the accentual rule for the *gaurādi* group does not apply to the word *śvan*.

And thus, even in the case of *śūnā*, since the acute accent (*udātta*) resulting from the substitution of *viḍ* does not apply here, there is no difference—either in accent or in form—between the elision of the *al* and the formation of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) by the rule of *pūrvarūpa*. Therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the rule "that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" does not serve as a justification for the single-substitute over the elision of the *al*.

Having reflected upon all this—namely, that in the list beginning with *gauḥ* and so forth, the word *śvan* is read as having its final syllable unaccented (*anudātta*)—it follows that there is an accent consisting of an acute (*udātta*) following a lost grave (*anudātta*). This refers to the accent prescribed by the rule "and where there is the elision of an *anudātta*, [the preceding syllable becomes *udātta*]," meaning that when an *udātta* has been elided, the *svarita* nature of the *anudātta* arises.

[From the *Jñāpakapāṭha*: "The instrument is that which is most effective" (Pāṇini 1.4.42). The inclusion of the word *tama* ("most") in this rule indicates that the comparative and superlative degrees (*taratama-yoga*) do not apply to the designation of *kārakas*.

[Objection: Since all *kārakas* are indeed "accomplishers" (*sādhaka*) by virtue of contributing to the accomplishment of some action or other, the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) would not apply to that which is not an accomplisher even if the word "accomplisher" were not explicitly stated. Therefore, the inclusion of the word "accomplisher" (*sādhakam*) must be understood to mean "the most effective accomplisher" (*sādhakatamam*); so what is the purpose of including the suffix *-tama*?

Anticipating the objection that—just as when it is said, "A girl should be given to one who possesses the form *aḥcdvddhddhed*," one understands "to one who possesses the most excellent form (*aḥḍddhdhḍiddh;arūpatamāya*)" through the inclination toward giving her to one who possesses the form *anaḥḍddhdhḍiddh;a*, even without explicitly mentioning the word "most excellent" (*tama*)—he says: "By the mention of *tama*."
And thus, by the mention of *tara* and *tamap* in this sūtra, it is indicated that in other sections concerning *kārakas*, the degrees of comparison (*taratamabhāva*) are not to be resorted to.

Otherwise, in the rule "The substratum is the locus" (*ādhāro’dhikaraṇam*, Pāṇini 1.4.45), since the technical term *adhikaraṇa* would already be established through its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), the explicit mention of the word *ādhāra* there would be purposeless. By the force of that mention, the meaning would have to be that the locus is called *adhikaraṇa* only when it is a physical container (*prakṛṣṭa ādhāraḥ*)—that is, a substratum which pervades all parts of the object contained within it.

If that were the case, [the rule] would apply only in instances such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) or "clarified butter in curds" (*dadhi sarpiḥ*), but it would not apply in instances such as "cattle on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaḥ*); this is the intended meaning. Thus ends the first chapter. Now begins the second chapter.

In the rule *yuvākhalatī* (Pāṇini 2.1.66), although the term "in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) is understood from the previous context, the mention of a term in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa-nirdeśa*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a compound is formed between a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) of a certain type and a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) of that same type.

It occurs as follows: by the rule *yuvā khalati-palita-valina-jaratībhiḥ*, the formation of a compound with the word *yuvan* (young) and the words *khalati* (bald), etc., is prescribed. And in that rule, the term *samānādhikaraṇena* (with a word in grammatical apposition) is understood to carry over.

Since a masculine word ending in *yuvan* cannot stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with feminine words such as *khalati*, the mention [of *yuvan*] in the Sūtra is inconsistent; this inconsistency serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in this context, the term *yuvan* refers to whatever kind of subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows it.

"Such a thing is understood. This means that because the subsequent member, the word *jaratī*, is feminine, when a compound with it is intended, only a feminine word such as *yuvati* is compounded with it. Even though in examples such as "the face is the moon," [the comparison is established despite gender difference].

The *Udyota* states that although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed even between words of different genders, this is not the case everywhere, but only in instances where there is agreement; furthermore, even in those cases, it occurs only when one of the two has a fixed gender—this is the intention of the *Bhāṣya*. The purpose of making this statement known is as follows:

It is stated in the Bhāṣya that the accomplishment of the grammatical operation occurs even without the *paribhāṣā*— "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. [Jñānapaṭala]

*Upapadaṃ tiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). The exclusion of *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) in this rule indicates that the rule *sup-supā* has been superseded by these two rules. [Objection: But surely, the mention of *atiṅ* in the sūtra *upapadaṃ tiṅ* need not exist. And if it were absent...

In the expression *kārako vrajati* ("the agent goes"), the word *vrajati* is designated as an *upapada* because it is included in the locative case (*kriyāyām*) within the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). Consequently, it is referred to by the term *kāraka*.

It must be stated that a compound should occur here, because the rule *sup supā* is also understood to apply in this case; thus, by obtaining the meaning of the sūtra— "an upapada ending in a *su*-affix is compounded with a capable word ending in a *su*-affix"—
the word *vrajati* lacks the status of being a word ending in a *su*-affix.
Anticipating the objection that a compound (*samāsa*) is not applicable here, [the author] states: "The prohibition is by the rule *atiṅ*.

Thus, since it would otherwise be redundant according to the method previously stated, the mention of *atiṅ* in this sūtra and the preceding sūtra "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the rule *sup supā*.

This indicates that [the word *samāsa*] does not follow [the previous rule]. Furthermore, since a compound (*samāsa*) would otherwise occur even for a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*) when that [restriction] is not followed, the mention of *atiṅ* (non-finite) is intended to prevent that; thus, it serves its purpose within its own scope. Now, one might object: "Since *atiṅ* is mentioned in this very sūtra..."

Let it be understood that *nivaḥ* (the prefix *ni*) is taught [as a *gati*] by implication (*jñāpyate*). If it is asked, "How is it understood that *nivaḥ* is taught as a *gati* in the previous sūtra?"—to this they reply:
In the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), there are two distinct applications (*yoga*): "kuprādayaḥ" and "gatiḥ."

It is divided [into two parts]. Therein, the meaning of the first sūtra is that *kuprādayaḥ* are compounded with a word ending in *su*. Likewise, the two rules "upapada" and "atiṅ" are divided. This term *atiṅ* applies to both "gati" and "upapada."
The word *śeṣāt* is understood [from the previous rule].

The term *sup* is excluded from both [rules] due to the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). The word *atiṅ*, ending in the nominative case, qualifies the compound (*samāsa*) introduced by the two preceding rules. And thus:

The meaning is that a compound consisting of verbal roots (*tiṅanta*) as its final member, as extracted from the two sūtras, does not occur. Consequently, since the word *ātiṅ* is connected with both sūtras,
the word *sup* [is also connected] with those two sūtras.

The intention is that this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the elision (*nivṛtti*) [of the rule]. And thus, since the elision of the term *sup* applies to both sūtras, the compound of *gati*s and *upapada*s is established even prior to the production of the case-ending (*sub*), according to the principle: "The *gati*, the *kāraka*, and the *upapada* [are compounded] with the verbal root (*dhātu*)."

It is stated in the Bhāṣya that the purpose of this [rule] is to provide the knowledge that the rule "the expression of a compound occurs before the production of case-endings" (*samāsavacanaṃ prāk subutpateḥ*) is established by the *paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, [this applies] even before the production of case-endings for the kārakas.

It must be stated how this compound is formed. Some say it is established through the principle of *ekadeśānumati* (acceptance by implication). Kaiyaṭa, however, maintains that the compound of the case-factors is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

It is stated [in the commentary]: "In that regard, because the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] occurs first, the compound is established prior to the arising of the *suP* [nominal suffix]. Since a compound with a *tiṅ*-ending word is not possible by the mere recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule 'of that which ends in *suP*,' it follows that [the compound] occurs only with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix."

Since the formation of a compound is already established, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes is for the purpose of forming a compound while the *kṛt* suffix is still in its intermediate state, even before the case-ending (*sup*) has arisen; so say some. [Pāṇini 2.2.24: *anekam anyapadārthe*].

The prescription of *dvigu* compounds for the final member (*uttarapada*) indicates that there is also compounding of words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) even when they do not denote the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). [Vi.]— But surely, since the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24) is governed by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of "sup supā" (Pāṇini 2.1.4), a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) existing in the sense of another word...

Since the meaning "it is compounded with that which ends in a *su*-affix" is obtained by implication (*arthāt*), the mention of the word "multiple" (*aneka*) would be redundant, as a compound of multiple *su*-affixes is understood. Nor [is it necessary] for those ending in *su*...

It should be stated that there is no compounding of multiple words [in a bahuvrīhi]. This is established by the very fact of the indicator (jñāpaka) that compounds [of this type] do not occur with indeclinables. The indicator itself is: "when it is the subsequent member" (uttarapade).

By the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), a compound is prescribed for a word expressing a number when it is followed by another word as its subsequent member (*uttarapada*) that is a noun ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) and stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For example: *pañca gāvo dhanaṃ yasya* ("one whose wealth consists of five cows").

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the three words *dhana-śabda-pare-tad-avayavayoḥ* within the *dvandva* compound *pañca-go-śabda-yoḥ*, there occurs a *dvigu* compound of the two members *pañca-go-śabdayoḥ*.

In that regard, first of all, in the absence of the three [conditions], the designation "uttarapada" (final member of a compound) would not apply to the word *dhana*. This is because the term *uttarapada* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to the final constituent of a compound. And thus, when [the word] follows as an *uttarapada*...

The formulation of the rule for *dvigu* compounds indicates that there is also compounding of words ending in *su*, even though they are not included in the list [of indeclinables]. And thus, for the sake of establishing the compounding of words ending in *su*, the term "consisting of more than one word" (*anekapada*) is not required here.
The venerable ones say, "This is correct. Regarding the rule for *dvigu* compounds: this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

By means of the sūtra governing the meaning of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the formation of a compound—consisting of a word denoting direction followed by a word ending in a case-suffix—is also prescribed when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows, provided the intended meaning is as stated.
It should be understood that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). [The rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29) serves as such an indicator.]
Because the word *ca* (and) signifies the inclusion of meaning, it is understood that when the sense of *ca* is present, the term *artha* (meaning) is also implied.

[Objection: But surely, by the rule "dvandva [is used] in the sense of *ca*," it is understood that a *dvandva* compound occurs wherever the sense of *ca* is perceived. And thus—while being carried away by the current...

In the verse, "He does not satisfy the cow, the horse, the man, or the beast, just as one intoxicated by liquor [does not satisfy others]," because the cow and the other items are construed with the act of leading (*nayana*) through their mutual connection, this applies even to the sentence: "The cow, the horse, the man, and the beast."

One might suspect that the technical designation *dvandva* would apply to words whose co-occurrence signifies a mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) consisting of reciprocal association (*parasparasāhitya*); however, this is precluded by the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) [in the definition]. This is the *dvandva*.

And by this much alone, since there is no occurrence of the effect [of the suffix] in the case of *ca* and *śas*, it will be understood that the suffix occurs when there is an object (*arthe*). Since this is already established,
the fact that he makes the mention of "object" (*arthagrahaṇa*) indicates that [the rule] does not apply to *ca*.

The meaning is that the *dvandva* compound occurs where [the sense of] "and" (*ca*) is present. By the mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*), a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended: the *dvandva* occurs only where the meaning [of "and"] has been expressed by that very [word]. However, in the case of "gām aśvam" (cow and horse), [it is not so].

The meaning is that the compound is understood as a *tatpuruṣa* by the very word "by means of" (*hetau*), and not as a *dvandva* because of the word "but" (*ca*); thus it is not a copulative compound. [Jñānapaṭala, Niḥṣṭhā (Sūtra 2.2.36):
"After words denoting genus, time, distance, and so forth..."]

By the rule prescribing that a subsequent *niḥṣṭhā* (past passive participle) is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable), it is indicated (*jñāpaka*) that in this context, the subsequent *niḥṣṭhā* is understood. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "niḥṣṭhā," there is the substitution of *cha* for a word ending in *niḥṣṭhā* when followed by a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a vowel or a soft consonant...

The rule regarding prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is being taught. Examples such as *kṣata-kṣīṇa* and so forth are cited. In that regard, in cases such as *sāraṅga-jagdhi*, *māsa-jātā*, *sukha-jātā*, *duḥkha-jātā*, and so on—
Since the posterior placement of the final member in *niḥśreṣṭha* would be incorrect, [the author] says: *jātikāla...*—
namely, by the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyo 'nācchādanāt ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

By this sūtra, the acute accent on the final syllable of a word ending in the suffix *kta* is prescribed when preceded by a genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), happiness (*sukha*), and so forth, as seen in examples such as *janman*, *bhūta*, and *sukṛta*. If the word ending in *kta* were a *nipāta* (an irregularly formed word) by the rule "niṣṭhā" [Pāṇini 3.2.102] prior to these [categories], then [the present rule would not apply].

In that case, since it would be difficult to find another word ending in a *kta* suffix [that could serve as a qualifier] for "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth, the prescription of vowel accents (*svaravidhāna*) by restating [the term] "another word ending in *kta*" would be untenable. Therefore, it is inferred that [this applies] to words such as *atikāla*, *sukha*, and others, which are formed with the suffix *kta*.

The application [of the rule] is precisely for that which lacks a visible example (*niḥsadr̥ṣṭānta*). Therefore, the intention is that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of forms such as *sāraṅgajagghī* is established. [Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.13: "The fourth case [is used] in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

[And by Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.36: "The fourth case ending [is compounded] with words meaning 'for the sake of that' (*tadartha*), 'purpose' (*artha*), etc. Thus, there is a compound of that which ends in the fourth case.

The rule for the formation of compounds with the word *artha* indicates that the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs when it signifies "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*). Precisely because the rule for compounding a word ending in the fourth case with a word meaning "for the sake of" is established there as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the fourth case is used in the sense of being for the sake of something.

Regarding the sūtra *caturthī saṃpradāne* ("the fourth case-affix is used for the recipient"), there is the vārttika: *tādarthye upasaṃkhyānam* ("an addition should be made for the sense of 'being for that purpose'"). In this context, the derivation of the word *tādarthya* is as follows: *tasmai arthaḥ* = *tadarthaḥ*; the state (*bhāva*) of being for that purpose is *tādarthyam*. In that regard, the phrase *tasmai*...

One might object that a compound with the word *artha* is not possible when it follows a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*), because a word ending in the fourth case rarely occurs in conjunction with the word *artha*, and because there is no such grammatical rule [prescribing it]. Anticipating this objection, [the author states] "the fourth case [is compounded] in the sense of 'for the sake of that' (*tadartha*)."

The formulation of the compound rule in the Sūtra (*caturthī tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ*)—which prescribes a compound with a word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*) alongside the word *artha*—is inconsistent if the fourth case is ungrammatical when used in conjunction with *artha*. Therefore, this inconsistency indicates that the fourth case is indeed applicable in such a construction. Thus it is said: "The fourth case [is used] in connection with *tadartha*, *artha*, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.36).

In that very same *Bhāṣya*, for the purpose of rejecting the *vārttika* "there should be an addition [to the rule] regarding the sense of being for that (*tādarthye*)," it is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the fourth case (*caturthī*) is valid in the sense of being for that. And the indicator is found in the rule "the fourth case [is used] with words meaning 'for the sake of that' (*tadartha-') and 'artha'" (*caturthī tadarthārtha*), which [prescribes the fourth case] for a word ending in the fourth case when combined with a word expressing "that for the sake of which" (*tadartha*).

The rule for forming a compound with that which ends in the fourth case is established by means of the term *tadartha*. If the fourth case were not used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*),
then because it would be difficult to find a word ending in the fourth case that is compounded with *tadartha*,
the prescription of compounding the fourth case with *tadartha* would be inconsistent.
Regarding this, it has been stated: "In that very same rule, [the word] ending in the fourth case [is used]. (Pāṇini 2.3.46):

*prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā*. Instead of formulating a single rule as "that which is in the vocative is called *āmantrita*," [the sūtra is divided into two]: "in the vocative" (*saṃbodhane*) and "it is called *āmantrita*" (*sāmantritam*).

(Sūtra 2.3.47–48) thus indicates that the rule for the application of case-endings (*vibhakty-adhikāra*) does not mean that the nominative case-ending (*prathamā*) occurs only when distinguished by [the presence of] an action (*karman*) and so forth. [Vivaraṇa: Now, regarding the section on case-endings (*vibhakti-vicāra*), there are two positions: the restriction of the suffix (*pratyaya-niyama*) and the restriction of the meaning (*artha-niyama*).
In that context, the restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*) is of the form: "the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is used only for the object (*karman*)," and so forth.

The restriction regarding the meaning (*arthaniyama*) is of the form: "the second case-ending is used only when the object is present," and so forth. Among these, in the view of the restriction regarding the suffix, if the word *mātra* were absent from the sūtra *prātipadikārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.3.46), [the following would occur].

The nominative case should also apply to the object and other factors. Although the rule "the accusative occurs only for the object" excludes meanings other than the object from the scope of the accusative, it does not exclude case-roles other than the accusative when applied to the object. And thus:

Having stated that the word "mātra" (only) serves the purpose of excluding [the application of] the nominative case even when [the object] is a *karman* (object), etc., the *Bhāṣya* refutes the aforementioned purpose of the word "mātra" by establishing the nominative case for *karman*, etc., through an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark).

Regarding this, [it is said] with the words "In the case of *saṃbodhana*," etc. The underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: if the nominative case were to occur even when there is a meaning in excess of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then, since the nominative would already be established by the rule for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha-sūtra*) even when there is an excess of the sense of address (*saṃbodhana*), [the separate mention of *saṃbodhana* would be redundant].
The rule *saṃbodhane ca* is redundant. It is not the case that this rule does not prescribe the nominative (*prathamā*) in the sense of addressing (*saṃbodhana*);

rather, it is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) for the purpose of prescribing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "vocative" (*āmantrita*). That which is the nominative in the sense of addressing receives the designation "vocative."

It should be stated that the meaning of the sentence [is established] through syntactic unity with the subsequent sūtra beginning with "syāt. If that were the case, he would have simply stated a single sūtra: "The vocative is [placed first] in the act of addressing. However, because of the division of the rules (yogavibhāga), [the status of the vocative] is determined by the first sūtra.

One must accept that the first rule prescribes the nominative case for the purpose of expressing the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), while the second rule prescribes the technical designation *āmantrita* (vocative) for that same case. Since the desired result is established by the aforementioned method, this sūtra, being otherwise redundant, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the nominative case does not occur when there is an excess of objects.

It must be said: likewise, in the case of the word *mātra*, the purpose is not the exclusion of the nominative (*prathamā*) meaning from among the objects (*karman*) and so forth. However, under the view that there is a restriction on the meaning (*arthaniyamapakṣa*), the stated purpose is even more clearly untenable; this is another matter. [Jñānapaṭala, verse 6cd] Furthermore, regarding the suffix *iñ*:
The mention of *bhārata* here [in Pāṇini 2.4.66] indicates that elsewhere, when *prāc* is mentioned, the mention of *bhārata* does not apply.
[Vi.Ṭ:
But surely...]

Regarding the rule *ḥcdvddhddhed;ahvaca iñaḥ*, [the question is]: in the expression *prācyaḥḍddhdhḍaddh;arateḥsdvdr1;u*, is it a *dvandva* compound or a *karmadhāraya*? If it is a *dvandva*, then [it refers to] that *iñ* which follows a *bahu-vrīhi* compound ending in *ḥcdvddhddhed;ahvac* (having two vowels) that occurs within a *prācya* gotra and a *bhārata* gotra.

The meaning of the sūtra is that there should be elision (*luk*). However, when it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, the meaning of the sūtra is that there is elision of the *iñ* suffix belonging to that which denotes an eastern gotra of the Bharatas. In that case, under the first alternative, the mention of "Bharata" would be purposeless, because [the elision] applies to those as well.
Anticipating the objection that "they are already included by the mention of 'Easterners' alone, for there are no barbarians elsewhere; thus,
in the second alternative, the mention of 'Easterners' would be redundant because there is an absence of non-Eastern barbarians," he accepts the *dvandva* (copulative) interpretation.
In this regard,

it has been stated by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra that the mention of "the great" (*mahat*) elsewhere in the Sūtra, rather than mentioning "the great" first, serves as an indicator of the meaning that the mention of the "great" does not apply to the [other] great elements.
To this, [the author] says: "In this context, the mention of 'Bharata' is for the sake of indication (*jñāpana*).
The purpose of this indication, however, is that the mention of 'Bharata' does not apply in the rule *iñaḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 2.4.60). Consequently, [the suffix does not apply] to *ĀṬḍālakāyana*.
In this case, the elision (*luk*) of the *phak* suffix does not occur. One named Uddālaka was born of the Bhṛgu lineage; his descendant in the male line is Āuddālaki, formed by the suffix *iñ*.
His son is Āuddālakāyana, [formed] by the suffix *phak* according to Pāṇini 4.1.101 (*yañiñośca*). And of that...

The elision (*luk*) of the *iñ* suffix that occurs after a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*) belonging to the easterners is not applied here; for although such elision would have been required by the rule "iñaḥ prācām" (Pāṇini 2.4.60), which means "there shall be elision of the *iñ* suffix when the lineage belongs to the easterners," the mention of "easterners" (*prācām*) in this context serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the mention of "easterners" does not apply to the present case.
Thus it is said: "He descends. This concludes the second chapter.
Now begins the third chapter:
[Jñānapāda] Perception (Sūtra 3.1.1).

The enumeration in the rule *eti-stu-śāsva-dṛśi-rujuṣ-aḥ kyap* indicates that the suffix *kyap* does not apply after every verbal root (*dhātu*). This is because it was stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *pratyayaḥ* and in the rule *hrasva-nasta-ca*.
Thus, because the suffix *ṣṭhā* is associated with the modification of its *t* into *ṣ*, and because the suffix *kyap*—
which is being brought forward from the preceding rule by the particle *ca* (*ca*)— is indicated as a reference to what has been previously mentioned, the prescription of *kyap* is untenable.
Anticipating this objection, [the author] provides the resolution: the word "dhātoḥ" (from a root), ending in the ablative case, is understood to follow here;
therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that the suffix *kyap* occurs after a root, with the letter *t* being elided. Thus, *kyap* applies because of the general nature of a root.

Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] *kyap* might apply again, the possibility of its occurrence is prevented by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because of the commonality of the verbal roots (*dhātu-sāmānya*). Thus it is said: "The enumeration [in Pāṇini 3.1.52] as *eti-stu-śāsv-as-...* [is the indicator]. For if *kyap* were to apply to any verbal root whatsoever, [this specific enumeration would be unnecessary].
Furthermore,

if [the suffix] *kyap* were applied to roots such as *etu*, the restrictive enumeration in the rule *hanaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.109) would be rendered useless. Moreover, that enumeration was established precisely so that *kyap* does not occur after every single verbal root.

The meaning is that it makes known. By the rule *kādy-anuṣaṅga-bandhāsañjanam* (the addition of the suffixes *ka*, etc., and the connection of the *anuṣaṅga*), it makes known that those elements which are absolutely unobserved (*atyantāparadṛṣṭāḥ*) are elided when they follow (*paraḥ*).
Regarding the rule *paraśca* ("and what follows"), there is the statement: "Or rather, for those that are absolutely unobserved..."
The author of the Vārttika has stated the purpose as "for the sake of the elision of subsequent [elements]":
let there be the elision (*lopa*) of those *kṛt* suffixes and others that are not observed anywhere by the subsequent, primary perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is the purpose of the sūtra *paraśca*. That being so, its meaning is that the grammatical operation (*kārya*) taught by rules such as *ṅkiti* would apply when the suffix *kviP* follows, and not otherwise. The author of the Bhāṣya [establishes] this vārtika through an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Having established the elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *kkip* and others that follow [the root], he rejected [the necessity of the rule] by stating: "The addition of the suffixes *ka* and so forth. For if the preceding elements were to be elided, then in the case of *kkip* and the rest—
The mention of the suffixes beginning with *kakāra* (the letter *k*) would be purposeless,
because every meaning of those suffixes is caused by a subsequent suffix (*parabhūta-pratyaya-nimittakatvāt*).
And thus, all those [suffixes] that undergo elision are elided only when they follow a suffix that causes their elision.

The meaning is that it makes known (*jñāpayati*). [Regarding the rule *ijādeśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.36): The statement of the *guṇa* substitution for the root *ṛcch* in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*)—as in the rule *ṛcchatyaśchor liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.4.11)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the augment *ām* does not apply to the *liṭ* of *ṛcch*. [Objection: But surely [the rule is] *ijādeśca gurumato'nṛcchaḥ*...?

In the Sūtra, let the mention of *ṛccha-* not be included. Nor should it be argued that in the absence of that [mention], the augment *ām* would also apply to the root *ṛcch*. For it is understood through an indicator (*jñāpaka*) alone that *ām* does not occur after *ṛcch*. The very indicator is this: "after *ṛcch* in the Perfect tense" (*ṛccher liṭi*).

By the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*, the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for the root *ṛcch* when followed by the *liṭ* suffix. If, however, the *ām* augment were applied to the *liṭ* of *ṛcch*, then because of the intervention of *ām*, the condition of being followed by *liṭ* would be absent, and thus the *guṇa* would not take effect.

The prescription of the *guṇa* [vowel substitution] would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, by means of this prescription of the *guṇa*, the absence of *ām* after the root *ṛcch* is indicated. And thus, since the desired form is already established by that very [prescription], the prohibition "after *ṛcch*" (*anaḥTktgrRN;ccchaḥ*) would be redundant; such is the underlying intention (*bhāva*).

[The suffix] *yak* [is applied] after a verbal root ending in a consonant before a *sārvadhātuka* affix (*Pāṇini 3.1.67*). Because of the prohibitive rule "the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not apply after roots ending in *du*, *ṛ*, *sn*, or *nam*" (*Pāṇini 3.1.89*), it is known that *yak* occurs when the agent is simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*). [Objection: But surely, in the case of expressing a state (*bhāva*)...

Furthermore, the affix *yak*, which is prescribed when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denoting the object follows, would not apply in the case of a *lakāra* (verbal ending) where the agent is also the object (*karmakartṛ*), because it would be superseded by *śap* when [the suffix] denotes the agent. To this, he says: "Not in the case of *duh*, *snuh*, *nam*, etc. [The rule states: "Not after *duh*, *snuh*, *nam*, etc."
By the rule *yak-ciṇ-au*,
*yak* and *ciṇ* are prescribed when the suffixes *ślu* and *liṭ* follow a root that has a *kartṛ-karman* (an agent who is simultaneously the object). Furthermore,
this prohibition [of *yak*] applies to the absence of *yak* when the root has a *kartṛ-karman*.
The intention is that the rule *prāptyabhāvād asaṃgataḥ san karmakartari yaṅ bhavati* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this point. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.93: *kradatiṅ*]

In certain rules for the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the mention of *tiṅ* in the rule "tiṅśca" (Pāṇini 5.3.56) is an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that suffixes such as *aṇ* do not occur after verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*. [Objection:
But surely, in the rule "kṛdatiṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.93), the mention of *atiṅ* need not exist. Nor...
In that case, even a *tiṅ* suffix would receive the designation of *kṛt*; consequently, because it would end in a *kṛt*, forms such as *paṭhati* would receive the designation of *prātipadika*.
This objection need not be raised, for even if they were designated as *prātipadikas*, there would be no fault regarding [the expression of] singularity and so forth.

Because *su*, *au*, *jas*, and so forth [are case endings] and because it is impossible to apply *ṭā*, *bhyām*, and so forth to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), since a verbal suffix lacks connection with femininity;
nor can it be said that primary suffixes (*cāṇādi*) or secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) would occur after those ending in verbal suffixes.

Because the formation of *taddhita* suffixes is prescribed for the purpose of denoting offspring (*apatya*) and so forth, it is impossible to bring about the production of a *taddhita* suffix from a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), since such a word lacks any connection with offspring and the like; or rather, [this is established] precisely through an *jñāpaka*.
For it would have been possible to prevent the derivation of *aṇ* and other suffixes from verbal forms (*tiṅanta*).

The very fact that [Pāṇini] provides an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, the rule "in some cases, when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is prescribed"—is proof of this. If verbal forms were also considered nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and thus secondary suffixes were to be derived from them, then [the author] would have mentioned them in the section on secondary suffixes.

The rule *tiṅśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56) would be redundant, since its purpose is already accomplished by the rule *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.3.55). Consequently, if *tiṅ* were designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then forms ending in *taṅ* (the personal endings of the verb) would also incur the designation of nominal stems.

The intention is that, because undesirable consequences (*doṣa*) would otherwise arise, the mention of *atiṅ* in the rule "kṛdatiṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.93) should be rejected. [Jñānapradīpa] Regarding the rule "kratyāḥ" (3.1.95),
the mention of *krtya* from that [preceding rule] is [to be understood here].

The evidence is that the designation *kṛt* occurs prior to the suffix *ṇvul*. [Objection: But surely, in the rule for *kṛt* suffixes, it should have been stated "prior to *ṇvul*"; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the designation *kṛt* applying even to *ṇvul*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Not so."

It would overrule [the rule]. If the designation *kṛt* were not established prior to the sūtra "ṇvultṛcau," then since *tṛc* would also possess the designation *kṛt*, [the rule] "those ending in *kṛt* are called *ah" would apply as well.

It is possible to formulate [the rule] thus; however, the separate mention of *taḥ* and *tācchīlya* would be purposeless. For, since the separate mention of *taḥ* and *tācchīlya* is made in the sūtra "aḍhaukādibhyaḥ kṛñaśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.169), it is inferred by that [fact].

Regarding the statement "the *kṛt* designation [applies] prior to *ṇvul*": it should not be argued that although the meaning "the *kṛt* designation applies prior to *taC*" is obtained through the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), the phrase "prior to *ṇvul*" is not thereby established;
for since an indicator depends upon a specific rule (*sūtra*), [it is restricted to] that which contains *taC*.

The intention is that since the section governing the technical designation *kṛtya* is known to precede the rule "ṇvultṛcau" (Pāṇini 3.1.133) by means of this very indication (*jñāpaka*), it need not have been explicitly stated as "prāṅṇvulaḥ. As for the reading "kṛtyāḥ prāṅṇvulaḥ" found in the *Kāśikā*:

It is established that such a reading of the Sūtra is not to be respected. [Jñāpakapradīpa, p. 86]—The prescription of *āluc* when *luṅ* is already established is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this [suffix] occurs after other [roots] as well.
[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: In the rule *sṛghasyado-masa-jitṛṣi-kṣipe-r-aluc*, why should the heavy suffix *āluc* not be prescribed? Let the suffix *lu* alone be prescribed.

Having raised the objection that once *śap* is applied, the form *spṛhayālu* is established by the rule "ato dīrgho yañi" (Pāṇini 7.3.101), which prescribes lengthening before the suffix *yañ*, [the author] says: "luśeti. Thus, the prescription of the suffix *āluC* indicates that the suffix *āluC* occurs even after verbal roots (*dhātu*) not explicitly mentioned in the sūtras.

And thus, forms such as *śayālu* are established. In that regard, because the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "after roots beginning with *ad-* and those ending in *prabhṛti*" (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is no possibility of the lengthening of the vowel following the elision (*luk*); therefore, the objection that the form cannot be accounted for due to the absence of lengthening is resolved. [Jñānapaṭala] The suffix *luṭ* is used for the non-current day (future). (Pāṇini 3.3.15)

The statement that *laḥ* has the designation *sat* indicates that *laḥ* is also *ṅit* when not referring to the current day (*anadyatana*). [Note: The sequence of the sūtras is "laḥ ṭaḥ saḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.78) and "satsaṃjñau bhavataḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.65), followed by "anadyatane luṭ" (Pāṇini 3.3.15). In this context, the rule should be divided as "anadyatane" and "luṭ. In the sūtra "anadyatane," the phrase "laḥ ṭaḥ saḥ" is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

The meaning of that [sūtra] is: "In the sense of non-today (anadyatana), the suffixes *la* are replaced by *śatṛ* and *śānac*, which are designated as *sat*. By this, forms such as "by one who will take up the sacred fires tomorrow" (*śvo 'gnīn ādāsyamānena*) and "by one who will sacrifice with Soma tomorrow" (*śvaḥ somena yakṣyamāṇena*) are established. Nor should it be asked how this is possible in the absence of an injunction prescribing *la* for the non-today tense.

It has been established in the Bhāṣya that by the very prescription of substitutes designated as *sat* through the exclusion of the *yogavibhāga* of "the *la*-suffixes occur in the non-current tense" (*anadyatane laḥ*), it is made known that the *la*-suffixes occur in the non-current tense. To this, [the following is said]: "The *la*-suffixes occur in the non-current tense" (*anadyatane laḥ*) [Jñāpakasamuccaya]; and "in the sense of hope, like the past" (*āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*, Pāṇini 3.3.132).

If it is argued that [the suffixes] are sufficient for *saṃbhāvana* (possibility), this is understood from the *jñāpaka* rule: "In *saṃbhāvana*, they are not sufficient" (Sūtra 3.3.154). [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra: Now, since there is no distinction between *āśaṃsā* (hope/expectation) and *saṃbhāvana*, those [suffixes] which are prescribed for *āśaṃsā* would also apply to *saṃbhāvana*, and those which are prescribed for *saṃbhāvana* would also apply to *āśaṃsā*.

Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the sense of "sufficiency" (*alam-artha*) is not invariably understood in the case of *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility), whereas it is not understood in the case of *āśaṃsā* (expectation); for even though there is no difference between the two meanings, a distinction exists based on the presence or absence of the sense of sufficiency. It should not be said that the grammatical application will be settled by taking that [distinction] as the basis, because the aforementioned fault remains.

If that were the case, then in the sūtra *saṃbhāvane 'lamiti cet* (Pāṇini 3.3.154), the qualification *alamiti cet* would be redundant. For if the meaning of *alam* were necessarily understood as "capacity" (*saṃbhāvana*) [in all instances], then, due to the absence of any other usage, the qualification *alam* would not have been prescribed.

The qualification [of the object] by means of "meditation" (*bhāvanā*) and "uncertainty" (*asaṃśaya*) is purposeful. And thus, since the capacity to produce that [result] is established for both meditation and uncertainty, it remains impossible to state a distinction [between them]. Therefore, [the author] says: "In that case, meditation... and so forth. What then?

If it is asked, "In the absence of these two [definitions], what is the resolution for the aforementioned lack of systematic distinction? Kaiyaṭa states that the systematic distinction is maintained because: *āśaṃsā* is a specific kind of desire (*icchā*) characterized by the form "May this happen to me," whereas *saṃbhāvanā* is a specific kind of uncertain knowledge (*aniścita-jñāna*) directed toward one of two alternatives (*ekatarakoṭika*). Thus, the distinction between them is consistent. [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.163: *tum-arthe sese...*]

The mention of "for the sake of another" (*tum-artha*) indicates that there is an agent distinct from the agent of the *tumun* suffix. [In the rule] beginning with "In the sense of *tumun*, [the suffixes] *se*, *sen*, etc. (*tum-arthe seseṇase-*, etc.), suffixes such as *se* and *sen* are prescribed in the Vedic section for the sense of *tumun*. In this regard, a doubt arises as to what the meaning of *tumun* is. It cannot be the agent that is the meaning of *tumun*.

If that were the case, the meaning of the sūtra would be that [kṛt suffixes] such as *sa* and *sen* occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed; in that event, the word *tum-arthe* ("in the sense of the infinitive suffix *tumun*") would be redundant, because the fact that those [suffixes] express the agent would already be understood by the rule *kartari kṛt*. Therefore, he says: "The mention of *tum-artha*..."

And thus, according to the manner previously stated, the mention of the sense of the infinitive suffix *tumun* (in Pāṇini’s rule) being otherwise redundant indicates that there exists another meaning of *tumun* besides the agent (*kartṛ*). That [other meaning] is the action (*bhāva*), and it is in the sense of action that suffixes such as *se*, *ena*, and so forth are prescribed. Therefore, the mention of the sense of *tumun* was made for that purpose; this is the underlying intention (*bhāva*).

The purpose of making this known is that the *vārttika*—"after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix *kṛt* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*)"—need not be stated. This is because, as is clear in the *Bhāṣya*, the fact that *ktvā* and other such suffixes denote an abstract state is established simply by the continued application of the mention of "for the sake of the sense of *tumun*" (*tumarthagrahaṇānuvṛttyaiva*). *kartari kṛt* (Sūtra 3.4.67).

The word *eva* in the sūtra "tayoreva" (Pāṇini 3.4.70) indicates that from this point onward there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). The word *ca* in the sūtra "ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.71) indicates that prior to this, there is a co-occurrence. [Viśvanātha: But then, what is the purpose of the word *eva* in the sūtra "tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ"?

One might object: "The word *sa* (he) should be stated [in the rule] so that *kṛtya* and the other suffixes apply only to the object (*karman*) and the patient (*bhāva*), and not to the agent (*kartṛ*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] replies: the exclusive particle (*eva*) is used to indicate that even when *kṛtya* suffixes are present, there is indeed an inclusion of the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). This is because the rule *tayoh* (Pāṇini 3.4.70) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), and thus the intended meaning is established by that very fact.

And thus, since the inclusion of the agent (*kartṛ*) would also have been obtained [by the rule], the particle *eva* is used for the purpose of its exclusion; therefore, it serves its purpose with respect to the verbal root portion (*dhātvaṃśa*). However, its purpose elsewhere is that in cases such as *bhavyādi* and *śabda*, there is also the cognition of the agent. For this very reason, both usages are justified: *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* (the boy is one who should sing the Sāmans) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and *geyāni māṇavakena sāmāni* (the Sāmans are to be sung by the boy) in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

To this he says: "The word *eva* in the rule *tayoḥ eva* [Pāṇini 3.4.70]. Thus, the intention is that the mention of the word *vā* in the rule *bhavyageya...* (Pāṇini 3.4.68) need not have been made. [Objection: But if this is being indicated, then in the rules *dāśagognau saṃpradāne* (Pāṇini 3.4.73) and *bhīmādayo’pādāne* (Pāṇini 3.4.74), a simultaneous application (*samāveśa*) would also result.

And likewise, the suffix *kta* would also apply to the agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, [the author] states "in the sense of the beginning of an action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) and so forth. Now, the meaning is this: let it simply be that the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the beginning of an action when denoting the agent; there is no need for the word "and" (*ca*). For the inclusion of the meaning of the word "and"—namely, the co-occurrence [of both senses]—is established by the previously mentioned rule itself, which is indicated by the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*).

However, the word *tu* (but) indicates that in the subsequent sūtras beginning with *ādikarmaṇi*, there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, in the case of *dāśa*, *goghnā-* and so forth, there is no co-occurrence with the meaning of the agent. Thus ends the third chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

[From the *Jñānapradīpa*: "Because of the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48), which prescribes the suffix *ṅīṣ*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not arise from this [base] (*praśasta*). [From the *Vivaraṇa*:]

In the commentary on the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*, the example *pracarī* is presented as an illustration of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. This means that when the sense is "the wife of a *praśasta*," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the word *praśasta*. [Objection: But [is it not so that] the wife of a *praśasta*...
In this sense, fearing that the taddhita suffix *aṇ* would apply because the meaning of "this belongs to him" (*tasyedaṃ*) is present, [the author] says: "by the introduction of the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
If, from the word *praṣṭha*, [the suffix were applied] by rule...

If the derivation of that secondary suffix (*taddhita*) were as you suggest, then because it would end in the suffix *aṇ*, the form would be established by the application of *ṅīp* alone under the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15); consequently, the prescription of *ṅīṣ* under the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48) would become purposeless.
Furthermore, there is no difference in form between the suffix *ṅīṣ* and *ṅīp*, nor is there any difference in accent;

for just as *ṅīṣ* is acute (*udātta*), so too *ṅīp* is acute by virtue of the rule "and [the vowel] of that which is unaccented, where there is the elision of an acute vowel" (*anudātasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ*). Consequently, the prescription of *ṅīṣ* being superfluous would not [be justified].

The intention is that [Pāṇini] makes it known that the formation of a taddhita suffix occurs after a word ending in *praśasta* (excellent), according to the rule "from a word denoting excellence" (*praśastādibhyaś ca*, Pāṇini 5.3.60). Furthermore, this is not [an application] of the rule "from a word denoting excellence" (*praśastādibhyaś ca*) for the sense of "this belongs to him," because [in that case] the suffix *cha* is prescribed by the rule "*vr̥ddhāc chaḥ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.114).

In the case of the suffix *ccha*, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, one might argue that the word *bhāvanīyā* is formed. In that situation, let the rule *puṃyogāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.48) serve to prescribe the suffix *ṅīṣ* by setting aside *ṭāp*.
If so, how can that [rule] be a *jñāpaka* (an indicator)? To this, it is said: *tarchi...* (then...).

Because the mention of the "end of a name" (ākhyāgra) would otherwise be purposeless. Being purposeless, it indicates that the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies after whatever word denoting a male refers to a female, even without the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In the case of *bhānavīyā*, that which denotes a male...
The word *anuśatikā* does not denote a female, and that which denotes a female and ends in the suffix *cha* does not have a masculine form;

therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied there. However, the word *praśasta* [denotes a female] even without a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), because it possesses feminine denotation; hence [the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies].
The intention [of the author] is that, because it is a *prathamā* (nominative) case-ending, it is ultimately established that this is not a *taddhita* suffix.
[Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.54:
"Also after a word denoting a limb of one's own body when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*)."

Because of the prohibitive rule "saṃhitāvidyamānapūrvācca" (Pāṇini 4.2.57), which serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), it follows that the suffix occurs even after a word that is not oxytone (*ānantodātāt*). [Vivaraṇa: Now, one might object regarding the rule "svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt":
The mention of *upasarjana* is redundant; for by simply carrying over [the word] *dvandva-vṛttiś ca antodāttāt* from the rule *dvandva-vṛttiś ca antodāttāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.52),
[the desired result follows].

Because [the word] *upasarjanāt* is present, there is no possibility of the simultaneous application (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭanyāya*) of the rule for words ending in an acute accent (*antodātāt*), which would otherwise follow from the context;
therefore, the term "*upasarjanāt*" is employed to exclude that. And when that term is employed, by virtue of its own force...

It should be stated that the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a mere secondary member (*upasarjana*) that ends in a word denoting a limb of the body, provided it has an acute accent on the final syllable, even if it is not [otherwise] anudātta. This is because the very mention of the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.54], which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), implies the necessity of the condition "having an acute accent on the final syllable" (*antodātāt*) for the application of the rule "and after a word denoting a limb of the body" (*svāṅgācca*).
This is because it is understood from the Sūtra that there is no *anu-vṛtti* [carrying over] here.
The indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the rule *sahanañ-vidyamāna-pūrvāt*.
From a word denoting a limb of the body (*svāṅga*) preceded by the triad beginning with *saha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

It is excluded [from the application of the rule]. Examples include *sakeśa* (having hair), *akeśa* (hairless), and *vidyamānanāsika* (possessing a nose). In these cases, when a word beginning with *sa-* or *a-* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first member of the compound (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*).

Since the final syllable of *svāṅga* does not possess the udātta accent due to the *śeṣanighāta* (the non-accentuation of the remainder), the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanāt* would not apply; therefore,
the prohibition [of *ṅīṣ*] is rendered purposeless.

The mention of "antodātāt" (ending in an acute accent) in that [sūtra] indicates the existence of a rule [prohibiting the application of the suffix]. Thus, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply even after a word that does not end in an acute accent if it is preceded by *sa-* or *ha-* etc., the sūtra containing the word *nañ* is meaningful as a prohibition against that very [application]. And so...

The intention is that since the requirement of the rule *upasarjanāt* is already fulfilled by the mere recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ṛk-pūraba-dvi-ratha* alone, the explicit mention of *upasarjana* need not be made. [Jñāpakapradīpa] Regarding the rule *ḍaki lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.133): this very rule indicates that the suffix *ḍhak* occurs after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*.

[Objection: But surely, from the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*, by the rule "there is elision of the final vowel" (*ḍhaki lopaḥ*), the form *paitṛṣvaseya* is intended [to be derived]. That, however, is not established, because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) prescribing the suffix *ḍhak* after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*.
