To this, he replies: "This very [suffix]," and so forth.

The intention is this: since the rule prescribing the elision of the suffix *pitṛṣvasu* (P. 4.1.132) would be inconsistent if the suffix *ḍhak* were not present when *ḍhak* follows, the very prescription of the elision of *pitṛṣvasu* before *ḍhak* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *ḍhak* indeed occurs after *pitṛṣvasṛ*. This is the underlying principle.

By this indicator (*jñāpaka*), one should assume that the reading *śubhrādibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.123) is intended as *śubhrādibhyaḥ pitṛṣvasuḥ*. Alternatively, it should be understood that in the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120), the mention of *strībhyo* is an inclusion of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). Thus, the author of the Uddyota established that the formation of *pitṛṣvasrīya* is thereby accomplished. [Jñāpakasamuccaya on Pāṇini 4.2.42: *brāhmaṇamāṇava-*.]

The prescription of *yan* that is stated here indicates that this suffix applies even to other words besides those [explicitly mentioned]. [Objection: But surely, by the rule "from *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, *vāḍava*, etc., *yan*" (*brāhmaṇamāṇavavāḍavādyan*), *yan* is prescribed after *brāhmaṇa* and others in the sense of a collection (*samūha*) and so forth. Examples include *brāhmaṇyam* for a collection of *brāhmaṇas*, and so on. In that rule, let there be no mention of *yan*.

This is because the form *iḥ* is established by the application of the suffix *yañ* through the rule *kedārādyañ ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.40). There is no difference between the forms or the accents of *ḍhyañ*, *yañ*, or *yan*. Nor should it be argued that there is a distinction such that if *yañ* were used, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply in the feminine according to *yañaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16), whereas it would not if *yan* were used; for it is stated in the *Kaumudī* that the suffix *ṅīp* applies only after a word ending in *yañ* belonging to the section on *apatya* (descendants).

Anticipating the objection that since *brāhmaṇa* and other such words are already *vṛddha* by their very nature, the *vṛddhi* [substitution] would apply even when *yañ* is present, and thus the specific condition "when *yañ* follows" would be redundant, [the author] says: "when *yañ* is the subject under discussion. Thus, the mention of *yañ*, though seemingly purposeless, indicates that *yañ* occurs after words other than *brāhmaṇa* and the rest as well.

By this, it is established that there is a collection (*samūha*) of those [words] ending in *praśasta*. And since the augment *vṛddhi* occurs when the suffix *yañ* is present—as in the case of *ādivṛddhi*—the mention of *yañ* has been made for the sake of its fulfillment (*cāritārthya*). Thus, the Vārttika stating "an addition [should be made] after *praśasta*" need not be composed, because the desired result is achieved through this very indicator (*jñāpaka*); such is the intention.

[The rule] *khaṇḍikādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.45) provides evidence that the rule of "extension to what ends with [a specific stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies here, and that the suffix *vuñ* precedes and the suffix *añ* follows. Since this cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is not contradictory for a single statement to provide evidence for both points.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: by the rule *khaṇḍikādi-bhyaś-ca*, the suffix *añ* is prescribed in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). In the *khaṇḍika*-group, the word *kṣudrakamālavaśaḥcdvddhddhedaga* is recited. What is the purpose of its recitation? For the suffix *añ* would be established from that very word even by the rule *anudātāder-añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44), since *kṣudrakamālavaśaḥcdvddhddhedaga* begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*). Its status as beginning with an unaccented vowel is as follows:

In the sense of "the offspring of the Kṣudrakas," there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix *viñ* prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.168 (*janapadaśabdād vuñ*). From *Mālava*, however, there is the suffix *ñyaṅ* characterized by *vṛddhi*. Then follows a *dvandva* compound. Kaiyaṭa maintains that because the final member of the compound is then accented (*samāsāntodātatva*), the word begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātāditva*). From that, the suffix *añ* is added in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).

Nor should it be argued that the recitation of that [word] is for the purpose of precluding the *vuñ* suffix prescribed by the rule "gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājāhuñ" (Pāṇini 4.2.39). For, since the rule "anudātāder añ" (Pāṇini 4.2.44) is subsequent, the *vuñ* suffix of the previous rule cannot apply in its domain; furthermore, the *vuñ* derived from "gotra" is not applicable after a word ending in "gotra" such as "kṣaudrakamālavaśa. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "For this very reason, the recitation [of the word] makes known that even the former..."

There are two statements: "vuñ is prescribed [in place of aṇ] after *paramat*," and "there is the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a suffix to a word ending in another word). Accordingly, it has been established in the *Bhāṣya* that, setting aside *vuñ*, the suffix *añ* is taught for the sense of "a collection" (*samūha*) in the case of *kṣudraka-mālava-śabde-pāṭha*. This is indicated by the rule beginning with "*khaṇḍikādi-bhyaś ca*."

Now, one might object: "How can two things be made known by a single statement? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "By the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapattyā*). That which serves as a communicator (*jñāpaka*) exists through the impossibility otherwise. The sense is that since the injunction of the *kṣudraka-mālavān* cannot be established without both [the two factors], it is possible to communicate both of them. Thus, the recitation is not merely for the purpose of communication.

However, the authors of the Vārttika have stated that this reading is for the sake of distinguishing the meaning: when there is a desire to express a collection (*samūha*) consisting of an army (*senā*), as in "the army of the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas" (*kṣaudrakamālavī senā*), [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied]; but when there is a desire to express a collection of something else, the suffix *vuñ* is used, as in "the collection of the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas" (*kṣaudrakamālavakam*). [Pāṇini 4.2.92: *śeṣe*]

The rule *pheś cha ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.149), which prescribes the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *phiñ*, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffixes *gha* and others do not occur in the sense of *apatya* (offspring). [Note: The governing rule *śeṣe* indicates that the suffixes *gha* and others to be mentioned hereafter apply in senses other than *apatya* and so forth.]

In the absence of this governing rule (*śeṣādhikāra*), suffixes such as *gha* and others would apply even in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, just like *aṇ* and others, because *gha* and the rest are exceptions (*apavāda*). Therefore, the governing rule for "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) has been established. However, the author of the Bhāṣya, by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), set aside the application of *gha* and other suffixes in the sense of "offspring" and so forth even in the absence of the governing rule for "the remainder," and thus rejected the necessity of that governing rule.

Regarding that, [it is said]: "pheś cha ca. By the rule "pheś cha ca," the suffix *cha* is prescribed after a word ending in *phiñ* that denotes a *sauvīra* gotra, in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*); by the word "ca" (*and*), the suffix *ṭhak* is also prescribed. For example: the offspring of Yamunda is *Yāmundāyaniḥ*. Since [Yamunda] belongs to the *tikādi* group, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. His offspring is *Yāmundāyanīyaḥ* or *Yāmundāyanikaḥ*; this is the illustrative example. In that case, let the rule simply be "pheḥ vā" (or "pheś ca").

The term *ṭhak* is carried over from the preceding sūtra, "vaḥṛddhāṭṭhak" (Pāṇini 4.1.148). Since *ṭhak* is already provided there, the suffix *cha* would have been applicable by the rule "vaḥṛddhāccchaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.114); therefore, the prescription of *cha* serves no other purpose. However, it functions as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in the absence of *aṇ*, the *gha*-class suffixes do not apply to [patronymic] descendants and the like.

And thus, since the suffix *ccha* would not otherwise apply, the provision of *ccha* is for the purpose of its attainment; this constitutes its utility within its own scope (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*). Consequently, since the desired result is established by this very rule, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "after *śi*" (*śeḥ*) may be rejected—this is the underlying intention (*bhāvaḥ*).

Even though there may be a suspicion that the aforementioned indicator (jñāpaka) refers only to those [sacrifices] performed for the sake of offspring, nevertheless, regarding other purposes as well, it is said: "The mention of *gotra* serves as an indicator for collective [rites], the mention of *daivayāta* for those related to the gods (*daivika*), and the mention of *bhāstrāyaṇa* for those related to the non-resident (*naivāsika*)."

The indicators (*jñāpaka*) stated by Patañjali should be considered here. From the indicator consisting of the mention of *Kalāpin* and *Vaiśampāyana* (Pāṇini 4.3.104), it follows that the designation of "pupil" (*antevāsī*) does not apply to the pupils of pupils.

[Commentary: Now, by the rule "kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca," the suffix *ṇini* is prescribed after words ending in the third case—namely, those denoting disciples (*antevāsin*) of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana—in the sense of "one who studies what was taught by him. Hṛidru is the name of a disciple of Kalāpin.

Then, by adding the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of "one who studies" (*adhyetṛ*) to the word *Hārīta*, the form *Hārītraṇi* arises. Vaiśampāyana’s disciple was Ālambhi; from that, by adding the suffix *ṇini*, the form *Ālambhina* arises. Among them, Kalāpin was one of the nine disciples of Vaiśampāyana.

Since the designation "Śaiśirīya" is observed in common usage for both the *Lokākṣi-śaiśirīya* and the *Yajña-śaiśirīya*, and since the inclusion of the *Hāridravīya* is already established by the mention of "disciples of Vaiśampāyana" (which includes the *Vaiśampāyanāntevāsins*), the explicit mention of "Kalāpin" in the Sūtra may be omitted.

Likewise, the sūtra "śaunakādibhyaś chandasi" (Pāṇini 4.3.106), which prescribes the suffix *ṇini*, also supports the aforementioned meaning; for the word *khāṇḍāyana* is also recited in the *gaṇa* of Śaunaka and others. And Khāṇḍāyana was a disciple of Vaiśampāyana, who was himself a disciple of Kaṭha.

And thus, anticipating the objection that—since the inclusion of Khāṇḍāyana is already established by the mention of the group of Vaiśampāyana’s disciples according to the logic stated previously, its recitation in the list beginning with Śaunaka is redundant—one demonstrates its utility as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by stating: "because of the mention of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana."

And likewise, in the Sūtra, by the term *antevāsin*, only direct pupils (*antevāsins*) are intended, and not the pupils of pupils (*antevāsy-antevāsins*). However, for the sake of establishing the suffix *ṇini* in the case of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana—who are respectively the pupils of Vaiśampāyana’s pupil—the separate mention of *tathoḥ* (the suffixes *ta* and *tha*) is made; thus, the rule achieves its purpose within its own scope.

However, there is a specific purpose [for this rule]: the suffix *ṇini* does not apply to the disciples of Vaiśampāyana’s disciples, nor to the disciples of Kalāpin’s disciples. These must be sought in the Purāṇas and other such sources. There are four disciples of Kalāpin: Chārītru, Chagalī, Tumbaru, and Ulapa.

Ālambī, Cūḍāla, Bheḍi, Kaliṅga, Kamala, Ṛcaḥḍābha, Āruṇi, Tāṇḍya, Śyāmāyana, Kaṭha, and Kalāpin—these nine are the disciples of Vaiśampāyana, according to the *Bhāṣāmanoramā*. Thus ends the fourth chapter. Fifth Chapter. [The first section begins:
5. The fifth chapter.

[Pāṇini 5.1.118: *upasargāc chandasi*] || The grammatical reference in [Pāṇini 6.3.34: *striyāḥ puṃvat*] indicates that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not apply in the sense of *vat*. [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa-sāra: Now, [one might object] regarding the words *strī* and *pums*: |||

In the case of the suffix *vat*, the forms *strīvat* and *puṃvat* are observed; however, these two cannot be established [by the rules]. This is because, according to the rule "From *strī* and *puṃs*, [the suffixes] *nañ* and *tañ* [are added] in the sense of 'being before'" (Pāṇini 4.1.87), those meanings which occur prior to that [suffix]—

The negative particles *nañ* and *snañ*, which are prescribed after all nominal stems (*sarvanāman*) with the specific sense of excellence (*prakṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), are superseded by every suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, they also supersede the suffix *vati* [prescribed] by the rule: "When there is equality with that, provided it is an action, the suffix *vati* is used" (Pāṇini 5.1.115).
Anticipating the objection that [if the rule were applied as stated] only *nañ* and *snañ* would occur, he says: "The mention [in the rule] is 'as in the case of the masculine' (*striyāḥ puṃvat*).
Thus, the sūtra "after *strī* and *puṃs*, [the suffixes] *nañ* and *snañ*" does not operate in the sense of the suffix *vat*.

The intention is that if [the rule] were to apply, then the designation "puṃvat" would be incorrect; this is the underlying thought. [Jñānapaṭala] Not [from] a tatpuruṣa compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. (Sūtra 5.1.121)

By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *naño guṇapratiṣedhe sampādyārhāglakṣaṇeṣu taddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.155), it is understood that all these secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) occur after a word that requires another word as its complement (*sāpekṣa*). [Vi.Ṭ] "Not..."

By the rule *nañpūrvāttatpuruṣādacatura-saṃgata-lava-mavaṭa-yudha-kata-ra-salaseḥ ṭyaṇ*, it is established that the suffix *ṭyaṇ*—which is prescribed by the rules immediately following this sūtra—is not applied after a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound. Examples include *apatitvam* (the state of not falling) and *apaṭutvam* (the state of not being clever).

In that regard, the author of the *Bhāṣya* established the non-application (*apravṛtti*) of the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) taught in subsequent rules—such as in the case of *īṣatpāṭavam* and so forth—in order to provide the justification for rejecting the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.106]. Thus: "on account of this indication (*jñāpaka*)."

The meaning is as follows: in examples such as *vatsebhyo na hriyate*, because there is dependence upon a negation (*pratiṣedha*), the capacity characterized by independence (*nirapekṣatva*) is absent; consequently, since the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) governed by the rule regarding "capable words" (*samartha-*) does not arise, the prescription that the word ending in a secondary derivative expressing meanings such as "to be accomplished" (*saṃpādya*) following the negative particle (*nañ*) is oxytone (*antodātta*) becomes untenable.

This indicates that when such a formation is being made, every secondary derivative (*taddhita*) generally arises with reference to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). However, in the case of *apatiḥ* (not a husband) and then *apatitvam* (the state of not being a husband), since the *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound lacks independence (*sāpekṣatvābhāva*), subsequent secondary derivatives cannot occur; thus, the forms *tvatalbhyām* are established even without them. Therefore, the rule "not from a *nañ*-preceded tatpuruṣa" (*na nañpūrvāttatpuruṣāt*) is fit to be rejected.

[Commentary on the Sūtra: The elision of *ya* [in the word *samāṃsamīnā*] indicates that there is no *luk*-elision here. [Vivaraṇa: Now, in the rule "samāṃ samāṃ vijāyate" (Pāṇini 5.2.12), the suffix *kha* is prescribed after the entire compound *samāyāṃ samāyām* in the sense of "giving birth every year. The example given is *samāṃsamīnā gauḥ* ("a cow that calves every year"). That cow which gives birth at each successive interval is described in this way.

In that case, because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix, it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.72), the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) belonging to its constituent part would have been required. However, since the form "samām" is established through the prescribed substitution (*nipātana*) of *ya*-lopa, it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that the case-ending is not elided here in the first member of the compound. If [the case-ending were elided]...

In that case, there would be elision of the *sup* suffix due to the fact that [the feminine suffix] *yāṭ* is a part of the *su*-suffix. Since the elision of *yalopa* would already be established by the elision of *sup*, the specific mention of *yalopa* in the rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that the elision occurs only of the letter *ya* and not of the entire suffix. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, there would likewise be no elision of *sup* in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as well; for it is accepted that the elision of *yalopa* applies only to the prior member (*pūrvapada*), and thus the audible form of *āḥ* does not occur in the subsequent member.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *samāhāra* (compound) in the rule with the suffix *visarga* (*yat*), which involves the elision of *y*, is inconsistent because the rule applies to the latter member of a compound. This is because the elision of *y* is optionally prescribed for the two members of a sentence (*vākya*), and the mention in the *sūtra* takes the form of a sentence. Thus, there is the statement regarding the elision of *y*: "After *yatas*, *etadas*, and *adas*, when expressing measure" (*yatadeteḥ parimāṇe*, Pāṇini 5.2.39).

The inclusion of the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) in the rule indicates that "proof" (*pramāṇa*) is one thing and "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is another. [Objection: But surely, in the sūtra "the suffix *vatup* is used after these [words] in the sense of measure," the inclusion of the term "measure" is redundant.

Anticipating the objection that the meaning of *parimāṇa* is already obtained by the simple anuvṛtti (carrying over) of the word *pramāṇe* from the sūtra *pramāṇe dvayasaJc* (Pāṇini 5.2.37), [the author] states *parimāṇagrahaṇam* ("the mention of *parimāṇa*") in order to make known that *parimāṇa* is distinct from *pramāṇa*.

That by which grain and the like are measured through its own inherent dimensions, such as *kāṣṭha* (a wooden measure) and so forth, is *parimāṇa*; it refers to measures such as a *prastha*. Kaiyaṭa states that *pramāṇa* is that by which the width of wood, cloth, and so on is measured, such as a *hasta* (a cubit). It is said: "Unmāna is indeed measurement by height, while parimāṇa is measurement from all sides."

"Length (*āyāma*) shall be the measure (*pramāṇa*), while the number (*saṃkhyā*) is to be excluded from all [cases]. Here, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "The suffix *ṭhak* is added after words denoting numbers, *go*, *puccha*, and measures" (Pāṇini 5.1.19) should be consulted. [Jñānapradīpa] Due to the rule "of this [stem ending in *an*]" (Pāṇini 5.3.5), which prescribes a substitute for the word ending in *an* before a suffix beginning with *th*, there is a *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) that the suffix *thamu* occurs here.

In this section, in order to establish the form *ittham* in the sense of "in this manner" (*etena prakāreṇa*), the rule-division *etadaḥ an* is formulated. Regarding that, the meaning of the sūtra *etadaḥ* is as follows: the sūtra *etetau rathoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.4) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). This means that the substitutes *eta* and *it* occur for the word *etad* when followed by a suffix beginning with the letter *r* or the letter *th*.

The suffix *reḍh* mentioned in the rule *anadyatane rhil anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.21) begins with the letter *r*. In that context, *etarhi* is the example. The suffix beginning with *th* is *thamu*. When this follows, the word *etad* undergoes the substitution of *id* [for its final syllable], resulting in the form *ittham*.

In this regard, one might raise the objection that since the suffix *thamu* is prescribed after the word *idam* itself by the rule *idamasthamuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.23), the prescription of the substitute *id-* for *etad-* before a suffix beginning with *tha*—which would otherwise not be applicable because *thamu* is not prescribed after the word *etac-chabda*—is inconsistent. However, precisely because of this [inconsistency], it is understood as an *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that even after the word *etac-chabda*, when a suffix beginning with *tha* follows in the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*), the substitute *id-* is indeed prescribed.

It must be stated how [the suffix] has the status of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) due to its meaningful occurrence. The meaning of the rule is that when a suffix beginning with *tha*—such as *thak* and others—is uttered following the word *idam*, there is the substitution of *ida-* for *etad-* when that suffix beginning with *tha* follows. It is not the case that *thāl* is mentioned here by way of restating the word *idam*; rather, only *thamu* is to be understood here.

Furthermore, since the prescription of the substitution of *id* for that [root] in the state of being *bhāva* would otherwise be untenable, it is understood by the force of that [prescription] that this [root] possesses the state of being *bhū*, which is called *bhāva*. Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
[Jñānapaṭala] Regarding the rule "the second [consonant] of a reduplicated root beginning with a non-jha letter" (Pāṇini 6.1.2),
the prohibition "not *n*, *d*, or *r* when they are the first members of a conjunct consonant" (Pāṇini 6.1.3) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

"In the case of a prior non-occurrence, there is a non-occurrence of the consonant. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* ("of the second [monosyllabic element] beginning with a vowel"), doubling is prescribed for the second monosyllable following the initial vowel; how then can it be said that "there is a non-occurrence of the consonant" in light of the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1)?
Thus, it must be stated that the doubling of the first *ekāc* (monosyllabic) element as prescribed by the Sūtra applies to the root *bādhate*.
In that case, since the doubling of the first *ekāc* together with its following consonant would be required,
such a doubling would be superseded by the second doubling [prescribed for the reduplication syllable].

And thus, the doubling of a consonant situated within the first monosyllable would not be obtained. Consequently, in the case of *aṭiṭiṣati*, the element *aṭ* constitutes the first monosyllable; and by the rule [regarding] "the second monosyllable," one would have to take the vowel *i* as qualified by the letter *ṭ*.
Fearing that the doubling of the consonant following the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) might not be established, he states: "not *n*, *r*, or *ḍ* at the beginning of a conjunct.
By the rule "not *n*, *r*, or *ḍ* at the beginning of a conjunct," [it is shown that] when vowels follow, these [consonants] do not undergo doubling.

The doubling of the letters *n*, *d*, and *r* following a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and so forth is prescribed. For example, in the case of "*ḥedyaṇ;rṇunāva*," although the doubling of the word "*rṇu*"— which is characterized by the letter *r*— would otherwise apply due to the rule concerning a second monosyllabic word (*ekāc-pada*), the letter *r* is excluded, and only the word "*nu*" is doubled.
Doubledness occurs [therein]. In that case, since the doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*)— which is included within the rule "the first monosyllable" (*ādyeṇaḥ*)—
is already established by the very fact of the doubling of the first monosyllable,
the prohibition of its doubling would be redundant.

This indicates that there is no doubling of a consonant in a preceding occurrence (*pūrvanivṛtti*). The meaning is that when the doubling of the first single vowel (*prathamaikācdvirvacana*) is being effected by means of the doubling of the second single vowel (*dvitīyaikācdvirvacana*), the doubling of the consonant contained within it is not effected. And so it is.
Since the letter *r* (repha) would also be subject to doubling, the rule "na ndrāḥ" was formulated to prohibit that.
Thus, in forms such as *aṭiṭiṣati*, the doubling of the syllable *ṭiṣ* is established without any obstacle; this is the underlying principle (*bhāva*). [Jñānapradīpa]
*Grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). By the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38),
which prohibits the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yakāra* of the root *veñ*, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* does not apply to the root *vyeñ*.
[He] says:

"It is transformed. Desiring to reject the inclusion of the root *vay* in the rule *vacy-ādeśca guṇaḥ*, the author of the Bhāṣya [Patañjali], based on the reading of *veñ* among the roots beginning with *yaj* (*yajādi*), [cites] the rule *veño vayiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.41).

Since the substitution of *vayi* is made for [the root] in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], by virtue of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it possesses the nature of *veñ*. Consequently, since the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is already established by the rule "vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.15), the purpose of the rule "grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca" is not for the sake of vocalization.
The recitation of *vayi* is redundant. Nor should it be argued that its recitation is for the sake of establishing *saṃprasāraṇa* before an affix marked with *ṅ*;

for since *vayi* is used only in connection with the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is no occurrence of it before an affix marked with *ṅ*. Furthermore, because the *liṭ* is *kit*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by virtue of [the root] belonging to the *yajādi* class itself.

He stated that [the form] is established. With regard to that, one might raise the objection: since the rule *veñaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.40) prescribes *saṃprasāraṇa* for the root *veñ* in the *liṭ* tense, this [substitution] would also apply to *vay*, and thus the reading of *vay* [in the rule] should be intended to prevent that very prohibition.
Anticipating this doubt:
He stated: "Or rather, the prohibition of *yakāra* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the non-prohibition [of other rules].
His intention was as follows: by the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38), the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yakāra* of the root *vī* is prohibited when followed by *liṭ*. In that context...
In the rule *veño vayiḥ*, if the mention of *vay-* were intended to include *veñ* by means of the mention of *veñ*,
then since the prohibition would be established by that very [mention], the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ* would be [redundant].

It was not stated [that way]. That *sūtra* indicates, by the inclusion of the root *veñ* in the *pratiṣedha-sūtra*, that the inclusion [of *veñ*] is not [intended to apply here]. And thus, by virtue of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), in the *pratiṣedha-sūtra* through the inclusion of *veñ*...

Even though the substitution of *vay* for *ve* is established by the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe*, the inclusion of *veñ* in the prescriptive sūtra *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* serves as a justification for including *vay*; thus, since there is no obstacle to including *vay*, the samprasāraṇa is established by that very rule.
"In the rule *vayigrahaṇaṃ pratyākhyeyam* (the mention of *vayi* should be rejected), all this has been stated with reference to the *yakāra* of the root *vayi*:
'ādeca upadeśe' (Pāṇini 6.1.45)."

In the rule *mīnāti-minoti* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the continued application of the term *ejgrahaṇa* (the mention of the root *ej*) indicates that an *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) does not occur when caused by a subsequent factor. Furthermore, the prohibition regarding the condition *aśiti* (when followed by a non-*śit* suffix) serves as an indicator that the *āya*-substitutions and others do not supersede the *ātva*. [Vi.]

Desiring to demonstrate the purposelessness of including the term "upadeśe" (in the state of being taught) in the sūtra *ṭhādeca upadeśe'śiti*, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "If the mention of 'upadeśe' were not made,
then even in cases such as *cetā* and *stotā*, [the substitution of] *guṇa* would occur."
Anticipating the objection that *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) would apply because of the absence of the status of ending in *ej* (*ejantatva*),

[the author] states that by the rule "mīnātiminotidīṅaṃ lyapi ca" (*Pāṇini 6.1.50*), the *cakāra* (the letter *ca*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *ātva* applies even to roots such as *mīnāti* that end in *ej*.

Since the form *mātā* and others would be established by the rule *ādeca upadeśe* simply because [the root] ends in *ej*, the rule *mīnāti*— being otherwise redundant— indicates that for a root ending in *aij* which undergoes substitution (*paranimittaka*), the substitution of *ā* does not occur.

And thus, since that which is already endowed with a guna caused by something else would not otherwise obtain the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the root, the rule *mīnāti* (Pāṇini 6.1.50) is meaningful as it serves the purpose of preventing that [substitution]. Consequently, in forms such as *cetā*, the single *e* is also already endowed with a guna caused by the subsequent *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

He established that the substitution of *ā* for the final element of that [root] does not occur by means of the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti*. He stated this regarding the form *tadāñchaḥ*—namely, that there is an anuvṛtti (carrying over) of the term *ej* [from the previous rule]. In this context, since the substitution of *ā* for roots ending in *ej*, such as *mī* and others, is already accomplished by this very [rule], that [subsequent] rule [is unnecessary].

The *Udyota* commentary should be consulted, which states: "Though this [term] is already established, it serves to indicate the meaning; thus, it is a *bhāva*-formation. In that very same *bhāṣya*, regarding the word *upadeśa* as being formed with a *karaṇa* (instrumental) suffix, it is said:
"By the term *upadeśa*, the *śāstra* (treatise) is denoted. And of the *śāstra*..."

Regarding the term *viśeṣaṇam*, because there is no application of the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to that which ends with the specified element), it is understood that the meaning is: "the substitution of *ā* occurs for that *ec* vowel which exists in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). In that case, the word *upadeśa* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, the word *upadeśa* denotes that which is being taught (*upadiśyamāna*). Of that which is being taught...

The mention of *viś* after "dhātu-ādeḥ" (beginning with a verbal root) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *ātvam*. Thus, by the rule of "specification of that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*), the meaning established is that *ātvam* applies to that which is taught as ending in *ej*. In this regard, whether one adopts the position that "the teaching (*upadeśa*) refers to *ej*" or the other alternative position, the form *glai* is derived from the root *glai* with the suffix *anīyar*.

In the case of *anīya*, since the substitution of *ā* is superseded by the subsequent rule [P. 6.1.45], *āy* would result; thus, the form *glānīyam* would not be established. Likewise, in the case of *niśānīyam*, one might suspect that the substitution of *āv* would apply. Anticipating this objection, it is stated that here too, the prohibition of the *śit* suffix [in P. 6.1.47] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
It has been stated that "the roots *nā* and others undergo *ātva* [substitution] when followed by an affix beginning with *ch*, *v*, or *dh*.

The purpose of prohibiting *ātva* before an affix marked with *śit* (such as *śap*) is seen in forms like *glāyati*, where there is no *ātva* substitution when *śap* follows. Even in that case, at the stage *glai a ti*, *ātva* would [otherwise apply].

Since the desired form is established by the substitution of *āy* due to its higher status, what is the purpose of the prohibition of the *śit* suffixes? And that prohibition is indeed made for the sake of indicating that the *āy*-substitutions do not supersede the substitution of *āt*. Consequently, when the substitution of *āt* is applicable...

Thinking this over, he says: "The prohibition [applies] by the rule *aśiti* (not before *śit*)," so that in forms such as *glāyati*, the absence of *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) is established, while in forms such as *glānīyam*, the presence of *ātvam* is established. This is what is intended.

[The Jñāpaka-ṭīkā: By the rule *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), which prohibits [the substitution of *ru*] in the case of the genitive singular (*ṅsi*) and the vocative (*buddhi*), it is indicated that the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is already established as applying to the elision of the letter *n*. [The Viśada-ṭīkā:]
In the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75), regarding the form *rājan-s*,

although the elision of the suffix *su* is already established by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (8.2.23), the mention of the nominative case (*prathamā*) serves that specific purpose [of ensuring the elision occurs].

Anticipating the objection that [the *n*] might not exist, and fearing that the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not be established because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when the elision of *n* is to be applied, the author of the Vārttika offered a solution; however, wishing to refute that, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "when the elision of *n* is to be applied..."

He stated that the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established because [Pāṇini], in the rule "not after *ṅsi* or a word ending in *su*" (8.2.8), teaches the prohibition of the elision of *n* in the formation of the vocative singular. This is with respect to the word *rājan*.

If the *saṃyogāntalopa* (elision of a final conjunct) were considered *asiddha* when the *nalopa* (elision of the letter *n*) was to be applied, then, because the *n* would not possess the status of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*), its elision would not even arise;
consequently, its prohibition would be purposeless. Therefore, that prohibition serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

When the elision of *n* (nalopa) is to be applied, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Consequently, in the case of *rājā*, since the desired form is established by the elision of the final cluster of *soḥ* alone, the purpose of the rule regarding the elision of *su*— namely, that the first [vowel] is long— is [not required] in the case of *rājā*.

The intention of the venerable teacher is that the purpose stated by Lāṭyāyana is not tenable. To explain: in the rule *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.4.7), there is a prohibition regarding the elision (*saṃbuddhi*). [From the *Jñāpakapāda*: *prathamayoḥ* (Sūtra 6.1.102)] "Not before *ādic*" (*nādici*).

The mention of *ij-gaṇa* (the group of vowels beginning with *i*) in [Pāṇini 6.1.104] indicates that the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule does not apply to *jas* and *śas*. [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra]: Now, in cases such as *vaḥTktgrRN;kṣāḥ*, when the form *vaḥTktgrRN;kṣaa-as* is established, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would be expected by the rule "pūrvasavarṇa," yet it would not occur [if the above point were not true].

Because it would follow that everything else would be a negation (*apavāda*) of the other form. As it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The *guṇa* and *yaṇ* substitutions are general rules (*utsarga*); the *vṛddhi*, *savarṇadīrgha*, and *pūrvasavarṇa* substitutions are exceptions (*apavāda*) to them. Of all these..."
Anticipating the objection that "the subsequent form [of the vowel] is an exception," he establishes the absence of the subsequent form by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), stating:
"the mention of *ij*. This refers to the purpose of mentioning *ij* in the rule *na ādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104), which serves as a prohibition against the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*).
In such cases, the purpose [of the rule] is the non-application of the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). If, in that instance,
the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) were to occur by superseding the homogeneous long vowel,
then since the homogeneous long vowel would not even be applicable, there would be no need for its prohibition.
What is the purpose of the mention of *ij* (*ijgrahaṇa*) as a means of preventing the application [of the rule] *bhavati*?

The intention is that this very mention serves to indicate that the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not occur when *jas* and *śas* follow. Nor [does the mention serve to prevent the application of] "dīrghājjasi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.105).
It should be stated that the mention of *ij* in the subsequent sūtra is for the purpose of including [the long vowel].

Otherwise, one should have employed the mention of *ij* right there [in the previous rule] by saying "after a long vowel, before *ij* and *jas*" (*dīrghādijjasoḥ*). If it were done here, it would serve no purpose at all.

It must be stated: since it has already been said that even that [prolongation] does not occur, the mention of *sadir* and so forth is useless and serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The detailed explanation is in the Bhāṣya. [Pāṇini 6.1.125: *plutapragṛhyā aci*. A *pluta* vowel is [treated] by its original nature...

Thus, by the rule (*jñāpaka*) prescribing the restoration (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the original form, the *pluta* vowel becomes subject to *prakṛtibhāva* due to the conflict with the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule. [Objection: Now, for what purpose is the restoration of the original form of the *pluta* vowel stated by the rule "plutapragṛhyāḥ"? It is not [the case that it serves no purpose].

It must be stated that vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) is taught for the purpose of establishing [the preceding rules]; for, because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "what precedes is non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*,
Pāṇini 8.2.1), only vowel-sandhi in the form of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) and so forth would otherwise apply.

To the objection that the prescription of the restoration of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would be purposeless, he replies: "The *pluta* [vowel] is by way of its original form. If the vocalic combination (*svarasandhi*) were to apply to the *pluta* because it is [otherwise] unestablished (*asiddha*), then the prescription of the restoration of the original form would be useless. Therefore, by means of this very prescription, it is indicated that the *pluta* is established; thus, it is made known that the *pluta* occurs even after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

And thus, the rule prescribing the *pluta* vowel for the occurrence of the *sandhyakṣara* (diphthong) as the result of the elision (*lopa*) of the *anudātta* is meaningful; this is the sense. [Jñānapaṭala] Regarding the rule *anudāttaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158): since the simultaneity [of accents] is already established by the rule *tavaicāntaśca yugapat* (Pāṇini 6.2.51), the fact that he teaches this simultaneity again indicates that accentuation does not occur simultaneously.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), it is said: "Of the augment (*āgama*), the substitute (*vikāra*), the base (*prakṛti*), and the affix (*pratyaya*)."

Having stated the purpose of the sūtra by means of the verse: "The accent of the word [prevails] except for one [element], for the sake of preventing the accentuation of the *pragṛhya* [elements]," [the author explains: "In a single word, the accentuation of the *prakṛti*, the *pratyaya*, and so forth would simultaneously apply; however, it is observed that there should be only one accent. Therefore, this sūtra is stated for that purpose. Having thus stated the purpose of the sūtra, [he then refutes it, saying: "This is not a valid purpose, because although the simultaneity is already established by the rule 'And *tavai* at the end and simultaneously' (Pāṇini 6.1.51), it teaches simultaneity again."

The Teacher [Patañjali] indicates this by stating, "the accent does not occur simultaneously," thereby refuting that purpose. His intention is as follows: by the rule *tavaic cāntaśca*, it is prescribed that for a word ending in the suffix *tavail* and having a member designated as a *gati*, both the final acute accent (*antodātta*) and the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member occur simultaneously; the example given is *anvetavai*.

In that regard, even without simultaneous apprehension, since there is no contradiction in multiple vowels being established within a single word at one time, the simultaneity of apprehension—being rendered purposeless—indicates that multiple vowels do not exist simultaneously.

And thus, in examples such as *anvetavai*, the simultaneous mention [of the two rules] is made for the sake of the simultaneous application of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) and the accent of the particle (*gatisvara*); therefore, its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope. By this, it is established that in other words, a simultaneous accent does not occur. Thus, the establishment of this point is achieved solely through the indicator (*jñāpaka*) provided by the author of the Sūtra. This is what is stated [in the commentary]: "Since this... and so forth.

Since the rule *ṭhrikte virdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.208) establishes that there is an option (*paryāya*) [regarding accent], the explicit prescription of this option serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that elsewhere no such option exists. [Objection: But even if multiple accents are established simultaneously by this indicator, an option regarding multiple accents would still result; however, only a single accent is desired. How, then, is that established? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

The word *rikta* is acutely accented on the first syllable. By the rule "in *rikta*, [the first syllable is] optionally acute" (*rikte vā*), acute accentuation on the initial syllable is prescribed for the word *rikta* when it occurs at the end of a compound. In the alternative case, it becomes oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

And if that [word] were to have various accents alternately, then—since the initial syllable would be udātta by the accent of the verbal root at one time and the final syllable would be udātta by the accent of the suffix at another time—the result of the optional rule (*vikalpa*) would already be established through this alternating occurrence of two accents. Why, then, is there the need for the sūtra *ṛk-te viḍ-dvir-ādhyāyāḥ*? That sūtra is indeed taught to indicate that multiple accents do not occur alternately.

Thus, when both the alternatives of successive application (*paryāya*) and simultaneous application (*yaugapadya*) have been refuted, it is established that the purpose of the *sūtra* is not [to state] that "among [the rules concerning] substitution, permanence, internal elements, and exceptions, each subsequent one is stronger"—for by this maxim, a vowel characterized by priority, permanence, and so forth, would already be obtained.

However, by means of these two indicators (*jñāpaka*), although the co-occurrence of multiple *udātta* accents in a single word is precluded, the remaining doubt persists that the co-occurrence of *udātta* and *svarita* accents might still occur. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya states: "Even in a *svarita*, there exists an *anudātta*."

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that when the alternation (*paryāya*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of the acute (*udātta*) are refuted by means of the *jñāpaka*, the same applies to the circumflex (*svarita*), because the acute quality exists within it; thus, the refutation of the alternation and simultaneity of both the acute and the circumflex is established. However, in this grammatical system (*śāstra*), by the mention of "acute" (*udātta*), there is no inclusion of the acute that constitutes a part of the circumflex (*svarita*).

For this very reason, the distinct mention [of *udātta* and *svarita*] in rules such as "udātasvaritayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.4) is appropriate. And thus, in order to preclude their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the *svarita*, the rule "anudātaṃ padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158) is indeed necessary. It was precisely with this in mind that the author of the Bhāṣya stated immediately after [the discussion of] "ārabhyamāṇe 'pyetasminyoge": [the subsequent remark].

Regarding this, the *Codyota* states: "By this, it is shown that the indication of the *svarita* accent for the *jñāpaka* (the indicative rule) is inconsistent. It should be noted that it is precisely based on this that the author of the *Bhāṣya* says, 'even when [the suffix] is being uttered,' thereby clearly demonstrating the necessity of the sūtra.

[From the *Jñāpakapradīpa*: Because the *anudātta* (unaccented) is prescribed for the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following *tasi*, it is understood as an *jñāpaka* that even the accent of a *vikaraṇa* (conjugational affix), though it is subsequent (*satiśiṣṭa*), does not supersede the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*.]

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: By the Vārttika, "When there is [a conflict between two rules], that which is taught later is stronger," it is stated that when one sound (svara) already exists within a single word, a subsequent sound taught [by a later rule] is stronger than the former. If this were so, then in forms such as *sunutaḥ* and *dhinutaḥ*, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* would supersede the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*.

Since the accent of the *vikaraṇa* is applied before the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*, one might suspect that once the *sārvadhātuka* accent has already taken effect, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* would be superseded by the rule "because it is seen" (*śiṣṭatvāt*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "after *tāsi*. By the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tāsi*, as well as that following a root taught with an indicatory *ṅ* or *k*, is unaccented" (*tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātam*, Pāṇini 6.1.186), the unaccented nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tāsi* is prescribed.

The citation "kartārau" and "kartāraḥ" [is given as an example]. If the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* were overridden by the accent of the *vikaraṇa* when the latter is acute, then, since the *vikaraṇa* suffix *tās* would be acute, the remainder of the word would be grave according to the rule "the word is grave," and consequently the *lasārvadhātuka* would already be grave. In that case, what would be the purpose of prescribing the gravity of the *lasārvadhātuka* following the *tās*?

And this [accentuation] being set aside, even though the *satiśiṣṭa* (the accent remaining after others have been applied) is a *vikaraṇa-svara*, it does not override the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*. Thus, in accordance with that, in forms such as *kartārau*, where the *sārvadhātuka* accent would otherwise apply, the rule becomes meaningful by prescribing *anudātta* (unaccented) status through its setting aside [of the former].

Furthermore, the intention is that the result of this rule is the establishment of the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) in forms such as *dhinutaḥ* by means of the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes. [Jñāpakapradīpa] *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167).

The inclusion of the term *chhalādi* in the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179) indicates that a svarita accent produced by a nipātana does not supersede an accent produced by a *bhakti* (suffixal) operation. [Note: Regarding the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, there is a Vārttika which states: "In the case of *caturaḥ śasi*, there is no prohibition regarding the feminine because of the nipātana of the initial udātta."]

This is its meaning: by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, it is prescribed that the word *catur* is oxytone (*antodātta*) when followed by the suffix *śas*. Consequently, in the feminine form *catastraḥ paśya*, the word *catasṛ* would also acquire an oxytone accent by virtue of being treated as identical to *catur* through the principle of "substitution" (*sthānivadbhāva*). A prohibition of this must be stated. [Objection: It need not be stated.

The initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) for the word *catasraḥ* is prescribed here. Since the word *catur* ends in the suffix *-uran*, it is already acute-accented on its first syllable; consequently, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute retains the properties of the original), the word *catasraḥ*—which takes the place of *catur*—would also have been established as acute-accented on its first syllable. Therefore, the prescription of the initial acute accent again is intended to override the final acute accent (*antodātta*) that would otherwise result from the rule *caturaḥ śasi*.

Regarding the term *bādhaka* (sublative): following this, just as the initial acute accentuation (*ādyudātta*) prescribed by the rule "caturaḥ śasi" is a sublative (*bādhaka*) of the final acute accent (*antodātta*) [otherwise required].

Just as, in this context, the rule *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167) sets aside the natural udātta accent of the stem by introducing an acute accent (*udātanipātana*) upon the word *catur*, so too would the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179) set aside the case-ending accent (*vibhaktisvara*).

And likewise, regarding the concern that in examples such as *catasraḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) would not occur, it is said: "The mention of *halādi* (beginning with a consonant) [in the rule] is for this purpose. The mention of *halādi* is made so that the acute accent on the suffix *śas* does not occur in cases such as *catastraḥ paśya*.

However, when one considers that the rule for the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudātanipātana*) has been long established, the intention is that the form *catasraḥ* in the rule *catasṛ* indicates the superior strength (*balīyastva*) of the acute accent on the first syllable.

Nor should it be said that the purpose of including *hal* and so forth [in the definition of *pratyāhāra*] is to exclude those suffixes beginning with *aj* which follow a base termed *ṣat*; for after bases termed *ṣat*, neither the dual nor the singular exists, and both *jas* and *śas* are elided by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of [suffixes] following *ṣat*" (Pāṇini 7.1.22). Thus, there is no need for such an exclusion.

In this way, since the word *tri* is also the subject of the rule regarding the [substitution of] *śas*, the dual and singular endings do not occur. As for the *jas* ending, it is excluded precisely by the qualification *asarvanāmasthāna*. However, in the case of *śas*, when the form *trayas* arises through the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), its status as udātta is already established by the rule "an ekādeśa [with an udātta vowel] is udātta"; thus, that too need not be excluded.

The same applies to the word *tisraḥ* even in the nominative case. As for the subsequent instance *tistraḥ paśya*, since the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is indeed established there by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174), that too is not to be excluded. Only *catastraḥ paśya* is to be excluded; and in that case, the desired result is achieved precisely by the method previously stated.

It is observed in the Bhāṣya that the mention of *ḍhalādi* (roots beginning with *ḍha*) and so forth in the rule *saduktavacane* (Pāṇini 3.2.108) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Regarding the sūtra *tāsyanudātet* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the mention of *anudāttaṅit* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) is an indicator that the property of being *anudātta* does not apply to those verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) whose phonetic form has been elided.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: "If it is the case that the *anu* (augment) is not included among those that are 'non-univocal' (*anekānta*), then since the root *śap* is also taught as having an initial vowel (*adupadeśa*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following it—in examples such as *juhoti*—would incur the status of being unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule *tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātam*. Anticipating this objection, he says: *anudātaṅdgrihaṇam*."

In rules such as *āste* and *śete*, the mention of "anudāteta" (having an anudātta vowel) in the sūtra *tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāt* is made for the purpose of establishing the anudātta nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes. However, both of these [the mention of *anudāteta* and *upadeśāt*] are redundant; for the anudātta nature is established simply by taking the status of being subsequent to the *śap* augment from that which has an *ad* vowel in its original enunciation (*adupadeśāt*).

Therefore, it indicates that when the *vikaraṇa* suffixes are elided, the subsequent *lasārvadhātuka* suffix does not become unaccented (*anudātta*). Consequently, there is no fault in the form *na doḥ*. [Jñāpaka on Pāṇini 6.1.223: *samāsasya*]

Having stated the rule *notarapade'nudātādau* (Pāṇini 6.2.142), there is a prohibition: *apaḥ pṛthivīrudrapūḥsarmanthiṣu*. By this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is established that what is prescribed for a word beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*) applies also to one beginning with a consonant (*vyañjanādi*), and what is prescribed for a word ending in an accented vowel (*antodātta*) applies also to one ending in a consonant (*vyañjanānta*). [Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "What is prescribed for a word beginning with an unaccented vowel and for one ending in an accented vowel would not apply to words beginning with a consonant or ending in a consonant, because properties such as being acutely accented (*udātta*) or gravely accented (*anudātta*) are properties of vowels (*aj-dharma*), not consonants."

Furthermore, regarding the word *dādhittha* in the phrase *dādhittham*, there would arise the following objection: [if the rule were stated as *samāsasya* alone], the suffix *añ* would not apply by *anudātādeśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.140), and the acute accent (*udāttatva*) prescribed for the third case ending (*ṭā*) and subsequent endings after the word *asti*—as in *paramavāc* and similar forms where the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) is acutely accented on its last syllable by *antodātādutarapadādanyatarasyāmanityasamāse* (Pāṇini 6.1.169)—would also not be established. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of the compound" (*samāsasya*), etc.

By the rule *notarapade'nudātādāvapaḥpṛthivīrudrapūḥsomanthiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.142), when there is a *dvandva* compound of deities (*devatādvandva*) where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), the simultaneous acute accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of both the preceding and the subsequent members—which was established by the rule *devatādvandve ca* (6.2.141)—is prohibited. In that context, the prohibition of the prohibition is stated by the rule *apaḥpṛthivīrudra*, etc., regarding the subsequent members such as *pṛthivī* and so forth.

Since the prohibition [of the suffix *ṅīp*] for words such as *apaḥ*, *pṛthivī*, and others—beginning with consonants—is already established by the very absence of the property of having an initial *anudātta* vowel, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not *apaḥ*, *pṛthivī*, etc. is redundant; being so, it indicates that whatever is prescribed for words beginning with an *anudātta* vowel and ending with an *udātta* vowel applies also to those beginning with a consonant and ending with a consonant.

The intention is that by this [rule], the purposefulness of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of forms such as *apaḥ* and *pṛthivī* is established, and the attainment of the *iṣṭa*-accent in forms such as *dādhityam* is also secured. [Jñāpakapradīpa] Regarding the rule *anigante’ñcatau* (Pāṇini 6.2.52): because of the prohibitory rule *anudātte ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.65), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix does not supersede the accent of the verbal root.

[Objection: Now, in the word *bhāḍavaśa* in the phrase *bhāḍavaśo nāma rājā*, by the rule *saptamī-hariṇau dharmye ’dhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.65)—which means that when a word ending in the locative case or a word denoting a "support" (*dhārī*) precedes a word signifying "law" (*dharmya*), the former is acute-accented on its first syllable—the word *bhāḍavaśa* ought to have its first syllable acute-accented.

Likewise, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix (specifically the *ṇyat* suffix) would result in the final syllable being *svarita*. In that case, because it is subsequent, the *kṛt*-accent would prevail, overriding the *dhātusvara* (the accent of the verbal root). However, what is actually observed is that the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is *udātta* by virtue of the *dhātusvara*.

To the question of how that [liberation] is established, it is said: "Because of the prohibition regarding 'deliverance' (uddhāra). This is the intended meaning: this *bhāḍava* is the son of *Bhāḍavā*. After his birth, that which is given for the sake of the body and the *puṣṭi* [offering] is called *uddhāra*, and it is also termed *hārya*.
In the analysis of the compound *bhāṭakasya āharaṇam* (the taking of rent), it becomes *bhāṭakāharaṇam*. One who accepts what is to be given is called a *hartṛ* (receiver).

Likewise, since the word *bhikṣāvasatha* denotes a location (*adhikaraṇa*), it acquires an acute accent on its first syllable by this [rule], provided that it is followed by a word denoting the substratum (*dharmī*) such as *haraṇa*. Similarly, by the rule *ano bhāvakarmavacanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.150), an acute accent on the final syllable of the second member would also have been applicable.

In that case, because it is subsequent, the *kṛtsvara* (the accent of the suffix *kṛt*) would be superseded by the *ādyudātta* (the acute accent on the first syllable) resulting from the final acute of the second member of the compound; since the *ādyudātta* would thus prevail, the mention [of the *kṛtsvara*] is for the purpose of excluding that [supersession]. Therefore, the *kṛtsvara* does not supersede the *ādyudātta*, but rather the *ādyudātta* itself [supersedes] the *kṛtsvara*.

This indicates that [the suffix] is added. Nor does the rule *gati-kāraka-upapadāt kṛt* apply here, for although the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix would prevail by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the rule *ano bhāva-karmaṇoḥ* applies as an exception (*apavāda*) when the word ending in *udhara* follows. Following the application of that [rule], it is stated: *saptamī-udhāriṇau dharmye udharaṇe*.

And thus, although it might be argued that by the rule "aḍ-ādy-udāttaḥ," the accent of *ā* (the *hrasva* vowel) in the word *an-aḥ* [in *anaḥ*] does not obstruct the accent of *ā* [from *ā-bhāva*], how can it be possible to indicate that the *kṛt*-accent does not obstruct the accent of *ā* [from *ā-haraṇe*]? This is what must be addressed.

When it is established that the accent of the rule *saptamī-hāriṇau* is more powerful than the accent of the rule *ano bhāva-karmaṇoḥ*—which itself is more powerful than the accent of the rule *kṛt-svaraḥ*—then, by the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), it is even more certain that what is more powerful than something more powerful is necessarily more powerful [than the original].

And thus, it is made known that in the general rule regarding the elision of *kha*, the *udātta* accent of *hrasva* (short vowels) is an exception (*bādhaka*) to every other accent obtained by any subsequent rule through the principle of "priority" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

In this way, even when *hrasva* follows an *udātta* sound, since the *udātta* accent would otherwise apply, the statement "in *hrasva*" is made for the purpose of setting aside that [subsequent rule]; thus, its utility is established within its own scope.

However, in other cases where there is a specific purpose—as in the example *bhāḍavaḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;aryam*—when the word *bhāḍavaḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;arya* follows [the first member], the accentuation of the initial syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) occurs by the rule "the locative case ending [is udātta] when followed by a word ending in -in" (*saptamī-hariṇau*), which sets aside the general rule regarding the acute accent on the final syllable (*kṛtsvara*). Thus, the first syllable of the preceding member becomes udātta.

[Pāṇini 6.2.143] *antaḥ*. The mention of *kapi* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the final syllable (*antodātta*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes acute. [Vivaraṇa: The rule *antaḥ* is a governing rule (*adhikārasūtra*). Being in syntactic unity with the subsequent rules, it conveys the meaning: "the final syllable becomes acute.

When the question arises as to whose final syllable is acute, the previously mentioned rule "of the compound" (*samāsasya*, 6.1.223) is also brought into play; thus, the meaning results in: "the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) optionally becomes acute."

In that case, regarding the view that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta, [it would follow that] in the rule *anaḥ ṭak chasprabhṛtibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), the accentuation prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74)—which prescribes the addition of the compound-ending suffix *apratyaya* and its subsequent udātta accent—would not be established. This is because [in that view] the vowel *a* [of the suffix *ap*] would be...

One might raise the objection that since [the suffix] *kap* is not a member of the compound (*samāsa*) but rather a member of the subsequent member (*utarapada*), the rule for its acute accent (*udātta*) would not apply. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "In the case of *kap*, there is a statement regarding what precedes. When the expectation arises as to whose end [is meant], the word "of the compound" (*samāsasya*) alone is connected, and not "of the subsequent member" (*utarapadasya*). Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is simply that the end of the compound is acute. The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the rule "in the case of *kap*, the preceding [is acute]" (Pāṇini 6.1.173). This is its purpose.

The meaning is that when *kap* follows, the penultimate syllable of the compound that follows the negative particle (*nañ*) or the privative particle (*sūḥ*) becomes acute (*udātta*). For example, in *sukumārīka*, the vowel *ī* is acute. This applies if [the rule] is intended to apply...

If it were the case that the final syllable of the *uttarapada* is acute, then—since the *kap* suffix is not a constituent of the *uttarapada* but rather a constituent of the compound as a whole—the vowel *ī* alone at the end of the *uttarapada* "kumārī" would become acute by the rule "nañ-su-bhyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.172); what, then, would be the purpose of the rule "kapi pūrvam"?

And that [rule] indicates that the udātta accent occurs at the very end of the compound and not on the other member of the compound. Therefore, the purpose of the sūtra *kapi pūrvam* is established, and the fact that the final syllable of the compound is udātta in examples such as *anaḥṭktgrRN;ca* is also accomplished; this is the underlying intention (*bhāva*).

However, in this view, regarding the word *idaṃprathamakāḥ*, the rule "ṣaṭ-kati-katipayasya-thuk" (Pāṇini 5.2.51)—specifically the portion "prathama-pūraṇayoḥ kriyā-gaṇane" (Pāṇini 6.2.162), which prescribes an udātta accent on the final syllable—would result in the addition of the suffix *kap* because it is a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). Yet, what is actually observed is the acute accent on the vowel of the word *maśaḥ*. That [result] would not be established [under this view].

Therefore, regarding that sūtra, one should state only "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*) and not "of the compound" (*samāsasya*). This is clearly seen in the works of Bhartṛhari and Kaiyaṭa. Furthermore, the mention of the absence of elision (*aluk*) in the rule *kāranāmni ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.10) indicates that a compound (*samāsa*) occurs here.

Regarding the rule *kāranāmni ca prācāṃ ḍhralope 'ḍhralādi* (Pāṇini 6.3.10), which prescribes the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending after a word ending in *ḍhra* when it is the name of a place in the eastern regions and is followed by a compound-final member (*uttarapada*) beginning with *ḍhra* or *la*, the authors of the Vārttikas deliberated whether this was an instance of a rule applying where [non-elision] was already established (*prāptavibhāṣā*) or where it was not yet established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), and concluded: "It is an injunction of compounding where [non-elision] was not previously established."

In examples such as *mukuṭekāḥ* and *śāpaṇam*, although the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending would not have applied by the rule "After a word ending in *ṛt*, the locative case ending is not elided when it forms a name" (*Pāṇini* 6.3.9), the statement that [the suffix] *vi* occurs results in the fact that it is not a name (*asaṃjñātva*). Furthermore, since a compound (*samāsa*) is difficult to achieve in that context, the compound must also be prescribed.

In the view that [the suffix] *viḍ* occurs when there is a name (*saṃjñā*), however, since the compound is already established by the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 2.1.44), the intention of the Vārttika is that only the absence of *luṅ* (i.e., the *aluk* elision of the case-ending) needs to be prescribed. But the author of the Bhāṣya says: "There is no fault."

This very point makes it known that a compound occurs here, because [the author] teaches the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending when the name of a cause is expressed—so say some. Even on the view that [non-elision] is not otherwise established, it is understood that a compound occurs precisely by the force of the rule prescribing non-elision (*aluk*), even though it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). Otherwise, since elision would simply not apply, the prescription of non-elision would be redundant; such is the intent of the Bhāṣya.

Regarding this, it is said: "This very [rule] regarding *aluk* is what [the author] intends. [Under Pāṇini 6.3.138, *cau*: This very [rule] makes known that *ca* does not apply to every individual constituent (*pratyaṅga*). [Objection: But in forms such as *prācā* and *dadhīcā*, after the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), since the rules for *ekādeśa* and *yaṇādeśa* apply by virtue of being *antaraṅga*, the condition of ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) no longer exists; therefore, the rule "in *ca*" (*cau*) for lengthening should not apply. To this, he says: "This very [rule] makes known... [That is, it serves as an *jñāpaka* that the *ca* rule applies even when the vowel-ending condition has been lost through intermediate operations.]

The meaning is that, due to its capacity for long-term persistence (*dīrghavidāna-sāmarthyāt*), that which is *antaraṅga* (internal) with respect to the rule "cau" does not [apply]. In reality, however, since it is understood from the mention of "cau" that this rule operates after the elision of the vowel *a*, it is inconceivable that this [rule] would apply before the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *yaṇ* and so forth, because they are incapable of operating after the elision of the vowel *a*. The term *pratyayāśraya* (dependent on an affix) denotes that which is *antaraṅga*.

[Pāṇini 6.4.46] *ārdhadhātuke*: The fact that the elision of the vowel *a* of the suffix *śap* does not occur in forms such as *bhavati* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since the elision of *śap* is prescribed after roots beginning with *ad-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.72). Alternatively, the prescription of its elision after roots ending in long *ā* is the indicator. [Vivaraṇa]: Anticipating the question, "What, then, are the purposes of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *ārdhadhātuka*? the Bhāṣya states: "The elision of the [final] *a*, the elision of *ya*, and the elision of *ṇi* are the purposes."

Having enumerated the purposes [of the rule] as "the *āllopa*, the *ītvam*, the *etvam*, and the status of being like the *ciṇ* substitute (*ciṇvadbhāva*) apply before the *sīyuṭ*," [the author] raises the objection that if the *lopa* of *a* were applied [by P. 6.4.64], then even in the case of *cikīrṣati*, the *a* of the *san* suffix would be elided because it falls under the jurisdiction of the *ārdhadhātuka* section. Having raised this, he then counters by suggesting: "Let there be the elision of the *a* of the *san* here; the *a* of the *śap* will still be audible. [To this, the reply is: let there be the elision of the *a* of the *śap* itself.

Having resolved that the section on *ārdhadhātuka* affixes exists for this very purpose, [the author] states: "This is not a valid purpose. The teacher’s intention makes it known that the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* of the *śap* suffix does not occur by this rule; for he teaches the elision (*luk*) of *śap* after roots beginning with *ad* and so forth—this has been stated. This is what is meant by the words: "not by this."

The meaning is: by the rule "atolopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.64), which falls under the jurisdiction of the section on *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. Now, one might object: if the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* of the *śap* suffix occurred in forms such as *vitaḥ* and *maḥ* (from *vindati* and *māti*), then by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), operations such as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would still apply. To prevent this, the elision (*luk*) of *śap* must be specifically prescribed; since there is thus another purpose for its prescription, how can this [elision of *a*] serve as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of those ending in the vowel *ā*."
Now begins the seventh chapter.

But surely, even in cases such as *śaṅkhaḥ* and *śaṇḍhaḥ*, the substitutes beginning with *āyan* would apply; for by the Uṇādi-sūtras beginning with "from the root *śam*, [the suffix] *kha*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 107), the suffix *kha* [is prescribed].

One might raise the objection that by the prescription of suffixes such as *ḍha* and others, since *kha* and so forth would become the initial elements of those suffixes, the rule *āyaneyī* (Pāṇini 7.1.2) would apply. To this, the author provides the following clarification: the prescription of the suffix *īyaṅ* for the verbal root *ṛti* (Pāṇini 3.1.29) is the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) that this is not the case.

The suffixes *āyan* and so forth occur after verbal roots (*dhātu*) and affixes (*pratyaya*). [Commentary: This is the meaning—the root *ṛti* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to feel aversion. From it, the affix *īyaṅ* is prescribed in the sense of the root itself by the rule "ṛterīyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.29).

The form is *ṛtīyate*. In that case, for the sake of brevity, one could simply have stated *ṛteśchaṅ*. By applying the substitution of *ī* for *ccha* according to the rule *āyaneyī*, the desired form *ṛtīya* would have been established quite easily. Therefore, having set aside this more concise formulation, [the author] instead provides *ṛterīyaṅ*.

The fact that he prescribes the heavier suffixation (garīyāṃsaṃ nyāsam) indicates that for those suffixes following a verbal root that begin with *ph* and so on, the substitutions such as *āyan* and so forth do not apply.
Consequently, when the suffix *chaṅ* is prescribed, the substitution of *īya* for the *ch* of *chaṅ* does not take place after the verbal root.
Thus, the prescription of *īyaṅ* is meaningful; by this, the rule "āyaneyī" does not apply in cases such as *śaṅkha*. [Jñānapaṭala, Sūtra 7.1.73] *ikoci* ||
The mention of *aj* (vowels) here indicates that,
like *bhavati*, some other suffix (*pratyaya*) also does not cause the application of the rule for the original form (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).
In the sūtra "iko 'ci vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.1.73), it was stated that the mention of *aj* is for the sake of subsequent rules.

Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika [states]: "In that regard, if the author of the Sūtra intended it for the sake of subsequent cases, he would have formulated it right there; since it is being formulated here, some purpose for it must be stated. Having raised this objection, [the purpose] is the prevention of the *num* augment in the case of *trapu* and *japu*.

Having stated the purpose, and because of the subsequent mention of the rule *bhasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.129), the augment *num* occurs only when followed by a *bha*-stem; for instance, in the case of *trapu* and *jatu*,
[the *num* does not apply] because the *bha*-designation has been elided by *luk*.

Since the suffix *num* will not occur precisely because of the absence of the condition of being followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the mention of the initial vowel (*ajgrahaṇa*) is redundant. Nor should one suspect that the condition of being followed by a case-ending might apply by virtue of the rule regarding the treatment of the suffix as part of the preceding stem (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). [This is because of the prohibition: "Not... (*na...*)

Anticipating the objection that this is because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *lumatāṅgasya*, [the author] says: "In that case, since the prohibition has been stated, the fact that [Pāṇini] prescribes the elision (*lopa*) indicates that there exists another way as well, namely, the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)."

And likewise, because [the rule] *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (P. 1.1.62) applies when a suffix follows, the mention of *aj-ādi* (beginning with a vowel) is made in order to prevent the application of *num* in cases such as *trapu*, where *num* would otherwise be required. Thus, the purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*) is that even in a case like *trapoḥ* (where the suffix *śas* has been elided), the substitution of *lopa* for the final vowel by *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (P. 7.3.108) does not apply by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*.

He stated that because it is caused by the subsequent addition of a vowel, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) is established. To this, he replied: "The mention of *ac* [in the rule]... [Jñānapradīpa]. And in the case of the feminine...
The prohibition in the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4) indicates that the substitution *rā* does not supersede the augment *nuṭ*. [This is discussed] in the rule *striyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.96).
Regarding the Vārttika: "The augment *nuṭ* [is applied] after *aci-ra-taḥ*, *tktgrṛn-jvad-ḍh-āveḥ*,
and *ḍh-ḍh-āveḥ* by way of prior contradiction (*pūrva-vipratiṣedha*)," the examples for *aci-ra-sya* are *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*.

In the case of *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*, although both the substitution of *r* by rule 7.2.100 (*aci ra ṛtaḥ*) and the augment *nuṭ* by rule 7.1.54 (*hrasvanadyāpaḥ*) would apply, the substitution of *r* takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of rules, and consequently, the augment *nuṭ* does not apply.

Therefore, the intention of the Vārttika is that, by overriding the substitution of *aci* through the principle of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the augment *nuṭ* occurs. Immediately following that is another Vārttika: "Or rather, [the objection does not hold], because there is no prohibition of *rapara* when *nuṭ* is intended."

It must be stated that the substitution of *r* does not supersede the augment *nuṭ*. Otherwise, just as the substitution of *r* would supersede the *guṇa* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*, it would likewise supersede the *nuṭ*—this is the intended meaning. This is as follows:

Refuting the two *vārttikas*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states that because the rule "not for *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*" prohibits the lengthening of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* when followed by a *nām* (genitive/locative ending), the substitution of *r* does not apply when *nuṭ* follows, as the condition for the *r*-substitution is not met.

He explained that even the prohibition of *rapratyaya* (the substitution of *ra*) for *nuṭ* need not be stated, and that the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding *nuṭ* by way of "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is likewise unnecessary. Taking that into consideration, he said: "No."
"Three," "four"—these indicate negation. [Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.17] states:
"The number of the qualifier applies to the qualified.
The division of the rule is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when the number belongs to the qualifier, it negates that qualifier.

[Commentary: Now, it may be objected that two sūtras—"āditaśca" and "bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ"—are recited in the eighth chapter [of Pāṇini’s grammar] (specifically at Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.16 and 17). Among them, the meaning of the first sūtra is that the augment iṭ shall not occur after the niṣṭhā suffixes following a root that begins with a vowel.

"Prasvinna" is the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*). In the absence of the second rule, the meaning would be that the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after the root *niḥ-sad* when used in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*) or in its original state (*bhāva*).
In that case, two rules need not exist: "After the root *vi-sad*, [the augment *iṭ* is optional] in the sense of the beginning of an action or in the sense of the state (*bhāva*)."

Let this be made into a single sūtra: "In the sense of the agent (*kartari*) and at the beginning of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*), *iṭ* is optionally added after a root. If it is asked, "How then is the prohibition of *iṭ* in the sense of the agent explained [in cases such as] *laviṣyate*?"—[the answer is: "Of that... [and so on].

It is established by the sūtra "viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.41). The meaning of that sūtra is that for a word where an *anunāsika* has been mentioned anywhere, the substitution of *iṇ* should not occur for the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*]. Consequently, from the beginning...

Since the substitution of *vi* for *bhū* and *ādi* in the sense of the action [of becoming] and the beginning has already been stated, the prohibition of *iṇ* is established by the rule "for that which has *vi*" (*yasya viḥ*) in the context of the agent (*kartari*).
And thus, having divided the *yoga*, the first sūtra is understood as being intended for the prohibition of *iṇ*.
Anticipating the objection as to why there is a description of the second [type of yoga] as being prescriptive, [the author] states:
