"For this very reason, although it is established by a single yoga, the division of the yoga is intended to indicate that when there is a distinction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is a corresponding negation of that limiting adjunct."

Just as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is produced as qualified by such-and-such a qualifier, so too can a negation (*pratiṣedha*) be understood as qualified by that very same qualifier. And in that case...

Because the option (*vikalpa*) is prescribed for the two conditions of the action itself (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "for that [verb] which has *niḥ* as its prefix" would not apply to the active voice (*kartṛ*).
This is because, in the case of the action itself and the passive as well, there is no occurrence of either the option or the prohibition.
Otherwise, there would be no prohibition [of *iṭ*], and consequently, the sūtra would be rendered useless. Therefore,

the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made in order to prohibit *iṭ* in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), and to optionally prescribe *iṭ* in the case of the absence [of the suffix] and at the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*).

The purpose of making known [the rule] *yadupādheḥ* is that, according to the rule *vidi-jñāne* (DhP 2.55) and *vibhāṣā gamahana-vida-viśām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.68), the suffix *vasu* optionally takes the augment *iṭ*,
resulting in either *vividivān* or *vividvān*.

Thus, because of this specific rule, in the case of *vidita* (in the sense of "known"), the prohibition of *iṇ* by the rule *yasya viḥḍddhdhḍaddh;āḥsdvdr1;ā* would have applied; however, that [prohibition] is set aside by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). This applies specifically to the root *vidlḥTktgrRN; lāḥḍddhdhḍaddh;e*.

The term *grahīṇam* refers to that very [root] with the augment *iṭ* by virtue of its being [listed] as such; however, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* applies to that very [root] when it has the sense of "seizing," and not to the root meaning "to know. Thus, the form *viditaḥ*—derived from the root meaning "to know"—is established.
This has been determined in the *Dharmapāda* and other such texts.
Regarding that, it is stated in the *Abhisandhi*: "In the section on Yoga. And here:
"Even though there is no practice of the *sādhana* for one who maintains a [different] philosophical view (*darśana*), nevertheless..."

The passage from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, “Because of the contradiction with the subsequent rule (*paravipratiṣedha*), the established distinction (*vyavasthā*) is not destroyed,” should also be considered here. [Jñānapaṭala] Regarding *svaratisūti* (Pāṇini 7.2.44),
in the context of *sanīvantardha* (Sūtra 7.2.49):

Because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the word *svaḥTktgrRN;graḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;ṇāt*, this rule does not apply to the exclusion of the prohibition characterized by *u*. [Objection: But surely, in the case of *svaḥTktgrRN;tvā*, by the rule "svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā" (*Pāṇini 7.2.44*),...

There is the contingency of an option regarding the *iṭ* augment. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of the *iṭ* augment because of the prohibition of *iṭ* after a root ending in a *u*-vowel by the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11); for the rule "svarati" (Pāṇini 7.2.44), according to the maxim of "that which applies where nothing else applies" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), [applies] to the prohibition of *iṭ* characterized by having a single vowel (*ekāj-lakṣaṇa*).
Anticipating the objection that [the rule] *śryukaḥ kiti* would likewise be an obstacle, making the occurrence of *iṭ* unavoidable, he says: "In the case of *sanīvantardha*."

The intention is as follows: by the rule *sanīvantardhabhrasjadamḍhḍhḍaddh;uśrisvaḥTktgrRN;yūrṇuḍhḍhḍaddh;arajñapisanām* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), it is stated that the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after the suffix *san* following roots ending in *iv*, as well as those beginning with *ṛdh* and so forth. The root *svaḥTktgrRN;* is also mentioned therein; its illustrations are *susvūḥsdvdr1;* and *sisvariḥsdvdr1;*ti.

In this regard, since the optionality of the augment *iṭ* is already established by the rule *svaratisūti* itself, the specific mention of the root *svṛ* is purposeless; being so, it indicates that the prohibition characterized by the term *vi* does not apply to the rule *svaratisūti*.

Consequently, since the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" would otherwise apply, the mention of the root *svar* in the sūtra "sanīvantardha" is for the purpose of establishing that [prohibition]. Thus, in the case of *svaḥTktgrRN;tvā*, because the optional application of *iṭ* does not occur, there is no possibility of *iṭ* due to the prohibition by "śryukaḥ kiti. [Jñānapaṭala: Taddhiteḥsdvdr1;vacāmādeḥ (Pāṇini 7.2.117)]

The inclusion of the *anuśatikādi* group in the list of words that undergo *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) indicates that when *vṛddhi* is to be applied to the initial vowel (*ādi*), the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final or penultimate vowel does not occur.

[Objection]: Now, in the case of the word *krauṣṭraka*—derived from *krauṣṭṛ* by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "tasyedam" (*Pāṇini* 4.3.120)—and from the word *jagat* by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "jāgatam" (*Pāṇini* 4.3.161), there is also the *vṛddhi* substitution for the first vowel of the base by the rule "taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ" (*Pāṇini* 7.2.117). In that situation, since the *ṛ* is the final vowel, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply to it by the rule "aco ñṇiti" (*Pāṇini* 7.2.115).

Nor can it be said that the *vṛddhi* substitution for vowels beginning with the initial [of the root] takes precedence over the *vṛddhi* of the final [vowel] and the *vṛddhi* of the *upadhā* (penultimate) vowel prescribed by the rule for the suffix *śatṛ*; therefore, in the case of *tathoḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.35), only the *vṛddhi* of the vowels beginning with the initial would occur. For, according to the principle of *yenanāprāpta*, a rule must be stated as an exception (*apavāda*) precisely because it applies where the general rule would otherwise have applied, and such a situation does not exist here.

Anticipating the objection that even where both the final-vowel-vṛddhi (antyalakṣaṇā) and the penultimate-vowel-vṛddhi (upadhālakṣaṇā) are applicable—as in *sauśruta* and similar forms—the former cannot sublate the latter because the vṛddhi of the initial vowel (*ācāmādivṛddhi*) has its own scope and thus remains uncontradicted, [the author] states: "by the rule *anuśatikādi-ṅīṣ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.20).

Now, the meaning is as follows: regarding the word *pauṣkarasādi*, which is derived from the base *pauṣkarasāda* in the sense of "offspring" (*apatyam*) by adding the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.96 (*bhṛgv-aṅgira-...*), although initial *vṛddhi* would have been required, the base *pauṣkarasāda* is listed among the *anuśatikādi* group so that there may be *vṛddhi* of both members of the compound (*ubhayapada-vṛddhi*), even in cases where the initial vowel of the first member does not undergo *vṛddhi*.

If [the rule] *upadhāvṛddhiḥ* were applied, then because of the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u* at the beginning of the word and the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *a* of the suffix *sā*, the form would result in *paúrusasādi*. Since the *vṛddhi* of both members of the compound would thus be established, the inclusion of this word in the *anuśatikādi* group—which is performed for that very purpose—would be redundant. Yet, since it is indeed included there, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned rule.

Although the reading of the word *upadhāvṛddhi*—which is [otherwise] meaningless—is sufficient to indicate only the *upadhāvṛddhi*, nevertheless, either by way of accepting a partial indication (*ekadeśānumati*) or by virtue of being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that depends on the general category, it is understood that the *vṛddhi* of the final letter (*antyalakṣaṇā vṛddhiḥ*) does not apply either. Thus it is reasoned.

The object of meditation. [Pāṇini 7.3.85] The prohibition of *guṇa* in the case of *ciṇ* and *ṇal* suffixes indicates that there is no *vṛddhi* for that which has not undergone *guṇa*. [Vivaraṇa: Now, one might object that in the form *jāgarayati*—derived from the root *jāgṛ* with the causative (*ṇic*) suffix and the present tense marker (*laṭ*)—the root *jāgṛ*...

When *jāgṛ* + *ati* is established, the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ṛ* occurs by the rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu*, and since *ra* follows as the subsequent element (*rapara*), the form becomes *jāgar* + *ati*. At this stage, one might suspect that *vṛddhi* would apply to the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *a* by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116). Anticipating this objection, he says: *ciṇṇaloḥ*. In the very rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu*, the application of *guṇa* is specifically prohibited when *ciṇ* or *ṇal* follow.

And as for the result [of that rule], namely *ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra*, in both cases the accomplishment of the *vṛddhi* substitution is preceded by the application of *guṇa*. Even there, since the forms *ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra* are established by the *vṛddhi* prescribed in the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* when the state [of the suffix] beginning with *a* is present—even though *guṇa* is applicable—what is the purpose of those two prohibitions of *guṇa*?

Furthermore, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] in the rule *kṛtaḥ* indicates that the *vṛddhi* prescribed by *ata upadhāyāḥ* does not apply to the vowel *a* produced through the substitution of *guṇa*. Thus, when *guṇa* occurs for *jāgṛ* in the case of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, the *vṛddhi* would not apply to the *a* that results from that *guṇa*-substitution; therefore, the prohibition of *guṇa* is made for those two cases.

Furthermore, since there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitute [by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*], the forms *ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra* are established by the rule *aco ñṇiti*; thus, the rule has its purpose fulfilled in its own domain (*svāṃśe caritārthatā*). However, the purpose for making this known (*jñāpanaprayojana*) is that in cases such as *jāgarayati*, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* does not occur—this is the intended meaning. [From the Jñāpakapradīpa: By the rule *puganta-...* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), the fact that the suffixes *knū* and *san* are marked with the *kit* designation serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs for roots of this class.

[Objection: Now, in the case of *dhitsati* and *dhitsitum*, where the suffixes *tumun* and *tumarthāśca bhāvavacanāt* apply, the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.86) would not result in the desired *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel.

Regarding the statement *ḍhita tuki* and *ḍhita tumi*, there arises the following objection: since the technical term *saṃyoga* applies to the immediate sequence of the final consonant of a verbal root and the initial consonant of an affix, the vowel *i* would receive the designation *guru* by the rule *saṃyoge guru* (Pāṇini 1.4.11). Consequently, the designation *laghu* would be sublated, and because the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) *i* lacks the status of being light, [the desired grammatical operation would not occur]. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: *knusanoh*.

In the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), the designation of *kn* as *kit* is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution in the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in forms such as *gṛdhnuḥ*.

In that case as well, since the suffixes beginning with a consonant and ending in a vowel (such as *kit*) would be designated as "conjuncts" (*saṃyoga*), the vowel *ṛ* would acquire the designation "heavy" (*guru*) by the rule "a [syllable] in a conjunct is heavy. Consequently, because the designation "light" (*laghu*) is sublated, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) lacks lightness, and thus no guna substitution would occur anyway. Therefore, the employment of the *kit* marker for the purpose of precluding guna is redundant.

Thus, the prescription of *kit* status for the suffix *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant following a *hal* consonant immediately after an *ic*-vowel, as stated in the rule *ḍhralope...* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), which is intended to prevent *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *didhikṣati*, would be rendered useless. This is because, given that the final *a* of the root and the initial *s* of the suffix form a *saṃyoga* cluster, the preceding *i* would be considered heavy (*guru*) due to that cluster; consequently, since the condition of being light (*laghu*) is absent, *guṇa* would not apply by default.

And thus, the fact that the *kit* designation for the suffixes *knū* and *san* is otherwise redundant serves to indicate that for such types of cases—namely, those involving the elision of the final letter of a root or the initial letter of an affix—the technical designation "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) becomes the cause for applying the designation "heavy" (*guru*), which in turn results in the occurrence of *guṇa*. In this way, the *kit* designation becomes meaningful as it serves to preclude that very *guṇa* which would otherwise have been obtained.

The intention is that the result of the *jñāpana* (informative indication) is the establishment of the *guṇa* substitution in cases such as *ḍhetā* and *ḍhetum*. [Jñāpakapradīpa] Because of the separate mention of the term *nadi* in the rule "ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.116), the designation *nadī* does not apply to the vowel *ā* (the nominative/accusative singular ending). [Vivaraṇa] By the rule "yū strayākhyau nadī," the designation *nadī* is prescribed for those stems ending in *ī* or *ū* that are invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*).

In that context, if the term *yū* were not stated, then for words such as *khaṭvā* and *mālā*, which are invariably feminine and end in the suffix *ṭāp*, the designation *nadī* would apply; consequently, in forms such as *khaṭvābhandaḥ* and *mālābhandaḥ*, the rule "nadī bhandauni" (Pāṇini 6.2.109) would result in the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*) being accented with the udātta tone.

However, since the word *khaṭvā* is derived from the root *khaṭ* with the suffix *kvun* (as taught in the *ĀṬṇādikas*), its form would end in *ā*; thus, because it does not end in *ī* or *ū*, the designation *nadī* would not apply to it. Consequently, the previously mentioned fault would remain. Therefore, the purpose of the rule *yū* must be stated. But that purpose is untenable, as the designation *nadī* for words ending in long *ā* can be prevented by means of an interpretive indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Likewise, [it is said]: "If even that which ends in *ā* were to receive the designation *nadī*, then in the rule 'ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ,' since the inclusion of that which ends in *ā* would already be established by the term *nadī* itself, the separate mention of *ā* would be purposeless."

And that [mention] indicates that the designation *nadī* does not apply to a word ending in *ā*. This is stated separately as "tadetadāḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;—iti paḥTktgrRN;thagiti. Thus, since the purpose of *thū* is not to prevent the *nadī* designation for a word ending in *ā*, one must state that its result is precisely to prevent the *nadī* status of the word ending in *ṛ* in cases such as *mātre* and *mātuḥ*. Its [purpose] is...

Regarding the status of being a river (*nadī*), it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that by the rule "āṇ nadyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.112), the augment *āṭ* should be applied to the subsequent suffix *ṅti*. In the rule "ṛtaśca" (Pāṇini 7.4.92), the use of the vowel *ṛ* with a following *t* (the *tapara* designation) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this is a qualification of the *aṅga* (the stem). [Viṭ: Now, in the rule "ṛtaśca," is the element "ṛtaḥ" a qualification of the *aṅga*, or is it a qualification of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)?

In the view that the term *abhyāsa* (reduplication) qualifies the root (*dhātu*), the meaning of the sūtra is that the augmentations *ruk*, *rik*, and *rīk* should apply to the reduplicated portion of a root ending in *ṛ* when there is *yaṅ*-luṅ (elision of *yaṅ*). In the view that the term *abhyāsa* qualifies the stem (*aṅga*), the meaning of the sūtra is that the augmentations *uk*, *at*, and *at* should apply to the reduplicated portion of a root ending in the vowel *ṛ*.

Anticipating the doubt as to which of these two positions is logical, [the author] states "specification of the stem" (*aṅgaviśeṣaṇam*). Regarding this sūtra, in the absence of the *tapara* (long vowel marker), in the case of the root *kṣi* ("to scatter") with *yaṅluk*, as in *cākarti*, the augment *rug* etc. would undesirably apply to the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*).

When *kśa* remains after the elision of *ya*, and the root undergoes reduplication so that *kśa* becomes *kśa-kśa*, the rule *aḍḍḍhḍhaddh;yāsa-hrasve* applies. Then, by the rule *urat*, the vowel *u* of the reduplicated syllable is replaced by *a*, resulting in *kar-kśa-ti*. Next, by the rule *ḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;lādi-śeḥsdvdr1;e cutve*, the *k* is changed to *c*, and by the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), the reduplicated syllable is lengthened, resulting in *cākśati*. Finally, by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, the *ṛ* is replaced by its *guṇa* equivalent, and thus the form *cākartīti* is established.

In that regard, on the view that the vowel *ṛ* is a qualifier of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*) would be redundant. The purpose of that [marker] is to exclude the occurrence of a long vowel in the reduplication; however, a long vowel does not occur in the reduplication because the rule "hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.59) prescribes a short vowel. Thus, the use of the *tapara* marker indicates that this [vowel *ṛ*] is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (the stem).

In that context, if the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) were not present, then even when there is reduplication (*abhyāsa*) and lengthening, since the root *kṛ* would have a long final vowel in the base (*aṅga*), the reduplicated portion of that base would undergo the augment *rug* and so forth, resulting in forms such as *carkarti*, *carikarti*, and *carīkarti* for the root *kṛ*. However, the form actually observed is *cākartī*. Therefore, the *tapara* marker has been prescribed.

And when that [reduplication] is reduplicated, since the *aṅga* cannot end in a short *ṛ*, the augment *rug* and so forth cannot apply to its reduplication; this is the sense. [Pāṇini 7.4.93: *sanvallaghuni*]

The rule *atsamaḥ kṛtvarāp* (Pāṇini 7.4.95), which prescribes the substitution of *it* for the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi*, indicates that the substitution of *it* occurs even when the root is separated by a *saṃyoga*. [Objection: But surely, by the rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), it is stated that when a *caṅ*-affix follows, the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) undergoes the same treatment as in the *san*-formation provided that there is a light vowel (*laghu*) following the *ṇi* and no elision of *ak* occurs.

And thus, in the case of *acakṣaṇat*, the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not apply. From the root *kṣaṇ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the formation of the imperfect (*laṅ*) with the augment (*iṭ*) and the reduplication (*caṅ*), after the elision of the initial consonant (*hal-ādi-śeṣa*) and the change of *ṣ* to *c* (*cutva*), we arrive at the form *acakṣaṇ i at*. Here, although there is a light vowel—the letter *a*—in the syllable *kṣa* which follows the causative suffix (*ṇau*) that is itself followed by *caṅ*, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not have this light vowel immediately preceding it, because it is separated by the letters *k* and *ṣ*, which constitute a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster).

Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "for the purpose of establishing *it*," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: by the rule *samaḥ-takr̥tvarapramradasta-spṛśām* (Pāṇini 7.4.95), the substitution of the vowel *a* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the roots *sam*, *takr̥t*, *var*, *pramrad*, *das*, and *spṛś* is prescribed when followed by a *ṇi*-causal affix that is itself followed by a *caṅ* (the aorist marker). Examples include *asasmarat* and others.

By means of the rule *sanvallaghuni*, the substitution of *at* is prescribed in order to prevent the shortening (*itva*) that would otherwise result from the extension of the *san*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāvātideśa*).

In that context, because the practice (*abhyāsa*) is separated by the conjunction of the letters *s* and *m*, it lacks the status of being followed by *caṅ*, *ṇi*, or a light vowel (*laghu*). Consequently, since there is no possibility of *it*-substitution due to the absence of the *sanvadbhāva* rule, the substitution of *at* (for *an*), which is prescribed for the purpose of establishing that [substitution], would otherwise be redundant. This redundancy serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *it*-substitution occurs even for those [practices] separated by a conjunction of consonants (*saṃyoga*).
And in the case of *acikṣaṇat*, the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) is desired for the *sul* [suffix], such is the opinion. Thus ends the seventh chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter.

[Jñānapāda 8.1.16] Regarding the word *pada*: the mention of the term "end" (*anta*) in the rule "There is elision of the final [n] of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, Pāṇini 8.2.7) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
[Objection:

Is it not the case that the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) "of a word" (*padasya*) applies to the subsequent rules? In that context, does "of a word" function as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) or as a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*)?
Thus there is doubt: [it is resolved] by the rule beginning with *nalopaḥ*.
In the sūtra *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, the term *pada* is also understood as a governing heading (*adhikāra*). If that were not the case, the mention of the word *anta* (end) would be redundant.

Thus, when [the condition] "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*) exists, it is a qualifier for the word "of the word" (*padasya*). The meaning of the sūtra is: "there is elision (*lopa*) of a word ending in *n* that bears the technical designation of a nominal stem. And in that context, by the rule of the elision of the final [element] (*alontyaparibhāṣā*), [it refers to] the *n* at the end of the word.
Since it is stated that "there is elision (*lopa*) of *n* when followed by a *dhātu*," what is the purpose of mentioning the word "end" (*anta*)?
Its mention serves to indicate that this is a qualification of the word (*pada*).
Consequently, the elision applies to the *n* that is a constituent part of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which forms a part of the word.

This is the meaning of the sūtra. In that context, because the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) does not exist, the rule of "the substitution of the final" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*) would not apply; consequently, the elision of the final *n* would not occur. Therefore, the mention of the word "final" (*antya*) is for the purpose of ensuring the elision of the final *n*.

The statement "it is performed" indicates that its purpose is fulfilled within its own scope. Furthermore, the purpose of the rule *viśeṣaṇam viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 1.2.52) being taught here is for another instance: in the sūtra *udātasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudātasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.4), because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the word *padasya*, [the term *yaṇaḥ*] refers to that [pada].

Furthermore, the meaning of the sūtra would be that when there is the status of being a *sthānivat* substitute for a vowel that is either *udātta* or *svarita*, the *svarita* quality is applied to the final syllable of the word (*padam*) following that [substitute], provided it is an *anudātta*. Consequently, that sūtra would apply only in cases such as *kumāryau*.

The word *kumārthaḥ* would not apply here. Thus, when *kumārī + āḥ* is established, in place of the acute (*udātta*) vowel *ī*, there occurs a *yaṇ*; following that is the grave (*anudātta*) vowel *āḥ*.
Of the word *kumāryau*, which ends with that [vowel], the final vowel is *āḥ*. Regarding that [vowel]:

Although the *svarita* quality is indeed established, nevertheless, in the case of *kumārī jas*, because the vowel *a* of *jas*— which follows the *yaṇ* substitute for the acute (*udātta*) vowel *ī*— is grave (*anudātta*), the rule regarding the accentuation of the case-ending (*il-svara*) does not apply here due to the absence of the condition [of being followed by a vowel].

Because the suffix (*vyañjana*) does not exist—that is, because of its absence—the word would not end in that [suffix]; since it would instead end in *s*, the svarita accent of the vowel of the *jas* ending in *kumāryaḥ* would not be established. However, if the term "of the word" (*padasya*) is taken as a qualifier for the [preceding rule], [the desired result follows].

The meaning of the sentence is this: when there is a *kaṇ* (the letter *n*) that occupies the place of an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel and is part of a word, the following unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*). In that case, since the unaccented vowel *ā*, which is a constituent of *jas*, is indeed a constituent of the word, its status as *svarita* is established. Thus, [in the rule regarding] "single-substitute" (*ekādeśa*)...

The purpose [of this rule] should also be understood in the case of *udātenedātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5). Regarding *anudātaṃ sarvamapādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18): because of the prohibitive rule *na luṭ* (Pāṇini 8.1.29), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *an* also becomes *anudātta*.

By the rule *gatyarthaloṭā* (Pāṇini 8.1.51), the fact that the particle *prati* is prohibited serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even a non-final syllable may become unaccented (*anudātta*). [Commentary: The sūtra *anudātaṃ sarvam apādādau* is a governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*). In that context, the inclusion of the word *sarvam* ("all")— [The remainder of the sentence appears to be cut off in the source text.]

If this were not done, then because this very sūtra is cited in the rule *tiṅṅtiṅḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), the statement that a *tiṅ*-ending following a non-*tiṅ*-ending is unaccented would apply only to the first syllable of the subsequent word, according to the principle *ādeḥ parasya*.

The initial syllable of the verbal root would not be [unaccented]. However, it is observed that every constituent part of a finite verb (tiṅanta) is unaccented. Therefore, the purpose for which the word "sarva" (all) is included must be stated. And this purpose is also established by means of an indicator (jñāpaka).
It is established by the rule *na luṭ*— "by the sūtra *na luṭ*,

it is stated that a finite verb (*luḍanta*) following a non-finite form (*atiṅ*) is not subject to suppression (*nighāta*). Furthermore, the possibility of suppression for a finite verb (*luḍanta*) arises from the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

It should be stated that this is by means of the *sūtra*. For if, by that *sūtra*, only the initial syllable were prescribed as having the anudātta accent, then the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the *luṅ* ending would be redundant;
because there is no *luṅ* ending that has an acute accent on its first syllable. [This applies] to the *tās* suffix following the *luṅ* ending.

Because the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), the *ās-* suffix is acute (*udātta*). In that regard, in forms such as *kartā*, when the *ṭi*-elision (*ṭilopa*) is applied, it becomes oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of the substitute (*udātanivṛttisvara*).
In forms such as *kartārau*, it is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). However, there exists no form ending in *luṅ* that is initial-accented (*ādyudātta*).

The obtained state of being *anudātta* (unaccented) would be subject to cancellation. Therefore, since the prohibition "not in the case of *luṭ*" (*na luṭ*) would otherwise be redundant, it indicates that the rule "of the subsequent [element], the first [syllable]" (*ādeḥ parasya*) does not apply in the rule "tiṅ before tiṅ" (*tiṅṅtiṅ*). And thus, even for that which is not the initial [syllable] of a word constituent, [the *anudātta* is not applied].

The state of being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) applies [to the entire word]. Consequently, in cases such as *kartā* and *kartārau*, where the state of being unaccented would otherwise apply to both the final and the middle syllables, the rule *na luṭ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71) serves the purpose of excluding that [unaccented status]. Therefore, the view is that the phrase *sarvasya* (of the whole) need not be stated.

[Objection: Even so, even if the rule *ādeḥ parasya* does not apply, by the operation of *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would still occur for the final [letter] alone; therefore, let the mention of *sarva* (the whole) be made in order to prevent that. To this [we reply]:

Regarding the phrase *gatyarthaloṭā*: by the rule *gatyarthaloṭā* (Pāṇini 8.1.51), the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) of a word ending in a *loṭ* suffix is prescribed. Furthermore, since every word ending in a *loṭ* suffix is *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable) due to the general rule that *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta* (unaccented).
Since there is no possibility of the attainment (*prāpti*) of a *nigāta* (a circumflex accent), the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is purposeless;

this indicates that the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) does not apply. Thus, by implication, because all [the syllables] would acquire the status of being unaccented (*anudātta*), the explicit mention of "all" (*sarva*) need not have been made.
[This is] the intention:

since, in reality, there exists a present-tense (*laṭ*) form ending in *kṣya* that is oxytone, and since the rule of non-udātta for the final syllable (*alontyanighāta*) would apply to it, the rule "by means of a loṭ [ending] expressing motion" (*gatyarthaloṭā*) is intended as a prohibition against that.

Because its purpose has already been served and because it would not otherwise serve as an indicator, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the mention of "all" (sarva) is necessary. [Pāṇini 8.2.7: *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*]. The mention of "all" (*sarva*)...

Alternatively, the inclusion of *rūpa*, *rātri*, *sthāntara*, and *sadṛśa* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *ru* does not apply to the word *ananta*. Having raised the objection that the elision of *n* prescribed by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* would also apply to the form *ahar-bhyām*, [the author] states:

The author of the Vārttika stated: "There is a prohibition of the elision of *n* in the word *ahan*. Now, it might be argued that this prohibition need not be stated; for in the rule *aḍvyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.3.67), since the substitution of *ru* takes precedence over the elision of *n*, the elision of *n* would not apply [in the case of *ahan*] anyway. Nor is there [an issue] regarding the elision of *n*.

It should not be argued that because the substitution of *ru* is *asiddha*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would apply; for the elision of *n* after *ru* (*roḥ*), being without any other occasion (*anavakāśa*), overrides it. Furthermore, if the substitution of *ru* were *asiddha* with respect to the elision of *n*, the prescription of *ru* would be purposeless.
Because at the time of applying *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) in the word *aḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;nśaḥcdvddhddhed;* (i.e., *ahaḥ*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would also apply; however,
since there is no such word as *aḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;nśaḥcdvddhddhed;* that is unfit for the application of *nalopa*, [the rule does not apply].

Nor should it be argued that, once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred in *aḍḍha*, let there be the prescription of *ru*-hood for the vowel *ā* following the vowel *ā*; and thus, since *ru* would have the form of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) as its scope, it would not be sublated by the elision of *n*. This is not to be said.
If the rule *aḍvyavāye’pi* intended to prescribe the substitution of *ru* for a non-final [nasal], then for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), it would have simply stated *aḍvyavāye*. Instead,
by not stating it thus and rather specifying the presence of the letter *n*, [the author indicates his intention].

By providing this explanation, he makes it known that the rule *na aḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;nityam* does not prescribe the substitution of *r* for a non-final [nasal]. Consequently, by that rule, the substitution of *r* must be prescribed only for the final *n*;
and for that very [final *n*], there is also the elision according to the rule *nalopaḥ pratipadikāntasya*, since [the former] would otherwise have no scope.

The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrated that the Vārttika—"there is a prohibition of the elision of *n* in *ahan*"—is unnecessary, because the elision of *n* is superseded by the substitution of *rutva*. He stated this in the form: "the elision of *n* in *ahan*. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But..."

The prohibition [of *ru*] in the case of *saṃbuddhi* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because the sūtra remains purposeful by prescribing *ru* in instances such as *he dīrghāho atra*. In that regard, there is the rule: "Not after [a word ending in] *ṅsi* or *saṃbuddhi*."
Thus, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is established. And so,

because the elision of *n* possesses an occasion for its application that is not superseded by the rule for *ru*, and because the rule for *ru* lacks any occasion for application [that would otherwise block it], there is no possibility of the elision of *n* being sublated.

When the elision of *n* (nalopa) is to be applied, because the substitution of *ru* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "what precedes is as if not having taken effect" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), the elision of *n* would apply in the case of the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2); therefore,
there is a prohibition against the elision of *n*.

The *vārttika* "or rather, there must be an addition for *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathantara*" is stated because of dissatisfaction [with the previous view]. Its meaning is as follows: in the case of *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathantara*, the substitution of *ru* for the final syllable is prescribed. Even there, if the *ru* were to apply to the non-final vowel after the elision of the nasal (*n*), then [the author] would have prescribed the letter *ra* itself, not *ru*.

Therefore, the substitution of *u* for the *ru* of another [word] is prescribed by the rule *ato ror aplutāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.113). However, if *ru* were substituted for the vowel *a*, then because that [substituted *ru*] would not follow the *a* immediately preceding *chāndasa* (*chāḥ*), the substitution of *u* would not apply; consequently, the rule would not prescribe *ru* as a means to achieve the substitution of *u*, but would instead merely prescribe the replacement by the letter *r*. Since the author has indeed prescribed the substitution of *ru*, he thereby indicates that *ru* does not occur at the end of a word (*anantyasya*).

Thus, since the substitution of *ru* applies specifically to the final *n*, its elision (*lopa*) would also apply to that same *n*. Consequently, because the substitution of *ru* is without scope for the elision of *n*, the form *ahnaḥ* is established by the rule *ahnaḥ saṃkhyā-vi-sāya-pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.133), and so forth; this constitutes its utility within its own domain. However, the purpose of this *jñāpaka* (indicatory implication) is that in forms such as *ahnāṃ* and *ahni*, there is no elision of *n*, but rather the substitution of *ru* occurs. [The rule] *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.97) and *āsandīvat* (Pāṇini 7.3.11, 8.2.12).

The rule *īvatyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.221) indicates that the substitution of *va* occurs in words such as *ḍddhdhḍaddh;avatyaḥ*, *ḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;īvatyā*, and so forth. [Viśiṣṭaṭīkā: Now, one might ask: regarding these two rules, "saṃjñāyām" and "āsandīvadaḥsdvdr1;ṭhīvaccakrīvatkakṣīvaddrumaṇvaccarmaṇvatī," are they part of a single sūtra or are they separate sūtras?

If it were a single sūtra, then for words not recited here—such as *aḍḍhīvatī* and *kapīvatī*—the substitution of *v* would not apply, because they would not be considered technical names (*saṃjñā*). If, however, it consists of two sūtras, it must be stated that by the first sūtra the substitution of *v* for the *m* of the suffix *matup* is effected, and by the second sūtra the inclusion of *āsandīvat* and others is established.

If that were the case, one might object that even in examples such as *ikṣumatī* and *drumatī*, the suffix *-vat* would apply by the first rule because they are proper names (*saṃjñā*). Anticipating this objection, the author of the commentary stated, "Let it be as you wish. Then, raising the question of how the application of *-vat* occurs in cases like *ahīvatī* under the view that [the two rules] constitute a single sūtra, he replies with the words beginning with *īvatyāḥ*.

By the rule *īvatyāḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable is prescribed for a word ending in *īvat*. Examples are *ahīvatī* and *munīvatī*. If the substitution of *vat* (the *vatva*) did not occur in forms such as *ahīvatī*, the very form of the word *īvatī* would be difficult to obtain; consequently, the restatement (*anuvāda*) "of *īvatyāḥ*" would be inconsistent.

And thus, the mention of *īvatyāḥ* indicates that words of this class indeed possess the suffix *vat*. If it is objected: "But since [the form] *āsandīvat* and others would require *īvatyāḥ*, how can this be an indicator?"—it is not so; for these words are not used in the feminine, and therefore they lack the status of ending in the word *īvatī*. This passage from the work of Kaiyaṭa should be consulted here.

[Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.56] *nudavidondatrabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanah*. This rule indicates that this grammatical operation applies only when [the suffix] follows these roots. [Viṭṭhala: Now, does the rule *nudavidondatrabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanah* prescribe the optional substitution of *n* for the final *ṣ* following the roots beginning with *nud*, or does it optionally prohibit [that substitution]?

Is this *yoga* a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) or a restrictive prohibition (*niyamaniṣedha*)? In that regard, if the position is that it is a prescriptive rule, then the substitute *naḥ* must be stated. Nor can it be argued that *naḥ* is understood by way of anuvṛtti from the sūtra "radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.42), because the *nakāra* has been interrupted by intervening rules such as "śuṣaḥ kaḥ" and "paco vaḥ" (sūtras 8.2.51, 52).

In the view that [the rule] prohibits [the substitution], however, whatever would otherwise apply to a *niṣṭhā* suffix beginning with *n* does not take effect; thus, even without explicitly mentioning the letter *n*, the prohibition of *n* is established. But in this view, the mention of the root *hnī* is redundant, because there is no possibility for a *niṣṭhā* suffix following the root *hnī* to undergo the substitution of *n*.

Since the three roots beginning with *nud*—namely *trā*, *ghnā*, and *hrī*—are all subject to the application of the rule *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43), it would be appropriate to exclude them all by that rule rather than the root *hrī* alone. Having raised this doubt as to which alternative should be adopted, the author first supports the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and then, in the Bhāṣya, establishes the negative prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) as well, stating: "Or rather, let there be a prohibition," and so forth.

It is based on that [view]. In that position, the mention of the root *hrī* is for the purpose of indication (*jñāpana*), namely: "The substitution of *n* occurs even for the suffix *niṣṭhā* following the root *hrī*. For a prohibition cannot apply to that which is not otherwise applicable; with this intention, he says: "the mention of *hrī*. [Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.45: *nityaṃ samāse*]

The phrase "of that which stands not in the final member of a compound" (*anuttarapadasthasya*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the sentence (*vākya*). [Objection: But surely, in the rule *nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya*, the expression "not standing in the final member of a compound" is employed for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ś* for the visarga in cases such as *paramasarpiḥ-kuṇḍikā*.

In that case, even though there is an absence of *sāmarthya*, the application of the rule *ṣatva* would follow from the sūtra *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44). It should not be argued that in that sūtra the term *sāmarthya* refers exclusively to the *sāmarthya* characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), because although the compound *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā* possesses the *sāmarthya* characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) due to its being a compound, the preceding rule does not apply because of the absence of the *sāmarthya* characterized by mutual expectancy.

Regarding the term *sāmarthye* (in the case of semantic connection): because the word is heard in its general form, both types of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) can be understood from the preceding rule. Nor, even so, does the inclusion of the suffixes *is* and *us* [in the rule] lead to the exclusion of suffixes by virtue of the mention of "suffixes" [in the definition of a compound], such that although *sarpis* ends in *is*, *paramasarpis* would not end in *is*—for if it did not, one would have to say *paramasarpiḥ-kuṇḍikā*.

In this regard, one might object that the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) does not occur by the preceding rule. Anticipating the doubt that, if this were so, the optional *ṣatva* would also be untenable by the preceding rule in the sentence "paramasarpiḥ karoti," he states: "There is a prohibition [of the preceding rule] regarding that which stands in a non-composite word (*anuttarapadastha*). The meaning is as follows: in the rule "nityaṃ samāse" (Pāṇini 8.3.45), the term "isusoḥ" (from 8.3.44) is understood to carry over.

In that regard, if the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) in the rule *is-usoḥ sāmarthye* were intended as a restrictive condition (*parisaṅkhyā*), then in the case of *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, the substitution of *śatva* would not occur for the word *paramasarpiḥ* simply because it does not end in *is*; thus, [the rule] *vimuktottarapadasthasya* would apply.

And this [rule] indicates that the prohibition regarding the mention of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply in the context of *is* and *us*. By means of this, since that [prohibition] also does not apply to the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), namely "isusoḥ sāmarthye," the substitution of *śat* is established optionally even for the sentence *paramasarpiḥ karoti*.

In the case of the word *viśrāḥ* in the sentence, there is the non-application (*apravṛtti*) of the prohibition (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), and so forth. And thus, in order to prevent the application of the rule for *ṣatva* in examples such as *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, one must rely on "syntactic expectancy" (*vyapekṣā-lakṣaṇa*) alone as the definition of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) in the preceding sūtra; this is the established truth (*tattvam*). [Now begins the commentary on] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59).
The prohibition of the *sāt* suffix by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.111) indicates that the status of being a word-initial (*padādya*) applies even to a portion of a suffix.

Regarding the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), there arises the following objection: if one adopts the view of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, that both the substitute (*ādeśa*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) must be the letter *s*—then in forms such as *kariṣyati* and *hariṣyati*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would not apply. This is because, although the *s* is a constituent of the suffix by virtue of the suffix being *sy*, it lacks the status of being a suffix itself. Anticipating this doubt, the Bhāṣya establishes the substitution of *ṣ* for a *s* that is a constituent of a suffix by means of an internal indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Regarding this, [the author] says: *sātpadādyoḥ*. By the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, the retroflexion (*ṣatva*) of the letter *s* belonging to a suffix (*sānta*) as well as that which stands at the beginning of a word (*padādi*) is prohibited. In that context, since the *s* belonging to a suffix lacks the status of being a suffix (*apratyayatvāt*), the prohibition by *sātpadādyoḥ* would be redundant with respect to the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (which prescribes retroflexion for *s* in substitutes and suffixes). This redundancy serves to indicate that even the *s* belonging to a suffix is subject to retroflexion by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*.

Consequently, since the *s* that is a constituent of the suffix *sāt* would also incur the status of being a *śatva*-eliding sound (*śit*), the inclusion of the term *sāt* is meaningful for the purpose of excluding that [status]. And thus, the intention is that the status of being a *śatva*-eliding sound will be established even in cases such as *kariṣyati*. In that very context, another interpretation has been presented: that the status of being a *śatva*-eliding sound applies to the *s* of both the substitute and the suffix.

In that view, having raised the objection that the formation of a compound between the word *prathamāntādeśaḥ* (the substitute for the nominative case) and the word *ṣaṣṭhyantapratyayaḥ* (the suffix ending in the genitive case) is untenable, the *Bhāṣya* provides a justification based on an implied rule (*jñāpaka*).

To this, it is replied: the mention of the root *ghas* in the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no compound between two roots possessing different meanings. In the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*, the substitution of *ś* for the *s* of *ghas* is prescribed; *jakṣatuḥ* is given as the illustrative example.

If the rule "of the substitute and of the suffix" (ādeśapratyayayoḥ) did not specify that the *sakāra* [is the one affected], then the meaning would be: "that which belongs to the substitute, for that there is the substitution of *ṣatva*. In that case, since the *ghas* root undergoes the substitution of *ad* as a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *sakāra* belonging to its constituent part would already have its *ṣatva* established by the rule "of the substitute and of the suffix" alone; consequently, the mention of the root *ghas* [in the rule] would be purposeless.

And this [use of *kṣatam*] indicates the meaning of the sūtra—that the substitution (*ādeśa*) and the suffix-part (*pratyayāvayava*) which is the letter *s* undergo the change to *ṣ*—and it further indicates that there is a compound (*samāsa*) between the substitute and the suffix when they have different case-roles (*nānā-vibhaktika*), but not when they possess the same case-role (*samāna-vibhaktika*).

And thus, since the *s* of the root *ghas* lacks the status of being a substitute (*ādeśa*), the rule *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) does not apply to it. Therefore, the inclusion of the root *ghas* in the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*—which has the effect of securing that *ṣatva*—is meaningful; this is the intended sense. Here, the term "substitute" (*ādeśa*) is compounded with the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) as a copulative compound (*dvandva*), where the suffix is understood as that which follows [the base]. Consequently, the compound consists only of two members that share the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktika*).

Nevertheless, it should be noted that because the word *pratyaya* (suffix) is used here figuratively to denote the meaning of the suffix ending in *ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive case), the statement regarding its having a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) function is made.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *ghas* and *grah* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) specifically for the rule "an affix following [a word ending in] a substitute is not [treated as] a part of that substitute" (P. 1.1.56), rather than for the stated maxim (*vacana*); or that it is an indicator specifically for the rule that a compound occurs only between two words of the same case-role (*samānavibhaktika*) when the affixes of the substitutes and the original words are identical. This is because the restriction of compounds to words of the same case-role is not something that must be established by an indicator.

In the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), there is a compound between two words of equal case-role (*samānavibhaktika*). Since it is established that in examples such as *kariṣyatīti*, a compound occurs with the word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) because the nominative case (*prathamā*) is untenable, one might raise the doubt: "Let the word *ādeśa* also be compounded only with a word of its own equal case-role. When this doubt arises, the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) establishes that the word *ādeśa* ends in the first case (*prathamānta*).

This is because the meaning results in the conclusion that a compound occurs between two words with different suffixes (*nānāvidha-pratyayayoḥ*). Furthermore, the reading of *aśva-* in the list beginning with *savana-* in Pāṇini 6.4.175 indicates that the substitution of *ś* for *ṣ* occurs even after roots that do not end in *iṇ*.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: In the rule prohibiting *śatva* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*), namely, "na rapara-saḥ-tkgrṛṇi-saḥ-tkgrṛṇi-jis-paḥ-tkgrṛṇi-śis-paḥ-tkgrṛṇi-ḥḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;śvanādīnām," the inclusion of *aśvasani* in the *savanādi* group is redundant. Nor can it be argued that in the absence of its reading there, the *sakāra* belonging to that word would incur *śatva*, because by the rule (Pāṇini 8.3.103), *ḥḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;*... [text truncated]

The attainment of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) must be explained. In that regard, because the term *iṇaḥ* is supplied by way of *anuvṛtti*, *ṣatva* is prescribed only for a *s* that follows a preceding member ending in *iṇ*. One might raise the objection that in the word *aśvasaniśaḥ*, since the *s* does not follow a preceding member ending in *iṇ*, *ṣatva* would not apply. Anticipating this, the author states "beginning with *savana*" (*savanādiṣu*) to show that the inclusion of that word in the list serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) for the validity of the rule.

And thus, it is indicated that in certain instances, the substitution of *śatva* occurs even for a following suffix that does not end in *ni*. Consequently, since *śatva* would also apply to the word *aśvasani* (in the sense of "one who desires horses"), its inclusion in the list beginning with *savana* is made for the purpose of prohibiting that substitution. The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is the establishment of *śatva* in forms such as *jalāśayaḥ* ("a reservoir of water") and *māśāḥ* ("desires"), as is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya*.
The prohibition in the rule *toḥ ṣi* (Pāṇini 8.4.43) makes it known that the sequential assignment (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) does not apply here.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: according to the rule *yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*, the meaning of the sūtra *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* would be that there is a correspondence based on numerical order—namely, that when a *s*-sound is joined with a *ṣ*-sound, a *ṣ*-sound is substituted, and when a *t*-class consonant is joined with a *ṭ*-class consonant, a *ṭ*-class consonant is substituted.

Furthermore, one might raise the objection that in examples such as *peṣṭā* (one who pounds), *rāmaḥ peṣṭā*, and so forth, the substitution of *ṣṭu* would not occur. Anticipating this, [the author] states: "The rule 'toḥ ṣi' is a prohibition. By the sūtra "toḥ ṣi," the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the dental class (*tavarga*) is prohibited when followed by a *ṣakāra*. An example is *san ṣaṣṭhaḥ* (he is the sixth).

Furthermore, if in the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* there were a correspondence according to the respective order of the letters (*yathāsaṃkhya*), then that rule would apply only to the conjunction of the *ṭa*-class with the *ṣṭa*-class, and not with the letter *ṣ*. Consequently, in cases such as *san + ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, since the *ṭa*-class would not be introduced, the rule *ṣṭoḥ ṣi* would be rendered useless.

That sūtra [Pāṇini 1.4.51] indicates that there is no application of the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyānvaya*) in the case of "seeing what is unseen" (*adṛṣṭena adṛṣṭasya*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that forms such as *rāmaḥ paśyati* are established. Thus ends the first section, the Supplement to the Compendium of Indications (*jñāpakasaṃgrahaparīśiṣṭa*).
[Section 2] The Supplement to the Compendium of Indications (*jñāpakasaṃgrahaparīśiṣṭa*) (2)
Here, even those forms not included in the *Dhātupāṭha* which are recited therein in the *Kaiṭabhī* (the commentary on the *Kāśikāvṛtti*) are collected and explained.
[Jñānapa. ṭ eoṅ, eāṬc || glāvam, glāvaḥ |]

The rule *āṬto'mśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.93) does not apply here. This is because the rule *aiāṬc* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) indicates that *o* and *au* are considered homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*). [Objection: But surely, according to the word *glośaḥ*, when *glau* is followed by *am*, the form *glau am* is established, and thus the rule *āṬto'mśasoḥ* would apply.
By the rule *sūtreṇa*, the single substitute *ākāra* would result for both *āṬ* and *a*. Nor should it be argued:
"How could the *ākāra* prescribed after *okāra* when followed by *am*, *śas*, or a vowel (*aci*) possibly apply when *āṬ* and *a* follow? [This is because of the rule] *odautoḥ*.

One might suspect that because the throat (*kaṇṭha*), chest (*uraḥ*), and place of articulation (*sthāna*) are identical, and because the effort (*prayatna*) is also identical, the term *okāra* would include *aukāra* as well under the rule *aṇudit sūtra* for the sake of designating homogeneous letters (*savarṇasaṃjñā*); however, this is not so.

Regarding the statement "it proceeds": if there were mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *e* and *ai*, as well as between *o* and *au*, then the separate rule (*pṛthaksūtra*) "ai-au-c" would not have been formulated. This is because [the rule] begins with *edaitoḥ* and *odautoḥ*.
There is no similarity [of form]. Therefore, the rule "āṬto'mśasoḥ" does not apply to the word *glau* when followed by the dual ending *au*; this is the intended meaning. [Pāṇini 1.1.22:
*taraptamapau ghaḥ*]

In the section on comparative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*), although one could have simply stated "the suffix *gha* after *tad*" or "the suffix *gha* after *pitṛ*," the fact that the rule is formulated as a heavy (*guru*) sūtra in a different context indicates that the suffix *tarap* is used even in its most absolute (*atyanta-svārthika*) sense.
By this, forms such as "that which has fewer syllables" (*alpāctaram*) and "the lighter elision" (*lopas ca balavattaraḥ*) are established.

For *alpāc* is indeed [treated as] *alpāctara*; however, the suffix *-tarap* is not used here when one wishes to express the comparative excellence of one out of two. [The meaning is clear. By the rule *sarvādīni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27), this designation applies even to that which ends in such a word, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *dvandve ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.31). [The meaning is clear.]

Now, an objection may be raised: by the rule *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*, the designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) applies only to those words such as *sarva*, *viśva*, and so forth that are listed in that specific group (*gaṇa*). Consequently, for the aggregate form *paramasarva*, since it is not included in that list, [the designation would not apply].

Since the designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal) would not otherwise apply, the suffixes such as *tratas* and *til*, which are conditioned by that designation, would consequently not be applicable; therefore, it is stated: "also [the designation applies] to that which ends in it. By the rule "and in a *dvandva*," the designation *sarvanāman* applies to a collective form (*samudāya*) whose final member is a word belonging to the class of *sarvanāman*.

The designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun) for a *dvandva* compound is prohibited in cases such as "varṇāśrametarāṇām" (of those belonging to the castes, stages of life, and others). In that context, although the word "itara" is included in the list [of pronouns], the designation of *sarvanāman* does not apply to a compound ending in it because it is not included in the list [of pronouns] as a whole; therefore, the prohibition is established.

It would be meaningless. Furthermore, by the rule *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām*, it is indicated (*jñāpyate*) that even those words beginning with *sarva* possess the designation of *sarvanāman*. Consequently, in the form *paramasarvatra*, the suffix *tral* is applied, and in *paramasarvataḥ*, the suffix *tasil* is applied.
The intention here is that *akac* is established in the case of *parama-aḍḍha-vakān*.
Although it might also be possible to state that the establishment of *akac* in *paramasarvaka* is a purpose [of the rule], nevertheless,
the view is that the establishment of the desired form is not possible through the suffix *kap*.

In the phrase *paramaḍddhdhḍaddh;avakān*, it should be understood that *akac* is stated for the purpose of providing an illustrative example. [Jñānapaṭala] *Sama* is a synonym for *sarva*; however, a synonym for *tulya* is not accepted here. This is because of the rule: "The designation corresponds to the number of items when they are equal" (*yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*, Pāṇini 1.3.10).
Because of the indicator [in the rule]. [Objection: But surely the word *samaśas* is recited in the *sarvādi* group.

And for that word, just as there is the meaning "all," there is also the meaning "equal. In that case, the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) would also apply to the word *samaśas* when it signifies "equality," since it is included in the group.

Anticipating the objection that this is because the specific meaning of the word *sama* has not been specified, he says: "the word *sama*. If the word *sama*, which signifies "equal," were also to receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), then...
The term *sama* should have been specified as having the meaning of "equal" (*tulya*), because the augment *suṭ* would apply [to it] by the rule "after a pronoun,
*suṭ* is added before the case-ending *ām*" (Pāṇini 7.1.52). Thus, by its not being so specified,
it is indicated that the word *sama*, which is a synonym for *tulya*, does not possess the technical designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
Such is the intention. [Jñānapāda, Sūtra 2.1.11]

It is precisely by virtue of this capacity that the compounds of the ancients are considered obligatory (*nityasamāsa*). For instance, the compound *sa-sūpa* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) is an obligatory compound, because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule prescribing such compounds as "an indeclinable" (Pāṇini 2.1.6). [Vi.Ṭ: Now, an objection...]

Why was the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *vigraha* not established immediately after the sūtra "prāk kaḍārāt samāsaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.3) and before the sūtra "saha supā" (Pāṇini 2.1.4)? [One might argue: Having first formulated some sūtras that prescribe compound formation (*samāsa*), [the author] then established the governing rule for *vigraha*.

Why does he introduce the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for compounds in the middle, when he intends to prescribe them later? Let the governing heading for compounds begin right from the start of the rules for compound formation.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "By the force of this [rule].

The meaning is that, by the very force of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the preceding rule, the status of these preceding compounds as obligatory (*nitya-samāsa*) is understood. Even though for those preceding this point there was an option (*vikalpa*).

Eternality is established precisely because of the absence of any means of valid cognition [to the contrary]. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this very point is being reinforced by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*). [Objection:
If this were the case, then the compound in "saḥ ḍhyupā" would also be an obligatory (*nitya*) compound. And consequently...

Regarding the phrase "ḥḍddhdhḍaddh;ūtapūrva" and so on, the demonstration of the colloquial analytical sentence (*laukikavigraha*) as "pūrvaṃ ḥḍddhdhḍaddh;ūtaḥ" would be inconsistent; therefore, it says:
"saḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd; supeti. If [the rule] "saḥḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;"...

If the compound prescribed by the rule *suṇa* for a word ending in *su* with another word ending in *su* were mandatory, then compounds such as those formed by rules prior to *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*—
namely *avyayaṃ vibhaktau* and so forth— would be rendered compulsory.

Since compounds that are prescribed by other sūtras and are considered obligatory would already be established by those very same sūtras, the formulation of compound rules such as "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a case-inflected word" (avyayaṃ vibhaktyā) would be redundant. Therefore, that formulation [of specific compounds] is intended for the compound governed by the rule "a word ending in a case-suffix is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix" (sup-ā supā).
The intention is that it indicates optionality. [Pāṇini 2.1.31: *pūrvasadṛśasamonārtha...*]

In the case of the mention of *miśra*, the mention includes that which is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), because in the rule "And *miśra* when not preceded by a prefix, provided there is no *saṃdhi*" (Pāṇini 6.2.154), the term "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is explicitly stated. [Vi.Ṭ: Now, one might object: in cases such as *guḍena saṃmiśrāḥ* ("mixed with molasses"), they are indeed *guḍasaṃmiśrāḥ*...]
The formation of a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word ending in the third case [the instrumental] using the term *saṃmiśra* would not be valid; rather,
it is by the rule "pūrvasadṛśasamonārthakalaha...miśraślakṣṇaiḥ" that a word ending in the third case is compounded specifically with the term *miśra*.

Anticipating the objection that this would result from the rule for the formation of *tatpuruṣa* compounds, he says: "In the case of the word *miśra*. By the rule "And *miśra*, when not preceded by a prefix, [is antodātta] in a non-sandhi context," the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) is prescribed for the word *miśra* when it follows a third-case form in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Examples include *tilamiśrāḥ* ("mixed with sesame") and so forth.

In that regard, if the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) were omitted, then even in cases such as *tilasaṃmiśrāḥ*, there would be an udātta accent on the final syllable; therefore, it must be stated that the mention of "without a prefix" is for the purpose of preventing that. [Objection: Since the compound *miśra* is accompanied by a prefix, a compound cannot occur at all; and since the accent prescribed for a *tatpuruṣa* compound would not apply here anyway, what is the use of mentioning "without a prefix"?

And that [mention of *kṛta*] indicates that when there is a mention of a mixed category (*miśragrahaṇa*), there is also a mention of the form with its prefix (*sopasarga*). Thus, in examples such as *tilasaṃmiśrāḥ*, the mention of the *anupasarga* (non-prefixed) form serves to exclude the accent [of the prefix], thereby fulfilling its purpose within its own scope.

However, there is a specific purpose elsewhere: because the word *saṃmiśra* is included under the term *miśra* in the sūtra beginning with *pūrvasadṛśa-* (Pāṇini 2.1.31), the third-case tatpuruṣa compound such as *guḍasaṃmiśra* ("mixed with molasses") is considered grammatically correct. [From the Jñānapradīpa commentary: *pūrvāparā-* (Sūtra 2.2.1): Every single part (*ekadeśa*) is compounded with the word *ahan* ("day"). This is indicated by the rule *saṃkhyāvisāya-* (Pāṇini 6.3.110).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: by the rule *pūrvāparādharottaramekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe*, a compound is prescribed for words such as *pūrva* when they denote a part in relation to a whole (*ekadeśin*) that shares the same locus. However, this compound would not apply in cases such as *madhyāhnaḥ* (midday), because in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) *ahno madhyaḥ* (the middle of the day), although the day is the whole, there is no [compound] with the whole [as the second member].

Anticipating the objection that since the rule for compound formation applies only to these four words—*pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, and *uttara*—which denote parts (*avayava*), the word *madhya* would not be eligible for compounding, [the author] says: "all of them" (*sarvo’pi*). Any word denoting a part, even if other than the four specified in the sūtra such as *pūrva* and so on, is compounded with the word *aṃśa*.
In this regard, the evidence is the rule *saṃkhyā-visāyapūrvasyāhnasyāhan anyatarasyāṃ ṅau* (Pāṇini 6.3.110), which prescribes the substitution of *ahan* for the word *ahnaḥ* when preceded by *sāya*.

In the case of *sāyāhnaḥ* (evening), which is analyzed as *ahnaḥ sāyaḥ avasānam* (the end of the day is evening), if the compound were not formed with the word *ahan* (day)—since the component *sāya-* is not included within the group of four beginning with *pūrva-*—then the substitution of *ṭyu* for *ahan* when preceded by *sāya-* would be inapplicable, as that [word *ahan*] would not have *sāya-* as its prior member. And yet, that [substitution] is indeed prescribed, provided that every single part [of the word *ahan*] is compounded with *ahan*.

This indicates that [the compound] is formed with *ahnaḥ*. Although one might raise the objection that by stating that the word *ahnaḥ* is preceded by *sāya*, it is possible to indicate that the compound is formed only with the word *ahar* and not with the word *ahan*, nevertheless, when the word *ahnaḥ*—which is preceded by *sāya*—is substituted for *ahar*...

The meaning is as follows: when the word *ahnaḥ* [from Pāṇini 5.4.88] is cited as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is necessarily implied that the compound in question is preceded by the word *sāyam*. Furthermore, since such a preceding word cannot co-occur with *ahnaḥ* in a compound, this serves as the intended implication. It is not only a specific part of the day (*ahnaḥ*) that is compounded with *sāyam*, but rather any general time period; for the indicator applies to the general case.

The author of the *Tattvabodhinī* states that another alternative view has also been proposed in the *Kaumudī*, according to which the correctness of expressions such as *madhyarātraḥ* (midnight) and *paścimarātraḥ* (the latter part of the night) is established. Although under that view forms such as *dinamadhyaḥ* (midday) and *rātrimadhyaḥ* (midnight) would not be established, he says this is to be resolved by the maxim: "That which is established by an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere."

[The Jñānapradīpa on Pāṇini 2.2.2]: "The word *ardha* is neuter" (Sūtra 2.2.2). Since its neuter gender is already established by the very mention of the word *ardham*, the explicit inclusion of the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) is intended to indicate that "in these sūtras, the mention of gender is not intended to be significant."

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of the explicit mention of the neuter gender in the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*, since the term *ardham* is presented in the neuter gender, the exclusion of other genders is established by that very indication (*liṅga*); therefore, the word *napuṃsakam* is redundant. To this, he replies: "*ardham*... [and so on].

And thus, being purposeless according to the manner previously stated, the mention of the neuter gender in the sūtras indicates that the specification of gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Consequently, in sūtras such as *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), because the mention of gender in terms like *idam* is not intended to be significant, the application of the sūtra is established even for meanings such as *tasyāyam*.

The rule "in the sūtras, gender and number are not restrictive" has its parallel in the *paribhāṣā*: [Pāṇini 2.2.11] *pūraṇaguṇa* (etc.). This exclusion by means of a quality (*guṇa*) is non-eternal, because of such indications as [Pāṇini 1.2.53] *tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt*.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: words such as *arthagauravam* (the weightiness of the meaning), *buddhimāndyam* (the dullness of the intellect), and so forth—which consist of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) "the weightiness of the meaning" (*arthasya gauravam*) and so on—are employed by the grammarians (*śiṣṭas*). Their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) would not be established, because words such as *gaurava*, *māndya*, and others denote qualities (*guṇavācaka*), and therefore they cannot form a compound with a word ending in the genitive case.

Anticipating the objection that a compound with a word ending in the sixth case-affix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not possible because it is established by the rule "pūraṇaguṇa... and so forth, [the author] states: "This is non-eternal. This prohibition of compounding with a word ending in the sixth case-affix when it is qualified by a quality (*guṇa*) is not universal.

Regarding the phrase "because it is a name (*saṃjñā*) and a measure (*pramāṇa*)," since the word *pramāṇatva*—which denotes a quality—is used in a compound with the word *saṃjñā*, which ends in the eighth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it is indicated that the use of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) in certain instances where a quality is expressed. Thus, the correctness of expressions such as *arthagaurava* ("the weightiness of the meaning") is established; this is the intended sense. [Jñānaprakāśikā: Sūtra 2.2.35: *saptamīviśeṣaṇe*]

Precisely because of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), there are also *bahuvrīhi* compounds consisting of words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). [Objection: But surely, in usage, we see *bahuvrīhi* compounds with words in different cases, such as "the discernment (*viveka*) born from the true scripture" (*sacchāstrajanmā viveka-lābhaḥ*), where the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has its birth (*janman*) from the true scripture."

How is its correctness established? Since it has been settled in the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24) that for words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the term *dvandva* is understood as *dvigu*, [the author] says: "Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)."

The prescription of the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of a word ending in the seventh case in compounds such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (the "neck-time" one) indicates that a *tatpuruṣa* compound can indeed occur between words that do not possess the status of being a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier) and a *viśeṣya* (qualified). Therefore, the intention is that the aforementioned usage is grammatically correct.

[Pāṇini 2.3.7] *Jñānapradīpa-ṭīkā*: The seventh and fifth case endings are prescribed when used in conjunction with the word *adhika* ("more than" or "in excess"). This is established by the formulation of the two rules: *tadasminn adhikam* (Pāṇini 5.2.45) and *yasmād adhikam* (Pāṇini 2.3.9).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: "In such expressions as *loke lokād vā adhiko hariḥ* ('Hari is superior to the world'), since there is no rule prescribing the ablative (*pañcamī*) or locative (*saptamī*) in connection with the word *adhika*, how can those cases be grammatically correct? For, when the relation of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is intended, the use of the ablative alone would be appropriate. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By the word *adhika*... (referring to the rule *adhikaṃ vyādhikena ca*).

And thus, the correctness of *tathā* and *u* follows precisely from the authority of the author of the Sūtras; this is the intended meaning. [Pāṇini 2.3.8: *karmapravacanīyayukte*] Although the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed by the subsequent rule [2.3.9], it is superseded by this [rule]. This is because, even though [the usage] is already established by the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna-* (1.4.90) and others, the force of the formulation of this specific technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [in 2.3.8] necessitates its application here.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, in the phrase *anu japaṃ prāvarṣat*, the term *anu* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84). Consequently, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is prescribed after the word *japa* by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.8). In that context, just as *japa* possesses the status of being a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator), it also possesses the status of being a *hetu* (cause).

And likewise, having raised the objection that by the third case-ending in the rule "after *para* and *apara*" (Pāṇini 2.3.23), the second case-ending might be replaced [by the third], he says: "even the *para* [is included]."

Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* is already established for *ati* when it signifies a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) by the rule itself—"when a characteristic or such a state [is indicated]" (Pāṇini 1.4.90)—it must be stated that the rule "anur lakṣaṇe" prescribes the *karmapravacanīya* designation specifically for *anu* when it signifies a characteristic.

And in that case, since the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would have been applicable, the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) which has the fruit as its result; thus, by the maxim *yenāprāpte*, the third case is superseded by the second case. Therefore, there is no fault—this is the established position. [Nyāsa-pañjikā] Regarding the rule *namaḥ-svasti* (Pāṇini 2.3.16): when used in conjunction with *pra-bhṛti* and other such words, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also correct.

This is because of the grammatical indications [nirdeśa] in the rules *tasmai prabhavati* (Pāṇini 5.1.101) and *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.78). [Objection: But surely, since the Vārttika on the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alaṃ-vaṣaṭ-vigrahācca* states that "the word *alam* is included here in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*)," it follows that when used with a word having the sense of sufficiency, the dative case alone is correct.

Having raised the objection as to how the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of forms such as *prabhuvanatrayasya*—which end in the locative case (*saptamī*)—is established, he states: "due to connection with *prabhu* and so forth."

Because of the grammatical indication (nirdeśa) in the rule *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ*, when the suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) is prescribed [by Pāṇini 2.3.39], the word *alam* in that very context signifies "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) and its opposite; and in connection with such a word, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is applied. However, to prevent the misconception that might arise—namely, that the fourth case is not used in connection with words signifying sufficiency, but rather only the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—the word *api* is employed in the phrase *ṣaṣṭhy api*.

And likewise, because of the use of the dative case in the expression "tasmai prabhavati," the intention is that the dative is grammatically correct when used in conjunction with the root *śak* (to be able) in the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). [Jñānaprakāśikā] Regarding the rule *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29): however, it does not apply when used in connection with a word denoting a part (*avayava*), as is evident from the formulation of the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Pāṇini 8.1.2).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: in the rule *anyārāditarartedikchabdāñcūttarapadājāhvyadvyupakṛte*, the term *dikchabda* (direction-word) refers to words observed to denote direction. Consequently, even when words such as *pūrva* and so forth—which are well-known to express direction but are currently used to express time—are joined with another word, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs.

By this, the explanation that "Phālguna is prior to Caitra" and so forth is established. If this were the case, however, the ablative (*pañcamī*) would also apply in connection with words denoting parts (*avayava*). Thus, in the expression *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body"), even though the word *pūrva* denotes a bodily part, since it elsewhere denotes a direction (*dik*), there would be the possibility of the ablative in its connection [with *kāyasya*], and consequently the locative (*saptamī*) would not be grammatically correct. Anticipating this objection, he says: "denoting a part."

In the sūtra *tasya paramāmreḍitam*, the word *tasya* refers back to the previously mentioned *dvirukta* (the reduplicated form). The term *para* denotes the subsequent member [of the reduplication]. If the ablative case were to apply even when joined with the word *para*—which signifies a member—then the use of the genitive case in the expression *tasya* would be inconsistent.

Furthermore, it is indicated that when the word *diś* (direction), which was previously seen to denote a direction, now denotes a part (*avayava*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) does not apply in connection with it. Therefore, the point is that there is no occurrence of the fifth case in examples such as *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* (the front of the body). [Jñānapañjikā] Regarding the rule *apādāne pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.28), because of the usage in the commentary *kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti* (starting from Kārtikī), the fifth case is applied in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti* (starting from).

[VI.Ṭ] But even so, in such cases as “*bhayāt prahṛṣṭaḥ, ārabhya vā sevyaḥ śrīhariḥ*,” how can the ablative case (*pañcamī*) be used, given the absence of association with words such as *anya*? To this, he says: “Because of the usage of the word *bhaya*. Likewise, here...

In the commentary on the sūtra *apādāne pañcamī*, having cited the vārtika *yataścādhvakālanirmāṇam* and given the example *kārtikyā āgrahāyaṇī māse*, [the author] introduces the rejection of that vārtika by stating, "this need not be stated," and then proposes: "This [usage] ought to be employed here, yet it is not used: *kārtikyāḥ prabhṛtyāgrahāyaṇī*."

It has been stated: "in the month. The meaning is that even in the absence of a word expressing motion (*prahṛti*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is established because the object [of the motion] exists. By speaking thus, the author of the Bhāṣya indicates the rule: "the ablative case is used in connection with a word denoting motion (*prahṛti*)."
