Otherwise, since the Vārtika would necessarily be required to provide the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*) in the absence of the word *prakṛti*, its inconsistency would be evident. And thus, the ablative occurs even in connection with words synonymous with *prakṛti*.

For this very reason, on the occasion of explaining the statement "kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti," Kaiyaṭa stated: "The meaning is 'starting from that' (tata ārabhya). Regarding this, the authors of the *Bālamanoramā* have asserted that the suffix *tasi* is applied to the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the word *tataḥ*.

Because of the rule for compound formation, *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed in connection with the word *bahiḥ*. [Vi.Ṭ] Thus, even though there is no specific sūtra prescribing the ablative case in connection with *bahiḥ*, the ablative is established by means of this indicator.

The rule *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* prescribes the formation of a compound with the word *ahi* joined by a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Since this prescription would be untenable without a fifth-case ending when used in conjunction with *ahi*, it indicates that the fifth case must occur in its connection with that word.

The intention is that by this [rule], the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of usages such as *grāmād āgataḥ* ("come from the village") is established. [Jñāpakapāda] Regarding the rule *adhi-i-arthānām* (Pāṇini 2.3.52): the mention of the prefix *adhi-* is for the purpose of indicating the following maxim: "The verbal root *iṅ* (to study) does not lose its status as a prefix when combined with another prefix. [Vivaraṇa] Now, an objection: there should be no mention of the prefix *adhi-* in the rule *adhi-i-arthānām*.

By the very expression *ig-artha* (meaning "having the sense of *i*"), the root *adhi-i* (from which *adhīta* is derived) is indicated; thus, the mention of *adhīti* is for the purpose of making known that the root *i*, meaning "to remember," must be employed only in conjunction with the prefix *adhi*. This is the intended meaning.

Although the mention of *iṅ* here might serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prefix *adhi-* does not combine with the root *ig* alone, but rather with *iṅ*, nevertheless, the inclusion of the root *iṅ* within the body of the statement is for the purpose of illustrating by example that just as the root "iṅ adhyayane" (to study) does not combine with the prefix *adhi-*, so too the root "ik smaraṇe" (to remember) does not.

It should be understood that the mention of *adhi* in the rule *ṇeradhyayane vaktavyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.26) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prefixes *adhi* and *upa* are not included in the sense of motion (*gati*). The root *nandi* in the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134) belongs to the extended group beginning with *pacādi*. This is because the roots *kṛ* and *ghaṭ* are employed in the rules *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare* (Pāṇini 4.4.143) and *karmaṇi ghaṭo’ṭhac* (Pāṇini 5.2.35).

And because the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) is prescribed when an *ac* affix follows. [Objection: Now, in the rule "lyu-ṇini-ac are added after roots belonging to the *nandi*, *grahi*, and *pacādi* groups," three groups are specified: the *nandyādi*, the *grahyādi*, and the *pacādi*. Among these, the *nandyādi* and *grahyādi* are not *ākṛtigaṇas* (open-ended groups). Why? Because... [text continues]

Fearing that because *pac* and others are explicitly mentioned [in the rule], the *pac*-class (*pacādi-gaṇa*) might not be an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), he establishes its status as an open-ended class by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): "The *pac*-class is an open-ended class."

From the usage of the word *kara* in the rule *śivaśamariḥsdvdr1;ṭasya kare*, which is derived from the root *kṛ* by adding the suffix *ac*—since it is not listed in the *pacādi* group—and likewise from the usage of the word *ghaṭa* in the rule *ghaṭo'ṭhac*, which is derived from the root *ghaṭ* by adding the suffix *ac*—it is understood that the *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).

Thus, by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ* is prescribed when the suffix *ac* follows a stem ending in *yaṅ*. Since there is no mention of forms ending in *yaṅ* in the *pacādi-gaṇa*, it would be impossible for the suffix *ac* to follow them. Therefore, the prescription of the elision of *yaṅ* before the suffix *ac*—being otherwise inconsistent—is intended to indicate that the *pacādi-gaṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). [Jñāpakapāda] *matiḥ buddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.188).

Furthermore, this does not contradict what has been stated, because of the indicator (*liṅga*) in the rule "upajñāte" (Pāṇini 4.3.115), which occurs within the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of "tena" (Pāṇini 4.3.112).

[Objection: But surely, by the rule *mati-buddhi-pūjārthebhyaś-ca*, the suffix *kta* is prescribed after roots meaning desire (*icchā*) and so forth when used in the sense of the present tense; and for those same roots used in the sense of the past, the general rule for the *kṛt* suffixes, *niṣṭhā*, would be an exception (*apavāda*) to that [present-tense *kta*].

Consequently, it would follow that usages such as "pūjito yaḥ surāsuraiḥ" (he who is honored by gods and demons) would be grammatically incorrect. Nor should it be argued that even there the suffix *kta* has exclusively a present meaning; for if that were the case, then by the application of the rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67), the genitive case [in "surāsuraiḥ"] would be ungrammatical. To this, the author replies: "this is not so."

By that [sūtra], the suffix *cha* is prescribed in the sense of "discovered by" according to the rule *upajñāte*; for example, *pāṇinīyam*, meaning "discovered by Pāṇini. In that instance, the third case ending is required after the word *upajñāta*, which is established as having the sense of the past tense (*bhūtārtha*) because it ends in the *kta* suffix.

Furthermore, if the suffix *kta* in its present sense, as cited in the rule *mati-buddhi-pūjārthebhyaś ca*, were to subvert the suffix *kta* in its past sense, then the grammatical reference *tenopajñātam* would be inconsistent; for the term *upajñā* also signifies the act of understanding (*buddhi*).

And thus, since Pāṇini prescribes the *kta* suffix after a root meaning "to understand" (*budh*) in the sense of "becoming," it is established that the *kta* suffix cited in the rule *matiḥ buddhiḥ* is not an exception to the *kta* suffix used in the sense of "becoming"—this is the intended meaning. [Jñānapradīpa] Regarding *yaj-yāca* (Pāṇini 3.3.90): there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *praśne cāsanna-* (3.2.117).

[VI.Ṭ] Now, one might object: from the verbal root *pracch*, by the rule "yajayācayatavicchapraccharakṣo naṅ" [Pāṇini 3.3.90], the suffix *naṅ* is applied; and by the rule "cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the *ch* is replaced by *ś*. Thus, the form *praśnaḥ* is observed.

In this context, since the suffix *pratyaya* has the marker *ṅ*, one might suspect that when *tis* follows, the *repha* (*r*) of the root would undergo *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule "graḥḍhddhic12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;jyāvayi" (Pāṇini 6.1.16). Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "And in the case of *praśna*, [the form is] *āsanna*. Thus, the fact that the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) is formulated in the Sūtra without *saṃprasāraṇa* indicates the absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* in this root; such is the conclusion.

[From the Jñāpakānuśāsana, Sūtra 3.3.95: *sthā-gā-pā-pacaḥ* (Sūtra 3.3.95). The form *avasthā* is [derived] as *saṃsthā* by virtue of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *vyavasthāyām* (Sūtra 1.1.34). [Vivaraṇa: Now, an objection: By the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (Sūtra 3.3.94) and the rule *sthā-gā-pā-paco bhāve* (Sūtra 3.3.95), the suffix *ktin* is prescribed for the root *sthā* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṅ* prescribed by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Sūtra 3.3.106). Thus, forms such as *prasthitiḥ*, *upasthitiḥ*, and so forth, are derived.

If this is so, one might object: "How can forms such as *avasthā*, *saṃsthā*, and *itthā*—which end in the suffix *aṅ*—be grammatically correct? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*avasthā saṃsthā*. Thus, by the mention of the word "in the sense of state" (*vyavasthāyām*) in the Sūtra, it is understood that the suffix *aṅ* occurs after the root *sthā* in the feminine gender to denote the abstract action (*bhāva*). This is the intended meaning. [From the Jñānapradīpa: *khano gha ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.125)]

The inclusion of the *ghit* marker is for the purpose of indicating that this [suffix] occurs even after other roots. By means of that, in the case of *bhujer bhogaḥ padam*, the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe ghaḥ*). [Objection: But surely, by the rule "khano gha ca," the suffix *gha* is prescribed. The example given is *ākhanaḥ*. In that suffix, the letter *gh* is marked with the *it* designation. And yet, there appears to be no purpose for that [designation] in the present context.

Anticipating the objection that since the root *dhā* is not included in the *caj* group, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) would not apply, [the author] states: "The inclusion of the marker *ṭ* (*ghit*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well, provided they are otherwise eligible for the *ku*-substitution. By this, when the suffix *gha* is applied to the root *bhaj* and the *j* is replaced by *g*, the form *bhaga* is established—this is the meaning of the phrase "the inclusion of the marker *ṭ* (*ghit*)."

[Pāṇini 4.1.14] *anupasarjanāt* [from that which is not a subordinate member]. This very rule makes known the application of the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) regarding feminine suffixes. [Vivaraṇa: Now, in cases such as *bhadrakurucarā*—meaning "that [city] in which the inhabitants of Kuru are auspicious"—where the word *kurucara* and others function as subordinate members (*upasarjana*), how can the feminine suffixes prescribed by rules such as *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15) apply?

The governing rule (*adhikāra*) "not being a secondary member" (*anupasarjanāt*) is prescribed for the purpose of excluding suffixes such as *ṅīṣ* and others. However, that [rule] is redundant, because the suffix *ṅīp* does not even apply after the word *bhāṣyakāracara*, precisely because that word does not end in a *ṭi*-suffix. Nor should it be argued that since the *ṭi*-suffix qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there would be an application of *ṅīp* even after something ending in a word that ends in a *ṭi*-suffix, by means of the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*).

Anticipating the objection that "in rules prescribing suffixes for compounds, there is a prohibition against [applying] the rule regarding that which ends in *nad*," he says: "This very [rule]. Since, according to the reasoning stated above, the heading *anupasarjana* (not being a subordinate member) would otherwise be redundant, it serves to indicate (*jñāpaka*) that in the case of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), the rule of "extension to that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Therefore, the heading *anupasarjana* exists for the purpose of excluding suffixes such as *ṅīṣ* in examples like *bhāṣyakurucarāḥ*; thus, its utility is established within its own domain (*svāṃśe cāritārthyam*).

However, there is a purpose elsewhere, such as in the rule *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7), where the suffix *raC* is required after words ending in *van*. Regarding the rule *strīpuṃsābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.87): the suffix *vati* does not apply in the sense of "like" (*vatyarthe*). This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *strī puṃvacca* (Pāṇini 6.3.34). Examples: *strīvat*, *puṃvat*.

By the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañ-snañau bhavanāt*, it is stated that for the meanings preceding those governed by *dhānyānāṃ bhavane* (Pāṇini 5.2.1), the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are respectively applied after the words *strī* and *pums*. These two suffixes are not employed in the sense of *vat* (as expressed in Pāṇini 5.1.117). However, the sense of *vat* refers to the meanings preceding *bhavana* (Pāṇini 5.1.115).

And so, raising the objection that the suffixes *nañ* and *tañ* would also apply in the sense of the suffix *vat*, [the author] says: "In the sense of *vat*, not. If *nañ* and *snañ* were to occur in the sense of *vat* after the words *strī* and *puṃs*, then the designation *puṃvat* (like the masculine) would not be appropriate; for the suffix *snañ* would have been excluded by the specific mention of *vat*.

Although the mention of *puṃvat* would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only for the case where the word *puṃs* itself is present, nevertheless, since an indicator depends upon the context of the rule (*sūtra*), it is understood here that the suffixes *nañ* and *snan* do not apply in the sense of *vat* after the words *strī* and *puṃs*. This is the intended meaning. [Jñāpakasamuddeśa, sūtra 4-2-4] *luḍbhaviṣye* (sūtra 4-2-4).

By the rule "vi-bhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrī-bhyaḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.23), it is indicated that this *lu* elision occurs specifically on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). Consequently, the form *pauṣī*—meaning the full moon day conjoined with the month of Pauṣa—is established.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection is raised: according to the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.3), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed; however, if by the rule *lupi yuktavad vyaktivacane* (Pāṇini 1.2.51) the specific sub-division of time consisting of six days (*ṣaṣṭidaṇḍa*) is not understood, then it is said that the elision (*lup*) occurs—as in the example *adya puṣyaḥ*. Herein, [the following is explained...]

Even when a specific distinction such as "not yesterday" or "not tomorrow" is understood, the *lup* elision does not occur because there is no comprehension of a subordinate temporal distinction consisting of a day and night (*ahorātra*).

Consequently, in the case of *pauṣī*—derived from *puṣyayuktā paurṇamāsī* (the full moon joined with the Puṣya constellation)—the *luP* elision of the *aṇ* suffix would also follow due to the lack of comprehension of a subordinate temporal distinction consisting of a day and night. To this, [the author] says: "In the case of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), however, there is no elision."

The meaning is that because the term *phālgunī* is used without elision (*lup*) in the sense of "the full moon day conjoined with the constellation Phalgunī," the intention is that the elision does not apply when the full moon day is conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Although an objection might arise—given that in that very same context the term *śravaṇā* is used with elision—how can it be possible to establish such a rule? Nevertheless, the intention is that although it is so stated there, the elision is merely indicated as being optional (*vibhāṣā*) in that specific case.

[From the Jñānapradīpa-ṭīkā: By the rule *na vyo liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.46), even though it occurs later in the order of rules, the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the vowel of the root *vyo* takes precedence over the subsequent rule regarding the substitution of *ḍhalādi* (the addition of *ḍha* etc.), because of the restrictive force (*grahaṇasāmarthya*) of the mention of *u* in the rule *ūḍhaḥ*.

[Commentary]: Now, one might object: from the root *vyeñ* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*), when the suffix *ṇal* of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is applied, we arrive at *vye-a*. Then, by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), *vṛddhi* is substituted for the vowel, resulting in *vyai*. When the reduplication of the root occurs, we get *vyai-vyai-a*. Here, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *yakāra* of the reduplicated syllable is applied by the rule *liṭi abhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17), followed by the formation of the single substitute *pūrvarūpa*, yielding *vivyai-a*. Finally, with the substitution of *āy* (*āyādeśa*), the form *vivyāya* is derived. Thus, the form is explained.

That is not established. One might object that, because it is subsequent to the *saṃprasāraṇa*, the substitution of *y* by *v* would occur first according to the rule *ḍhaladiśeṣeṇa*, and once the *v* has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa* to become *u*, the form would result in *uvyāya*; anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though it is subsequent."

In the sūtra *liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), because of the very recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of both *vacisvapiyajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) and *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhajjatīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), when there is the elision (*lopa*) of the [augment] *uṭ*, [the rule applies].

The repetition of the rule regarding the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is for the purpose of restating it. Thus, there is a double prescription: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], there shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication of roots such as *vac* and roots such as *grah*. Among these, the second prescription is for the sake of restriction: "In the case of the reduplication of roots such as *vac*, there shall be vocalization only, and nothing else."

And thus, by displacing the *ḍhalādi* group [of suffixes] and applying *saṃprasāraṇa* to the vowel *i* of the root *vyadh*, the form *vivyādha* is established; this is the intended meaning. [From the Jñāpakapradīpa: Regarding the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75), this augment *tuk* applies after a long vowel (*dīrgha*), but not after the suffix *cha*. This is known from the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *senāsurācchāyā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25). [From the Vivaraṇa: Now, an objection: in the rule *dīrghāt*, the word *che* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*) from the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73).

In a situation where there is a mention of both the ablative (*pañcamī*) and the locative (*saptamī*), the ablative mention is more authoritative; thus, by the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.75), the ablative would determine the status of the locative *che* (Pāṇini 6.1.73). Consequently, the meaning of the sūtra would become: "the augment *tuk* is added to the *ch* that follows a long vowel."

One might raise the objection that in cases such as *cchidyate*, the augment *tuk* should follow immediately after the letter *ch*, and not immediately after the long vowel. To this, [the author] replies: "This *tuk* follows the long vowel. Although, in the case of a reference by means of the ablative (*uḥ*), a reference by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is stronger, nevertheless, in this rule (*sūtra*), by relying on the strength of the locative reference (*saptamī*), it is accepted that the ablative reference is interpreted as being in the sense of the locative (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

In this regard, the proof is the grammatical rule of Pāṇini: *senāsurācchāyā*. If the augment *tuk* were to apply after the long vowel *ī*, then the letter *c* would have been specified above the *ch*. However, the fact that the letter *c* is specified above the long vowel *ī* indicates that this *tuk* belongs to the long vowel itself; such is the underlying intention (*bhāva*).

The ultimate point is this: because of the rule *senāsurācchāyā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25), which mentions the word *dīrghāt* in the ablative case, it is made known that the suffix *ṣṭhaḷ* follows a long vowel; thus, it is indicated that this *tuk* augment belongs to a long vowel. In the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) for the substitution is not attributed to the *ik* (the original element). This is known from the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of rules such as *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) and *vāṭvaḥṣṭutpitṛṣvasuḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.31).

[Commentary on VI.1] Now, in the word *dhātraṃśaḥ*, regarding the letter *ra*, there arises the possibility of doubling by the Vārttika rule "yaṇo mayo dve vācye," where the word *mayaḥ* is in the ablative case and *yaṇaḥ* is in the genitive case. Just as that doubling is prevented because its status as the effect (*kāryitva*) is set aside by its being directly heard as the cause (*nimittatva*) in the rule "aco raṛbhyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.46), so too in the word *sudhyupāsyaḥ*, the doubling of the letter *u* would likewise be prevented by the rule "iko yaṇaci."

Since the status of being a cause (nimittatva) is sublated by the status of being a substitute (sthānitva) when it is heard, the substitution of a semivowel (yaṇ-ādeśa) for the vowel *ī* would not occur when that [cause] follows; therefore, he says: "by virtue of being a substitute."

The point is this: because the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *i* is prescribed in the rule *ityuttarasya* when followed by *u*, and because the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *ṛ* is prescribed in *pitṛḥsadṛśaḥ* when followed by *u*, these two instances serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) that the status of being a *sthānin* (the element to be replaced) does not constitute a cause (*nimitta*) for the application of a grammatical operation. Thus it is made known. [From the Jñāpakapradīpa: Regarding *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau* (Pāṇini 6.1.137): the augment *suṭ* is applied even in some cases where the root *kṛ* is preceded by *sam*.

This is because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.2.16). [Vivaraṇa: The suffix *sūṭ* is prescribed after the root *kṛ* preceded by *sam-* or *pari-* in the senses of "preparation" (*bhūṣaṇa*) and "collection" (*saṃghāta*), according to the two rules: *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe* and *samavāye ca*.

The augment *suṭ* is not applied only to the two meanings already mentioned; it is observed even in other senses, as in examples such as "the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared in the potsherds (*kapāleṣu*)," where *suṭ* is seen. To justify this, [the author] states: "of that which is preceded by *sam*."

In the sūtra *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*, the meaning of the word *saṃskṛta* is that which has its purpose manifested as an action resulting in [use for] eating and so forth; this is because of the example cited: *saṃskṛtā bhrāṣṭre yavāḥ* ("barley grains prepared in a frying pan").

The intention is that, likewise, because *suṭ* is explicitly mentioned even in the rule for *ad-bhū*, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is thereby known. [Jñāpakapradīpa] Regarding *vīra-vīryau* (Pāṇini 6.2.120): the word *vīrya* ends in the suffix *yat*. In that case, the rule "the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to the vowel following *yat*, except in the case of *nau*" (6.1.213) would not apply; thus, the specific mention of *vīrya* is an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark). For if that were not the case, the desired result would already be established by the preceding rule alone.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: in the case of *suvīraḥ* and *suvīryaḥ*, where the words *vīra* and *vīrya* follow a word ending in the nominative case (*su-*), the rule "vīravīryau" prescribes that the first syllable is acute (*ādy-udātta*) in the compound. In that context, the prescription of the acute accent on the first syllable of the word *vīrya* is redundant.

One might object that, by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.213], the word *tasya* is initially acute (*ādyudātta*), and that by the rule *ādyaudātaṃ dvyac chandasi* [Pāṇini 6.2.119]—which means that in Vedic usage, a two-syllable word (*dvyac*) that is initially acute takes the *udātta* accent on its *su*-suffix—the initial acute nature of *tasya* is established. Anticipating this objection, it is signaled that for this very reason, the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* does not apply to the word *vīryaśas*.

[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein being *sat*" means: when there is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) as in the rule "from *anāvaḥ*" (*yato 'nāvaḥ*), etc. "By the preceding rule alone" means: by the rule "in the Veda, a word ending in two vowels has the acute accent on the first syllable" (*ādyaudātaṃ dvyac chandasi*), etc. [Pāṇini 6.2.160: *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca*].

In the case of *khiṣṇuc*, even though it belongs to the *vyanjanādi* (consonant-initial) group, its inclusion [in the list] is due to the force of the rule prescribing that it begins with the vowel *i*. It is not accepted as being *vyanjanādi*.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, in the case of *anādṛḍhaḥ āḍṛḍho bhavati* and *āḍṛḍhibhaviṣṇuḥ*, where the sense of becoming (*bhū*) is intended and a word ending in the suffix *san* is the upapada, the suffix *khiṣṇuc* is applied to the root *bhū* by the rule *kartari bhuvah khiṣṇuckhukañau* (Pāṇini 3.2.57).

In that case, regarding the negative compound *anāḍhya-bhaviṣṇuḥ* (not becoming wealthy), according to the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca*, an udātta accent on the final syllable would be required; however, that would not occur [if the compound were analyzed as *na āḍhyaḥ*].

Anticipating the objection that since *vyanjanāntasya* (of that which ends in a consonant) is mentioned there, the suffix *khiṣṇuc* would not apply to *vyanjanānta-vyadh* because *iṣṇuc* alone is prescribed, [the author] provides the suffix *khaṣṇuc* for the root *bhū*, arguing that the initial *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) can be established by the augment *iṭ* itself; thus, the prescription of an *ikāra*-initial *iṣṇuc* by the rule *iṣṇuc* applies to *khiṣṇuc* as well.

He indicates that this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Therefore, there is no fault, as he says: "in the case of *īṣatpāna*. [Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.11: *aptaḥ-tṛntṛcau*. Since the form would have been established by the rule *taḥ* alone, the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* after *aptaḥ* is for the purpose of indicating that even when a general term is used, only a specific instance is sometimes intended to be understood.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: in the rule *aptṛntṛc* (*Pāṇini 6.4.11*), instead of reading *tṛntṛcau*, one should simply read *tṛ*. By this general term *tṛ*, the inclusion of both *tṛn* and *tṛc* will be accomplished. This is just as in the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (*Pāṇini 6.4.154*), where *tṛ* [is used].

By this [statement], it is indicated that in the rule "tadvat" (Pāṇini 5.1.116), there is a general mention of both *ta* and *tac*; thus, it is understood that in some cases, even when a general term is used, only the specific form is intended. Therefore, the separate mention of *ta* and *tac* is for the purpose of making known that even where there is a general designation, only the specific [form] is to be taken.

The purpose of this indication is as follows: although the term *ka* is mentioned in a general sense in the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.37), it refers specifically to the *ka* of a *taddhita* suffix and not to [the *ka*] of a *kṛt* suffix. Consequently, in the case of *pākabhārya*—meaning "one whose wife is a cook"—there is no prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). The word *pāka* is a *kṛt* derivative.

The suffix *kap* is prescribed as an *uṇādi* formation; therefore, the rule "In the prohibition regarding words ending in *ka*, the mention of *taddhita* [suffixes] is for the sake of including those beginning with *vuñ*, *ṛ*, *añ*, and *yaṇ*" becomes justified. Others, however, say: since it would have been sufficient simply to say "after *aptṛ*," the separate mention of "ending in *tṛ*" and "before a *jiti* [suffix]" is for the purpose of excluding the case of *arvaṇas-tṛ*.

Although the exclusion of that [meaning] is established by the phrase "provided it has a meaning," nevertheless, those two are mentioned separately in order to indicate the non-eternality of that exclusion.

Therefore, they say that it is established by the rule: "The suffixes *ani*, *na*, *as*, *man*, and *gra* cause the application of the rule regarding what ends in them, whether the preceding element has meaning or is meaningless. This alternative view is also set forth in the *Tattvabodhinī*. [Jñānapradīpikā] Regarding the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112):

In the rule *āta āṬ ṇalaḥ*, although the form would have been established by simply using *o*, the prescription of *āṬ* is for the purpose of ensuring its audibility when the *ṇal* suffix is elided after the root *daridrā*. For this very reason, some maintain that the augment *ām* does not apply here, based on this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). [Commentary: Regarding the root *daridrā*, the form *daridrāñcakāra* is stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *kāspratyayāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.35), following the Vārttika: "The augment *ām* is applied after roots ending in *kāsu* and those with more than one vowel, as well as after *lup* and others. Thus, the form *daridrāñcakāra* is produced in the Perfect tense (*liṭ*).

Kaiyaṭa, however, not accepting the form *āma*, maintains that forms such as *dadaridrau* alone are correct. Likewise, he states: "In the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34), since there is no reason for the nominative case [of *ātaḥ*], it would be more appropriate to prescribe the vowel *au* alone. This is because forms such as *yayau* could be established by the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *vṛddhireci* (Pāṇini 6.1.88) itself, [applying] to both the *ā* and the *au*."

Therefore, the prescription of *au* [in Pāṇini 7.2.68] results in the hearing of the vowel *au* in the form *dadaridrau*, because of the elision of *ā* in the root *daridrā* by the rule "the elision of *ā* for the root *daridrā* should be stated before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. However, if *o* were prescribed instead, then once the elision of *ā* had occurred, there would be no occasion for Vṛddhi, and thus only the vowel *o* would be heard in the form *dadaridro*. He refutes that view with the words "at the point where it says *āta au ṇalaḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.1.34). "For this very reason" refers to this same point.

From this very rule prescribing *au* for the purpose of hearing the sound *au* in the root *daridrā*—namely, the prescription of *au* in *daridrā*—it is understood that there is no *ām* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense of *daridrā*. The intention is that if *ām* were present, the substitution of *ṇal* would not even be applicable. [Jñāpakapāda] "The *au* of the roots *ṛ*, *ṣṭṛ*, and *gā* [Pāṇini 7.1.16]: the mention of the short vowel *a* (*atva*) indicates that the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) occurs in place of the nominative plural suffixes *jas* and *śas*."

In the rule *āṬś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the term *āṣṭāḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the word *aṣṭan* in its state of having undergone the substitution of *kṛt* (the *ṭā* suffix). Consequently, the meaning of the rule is established as follows: *auś* is substituted for the nominative plural (*jaś*) and accusative plural (*śas*) endings when they follow the word *aṣṭan* after the vowel *ā* resulting from that *kṛt* substitution.

In that regard, since the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* prescribes the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* only when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a vowel (*ch-ay-aṇ*), the substitution of *ā* does not occur for *aṣṭan* when followed by the case-endings *jaś* and *śas*. Therefore, how can it be inferred that the case-endings *jaś* and *śas* also follow a form of the word *aṣṭan* ending in *ā*?

Regarding the phrase *kṛtatvāt*: one should not say that this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the state of being already formed (*kṛtatva*), but rather that this [form] is established by virtue of the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇavaśa*). For if that were the case, since the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* is optional, one would have stated simply as "aṣṭabhya auś" for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*); such is the intention. [Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.53: *trestrayaḥ*].

Since the substitution of *traya* is already established by the very mention in the rule *ṇijāṃ trayāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.4.75), this present sūtra is intended to provide the technical instruction (*jñāpaka*) that "there are also nipātanas that serve as exceptions. By means of this, the form *purātanam* is established. [Viṭṭhala: Now, one might object: since there is doubt as to whether the word *traya* in the rule *trestrayaḥ* ends in *a* or in *s*, the determination that it ends in *a* should have been made by the mention in *ṇijāṃ trayāṇām*.

If that were so, one might object that since the substitution of *traya-* for *tri-* would be established by the very rule prescribing the augment *nuṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel, the sūtra "trestrayaḥ" would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "by the very indication [of the sūtra]" (*iti nirdeśādeva*), asserting its purposefulness as a means of making known a specific technical term (*vacanaviśeṣajñāpanārthatayā*).

And likewise, because the substitution of *tray-* for *tri-* would be an exception (*apavāda*) [to other rules], the form *trīṇām* would also result as an alternative possibility; therefore, the rule *trestrayaḥ* is formulated to prevent that. The purpose of this indication (*jñāpana*), however, is the establishment of the archaic form *purā*. Otherwise, from the word *purā*, by the rule "after *sāyam*, *ciram*, *prāhṇe*, *prage*, and indeclinables, the suffixes *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* are applied, along with the augment *tuṭ*" (Pāṇini 4.3.23), [the form *purātanam* would not be established].

Regarding the rule *Purāṇaprokteṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105), the intention is that although the suffixes *ṭaḷ*, *ṭuḷ*, and *ṭuḷ* along with the augment *tuṭ* would have been applicable by the rule [4.3.23], this specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) establishes the form as *bhāva*. And regarding the rule *Dvārādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.4): [the example is] *śauvastikam*. Among the suffixes beginning with *vuñ* and *chaṇ*, the fact that the *ṭhaC* suffix is marked with the *cit* indicator makes it known that the substitution of *iK* is more powerful than the internal (*antaraṅga*) operations.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: from the word *śvas*, by the rule *śvasastuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.15), when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, since the augment *tuṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) due to being conditioned by the presence of the suffix itself, it would apply prior to the substitution of the vowel *i*. Consequently, because the letter *ṭha* would no longer be the initial element of the suffix, the substitution of *i* would not take place—as it does not in the case of the *ṭha*-sound in *karmaṭha*. Thus, one would expect forms such as *śvastika* rather than *śauvastika*. How is this resolved?

One might raise the objection that, according to the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50), an *ikāra* substitution is prescribed only for the letter *ṭha* following an *aṅga*; however, this is not to be feared, as indicated by the mention of *vuñ, chaṇ*, and so forth. In the rule *vuñ-chaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80) and others, the addition of the *cit* marker to *ṭhak* is for the purpose of making it *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable).

In that case, even though the marker *cit* is redundant—since the acute accent (*udātta*) on the letter *a* of the suffix *ṭha* would be established by rule 6.2.39 (*ādyaudātaśca*) due to its being *antaraṅga* prior to the substitution of *i*, after which the final acute accent would be achieved by the substitution of *i* itself—nevertheless, its inclusion serves to indicate the maxim: "The substitution of *i* is stronger than [operations resulting from] *antaraṅga* rules."

Furthermore, since the accentuation rule "ādyaudātaśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.3) would apply immediately after the substitution of *i* for *ī*, the vowel *i* itself would become acute (*udātta*), rather than the final syllable; thus, the inclusion of the marker *c* serves its purpose within its own domain. However, its actual utility lies in cases such as *śauvastikam*, where by applying the substitution of *i* for *ī* even before the internal *tuṭ* augment, the desired form is established.

In this context, the fact that *ṭhac* is marked with the *cit* designation is merely an illustration; the *cit* designation of *ṭhac* is a general indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule: "Suffixes, augmentations, and substitutes are stronger than internal operations" (*antaraṅga*), as seen in the *Śabdakaustubha*. [Jñāpakapradīpa] Regarding *yaj-yāc-...* (Pāṇini 3.1.90): *arcyam*. Even though the root has a short *ṛ* in its penultimate syllable, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied precisely because of this very indicator.

[VI.Ṭ] Now, an objection: from the root *arc*, by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; then, although the substitution of *k* for *c* would apply by the rule *cajoḥ ku* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), it is barred by the rule *yajayācarucapravacarcaśca*. Following this, with the addition of the penultimate vowel *uṇ* (*guṇa*), the form *arcyam* is traditionally taught. That, however, is not established.

Anticipating the objection that, by the rule *ṛdupadhāccākḷpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110), only the suffix *kyap*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇyat* and is characterized by having a penultimate *ṛ* vowel—should apply, he says: "even though it has a penultimate *ṛ* vowel."

The intention is this: since the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*) for the *ṛ* of *ṛc* when followed by the suffix *ṇyat*—as stated in the rule prohibiting that substitution (*kutvaniṣedha*)—would otherwise be inconsistent in the absence of the suffix *ṇyat*, it is understood through that prohibition that *ṛc* takes only the suffix *ṇyat* and not *kyap*. In this context, the rule "anunāsika" (Pāṇini 8.3.2) applies. The mention of the word "vāk" is for the sake of clarity.

[This is] established by the very *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark) of the rule *anunāsikātparaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.4). [Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra: Now, one might object: "In the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā*, the mention of the word *vā* (optionally) need not be made."

Even in the absence of that [nasalization], in the rule *anunāsikātparo'nusvāraḥ*, by relying on the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the analysis of *anunāsikāt* as a *lyap*-elision (i.e., *anunāsikād*), and by explaining it as "after a nasalized [consonant]," the meaning is "in the case of the absence of nasality," because that [nasality] is optional; for if nasality were not optional, the case of its absence would simply not occur, and thus its optionality would be impossible.

Regarding the word "siddheḥ" (because it is established) here, the following is said: the mention of *vāk* is for the sake of clarity. To indicate this very point, the author did not say "tu vā" in the commentary (*vṛtti*), but rather stated simply that "there shall be an anusvāra for what precedes *r*. [From the *Jñānapradīpa*: Regarding the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15), by the principle of "treating as the end of a word" (*antavadbhāva*), there is no *visarga* for the *repha* at the end of a word when followed by another word.]

This is because of such grammatical indications as *uḍddhdhḍaddh;ayatharkṣu* (Pāṇini 8.3.8) and *kartari carḥsdvdr1;idevatayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.186). [Vi.Ṭ] Now, in cases such as *praaṛccchati*, after the vṛddhi substitution by the rule *upasargādṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91), the form *prārcchati* is established. Since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ār* is treated as if it were the end of the preceding member (*pūrvāntavat*), the *r* is at the end of a word (*padānta*). Consequently, by the rule *kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15), a *visarga* should occur.

Anticipating the objection that [the rule] would apply, [the author] says: "by way of having a final [sound]. For a *repha* (the sound *r*) that has attained the status of being a word-final (*padānta*) by way of having a final [sound], a *visarga* does not occur. This is because of the grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) in the rules "uḥ ṛtviyarkṣu" and "carṣaṇīdevatayoḥ. When the form "ubhayathā ṛkṣu" is present, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by its *guṇa* substitute according to the rule "ād guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), resulting in "ubhayatharkṣu."

In this case as well, because the single-substitute *ar* is treated as if it were the final part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*), the *repha* would be considered a word-final (*padānta*) sound; consequently, the rule *uḥ after two or three consonants becomes *kṣu* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) would have required the reading *uḥ kṣu*. Since it is not so stated, the underlying intention is that the *repha* at the end of the word does not undergo *visarga* due to its being treated as the final part of the preceding element. [Jñāpakapradīpa] *dvi-tri-catuḥ* (Sūtra 8.3.43).

The mention of the term *artha* (meaning) when [the word] *kṛt* is present is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) [of terms] is not a restrictive factor in all cases. By this, in the rule "dīdhīvevīṭām" (Pāṇini 1.1.6), although there is co-occurrence with verbal roots (*dhātu*), the augment *iṭ* is included.

[Objection: But surely, because of the co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the two words ending in *suc*—namely *dvis* and *tris*—the word *catur* must also be understood as ending in *suc*. Consequently, since it occurs in the sense of number (*kṛtvo'rtha*), the mention of "in the sense of number" (*kṛtvo'rtha*) in the rule *dvistriścaturiti kṛtvo'rthe* would be redundant. Therefore—

Regarding the phrase "the mention of the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix" (*kṛdarthagrahaṇam*): since the *sāhacarya* (association) rule does not serve as a restrictive factor in all cases, the mention of the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix was made so that the term "fourth" (*caturtha*) might not include even that which lacks a *kṛt* suffix; thus, it fulfills its purpose within its own scope.

Otherwise, there would be a purpose [for the rule]—namely, "by that" (tena). Since the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* belong to the class of roots beginning with *dhātu*, there arises the possibility of taking the root *iṭ* from the *bhūvādigaṇa* which has the meaning of motion, due to the principle of association (*sāhacarya*). However, because it is accepted that association does not always serve as a restrictive factor, only the augment *iṭ* is taken here.

This is the intention behind the rule *dīdhīvevīṭam*. [In the *Jñāpakapradīpa*: Regarding the root *cit* in the sense of remembering (*smṛti*), although one should have read it as *cint*, the inclusion of the marker *it* is an indicator (*liṅga*) that the addition of the causal suffix *ṇic* is optional. Consequently, in forms such as *cintyāt* and *cintyate*, there is no elision of the nasal (*n*). Some hold that this indicator refers to the rule in its general application, while others maintain that it refers specifically to particular cases. [In the *Vivaraṇa*: Now, an objection: in the *cur-ādi* class, the root *cit* in the sense of remembering is recited with the marker *it*. Let the inclusion of that *it* be omitted.]

For the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyālāghava*), one should simply read "cinti smaḥ" [in place of "cintayāmaḥ"]. Nor is there any need for the inclusion of *ni* (the augment) to prevent the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), because such elision does not apply here. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the *it*-designation (indicating the presence of *i*) is intended to prevent the elision of *n* in the following cases: in the form "cintyāt" (where the suffix is the benedictive *liṅ* without *ṇic*), and in the form "cintyate" (where the suffix is *yak* in the passive voice).

Since the usage *cintyate* from the root *cint* alone—without the suffix *ṇic*—is as impossible as the horns of a hare due to its being eternal (*nityatva*), [the author] says: "cinta," etc. By the word "tena" (by that), the meaning is "by way of being optional" (*pākṣikatvena*). Thus, because the usage *cintyate* from the root *cint* does occasionally occur, the purpose of designating it as having the marker *it* is for the sake of preventing the elision of *na* (*nalopa*) in that instance; this is the intention.

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule] does not have as its scope only those instances within the *cint* root where the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is applicable, but rather it has as its scope the *cint* root in general; for this very reason, the correctness of the usage of the causative forms *cintayati* and *cintayet* is established. Alternatively, it refers to the commonality of belonging to the *curādigaṇa*.

For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita stated in the commentary on the sūtra *ata ekahalaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.120): "And this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)," with the underlying intention that [the rule] refers specifically to the verbal roots *keti* and *citi*. This indicates the optionality of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) only for those two roots, and not for the entire class of *cur*-class roots in general.

Otherwise, since there would be an option for the addition of *ṇic* after every root of the *curādi* class, they maintain that the rule providing an optional *ṇic* for those roots read within specific sub-groups of the *curādi*, such as "after those beginning with *ādhṛ*" (Gaṇasūtra), would be rendered purposeless. Regarding their view, it is said: "Others [hold] that it depends on a specific [qualification]. This is the interpretation favored by the *Bālamanoramā*. Between these two views, the position that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends on a specific qualification is indeed the more logical one.

And it should not be argued that, if that were the case, how could verbal forms such as *jagāṇa* and *jagaṇatuḥ* be grammatically justified; for since the root *gaṇ* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class, which is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*), those forms are established from that very root within that class.

Regarding the view that [the rule] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with respect to general cases, the author of the *Natu-bodhinī* does not maintain that there is the laborious necessity of postulating such things as: "In order to justify the utility of the sūtra 'ādhaḥsthād vā', one must rely on the fact that what is established by an indicator is not universally applicable; thus, for those [roots] beginning with *ā-dhā*, the option is optional at will (*icchika*), whereas for others, it is restricted by the usage of the masters (*śiṣṭa-prayoga*)," and so forth. [Jñā.pā.ṭ 81].

Even though the state of being double (dvitva) is eternal, it is superimposed by means of a quality (*guṇa*). The operation of the *upadhā* [strengthening] takes precedence over doubling, because the marking of the root *oṇ* as having an *ṛt* vowel (*ṛdit*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general consideration. [Commentary: Now, one might object: when the suffix *san* is added to the root *īṣ*, since there is no *halādi* [beginning with a consonant], the *kit* status is absent, and consequently, there would be no *guṇa* in the reduplication (*graṇe*).

When *isa* is established, by the rule "the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), the doubling of *is* occurs; then, after the elision of the initial *i* (by *halādiśeṣaḥ*) and the substitution of *s* for *san*, the form *isisiṣati* is expected. However, that is not achieved.

An objection is raised: since the substitution of *guṇa* applies whether doubling (*dvitva*) has occurred or not, and because it is *nitya* (invariably applicable), it would preempt the doubling; thus, once doubling has taken place in *ādi*, the *ik* vowel of the verbal root (*dhātu*) would no longer be an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel), and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution would not apply. Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Even though it is *nitya*... [and so forth].

Since the operation of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is more powerful than doubling (*dvitva*), the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel occurs first, and doubling follows immediately after; therefore, there is no fault. The fact that the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the operation of the penultimate vowel is more powerful than doubling.

Likewise, regarding the rule *ḍhddhac12;ḥdyaṇoddhd;#—oṇiḥTktgrRN;dātorṇyantālluṅ ciṅ "ṇo ciṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ'*: when the luṅ (aorist) suffix with the ciṅ (caṅ) augment is applied to the causative form of the root *oṇ*, and the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) is prohibited by the rule "*ṇo ciṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ*", the form stands as *oṇi-at*. At this stage, if the reduplication (*dvitva*) of the syllable *ṇi* were to occur, the resulting form would be *oṇiṇat*. To prevent the shortening of the penultimate vowel in this context, the root *oṇ* is marked with the *ṛt* indicatory letter (*ṛdit*). If the shortening of the penultimate vowel were applied, the form would stand as *uṇ-i-at*; then, if the reduplication of *ṇi* occurred, the result would be *uṇiṇat*, which is incorrect. Therefore, the *ṛt* designation is for the purpose of prohibiting the shortening of the penultimate vowel. Once the shortening is blocked, the form remains *oṇ-i-at*, and upon the reduplication of *ṇi*, the correct form *oṇiṇat* is obtained. If the shortening were allowed, however, the form would be *uṇiṇat*.

The established rule is that the sound *o* should be heard [in the reduplicated form]. However, if—due to the permanence [of the grammatical operation]—doubling were to occur prior to the shortening of the penultimate vowel, that is, while the form is still in the state of *oṇi at*, then because the penultimate vowel would no longer exist as an *o*, the shortening would not even be applicable. Consequently, the doubling prescribed for the purpose of excluding that [shortening] would be rendered useless. Therefore, it is understood that the penultimate modification consisting of shortening takes precedence over doubling.

Now, one might object: "Since the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) is [already] established by the previously mentioned *jñāpaka*, and since the doubling (*dvitva*) of the *pra-* [augment] occurs when there is no doubling of the *la-* [root], how can the doubling of the penultimate vowel-guṇa (*upadhā-guṇa*) be considered non-existent due to that doubling? To this, the author replies: "With reference to the general rule (*sāmānyāpekṣā*). Those statements which were not observed in the collection of *jñāpakas* have been set forth here in this first section (*pariśiṣṭaka*).

Following the sequence of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* itself, along the path favored by Nāgeśa, and in conjunction with my own commentary, I have compiled this collection of examples according to my understanding. Furthermore, certain statements from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources that were not previously observed have been established through *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) by the most eminent Dīkṣitas in their *Kaumudī*. Their utility in determining the correctness (*sādhutva*) of words is also demonstrated here.
Having observed this collection of indicators (*jñāpakasaṃgraha*) in the second supplement (*pariśiṣṭaka*), [ends] the second *jñāpakasaṃgrahaparisiṣṭa*.
